items.label: January 1930
items.sum: Opening club notes: congratulations to the Surrey Youths' Race team, T. W. Green, Len Fletcher and Bert Footer, new members and marriages, the new official Club tie, the dropping of the April Open Meeting, the Club Dinner date and an extra July handicap.
items.s: Opening club notes: congratulations to the Surrey Youths' Race team, T. W. Green, Len Fletcher and Bert Footer, new members and marriages, the new official Club tie, the dropping of the April Open Meeting, the Club Dinner date and an extra July handicap. Congratulations are due this month to our Surrey Youths' Race team, to A. L. Fletcher, H. E. Footer and, of course, T. W. Green, who merits our congratulations as regularly as our Gazette appears On this occasion it is a wonderful effort in the "God-stone" Walk on Boxing Day. Although he started 11½ minutes after the rest of the competitors (owing to a train which was an hour and a half late), he managed to catch all but four competitors and beat the existing course record by 40 secs. Whether this time will be accepted as a new record for the distance, owing to the late start, is doubtful, but nothing can detract from the merit of the performance Len Fletcher, walking for the Army and Navy Co-operative Stores, accomplished a fine performance by winning the London Business Houses championship. L. G. Sandy, the Police champion, whom we all know to be a good walker, was well beaten. Bert Footer, after many years of trying, has won the Club 7 miles Cross-country championship His win is a reward for perseverance and one which holds a moral for all of us All his club-mates are unanimous in saying "Well run, Bert." Our junior team of runners, Messrs Garland, Jacobs, Clubb and Thorne, by dead-heating in the Surrey Youths' Race with Mitcham A.C., showed that our younger members may be relied upon to uphold Belgrave prestige, and in time will prove worthy successors of the present seniors * * * * * W. Plant, J W. Haggar, B. Langley, L. C Price, H. J. Grimwood and W. Mellish were elected to the Club at the last Committee meeting and are cordially welcomed. * * * * * We have to congratulate A. W. Godfrey and E. A. Saward upon their recent marriages and wish them many years of happiness. The official Club tie has now made its appearance and may be obtained from the Hon. Editor. The tie has been specially woven to the Committee's specification and is moderately priced at three shillings (or 3/3 by post). All loyal Belgravians are expected to wear the Club Colours at the Open Cross Country and Road Walking Championships which will soon be taking place. Please note that the official Club tie can only be had from the Hon. Editor, whose address appears on page 1. * * * * * The Committee have decided not to hold an Open Meeting in April this year When we first promoted this meeting it was because athletes were not catered for so early in the track season. Now, however, other promoters have come forward and, as our meetings are always bound to result in a heavy financial loss, owing to the fact that there is no "gate," we have decided to discontinue it. In its place it is hoped to arrange an attractive programme of match events, supplemented by some Club handicaps It is probable that the Club Dinner will be held on Saturday, April 26th, following upon this meeting, so all our members should make a note of this date. * * * * * In response to the requests of many members, an extra handicap meeting has been arranged during the Summer. This will take place in July—usually a blank month as far as Club fixtures are concerned A. L. Fletcher A. L. Fletcher H. E. Footer H. E. Footer T. W. Green T. W. items.s: SURREY COUNTY YOUTHS' CROSS-COUNTRY RACE. Report and result of the Surrey County Youths' cross-country race on Putney Heath, where Belgrave's juniors tied with Mitcham A.C. for first place on 22 points (Surrey A.C.'s printed positions add to 85, though 81 pts. is printed). On December 14th, our Juniors competed in the above race on Putney Heath (the race being re-run on this date owing to the runners losing the trail on the preceding Saturday) It was a fine afternoon and excellent for country running. We had a full team of eight running and from the start our boys got into the leading positions. Things were looking very hopeful after about half a mile of the outward journey. On the return of the runners they were headed by Gittings, of South London H. with Garland in fifth position, an improvement on his running in the same race last year. In the team race Garland was placed fourth, Jacobs fifth, Clubb sixth, and Thorne seventh, aggregating 22 points, and thus tieing with Mitcham A C. for first place. Our boys packed very well and Thorne put in a great finish to beat the last two Mitcham scoring men in the straight; thus gaining us two points and pride of place with Mitcham. Well run Bels. ! items.s: THE FIVE MILE NOVICE WALK. Report and result of the Five Mile Novice Walk, won by G. Tucker of Belgrave from J. L. Wells of Surrey W.C., with Larman disqualified near the finish. The much-discussed Novice Walk, after much advertising and splendid response from certain of our Club officials who presented the prizes was, from a numerical point of view, a failure. Consolation was found, however, in the splendid racing that followed G. Tucker, the winner, walked a brainy race against L J. Wells, of Surrey W.C, who gave a plucky display of determination in trying to hang on to Tucker when the latter made his final effort. Meanwhile, a splendid race for third was taking place between Harley and Larman, who were fighting it out stride by stride over the last stages. Within sight of the tape Larman came under the ban of the judges, allowing Harley to take third place. Larman learnt a lesson from his disqualification as was proved the following week when he gained a prize in the sealed handicap held in conjunction with the seven miles Junior Championship. items.sum: Report and result of the club's Seven Miles Junior Walk Championship for the Horwood Cup, won again by holder Frank Elson from E. Saunders, with the sealed handicap won by Saunders (E. Stringer's printed allowance 4 50 does not match his printed handicap time 60 48).
e: Club Seven Miles Junior Walk Championship
items.s: THE SEVEN MILES JUNIOR WALK CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the club's Seven Miles Junior Walk Championship for the Horwood Cup, won again by holder Frank Elson from E. Saunders, with the sealed handicap won by Saunders (E. Stringer's printed allowance 4 50 does not match his printed handicap time 60 48). Twenty juniors faced the starter and this must be considered a very good field when one remembers that many of our members are not allowed to compete in this race, by reason of their having reached "Senior" status under R.W.A. rules. The number competing and the good racing seen gives visions of a double win in the Junior and Senior championships this year. Elson started off at a very fast pace, followed by Field and Saunders, with Khlopin close behind. Towards the end of the first lap Field was in the lead, but he suffered disqualification, and this again gave Elson the lead, closely followed by Saunders. Saunders at one time looked likely to prove the winner, but Elson managed to gain a few yards lead up the last hill and retain it to the end. Thus Frank Elson, the holder, by his narrow win again won the "Horwood Cup," but surely Saunders will add his name to the trophy in the course of time unless, or course, he loses his Junior status later in the season, which appears very probable. Khlopin's improvement continues, a remark which applies to many of those who followed him Harley and Larman again had a close race, the latter winning on this occasion by a yard, and showing that the words of advice given by one of the judges the week before when he was pulled out had proved beneficial. The sealed handicap turned out to be a very close affair as the appended results show Saunders deservedly took first prize and Larman is to be congratulated upon winning his first prize A second behind him came R G. items.s: THE THIRD INTER-CLUB RACE Report and result of the third inter-club cross-country race with Ashcombe A.C. and Thames Valley H. from Roehampton, won by Belgrave with A Allum and J E Flower dead-heating first (T.V.H.'s 20 printed positions add to 599, not the printed 578; Ashcombe's 18 printed positions add to 653, not the printed 698, position 45 being unaccounted for). The final Inter-Club race between Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and ourselves was held from The Angel, Roehampton, on December 14th. The race started from the Flagstaff, on Wimbledon Common, towards the Kingsmere, which had to be circled twice before going out down the track to Beverley Brook. A wild scramble ensued at the commencement with Cohen, of Ashcombe, cutting out the pace. Jack Flower and Arthur Allum were close behind him while F. R. Webb and Dewberry were also near the leaders. Nearing the brook Footer moved up with Nuti and Bicknell of Thames Valley just in front of them. After crossing the bridge the long drag up the "Toast-rack" commenced and it was here that Flower and Allum overtook Cohen. Warboys also gained some positions here while Duffett and F. R. Webb running together gradually decreased Bicknell's lead on them On the stretch home across the common our leading two got well away from Cohen, whom Footer also passed, although he was unable to catch the leaders, much to his regret, judging by his remarks after the race. Mitchell and Warboys ran well, the latter being troubled by a badly-cut knee sustained in a fall during the race, and F. R. Webb also displayed fine form and on this running will be a decided acquisition to our senior teams. Sid Chorley was another to do well. Canard and Dewberry both had off days, the latter's old fault of dashing off at the start again led to his own undoing and until he curbs his impetuosity and runs more evenly he will find it difficult to last out a race. We had (for us) a poor muster, only 21, and as it was decided that 19 aside should score we were a little apprehensive as to our finishing a full scoring team. However, that old stalwart George Still and veteran George Tyrer both did their bit, and we came out on top, winners by a fair margin of points m s 1 A Allum B 28 41 1 J E Flower B 28 41 3 H E Footer B 28 53 4 L J. items.h: THE H. T. BLACKSTAFFE SHIELD RACE.
items.sum: History of the H. T. Blackstaffe Shield, report and full result of the 18th Club 7 Miles Cross-country Championship won by H. E. Footer (who also won the handicap), and a list of the first three from 1920 to 1928 (printed handicap figures for W. G. Webb, E. A. Duffett and A. J. Flower do not agree with their printed positions or sums).
items.s: THE H. T. BLACKSTAFFE SHIELD RACE. History of the H. T. Blackstaffe Shield, report and full result of the 18th Club 7 Miles Cross-country Championship won by H. E. Footer (who also won the handicap), and a list of the first three from 1920 to 1928 (printed handicap figures for W. G. Webb, E. A. Duffett and A. J. Flower do not agree with their printed positions or sums). The Club 7 Miles Cross-country Championship is the oldest championship event of which any tangible record is available. Until 1909, however, there existed no trophy for the event, and then Mr. H. T Blackstaffe, the Olympic Sculling Champion of 1908, and President of our Club in 1909, presented the Shield that bears his name. This was competed for on January 22nd, 1910, for the first time, from "The Spencer Arms," Lower Richmond Road, Barnes Common, then the Club headquarters, and won by C F. Blow The 18th race for the Shield (3 years lapsed owing to the late war) was held at Wimbledon on December 21st The course modified a little from last year's and the weather was in accordance with usual Championship day weather—damp, dark and dismal. A fair field of 28, considerably less than should be expected, started; the most notable absentee being A Penny, who was nursing an injured knee. The course, after a half-lap of the starting field, lay across the Golf Course to Gravelly Hill, down to Beverley Brook, along and up the Horse-ride to the Flagstaff, thence via the Windmill to the Village. Out again over the same lap and then home to the starting point. The start was comparatively a slow one, with the result that the field were fairly well bunched for the first two miles At this point a leader could scarcely be defined and a fairly small distance covered the majority of the runners, with the three veterans, G. Still (who incidentally won a Club 7 in 1908, but not being first-claim at the time, did not qualify for the Championship Medal), H. Goodfellow and G. Tyrer bringing up the rear in that order Thence the field gradually spread out, with J. E Flower, Footer and Allum taking up the lead At 4½ miles, these three were still together and then after a fair interval came Mitchell, then the brothers Webb, Warboys and Duffett. T. J Flower, who had been maikng the running for "A.J ," had made up a little ground, but at no time had a hard race. With two miles to go the leaders were still together and thus they went from view up the long rise towards the Flagstaff. Footer piled on the pace up the sharp hill and opened up a gap, but "J E" hung on grimly and when on level ground closed up again with the leader. Allum had been dropped, but was in striking distance and it was still anyone's race. Bert however, is determination itself He had obviously "a bee in his bonnet," and nothing was left to chance or a "social" finish, and, making another effort, resisted all efforts to hold him and gradually drew away to record his first victory in the "7." He has, however, two 10's to his credit. No one will say other than that his win was well merited and deservedly popular, for none have been more stauch than he in his efforts for the Club in open Cross-Country Championships, and this win is but a reward for his rather unfortunate experiences in previous years, for on three consecutive occasions he has been second. In 1925 and 1926 he ran second to K. B O'Kell, and in 1927 to A. Clark, and yet in each of these three years he was first home for the Club in both the South of the Thames and Southern Counties Championships. Jack Flower ran exceedingly well in what was probably his first serious attempt at the distance and Arthur Allum, third, probably ran well enough to have won the race seven years out of ten. The keenness of the struggle between the first three may be judged from the fact that they drew well ahead of the rest of the field and filled 3 of the first 4 placings in the handicap in which Footer achieved the rare success of the "double " W. Mitchell, our 10 mile champion, finished 4th, but he probably was not yet in top form, which may be said of our Captain, W. G Webb, and the running Hon. Sec., E. A Duffett, the previous year's winner. F R Webb ran in good form and finished well up 5th in both championship and handicap Of the others, a few were below their best, but of the longer markers, T Cotton stepped up in the placings and gained 3rd prize in the handicap The full details of the finish are appended, and there remains only to be stated that our President, Mr. E. Gordon, presented the trophy and prizes and that Bert made a short and pithy speech in response to the general request * * * * * A summary of the results of the Seven Miles Championships from the year 1920 until last year appears below :— *The second race in 1928 was due to running the Championship early in the new season. The first race took place on January 7th, and the second on December 22nd, in the following cross-country season. Times have not been given as they do not convey any comparison, owing to alterations in the course. items.sum: Report and results of the club's Boxing Day meeting, with Jim Tosh winning the sprint, C. R. Redgrave the walk and Arthur Allum the two miles.
items.s: THE BOXING DAY MEETING. Report and results of the club's Boxing Day meeting, with Jim Tosh winning the sprint, C. R. Redgrave the walk and Arthur Allum the two miles. Our usual Boxing Day meeting took place this year in fine weather which attracted many hundreds out-of-doors and resulted in us having a very large crowd on the rails. Firstly, the heats of the sprint were decided. The fastest time was accomplished by Jim Tosh, who beat Tommy Hampson, the International half-miler and Oxford Blue, in 12 secs. Tosh repeated his time later in the final, beating J. E. Mackie, our field events vice-captain, by a narrow margin with a comparatively new member, J. G. Barrett, inches behind. Barrett is powerfully built and should meet with further success. It was pleasing to see an old friend, George Maryon, get into the final from the five yards mark, and it is hoped that he will have a successful Summer season. A fair number participated in the Walk, which was won by C. R Redgrave with 620 yds. start. The veteran Vigor held the lead until he retired with two and a half laps to go, leaving A. A. Harley the leader. This he held until about two hundred yards to go, when Redgrave challenged. These two walked together down the straight, and Redgrave won by a yard. R. F. Elson was third. This race was won last year by Redgrave with 760 yds. start, the time being 22 mins. 31 secs. This year he won from the 620 yds. mark in 21 mins. 56 secs.—a vast improvement in the course of a year. The last race of our meeting was the two miles run. The Hon. Handicapper, L E. Fletcher, led for some time, but the back markers were steadily gaining. Eventually Arthur Allum took the lead and won in 10 mins. 10 3-5 secs Jack Flower was second off 5 yds., beating his brother Albert down the straight. So concluded a very successful meeting, the number of entrants and quality of the racing being well up to standard and a credit to the Club. 120 Yards Handicap—Heat 1, S Garland, 13, 12 1-5 secs , Heat 2, A J Powter, 8, 12 3-5 secs , Heat 3, J E Tosh, 8, 12 secs , Heat 4, J G Barrett, 7, 12[illegible] secs , Heat 5, G R Maryon, 5, 12½ secs , Heat 6, J E Mackie, 11, 12 1-5 secs Final 1, J E Tosh; 2, J E Mackie, 3, J G Barrett Ins , 2 yd , 12 secs Three Miles Walk Handicap—1, C R Redgrave, 620, 2, A. items.s: BELGRAVE HARRIERS v. METROPOLITAN POLICE. Walking match against the Metropolitan Police at the Crooked Billet, Walthamstow, which the Police won 35 points to 43, T. W. Green winning. This fixture was originally intended to take place at Imber Court, but owing to floods and other difficulties the venue was changed to "The Crooked Billet," Walthamstow. Unfortunately there appeared to be a misunderstanding among our men, for only three of our members—T. W. Green, H J. Fletcher and A. A. Harley—and two supporters turned up. This was most disappointing both to the Police and ourselves, and in order to make a sporting match of it we "borrowed" two of our own members, J. Rathbone and J. C. Bidgood (who had turned up to assist the Police), and three others At the end of the first lap Green was leading with Holland. Then came Rathbone, and Bidgood, Harley and Fletcher walked together, filling 8th, 9th and 10th positions. At the end of the second lap Tommy had a five yards lead from Holland, the other positions being unchanged. Bidgood then retired, and the first dozen positions remained the same until the end. Green drew away from Holland over the last lap, beating him by 39 secs. Throughout the race a gale raged and heavy rain fell. The course, which contained no hills, was reputed to be 7¾ miles long. After the race our walkers were entertained to a meat tea by the Police, and it is regrettable that there were not more present to accept the hospitality so warmly bestowed. m s m s. 1 T W Green B 60 35 10 P -C. items.label: January 1930
items.sum: Walking notes on the club Junior race, the Boxing Day walk, the Godstone walk, the Police match, the London Business Houses walk, T. W. Green's Southern Railway course record and coming events.
items.s: WALKING JOTTINGS. Walking notes on the club Junior race, the Boxing Day walk, the Godstone walk, the Police match, the London Business Houses walk, T. W. Green's Southern Railway course record and coming events. In the Club "Junior" race held over the same course as was used in our "Open 7," Elson, the holder, was seriously challenged by E. Saunders, and only won by the narrow margin of 3 secs. Saunders well deserves any success that comes his way, for he puts in some hard training, and it is he who was chiefly responsible for turning the third man, Paul Khlopin, into the fine walker he is. Although Elson had been troubled with his foot he improved by 22 secs. on his performance in our Open, while Saunders was half a minute better than on that occasion. Quite a number of our walkers competed in the 3 mile track race on Boxing Day and C W. Redgrave, who won the previous year's race, was again the winner, but this time in a tight finish with A A Harley. Redgrave has improved a lot during the past 12 months and should do better still in a year or two. Harley, too, has not yet shewn us his best, and having the advantage of long legs, should soon overshadow those of us that have but "legendary" records Another of our young members, R F. Elson, was third and he will, no doubt equal his brother's performances in the not too distant future. Len Fletcher was, of course, on scratch, but although he put in some fast walking he failed to get into the placings. T. W. Green, P. Khlopin and G Tucker were our only representatives at Croydon for the Surrey Walking Club's "Godstone" walk, and Tommy was unfortunate enough to arrive late and so he started 11 mins. 32 secs. after the rest of the field and yet managed to get fifth in the scratch race. His time, 2 hrs. 47 mins. 58 secs was, of course, taken from the start of the field, but after allowing the 11½ mins. he was found to have covered the distance in 2 hrs. 36 mins. 26 secs , which is 40 secs. better than the record set up by H. L. V. Ross in 1910. Khlopin finished 7th, and Tucker 24th, the team being placed third When Enfield A.C. beat the Police in a walking match a few weeks back, one of the sporting papers said that this was only the second defeat suffered by the Police in four or five years, the other beating being by the Belgraves two or three years. As a matter of fact, this statement is not correct, we having beaten them in 1927 and 1928 in the only two matches we have had with them previous to this winter. This being so, it was hoped that we would administer still another defeat on December 28th, Unfortunately, as mentioned elsewhere, only a few of our walkers turned up owing to a misunderstanding, and we suffered defeat, although Tommy Green was first home. It was extremely regrettable that this match, which is one of the most sporting of our fixtures, was so poorly supported, and we must make amends by turning out at full strength for the return match at Wimbledon on February 22nd. It seems very strange that a club with a large walking section such as we have should have been so sparsely represented in this race and in the "Godstone" If this continues we shall have to look to our laurels. On Saturday, January 4th, several of our club-mates competed in the London Business Houses walk (7 miles), and Len Fletcher won both the Championship and the sealed handicap. Well walked, Len! E. Saunders was 6th and H. F King, who won this race in 1927, was 7th. Our other members were J. B. Carne 15th, A. H Field 18th, and R E Wills 31st. On the same day T W. Green was making still another course record, this time in a Southern Railway race from Shoreham to Brighton. His time for this 7½ miles was 53 mins. 45 secs., which is more than 2 mins. better than the previous best for the course Another Belgrave, J. F. King, was 3rd. Coming events include the Cambridge Harriers Open 7 miles handicap at Eltham on January 18th, a race in which we have always secured a good share of the spoils. Our Club 10 mile championship is to be held on February 1st with the usual sealed handicap in conjunction, and by then all of our "Juniors" who hope to raise their status on March 1st, should be capable of shaking up most of the seniors So, we should see a very good race. e: Belgrave Harriers v. London Athletic Club
items.s: SPORTS JOTTINGS Sports notes by "Observer" on the South of the Thames and Southern Counties cross-country championships, field events plans, and pen-portraits of J. D. Andrews, C. W. Redgrave and A. J. Flower. The serious side of the cross-country season has now commenced and our boys are hard at it every week in preparation for the coming championships. The South of the Thames race on February 8th is one which we have high hopes of winning, so repeating our performance of last year. As the winning team is barred each year, to do this is a rare feat. We have a good team to represent us, the fifth and sixth men being the doubtful places, but as we have several of equal ability, it is hoped that they will try to pull out a bit extra and so bring the team up to winning strength. Our greatest rivals appear to be Herne Hill Harriers and South London Harriers, so now, boys, don't forget we want to see Belgrave FIRST. The Southern Counties Championship on February 22nd is to be held at Brighton. This will be rather a stiff course, I should think, but one of which some of our boys have had experience, as the South of the Thames race was held there in 1924. There are no barring clauses in this race, hence the Club will field their full strength and with our lads fit they should certainly give the other clubs the shock of their lives. So often in this race, however, have we expected to do well and yet have finished well down the list. Several excuses have been put forward to account for this staleness, which as regards last season was probably correct, lack of training over the distance, which is also partially true of our boys, and so on. In both the South of the Thames Championship and the Southern Counties Championship, there are trophies awarded to the first club to finish their twelve men We are holders of the "Sir Jeremiah Colman" Cup given in connection with the former race, and this year we want to make a double of it by securing the "Odling-Smee" Cup awarded for Surrey clubs in the Southern Counties race. Thus not only are the supposed scoring team interested in these races, but every man of the twelve can do his bit towards helping the Club to gain honours; and we shall not be satisfied until we have gained the blue riband of the cross-country world, namely the National Championship. It is to be hoped that members of our Field Events Section will soon commence training in earnest. The coming season is likely to see a great advance in the number of field events provided, and we hope our members will appreciate this and shew a corresponding advance in their performances. As our readers are doubtless aware, the Club is not holding their Open Track meeting this year, the date being filled by an attractive fixture with the London Athletic Club. This will be much on the same lines as last season, which included two field events, namely, Javelin and Long Jump. There will also be Club handicaps, one of which will presumably be for the field event members. Then, again, it has been mentioned that a Field Event Section of the Southern Amateur Athletic League will probably be formed and if this matures we shall wish to see our club participating. In fact, the coming year appears to be the one the field event men have been waiting for and it is hoped that we shall see more numerous entries in connection with the "Harry Wright" Shield Competition. My next three Club members are :— J. D. Andrews, a prominent performer for the Club a few seasons back and scored in our winning Surrey County teams. Always ran consistently well over the country and now that he has commenced training again we hope he will find some of his old-time running form, and so show some of our newer members that the "old brigade" are not finished yet. I only hope that Micky Pyer and Harry Bruce will follow Jack's example. C. W. Redgrave, a very promising young member of our walking section Has a very neat style and should improve with age, being as yet rather on the frail side. Should do well in "Opens" next summer and the Club Handicapper will also have to keep an eye on this young man's performances. A. J. Flower, an elder brother of "T.J." and "J E" Of much the same build as his brothers, being, in fact, the tallest of the three Is as yet in the Novice stage, but shews promise of developing into a useful track runner Has long stride with rather lumbering gait which he will no doubt improve upon with experience. e: Belgrave Harriers v. Royal Air Force
Belgrave Harriers v. St. George's Services S.C.
items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. Notice of coming fixtures from the Hon. Running Secretary: matches with the R.A.F. (Kenley) and St. George's Services S.C., the Macher Shield 10 miles, a social run at Croydon, the South of the Thames race and a road race to pick the Brighton Relay team. On January 18th we have two fixtures arranged, one being with the Royal Air Force (Kenley). This will take the form of a five miles race between teams of eight men to run, with five to count. If possible our prospective "Senior" team will do duty here, so giving them a useful try-out against the Air Force lads, prominent among whom is Cpl A. P. Whale, the well known Surrey A.C. runner. The other fixture is a five miles race versus St. George's Services S.C. from their headquarters, "Bishopsford," London Road, Mitcham It was originally intended that the London Scottish A C. should also take part, but they have now fixed their own championship for that day. In the race with St George's an all-to-score rule will operate, so I hope that all members will support this fixture The 25th sees the second and final Club championship over the country, namely the 10 mile race for the "Macher" Shield (holder, W. S Mitchell). This should be a more level race than was the 7 miles, and although Bert is tipped for the double he will have to stave off many challengers. A sealed handicap will be run in conjunction with the race and I hope all members will make an effort to turn out and support the last handicap of the season so far as cross-country is concerned. See Social Hon Sec 's notes re Social after the run. On February 1st we have a social run with Croydon H., Mitcham A.C and Epsom H. from the former club's headquarters at Wickham Road, Croydon Their course over Addington and Shirley Hills is a pretty adventurous one. I sincerely hope we don't meet any Alsatians, and I recommend members to come along for an enjoyable run. I understand there will be a Social afterwards. February 8th brings the first of the "Senior" championships, this being the South of the Thames race over a 7 miles course. Venue has not, at the time of writing, been arranged, but Horsham appears likely to stage the event I hope that our loyal supporters will turn up in force, the same as last year, when it was generally agreed that they largely contributed to our team's victory. I wish to remind members of the fixture arranged for some time in March, in connection with selecting the team for the Brighton Relay. This will take the form of a 5 miles Scratch Road race, with a Sealed handicap in conjunction. Thus not only are the cracks concerned, but the long mark men are given another opportunity of winning a prize before the season finally ends All enquiries to E A. items.sum: Social notes from the Social Hon. Secretary on the poorly supported Battersea dance, the coming Wandsworth Town Hall dance and the last Social of the season at Wimbledon.
items.s: THE LIGHTER SIDE OF THE CLUB. Social notes from the Social Hon. Secretary on the poorly supported Battersea dance, the coming Wandsworth Town Hall dance and the last Social of the season at Wimbledon. The Extra Dance held at Battersea Town Hall did not prove the success expected This was probably due to the night—Tuesday—which, of course, is a regular training night, and I suppose the very bad weather must also be considered At the same time, it was really disappointing, after the success of our first dance of the season, to think we cannot run a dance, independent of the night, the weather and outside support, successfully. Our membership is well over five hundred; it only needs two hundred to overcome the expense of these dances. I am sure there is no difficulty in obtaining tickets, so I sincerely hope better support will be forthcoming for our next dance. This will be held at Wandsworth Town Hall on Friday, January 31st. Our last Dance at this Hall was a huge success. Apparently, our members are more at home here, for the fact remains that every Dance held here has been successful. I think that the far more comfortable and pleasant surroundings must account for it, so again I hope the sequence will not be broken. A few days before our next Dance we hold our last Social of the season, at Wimbledon. This has been brought forward from the original date, February 15th, to January 25th, to enable a few regular lady supporters to come along. Also one has the added attraction of the Club's 10 mile Running Championship being held in the afternoon. Everybody who saw last year's race at this distance will agree that this alone is worth the trip to Wimbledon, and our races already held this season suggest that it will be even more uncertain as to who will eventually take the Shield, and I can assure you that after spending an hour or so on Wimbledon Common one is quite ready for tea This is laid and served punctually at 5-30 p.m. Later a dance band arrives and quite a good opportunity is provided for anyone to polish up their dancing ability. Nobody is critical, everybody is willing to try a few steps. Dancing is interspersed by vocal efforts from various members, and a really enjoyable evening is spent. So, now, don't forget, you track men; come along and see the fellows who keep the Club's name in print during your close season perform seriously and then, a little later, flippantly. W. A. items.s: THE SURREY COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIP. E.G.'s report of the Surrey County cross-country championship at Epsom on January 11th, won by H. E. Footer in a snowstorm with Belgrave taking the team title, and a tribute to Capt. W. H. Ellison for driving H. S. H. Cook to the race; the printed Surrey A.C. placings (2, 23, 14, 15, 16, 21) add up to 91, not the 80 pts. printed, and the Belgrave team line lists a sixth scorer at 18 though H. E. Wills is printed 21st. Saturday, January 11th. What a day of contrasts! an early promise of a fine day right up to the time we arrived at Epsom, and then the weather did its worst. Our boys, on the contrary, rising to the occasion, did their best, and so good was this best that our old pal "Joe" tipped them for the Southern. With regard to the race one could only see the start, and then, by a route march to the Grand Stand, see the runners in the distance, a series of straggling dots on the sky line. We know that L. H. Weatherill (S.L.H.) and H. S. H. Cook (Bel.) took the lead and then over-ran the trail, having to double back and so lose a lot of ground. Then we struggled down to the winning post. By this time the conditions were appalling, snow blowing straight into the faces of the runners; and visibility was so bad that one could only see about twenty yards. Snow-covered judges and spectators stared into the mist, waiting. At last a runner, and (cheers!) it is Footer, spreading badly, rolling a bit. but with chin thrust out and that do-or-die look on his face that we know so well. Bravo, Bert! Following him came J. A. H. Sutherland (Surrey A.C.), G. H. P. Thompson (S.L.H.) and L. H. Weatherill (S.L.H.). Then we danced with joy as W. S. Mitchell, A. Penny and H. S. H. Cook all raced in together. Four in seven! Our feet were quite warm now. Two more, L. J. Cohen (Ashcombe A.C.) and G. W. Tolley (Epsom), and then E. A. Duffett, finishing like a train. Five in ten! Before we had time to chill again, H. E. Wills raced in and completed our scoring six. Congratulations to all the team. We are proud of the splendid way you upheld the prestige of the Belgrave Harriers. RESULT. And now may we be permitted to pay tribute to a splendid sportsman. It was H. S. H. Cook's misfortune to be working right up till 2 p.m. on the day of the race. On Tuesday night we discussed ways and means of getting him to Epsom by 3 p.m. Trains were out of the question as he was fixed at Goldhawk Road Shepherd's Bush. Capt. W. H. Ellison was appealed to by phone on Wednesday and replied with a cheery "I'll be there, boy." He was; and thanks to the skilful driving of Reg. Freestone, Cook was in the dressing room, warm and dry, at 2-30 p.m. This is not the first time that the Captain has placed his car and time at our disposal, and he has never let us down. items.sum: Light-hearted account of the January 18th fixture against the R.A.F. at Kenley, followed by Arthur Penny's report of the match against St. George's S.S.C. at Bishopsford, which Belgrave won 55 pts. to 127, with full result.
e: Belgrave H. v. St. George's S.S.C.
items.s: THE KENLEY AFFAIR. Light-hearted account of the January 18th fixture against the R.A.F. at Kenley, followed by Arthur Penny's report of the match against St. George's S.S.C. at Bishopsford, which Belgrave won 55 pts. to 127, with full result. On January 18th eight burly Belgravians (not to mention officials) went Kenley-wards in search of sausage-and-mash and similar epicurean delicacies, and I understand the fixture was a great success. I am assured that our team (again not forgetting the officials) acquitted themselves well and showed our R.A.F. friends that they might be relied upon to maintain Belgrave prestige, no matter what the cost (physical, not monetary, of course). This fixture is certainly becoming very popular, and even keener competition for a place in the team seems probable next year. Trials may even have to take place in order to choose our men to oppose the R.A.F. But, I forget, there was to have been a race! It appears that the runners left the right trail and followed that in use in the S.L.H. v. Cwmbran H. match. Thus, the run, from a racing point of view, proved a fiasco, but from the appetite-producing viewpoint was a decided success, and our boys are confident that they can give an equally good account of themselves over a five-course meal as they can over a five-miles course. And so we will leave them with their exultant shouts of "We had eggs on toast this time" still ringing in our ears, and learn from the pen of Arthur Penny how the runners fared at Bishopsford. Our team was rather a weak one, owing to the fact that several of the stars were representing the Club at Kenley v. the R.A.F. However, we had quite an enjoyable run over a rather short course, perhaps; but nevertheless our team managed to score a handsome win, scoring 55 pts. to St. Georges' 127. One of our team, Coleman, had the misfortune to sprain an ankle early in the race and was forced to retire. The rest of the team ran very well and more or less up to form over a strange course. The social side proved a success, our good friend "Dug" Sloper doing more than his share towards it, as is his usual custom, being "a sociable sort of fellow." A brisk wash and rub-down, then a very welcome cup of tea and a chat about race ended the day very satisfactorily. 1. A. W. Penny B.H. 25 1 2. W. G. Webb B.H. 26 0 3. F. R. Webb B.H. 26 20 4. N. items.sum: H. E.'s report of the Cambridge H. Open Walk at Eltham, where Belgrave walkers won eleven of the twenty-two prizes and the scratch team award, with individual and team results.
items.s: THE CAMBRIDGE H. OPEN WALK. H. E.'s report of the Cambridge H. Open Walk at Eltham, where Belgrave walkers won eleven of the twenty-two prizes and the scratch team award, with individual and team results. We had 18 starters out of 132 in this event, held at Eltham, and had the extreme satisfaction of taking away eleven of the twenty-two prizes awarded. We usually fare well in this race, but on this occasion our walkers surpassed themselves. Len Fletcher and Tommy Green were chasing Hyde from the commencement of the race, but were not able to catch him. These two, with the help of Paul Khlopin (17th) and Frank Elson (20th) gave us the scratch team awards, whilst C. H. Speechley (second in the indvidual handicap), S. L. King, P. N. Khlopin and A. L. Fletcher formed the quartet gaining second prizes in the handicap team race—beaten by eight seconds. If R. G. Hillier, who is rapidly improving, had been included in the "A" team we should have taken premier awards, but it is, of course, impossible to foresee an incident of this nature. It is necessary to state that the course was short of the stipulated seven miles as is evident from the times returned. Fletcher had a good day, taking away no less than three prizes, whilst Sid King took his first prize since staging a "come-back." Speechley maintains his improved form and this season looks like being the best of many for him. Khlopin in the last quarter of a mile seemed to have shot his bolt but by sheer pluck managed to finish the course and help the team win. And now a word to some of the younger walkers. Remember that the judges are just as strict in the last hundred yards as they are at the start.. My advice is: "Use your speed during the race, and not wait until the last bit is reached." H. E. Pos. items.s: THE TEN MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the club ten miles cross-country championship on January 25th, won easily by Bert Footer from J. Flower and Allum, with actual and handicap results; some printed handicap figures do not agree with the times (A. Penny shown 4th in handicap, S. R. Chorley's 61 48 and C. W. Tame's 65 36 do not equal time less start), followed by a table of the first three in the championship each year from 1923 to 1929. January 25th; cold, windy, and wet underfoot—such was the condition of the weather for the Club Championship. Footer was naturally a firm favourite owing to his greatly improved form, but nobody was certain. The race started at quite a moderate speed with E. Duffett in the lead after the first mile. The course was over two laps, and at the end of the first Jack Flower, Allum, Mitchell, Penny and Footer were grouped well together some fifty yards ahead of Warboys, who was running well and seemed quite fresh. After completing the mile lap they started on the second lap. The leaders were still grouped together with Allum, who seemed to be running a little too fast for himself, now in the lead. Warboys was still picking up. Ernie Duffett had found the going a little hard and had retired. Dewberry was running very well and although some distance was picking up very quickly. F. R. Webb was dropping back and later dropped out on the far side of the Golf Course. From the appearance of the competitors, the going was very hard and muddy, and one or two of the Juniors were evidently feeling it. Apart from the group in the lead the others were strung out, in some cases very widely. At the finish Bert Footer came in an easy winner by about 50 yds., with J. Flower and Allum filling 2nd and 3rd places. items.label: February 1930
items.sum: Report by J.B.B. of the club 10 miles walking championship for the R. Murphy Shield, won by inches by Len Fletcher from Tommy Green, with S. L. King winning the handicap, and the full actual and handicap result.
items.s: THE "R. MURPHY" SHIELD RACE. Report by J.B.B. of the club 10 miles walking championship for the R. Murphy Shield, won by inches by Len Fletcher from Tommy Green, with S. L. King winning the handicap, and the full actual and handicap result. "History repeats itself!" we say—too often grumblingly—but at the fight for the Club 10 Miles Walking Championship and the Murphy Shield, History was in its most gracious mood, and in giving us a repetition of the 1925 and 1926 races, we were treated to all that the hearts of sportsmen could desire.. In those years the obstinate fellows were R. D. McMullen and E. L. Reeve, and "Mac" was the victor on each occasion, winning by two seconds on the first, and being compelled to walk 38 seconds faster in order to win by one second the following year. In both cases they had a dour, side-by-side struggle throughout; and all of this was provided for us again by Len Fletcher and Tommy Green in this year's race. Even more stoutly did these two dispute for the leadership for every inch of the journey, and Len eventually won by inches only. Entering the road for home he led by a yard, and Tommy almost caught him at the tape. In congratulating Fletcher we must hasten to add "Bravo both!" F. Rickards, J. G. Scamell, J. Rathbone, J. E. Field and B. J. T. Knifton, all of whom have walked well in former Club championships, were not present, but otherwise the field of 26 starters was representative of the present strength of the Club. Containing, as it did, former winners in H. F. King (four times), Tommy Green (twice) and R. D. McMullen (twice) in addition to A. L. Fletcher, the London Business Houses Champion, it was indeed the most classic field that has ever contested this race. Fletcher, Green and H. F. King set a fast pace at the start, F. H. Elson being only a few yards behind at a mile. At two miles Elson had dropped back a little more and H. F. King was finding the pace too warm. He fought tenaciously, however, and prevented the leaders from opening a gap of more than 20 yds. in the next mile. From about the 6th mile, however, the two leaders drew well away, and Harold was eventually beaten by about 400yds. Elson developed a strain when lying 4th, a mile from home, and retired. Charlie Speechley walked very prominently for about 8 miles, but then fell away considerably. S. L. King walked very evenly throughout to finish 7th and win the handicap. In this our Editor, by setting his teeth and walking up to the colour of his hair, gained second place, with Len Fletcher third, in addition to winning the Championship, R. D. McMullen and E. G. Cooper both walked pleasingly, and they should be fit for the National Championship in May. H. F. King has also set his mind on helping the Club in this event and he should strengthen our team immensely. His walking in the race under review was one of the outstanding features of the season. Previously he had raced but once this winter, yet the form shown over the first 8 miles was so good that it is questionable whether he walked better or faster during the years 1923, 1924, 1927 and 1928, when he was rarely beaten at 7—10 miles on the road. J. F. King, who won the Godstone race in 1925, was making his first appearance as a Belgrave, but he was obviously short of training and could finish no nearer that 11th. No doubt "Mac," the Club captain, deems himself an Emperor, now that he has such a team, and three Kings, under his care. A new course was used this year. From the times returned it would appear that the distance covered was from 500 to 700 yards short of the stipulated ten miles. Pos. Name Actual Time Start H'cap Time Pos. in H'cap 1. A. L. items.label: February 1930
items.sum: Report of the South of the Thames cross-country championship, won by Bert Footer as the first Belgravian ever to win it, with Belgrave second to South London Harriers in the team race, and the Belgrave finishers and team scores.
items.s: THE "SOUTH OF THE THAMES." Report of the South of the Thames cross-country championship, won by Bert Footer as the first Belgravian ever to win it, with Belgrave second to South London Harriers in the team race, and the Belgrave finishers and team scores. Congratulations to the South London Harriers on again winning the "South of the Thames" Championship. Also on again becoming holders of the "Colman" Cup for the team to finish twelve men first. Congratulations are also due to our team for their splendid performance in obtaining second place, for it must not be forgotten that as we won the last year, the scoring six were barred from competing again this year. And to be beaten by the S.L.H. combination is no disgrace. To "Our Bert," on his magnificent win, congratulations are again due. He must be a Multum in Parvo, for where he finds it, I don't know. The day very cold, but otherwise fine, and the draw for position favoured our team, for we were on the extreme right and the first turn was right-handed. Our men were prominent at the end of the first small lap of a mile, Footer laying fourth, quite comfortable with the others not far behind. The next lap took the runners right out into the country, and from the top of the hill where our supporters had gathered, a splendid view of the race could be had down the hill. The runners traversed several S bends, then striking across to the river to return up the hill again. The position of the leaders changed considerably hereabouts, and it could be seen that several took the lead in turn, but Footer and J. E. Flower, running as much with heads as their legs, were within striking distance. On the return journey Footer was laying second and was given a great ovation by his friends with bells and rattles. At this point Jack Flower was 4th, Warboys 8th, Duffett 16th, Joe Flower 31st, and our next two, Bayliss and Rice, were well back. The last lap saw the leaders racing in real earnest, Tebbutt (S.L.H.) going away with Bert in close attendance until Bert made his big effort and went away to win a glorious race in 46 mins. 9 secs., about 80—100 yds. ahead of the second man. Bert received a tremendous ovation from the crowd and Club supporters and I am quite safe in saying he has made Club history, being the first Belgravian to ever win this race, although we have regularly competed from the foundation of the Championship. "J.E." came along next, 4th and Sid Warboys, who had picked up several places, next, 5th, still smiling. Three in five! Duffett 16th, T. J. Flower 36th, and W. L. Bayliss, who had picked up perhaps twenty places, 60th, completed our six. But the team race was already won by S.L.H. with six men in twenty-five (Great running! Last year we had six in twenty-six), and their twelfth man was home before our eighth. And so we returned, feeling that, all things considered, we had done very well and that something more had been done to add to Belgrave history. 1. H. E. Footer 46 9 66. A. C. Canard 49 35 4. J. E. items.s: THE ASHCOMBE A.C. WALK. Report of the Ashcombe A.C. open walk in Richmond Park, where Len Fletcher beat A.A.A. champion C. W. Hyde and Belgrave won the team handicap, with P. Khlopin winning the handicap, and the Belgrave results and team handicap result. We had twenty-two entries out of 93 in the Ashcombe Open Walk, held over a 10½ miles course in Richmond Park, and did our best to confiscate all the awards. We were the first team to finish four men (in fact, we had six in thirteen); won the team handicap; supplied the individual winner and the winner and second man in the handicap. The wonderful feature of the race, from our point of view, was the defeat of C. W. Hyde, the A.A.A. seven miles champion, by our champion, Len Fletcher. Len led at two miles, was over fifty yards behind at seven miles, and yet won by over two minutes, recording 83 mins. 46 secs. for the 10½ miles—surely his best performance yet. Khlopin finished seventh in the scratch race—his best yet—and so won the handicap, whilst Fletcher gained second prize on the toss of a coin from P. W. Collier, of the London Vidarians. Pos. items.s: FIELD EVENTS. Field events captain's call for members to start training, announcing a long jump and javelin match against the London Athletic Club and a long jump handicap at the first meeting on April 26th. It is now time for all members of the Field Events Section to commence training. At our first meeting, on Saturday, April 26th, there will be two field events included in the programme. These are a long jump and javelin throw versus the London Athletic Club, and also a long jump handicap open to all members. Consistent and persistent training is the only secret of success in field events. To become a champion it is necessary to devote much time and thought to training; if this is done eventual reward is certain. If any member is not successful at running or walking, I would strongly advise him to take up a field event. Messrs. Thompson, Hegarty, Noble and Mackie should all show improvement with the javelin this season. Javelins, a discus, a shot, and a pole for jumping are all available at the Park, so get down to it and let's have some really good performances. G. H. Powell G. H. items.label: February 1930
items.sum: History of Belgrave's record in the R.W.A. Junior walking championship from its first race in 1909, including the 1922 individual and team double and Tommy Green's 1927 win.
items.s: THE R.W.A. JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP. History of Belgrave's record in the R.W.A. Junior walking championship from its first race in 1909, including the 1922 individual and team double and Tommy Green's 1927 win. The R.W.A. Championship has attracted the attention and efforts of the Belgrave from the very beginning of its history, for when the first race of the series was promoted in 1909, the team was placed second, and we supplied the winner in the person of Harry Evans ,who is now known better as a judge than as an active walker. Nothing further is known of the Club's performances until after the War, since when we have a very fine record, although our number of actual wins is not so great as might have been. The first post-war Championship was held at Blackheath in 1920, and that year we drew our first blood as winners of the team event. In 1922 we secured a "double," for H. F. King headed the field and with the assistance of A. F. P. Spendlove (who finished 3rd), J. Miles and our ex-President, Harry Hare (16th and 18th respectively) won the Team Championship for the Club for the second time. Their score of 38 points is still the lowest aggregate of any Belgrave team in the "Junior." On two occasions our Club has been placed second; in 1925, when we were beaten by only 5 points, and again in 1929, when our scoring four were in the first twenty-one. Third place has been our lot no less than four times, these being in 1921, when George Cooper, who was at the time representing another club, won the individual title; 1924; 1926 and 1928. In 1927 Tommy Green, who had not been with us long enough to qualify as a team man, beat Len Fletcher by two seconds for the championship after a thrilling struggle all the way. On this occasion the team was fourth, although their score of 69 pts. would have gained them a place in any previous year. The only Belgrave, other than those already mentioned, who has been in the first three is F. W. Thorn who walked into third place in 1924 when competing as an individual. The number of entries for this race has greatly increased since 1920, the record being in 1928, when no less than 328 competitors faced the starter. These larger fields lead to fiercer competition, and the winner of a present day Junior Championship can claim to be a walker of great merit. Harry Evans Harry Evans won the first R.W.A. items.sum: Walking section notes: the Police v. Railways match, "Joe" King's Southern Railway 10 miles win, and the coming R.W.A. Junior and Surrey road walking championships.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking section notes: the Police v. Railways match, "Joe" King's Southern Railway 10 miles win, and the coming R.W.A. Junior and Surrey road walking championships. Nothing much has happened in the Walking Section other than the Cambridge Harriers Open, the Club 10 Mile Championship, and the Ashcombe A.C. Open. On January 25th a match between the Police and the Railways brought out more of our club-mates than did a similar race between Police and Belgrave. Tommy Green went off the course when holding a good lead and eventually finished 11th. Other Bels. were Rathbone, 4th; Rickards, 12th and Bidgood, 13th, for the Police, and J. F. King for the Railways. "Joe" King, one of our recent recruits, won the 10 miles Championship of the Southern Railway on February 8th. Tommy Green, the holder, did not start. The big event of the near future is the R.W.A. Junior Championship, which is to be decided on March 1st at Enfield, and we shall as usual be strongly represented in an endeavour to add another win to our creidt. Supporters are especially welcome on this occasion. The Surrey County Road Walking Championship is to be held on March 22nd, and it is hoped that on this occasion we shall record our first team win. items.sum: Sports notes by "Observer" on the new three-division Southern Amateur Athletic League and its field events contests, a proposed Birchfield ten-a-side mile challenge, Belgrave's ten best milers and pen portraits of three club members.
items.s: SPORTS JOTTINGS Sports notes by "Observer" on the new three-division Southern Amateur Athletic League and its field events contests, a proposed Birchfield ten-a-side mile challenge, Belgrave's ten best milers and pen portraits of three club members. At a recent meeting of the Southern Amateur Athletic League it was decided, in view of the numerous applicatons for membership, to form additional divisions with promotion and relegation. It has now been decided to form three divisions to accommodate the eighteen clubs, as follows :— Polytechnic Harriers, who won last season's competition by two points, South London H., Belgrave H., Herne Hill H., Surrey A.C., and Highgate H. will form the first division. Second Division: Woodford Green A.C., Queen's Park H., Finchley H., Fitzroy Lodge A.C., Cambridge H. and Ilford A.C. Third division: Mitcham A.C., Ashcombe A.C., Enfield A.C., Mary Ward A.C., Southgate and Wood Green A.C. and Essex Beagles. The winners of the second division will gain promotion, displacing the last club in Division I., but two clubs will be relegated from Division II. and promoted from Division III. The clubs in the second and third divisions will arrange the events in which they compete, but in the case of the first division each of the six contests will be allocated to an important sports meeting. Polytechnic Harriers will include the 4 x 220 yds. Relay in the programme for their Marathon and Kinnaird Meeting at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, May 31st, and the Civil Service A.A.A. will stage the 1 mile team race at their meeting on Saturday, June 14th, at Stamford Bridge. The first division have also instituted a series of inter-club competitions in field events, and it has now been arranged to hold the following events :— High Jump, May 8th, at Herne Hill H. Meeting at Herne Hill Track. Putting the Shot, June 26th, at Poly H. Meeting, Paddington Track. Javelin, July 2nd, at Belgrave H. Meeting, Battersea Park Track. Long Jump, July 23rd, at Highgate H. Meeting, Finsbury Park Track. Discus, July 28th, at Surrey A.C. Meeting, Battersea Park Track. 120 yds. Hurdles, August 20th, at South London H. Meeting, Battersea Park Track. It has been decided that 3 men should compete for each Club in each event, 2 to score. In the Hurdles events the scoring will 4, 3, 2, 1 points, the club with the highest score winning the event. Another interesting item of news is that Birchfield Harriers propose to come to town for the L.A.C.'s Spring meeting with ten mile runners to compete against the next best ten in the country. The race would presumably be run in relay fashion, and whether this would very entertaining to watch is open to doubt, especially if one team set up a good lead over the other. While on the question of mile runners I should like to say that I consider our own Club could give any team in the country a run, counting ten aside. Our narrow defeat last year in the Victory Cup showed the strength of our boys and the more to count the better we like it. Take the following ten names—there are, no doubt, others, but these will do for an example: T. J. Flower, W. A. Rice, W. G. Webb, J. E. Flower, H. E. Footer, E. A. Duffett, A. Allum, A. W. Penny, W. S. Mitchell and A. D. Pyer. Here are ten men of proved ability over the distance, namely 1 mile, and I should say that fit and well this team would average well inside 4 mins. 40 secs. I say would average, mark you, and if you reflect that the Victory Cup was won by a team, of four men, averaging about 4 mins. 38 secs., you will readily agree that our team would take some beating with ten aside running. My next three Club members are as follows :— W. H. Eastman, a promising recruit to our cross-country section and one who should show a big improvement on the track this Summer. Has done a little running in Scout events before he joined us, but it has been during the Winter season that he has shown signs of developing into a very useful distance runner. Is on the young side, so would be wise not to force matters just yet but to let his improvement come gradually. F. R. Webb, a brother of our respected cross-country captain and has a big advantage over "Bill" by the fact that he has youth on his side. Was formerly a member of the Ashcombe A.C., and did well in Opens on the track when competing in their colours. Has now become eligible to run for us in team events and we hope he will do better in the "Claret and Gold" than he did in the "Chevron." R. G. Hillier, another of our youthful members of the walking section. Has gained some successes in Club handicaps and has been walking well during the present season on the road. Is of good build for walking and if he gives his mind to it should do much better in the future. T. J. Flower T. J. Flower named among ten Belgrave milers of proved ability W. A. Rice W. A. items.label: February 1930
items.h: THE LIGHTER SIDE OF THE CLUB.
items.sum: Social notes by W. A. Rice on the last Wimbledon social of the season, the third dance at Wandsworth Town Hall and the date and venue of the Annual Dinner.
items.s: THE LIGHTER SIDE OF THE CLUB. Social notes by W. A. Rice on the last Wimbledon social of the season, the third dance at Wandsworth Town Hall and the date and venue of the Annual Dinner. The last social of the season, held at Wimbledon on January 25th, was, from an entertainment point of view, the best of the series. In fact, with so many performers at hand it was a job to work them all in without giving the dancing fraternity a long wait. The programme was well varied, as we had dancing, vocal and instrumental artistes. Billy Williams, with new songs, scored his usual success. His inebriated actions are very realistic (no offence, Billy !). Then came the surprise item. This was a troupe dance. Miss Parsons of the "L.O.'s" had very sportingly asked some of her friends—members of a gymnastic class—to come along and give us a demonstration of a "Tarantella" dance. This is a very intricate troupe dance, and the state of our floor did not help. Anyway, judging by the reception, it was very much appreciated and only the strenuous efforts of the dance prevented an encore. Tom Cotton has firmly established himself as a favourite. His songs were well chosen and sung. Another surprise item was the ability as a trumpeter of A. T. Webb, who with his accompanist, helped us over that period between tea and the arrival of the dance band. Then came Miss Grace Kirkpatrick. I think everybody knows how well she can sing, and it was with general regret that time prevented her from singing more than two numbers. R. F. Elson, as a parson, surprised and amused us all, and then when Perce Cook came on to the dance floor with efforts to emulate Ben Blue, I was forced to alter my opinion regarding the talent we have in the Club, and with encouragement we ought to unearth some more. We had quite a good number present, and with the entertainment that was provided, it was really a good wind-up to our socials for 1929-30. Our third dance of the season saw us back at Wandsworth Town and again we had a great crowd. On such a night it would have been quite pardonable to have had a few dozen there only, but we had round about three hundred present. Now about our Annual Dinner. This has been definitely fixed for Saturday, April 26th, in the evening, after our opening track meeting. This should provide a great filip and I do hope the dinner will be representative of all sections this year. The venue is very accessible, being at the Crighton Restaurant, Clapham Junction, and the price of the tickets will be reasonable. Further details shortly. W. A. Rice. items.sum: Fixture notice listing the National Cross-Country Championship at Sheffield, a social run with Herne Hill Harriers, the 5 miles road race trial for the Brighton Relay team, the International at Leamington Spa, the Inter-Counties at Wolverhampton and Brighton Relay day.
items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. Fixture notice listing the National Cross-Country Championship at Sheffield, a social run with Herne Hill Harriers, the 5 miles road race trial for the Brighton Relay team, the International at Leamington Spa, the Inter-Counties at Wolverhampton and Brighton Relay day. The cross-country season is now drawing to a close and Saturday, March 8th, sees the grand finale so far as the team championships are concerned. On this day the National Cross-Country Championship will be held at Graves Park, Sheffield. A special train will leave London (St. Pancras) at 9-55 a.m., arriving at Sheffield at 1-23 p.m. Third class return fare, 14/-. Our team and supporters will travel by this train. On March 15th we have a social run with Herne Hill Harriers from their headquarters at Mottingham. This will take the form of a road run, in view of the close proximity of the Brighton Relay, and it is hoped that all members keen on securing a place in the team will turn up and support this fixture. The 5 miles Road Run with Sealed Handicap in conjunction, will be held on March 22nd. This has been brought forward from the 29th as this is the date fixed for the Inter-Counties race at Wolverhampton. Our 5 miles Road Race will be in the nature of a trial for the 10 places in the Club's Brighton Relay team. The Handicap was put on for the benefit of those members who wish to have a run and I hope that we will have a bumper entry. Entries close 18th inst. An additional attraction on the 22nd is the International race at Leamington Spa. Special train from Paddington at 11-18 a.m. Return fare 5/-. We have one International in the Club and it is not without the bounds of reason that we might have another; it all depends on how "bad" Bert feels on the day of the race. The 29th is the day of the Inter-Counties Championship at Wolverhampton. We hope to have at least four Club members competing for their respective counties and the Belgrave element should be well to the fore. Don't forget April 12th. This is Brighton Relay day. Book your seats early for the trip to Brighton. All enquiries to E. A. Duffett, Hon. Running Sec., 138 Frant Road, Thornton Heath. E. A. Duffett E. A. Duffett Hon. North of the Thames Cross Country Championship
items.s: CORRESPONDENCE. Letter from K. B. O'Kell in Newcastle-under-Lyme recalling his running career from a 1914 Scout camp race to his years with Belgrave, praising Footer and Tommy Green and urging that a club history be compiled. Newcastle-under-Lyme. My Dear Belgravians, In various papers (almost as well edited as our own Gazette) one invariably sees a controversy as to which is the most exciting sport or pastime. Well, from my own experience, I would say that there is no sport to equal running as far as excitement is concerned, although I consider tennis the most congenial pastime, if played as such. Perhaps it would interest some, especially the novices, to know of my experience in the running world, and give them some encouragement. In the year 1914, at the age of thirteen, I was in Camp with Boy Scouts, and if we left our towels outside the tents after 11 a.m. we were fined a halfpenny. Eventually this sum grew and it was decided to hold a sports meeting "to share the spoils." I entered several events and was placed second in the mile to a fellow named T. C .Crossland. About four or five years later I saw reports, "Sensational sprinting by T. C. Crossland." Writing from memory, I believe he won an "Open 100" in 9 4/5 secs. and I thought "If he can run, so can I." Before going any further I should mention that Crossland became a member of Surrey A.C. and ran for England v. France in an unofficial match. I, with many others, was deeply grieved to hear of his untimely death through poisoning, attributed to a scratch on the arm. This was about 1921, I believe. Anyhow, after reading the paragraph mentioned, I promptly invested in a cheap pair of spikes, got up at 6 a.m. in the morning and proceeded to run round Wandsworth Park as fast as my ignorant legs would allow me. I had the assistance of two very decent brothers, who would turn out and time my efforts. Needless to say, my idea of speed was very meagre, but full of hope I entered an "Open" at Kingston. After a mild disappointment at not being on limit, the race began and at the end of a lap I was last. I wondered at what speed a mile was run, but as I was really "groggy" I was persuaded to give up running. This was in 1919. Later, at business, I became associated with A. A. Gordon, son of our present President. We decided to "wipe the board" with the other departments at the firm's sports meeting, so I again set my heart on the mile, and A. Gordon concentrated on the short distances. Under the coaching of our President I got quite fit and won the race very easily, although I had "wind-up"—100 per cent. At this point I would like to mention to all Belgrave novices—be advised by the older members. As you see, when I thought I was a potential "Sensational runner" I was doing myself more harm than good, but when I came under the guidance of the Gordon family, I reaped the maximum reward—prizes, and then "scratch" mark. Here, also, I should like to mention that at the time of my first venture at Kingston, I had joined a famous club which was then "all the rage"—a Surrey club, by the way—but all the advice I ever received was a note asking me to turn up for a club photograph. I can assure you that it was a different reception at Belgrave. I, like most novices, was quite unknown, but reported as "promising." I was cordially welcomed and given advice and information on all hands. In 1923 I had a very successful summer and later on in the following winter began cross-country running. Up to this time Belgrave had never won a team championship and we hoped to break the spell with the "South of the Thames" Junior—but we were beaten into second place. At this time A. D. Pyer was the "star," with a dogged little chap named Footer always after his body. Well, one day Footer beat Pyer, and I cannot recall him playing second fiddle since! Gradually our strength grew and we scored our first win at Epsom in the Surrey County Championship on January 2nd, 1926. Since that day Belgrave have advanced beyond all anticipation and it is with a great deal of regret that I cannot now share all the thrills that the various events offer. Running offers more thrills than most other sports. The thrill of passing your antagonist "up the straight" (although from my experience it is invariably the action of others), even if it only happens once or twice a year, is a grand sensation. Last night, I was having tea after a rotten game of football, and "London was calling" on the wireless. The announcer came to "Cross-country running," gave the North of the Thames result and then said "South of the Thames was won by H. E. Footer, Belgrave Harriers." Since my last race with the "Bels." this was my first thrill. Needless to say, your champion Footer is practically a club by himself and an inspiration to any athlete. What he lacks in lineal measure he overcomes with (put as D. G. A. Lowe once did) the "guts" of a lion, not to mention the whole-hearted club spirit he shows. On Boxing Day morning I visited Battersea Park—the scene of many of my most enjoyable days. During a conversation with our President I remarked how wonderful it was that all the "Old Brigade" still cling to the Club. He said, "Well, Ken, it's a treat to come down here; they are like a big, happy family." Personally I have always found that so—in our disappointments and in our victories—and I'll bet any money that there is not another club that can say the same for a long way round. Running has many disappointments, as well as thrills. Take Footer's case; times when he could not "raise a gallop," but there is always hope, and I am convinced that it takes at least three or four seasons to find the best methods of training. So, you young runners, don't get down-hearted if you run badly. Try another method of training, with the advice of the members. Your history in athletics since 1919 is really remarkable and something for everyone concerned to be proud of. This winter I have been playing football, but I've had enough and next year I'll be back to the greatest winter pastime (for "old 'uns")—cross-country running. I would classify it as "greatest sport." I have had quite a lot to say about running; of course, like all of you, I get equal thrills out of our walking section. I pick up a paper quite casually and see a smiling portrait of Tommy Green, Belgrave Harriers, etc. And, then, when it's one's misfortune to be away from the centre of activities, we have the Club Gazette, also the work of whole-hearted club fellows. No doubt to many of you the Gazette is old news, but I get many pleasant hours looking through old editions and wishing I were in the swim again. The average club does not have such an appeal, no "happy family" spirit, and I can assure you that it is with great pleasure that I receive the familiar Claret and Gold edition. As I am out of reach of most of you, I suggest that it's worth 8d., and I am sure the present edition is at least worth a Bob!!! (No "cat-calls" from St. John's Hall, please). All you younger members have a lot to be thankful for: splendid organisation, unselfish devotion in club interests by men whose only enjoyment is to see the club's activities increase, and attain fame in the athletic world. I was interested to see more of our benedicts "hauled into the net." How many little black books has H. Parker filled? Are Belgrave—"unofficial matrimonial agents"—inviting London Olympiades to their socials? Evidently our far-seeing Committee mean England to shine in the 1952 Olympic Games! It has often been suggested that our club history should be compiled. Would it not make a very interesting "serial" for our Gazette? Now Messrs. Evans, Horwood, Gordon, Macher, H. Parker and Co.—what about it? We all know a good deal, but there is nothing like history. In concluding, I can do no more than wish you all a continuation of the very interesting headlines you have a habit of having inserted in our leading sports papers. Naturally, we all look forward to the result of the Southern, Brighton Relay and the R.W.A. "20." Although a long way off, the eternal cry "Up the Bels." is a constant thought, and I can well picture the enthusiasm at such victories as Bert Footer's and Tommy Green's. Keep it up, Belgrave; you make the older members very proud to show the deeds to their friends. Sound foundations have been laid; you have some jolly fine fellows among you; no class distinction, no jealousy, no enmity. I, like many more, hope that you will smash any attempt to place such an ideal combination in danger, and with speedy promptitude, and so maintain that great club cry, and the position it now holds in the athletic world. Up! up! up! Belgrave!!! All the best, K. B. O'Kell. K. B. O'Kell K. B. items.sum: Opening club notes on the cross-country and walking successes of the past month, congratulations to Len Fletcher, Joe King and S. H. Warboys, the summer fixtures, a new member, club ties and a reminder about subscriptions.
items.s: Opening club notes on the cross-country and walking successes of the past month, congratulations to Len Fletcher, Joe King and S. H. Warboys, the summer fixtures, a new member, club ties and a reminder about subscriptions. The past month, the climax of the winter season, has been wonderfully successful for our runners and walkers. The cross-country men have been placed in the “Southern” for the first time in the Club’s history and followed this up by what is, perhaps, an even better performance—sixth in the National—another “best yet.” The walkers have won the Junior Championship again and now Belgrave hold both Senior and Junior Championships. Incidentally, we are the first Club to have won the Junior title three times. A team went to Birmingham on March 22nd and brought back the “Bishop of Birmingham’s Cup”—our first visit to the Midland town for this race since 1921, when we won the trophy for the first time. “This ’ere Progress, it goes on,” wrote H. G. Wells, in one of his novels and this is a phrase which we could very well adopt in connection with our Club’s activities, even at the risk of departing from the famous novelist’s original meaning. Long may it continue; and congratulations to all those concerned in the past month’s contribution to the Club’s progress. * * * * * Congratulations to Len Fletcher upon again winning the Surrey County Ten Miles Champioiship, and also to Joe King upon again winning the Sussex Twenty Miles Championship and beating the County record for the distance, which he held. S. H. Warboys also merits our congratulations upon being placed sixteeneth in the Inter-Counties cross-country race and being the second man of the Middlesex team (who were placed second) to finish—a splendid performance. * * * * * Our Summer season will open with a match v. Old Emanuel A.C. at Wandsworth on Thursday, April 24th, and will be followed on Saturday, April 26th, by our match v. L.A.C. and handicap programme. A. E. Strank joins our ranks this month and we extend a cordial welcome to him. * * * * * And now for the Brighton Relay Race on April 12th, when we hope to record another “best yet” performance. * * * * * Club ties may be had from— A. A. HARLEY, 44 Rosebury Road, S.W.6. Price 3/-. By post 3/3. * * * * * Have YOU paid your subscription? Without oil an engine won’t work—without subscriptions a club cannot carryon The Summer season is now upon us, which means that six months of the year have gone by—and still a large number of members have not yet paid. Have you paid? If not, do so at once and so help the Club and save the Hon. Treasurer the trouble of writing for it. H. G. Wells H. G.
