items.label: April 1930
items.sum: Special correspondent S.D.'s lap-by-lap account of the Southern cross-country championship at Race Hill, Brighton, where Belgrave placed 3rd, the club's first placing in the race, with results and team placings.
items.s: “THE SOUTHERN.” Special correspondent S.D.'s lap-by-lap account of the Southern cross-country championship at Race Hill, Brighton, where Belgrave placed 3rd, the club's first placing in the race, with results and team placings. (From our Special Correspondent). Race Hill, Brighton. I have travelled down here by the “Race Special,” in one of the first-class compartments reserved for Belgrave Harriers, and then from the station by special tramcar to the course. Having ascertained our team, the last place in which was in doubt until the arrival, amid cheers, of Hon. Sec., Wally, I made my way to the turning point for the first short lap—a little more than three-quarters of a mile from the Grandstand. The day, though bright and sunny, is cold, and the spectators, who line the course in large numbers, are glad to avail themselves of any little shelter they can find from the easterly wind which faces the runners at the start. In spite of the wind, however, there is a haziness which obscures the view of the sea, which lies at the foot of the valley on my left, and also the Grandstand where the “field” is now lining up. “They’re off!” Someone standing near me with glasses has seen them start and I can see a solid mass moving steadily down the course, which dips slightly before rising to the bend where I am standing. Here they are—the whole 300 in a bunch—led by Broadley and Payne. I look for the claret and gold. There’s Allum......Jack Flower close to him......there’s Sid Warboys and Ernie...... I watch them turn through the rails. There is a doubt—the pointsman is not clear—the leaders break out in different directions and cast about like hounds in search of the trail. They find it, and the sudden change of direction catches unawares a horseman who is watching the scene and he suddenly finds himself engulfed in a sea of runners—his horse shies, but he can do nothing but let the race flow round him. Arthur Allum has gone wide on the turn and Jack Flower is first of the Bels. as they return to the starting-point to complete the first lap. They come down the course again, the mass a little less dense now, but still well together. Broadley still leads; Flower, Allum, Warboys and Penny lie well packed inside the first 40. Where’s Bert Footer? Here he comes. but well back and not looking any too happy. Go on, Bert! Up the Bels! They have gone nearly 2½ miles now and leave the racecourse for a stretch of plough, which, though dry and light, begins to string the runners out. They disappear over the hill, and I move on half a mile to see them as they return on the first long lap (at about 4 miles). Suddenly the leaders appear again; Oddie, Tomlin, Weatherill and Broadley......S.L.H. have three in seven......there is a gap......Harry Payne 9th......What about Belgrave? Syd Warboys, running strongly, is 26th; Jack Flower 39th; Allum, Duffett and Mitchell, 44, 46, 48. Bert is somewhere up with Jack, who probably “eclipsed” him as they passed (I missed seeing him). Penny, Rice and Smith are together in the nineties. A wait while the race goes back once more to the Grandstand (Footer, Mitchell and Flower are together here,, 39, 40, 41, I am told) and out on the second lap and making 6½ miles when I see them again, where they cross the road near Warren Reservoir and plunge down a steep hill—rough going and a wire fence to negotiate at the bottom. The same four are leading, but now the order is Tomlin, Broadley, Weatherill and Oddie, followed by Saunders and Ferris, of Wycombe Phoenix H. Warboys has picked up ten places in the two miles and is now 16th—he smiles happily at me as he glides down the hill. Arthur Allum has put in some good running, too, and now lies 31st, with Footer and Flower at 34 and 36, Mitchell 41, Duffett 50. The long line of runners winds across the fields and round a copse lying in a fold of the Downs and they are in view till they come for the second time to this hill, which is the steepest I have ever seen in a cross-country race; Tomlin and Broadley still have the lead. Oddie is third, but has dropped into a walk (like many others) on the steepest part of the climb and is closely followed by his clubmate, Weatherill. Ferris and Saunders come next......Payne is 12th......Sid Warboys is still 16th and going strong. Bert’s position is likewise unchanged at 34th, but a “Footer finish” will remedy that! Allum is with Bert, followed by Ernie, 39, and Flower, 41......Mitchell, our sixth man, is 54th; Bill Rice finds the hill a very severe test; Webb and Smith are also feeling the strain; Arthur Penny is having a “bad time” and has dropped back to about 150; Bayliss and Chorley are still sticking it gamely in the rear. The race is over! Tomlin is the individual winner, S.L.H. the team champions, with Wycombe Phoenix 2nd, and Belgrave 3rd. Well done the Bels! Jolly well run, you fellows! This is the first time in history that we have been placed in the “Southern”—our nearest effort being 7th in 1904. A point that strikes me on looking at the figures is the number of places our boys picked up in the last mile. Notably Bert, with a gain of 13, Mitchell 5, Rice 11, Webb 8, and Chorley 12. Another noticeable feature was the promptness with which the detailed results were made known; only 26 minutes elapsing between the time Tomlin passed the finishing post and the distribution—at 1d. a time—of sheets giving the placings of the scoring men of the first dozen teams. We have all had tea at a pastrycook’s in North Street, where Harry Parker distinguished himself by his efforts to hustle a service which was not adequate to lusty Belgravian appetites. We have strolled, at a leisurely pace, round the town; bought our Brighton Rock; said good-bye to our week-ending friends and we are now returning to London is a satisfied mood and a first-class carriage. I have one regret—I have not seen the sea! S.D. 1. S. A. Tomlin (Highgate H.) 56 47 2. J. A. Broadley (Hampstead H.) 56 55 3. B. C. V. Oddie (S.L.H.) 57 10 13. S. H. Warboys 58 28 21. H. E. items.s: THE M.P.A.A. VISIT. Report and full result of the cross-country match against the Metropolitan Police at Wimbledon on February 22nd, won by Belgrave 84 points to 130 (the report says only one Belgrave man placed between 8th and 20th, though the team placings list two, 8th and 12th, and the result marks 11th F. Rickards B although the Police scored 11th), with a note on members in the Police Ten Miles Championship. On February 22nd we entertained the Police team at Wimbledon. About twenty-five members of the Force turned out, whereas our numbers were fewer than usual, and only just over a dozen of our men were present. The course used was the old seven mile Club course and we placed the first six men home, headed by Len Fletcher. T. J. Caffrey, the Woodford Green walker, was the first M.P.A.A. man to finish, in the seventh position. With ten aside to score, we placed our men in the first 22, scoring 84 points; but the Police placed their ten in eighteen and scored 130 points. This showed our weakness to be in the middle section of the final placings; in fact, between positions 8 and 20 we placed only one man. However, our first six positions placed defeat out of the question. Final positions are appended, and many “Belgrave” names may be seen in the Police team. * * * * * In the Police Ten Miles Championship held earlier in the month three of our members, Messrs. items.label: April 1930
items.sum: Account of the R.W.A. Junior walking championship at Enfield on March 1st, in which Belgrave beat Enfield 33 points to 38 to win the Garnet Cup for the third time, with the result, team placings and a table of the club's record in the race since 1909.
items.s: THE R.W.A. JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP. Account of the R.W.A. Junior walking championship at Enfield on March 1st, in which Belgrave beat Enfield 33 points to 38 to win the Garnet Cup for the third time, with the result, team placings and a table of the club's record in the race since 1909. Maybe that it was but idle fancy, or possibly the long run of successes in the past few months had blunted the edge of enthusiasm for March 1st, the day of the R.W.A. “Junior” Championship, found me somewhat more apathetic than usual, a state of mind not improved by a journey to Enfield in solitary state. However, once at the venue, one sensed a different atmosphere, especially in the dressing-room, where the pungent smell of “speed oil” immediately aroused me to be up and doing. Our team, when found, and a slight misunderstanding rectified, quickly raised some enthusiasm. Certainly, on paper, our chances appeared outstanding and quite equal to those of 1922, the year of our last victory. So, in spite of a number of regretted absentees that prevented us starting a “B” team, everything appeared satisfactory. Up to a point. The course had been mapped out over one large lap of 10 miles and, in consequence, being without a conveyance, one saw a surging mass of walkers some 300 yards from the start and was then hopelessly left. Eventually, by tracing the course the reverse way, the 8th mile point was reached and here the leaders were seen for the first time. Who is that coming along in front? A group of three, it seemed. Yes; and who is that just leading? A cheery little individual we know so well; F. H. Elson. A pleasant smile, widened for our benefit, and he is gone, closely followed by Amies of Enfield and D. Gum of Essex Beagles (I nearly said G.L. and Coke). Then began the anxious moment. How are the team placed? The next competitor was Turtle, Herne Hill H.; then came Bonnett, Ashcombe; Vidofsky, Derby, and then another tonic, E. Saunders, of ours. A hasty “Where am I?” and away he went. Then came Caffrey, Woodford Green, followed by A. Bye, Enfield, our J. E. Field and the Enfield man, Marler. This made Enfield and ourselves 3 each in the first 11. Another Derby man, then 2 from Sheffield, another Midlander from Birmingham, and then, Oh Heavens! another Enfield man. Surely they, with 4 in 16, were going to do the trick. But we live; here comes (following a Leicester man) our versatile performer, S. L. King, 18th. Excellent; the score is 36 to 38 in our favour, and no other team near. A wait—where is our 5th man? Where is Paul Khlopin? No signs. The 5th Enfield man has already gone. We run, always with an eye to a conveyance; but no, our luck is not in. Panting and hot, we reach the 9th mile, but again no, the anticipated “lift” has gone. “What has happened?” “How are we placed?” “Oh, we are all right; 4 in 16.” “But what of Enfield?” Nothing is known. “Who is leading?” “Amies, with Elson second.” There goes 2 points and our lead wiped out. “Where is Saunders?” “7th.” Right. Field? “11th.” Hell! Enfield’s third has passed ours and we are 2 points down. Where is King? Where is No. 92, Enfield’s 4th man? It is too late. The end is approaching and being helplessly left, nothing can be done. There is, however, an immense faith in the capabilities of our 4 to stay home and not to concede any ground, and, moreover, in S. L. King to make up some placings. We continue our walk towards the finish. “Where is No. 92?” is the burning question, but no one seems to know. The finishing point is reached and hastily we check some more unofficial figures and still no signs of the important number. The dressing-room, and we are volunteered the information that “Enfield has won.” No, we cannot believe that yet. More enquiries and eventually the official placings are unearthed. We are there—33 points to 38. King has made up the necessary and beaten Enfield’s 4th. The fatal No. 92 has fallen back and has been supplanted by what was Enfield’s 5th man at 8 miles. Thus after a lapse of 8 years we again become possessors of the “Garnet Cup” and now gain the title of Junior Champions, in addition to National Champions, for the first time. It has been a truly wonderful season and all credit is due to our winning team for a very fine performance. F. Elson made a very gallant effort to gain the individual title, but the local man probably judged his effort at the right point, in which respect knowledge of the course undoubtedly helped. Saunders has justified our faith in his capabilities and J. E. Field has redeemed what has been for him a somewhat disappointing season. Of S. L. King, well, we always knew he would do it and he doubtless would have been as delighted with the result even had he not scored. His participation therefore is doubly satisfactory and some slight return for his services as Hon. Secretary of our Walking Section in the Season 1927-28. In congratulating our team, we must tender sympathy to Paul, who had been expected to finish close up to the leaders. He was unfortunate to incur the displeasure of one of the Walking Judges early in the race. Comment thereon is, of course, impossible. It is obviously a matter of fact, not of rule. Bearing on this subject, however, an interesting article by a Northern writer appeared in a Sheffield paper that I was fortunate to secure on the occasion of our visit for the National Cross-country Championship. In this he writes: “You may remember that I tipped Belgrave in this column a fortnight ago, and my reason for this is that Belgrave seem to have fewer disqualifications than other Clubs. They are a team that adopt a similar style, and that one attractive to see. But if my admiration was for Belgrave, my sympathy went to Enfield.” It is pleasing and satisfactory, therefore, to know that our walkers have a good reputation up North, both for style and speed. Whilst not going so far as to say that my sympathy went to Enfield, we must congratulate them on making a very fine effort. Third last year, second this year, their turn will surely come, and although I have recollections of having competed in an Enfield “Open 7” in 1920, I believe it is only in the last 3 or 4 years that a walking section has been actively in being. The second man in their team, A. Bye, who finished 9th in the race, is of course the old Belgravian who left us owing to residential difficulties to join Southgate and Wood Green. In conclusion, our success is the third since the race was established and this gives us a new record, for no other Club has won on more than two occasions. items.sum: Account of the National cross-country championship at Sheffield on March 8th, followed round the course, in which Footer finished 20th (17th team scorer) and Belgrave's seven placed 6th of 37 clubs with 320 points, the club's best yet, with the result, team placings and the club's previous National records from 1920.
items.s: THE NATIONAL CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Account of the National cross-country championship at Sheffield on March 8th, followed round the course, in which Footer finished 20th (17th team scorer) and Belgrave's seven placed 6th of 37 clubs with 320 points, the club's best yet, with the result, team placings and the club's previous National records from 1920. There existed a considerable element of doubt as to the wisdom of entering a team in the “National” at Sheffield on March 8th, especially in view of the unfortunate experience at Beaconsfield last year ,but even had the question not already been settled, there is little doubt but that our place in the “Southern” would have turned the scale. Once entered, however, difficulties still had to be overcome, for J. E. Flower desired to rest, A. Penny was temporarily disabled, and W. Mitchell was in a similar plight and consequently matters did not appear very satisfactory up to a few days before the race. Eventually we raised 7, and what was lacking in numbers was made up in determination. What were our prospects? Well, to be frank, so far as chief placings were concerned, nil. But this is not always our chief concern. Progress is not always rapid and if we achieved a best performance to date, then the result would be considered generally satisfactory. This was done to some purpose, as will be seen. We will pass over the 3½ hour train journey to Sheffield and the incidents that enlivened the time en route, also the trip up to the course and the remarks thereon. Comment on the dressing accommodation would not be complimentary, whilst the heated atmosphere of the room, shared with 7 other clubs, was positively overpowering and leaves us speechless. No words of mine can adequately describe the scene of the grand march of competitors from the dressing rooms to the starting point, some half mile away, headed by a Piper, and with each Team Captain carrying a small staff with card bearing the name of the Club. Incidentally, I became promoted Captain before the course was reached, whilst what happened to the Piper I failed to ascertain. Possibly he had enough for one day, for a 3 mile Youth’s race preecded the big event. However, once at the starting point, little time was lost. The scene was very animated and inspiring and it seemed that nearly all Sheffield had turned out to witness the race. Certainly it was one of the largest crowds I have seen for a cross-country event. The course of 10 miles was over parkland, a rough figure 8 in shape, with a small lap of 1 mile and 3 of 3 miles. Drawn reasonably well and away, Syd Warboys decided to get into the picture and at one point was actually leading the field. Thereafter the runners disappeared round the crest of a hill and came into sight at the end of the first mile, where J. A. Burns (Joe Bink’s selected) had a slight lead of Bailey and Platt, both of Sheffield. It was almost impossible to place our team at this point, but Footer was 63rd, Warboys 100th, and the others, whom I could not both place and name, 128, 140, 150, 175. Again the field went from sight; this time for 2 miles. Thus at the end of 3 miles the first to appear was Holden, of Tipton; Howard, of Kettering; Beman, Birchfield; and Evenson, of Salford. Our Bert was here definitely 62nd, Warboys 85th, Allum 97th, Bill Webb 101st, Ernie Duffett 128th, Frank Webb 137th and Bill Rice 182nd. The team score, ignoring individuals, 610. We see them again a little more than a mile further on. Beman is now just in front, Howard is still second, Holden third, Harper, the holder, is 5th, Winfield, of Derby, 6th, whilst the first Southerner, Broadley, of Hampstead, is 8th. Webster, of Birchfield, is “on the ground” in distress but quickly rises and goes on. Footer comes along, now 49th, Syd Warboys, 72nd, Arthur Allum, 87th, “W.G.” 103rd, “E.A.” 110th, Frank 120th, and Bill Rice 185th. At 6 miles Howard has taken the lead and Harper has dropped to 6th place. Bert is now 31st, our friend Bert Cook is observed 42nd, Warboys 63rd, Allum 77th, Bill Webb 90th, Duffett, 108th, and Frank Webb down to 110. The team score is down to 479, which appears very satisfactory. Once more we check, we do not mind whilst we continue to knock off the points. 7¼ miles. Howard is still leading and, Broadley has moved up into second place, Beman is third, Harper fourth, Footer is 25th, and our others in the same order, 56th, 73rd, 90th, Frank Webb has, however, now passed Duffett, their positions 95th and 104th. There is little time for more; we have to return to the finishing point for the discs. One last brief effort and at 9¼ miles Footer is seen still 25th. Howard is leading by some 30 yards from Harper, who is making a determined effort. With some difficulty we reach our appointed spot, and soon a mighty shout goes up. “Harper.” “Harper.” But Howard is not yet beaten, and although he has seemingly had a hard race all the way he holds on to a slight lead and makes his way through the funnel, beaming with delight. Broadley is practically carried through, 3rd. We wait. Cheers, here’s Footer. All in, as usual. We clutch his hand, a hasty grasp, and then the disc. Cheers again, 17. Then follow with wonderfully welcome frequency the others. Warboys 36, Allum 47, W. G. Webb 65, F. R. Webb 74, Duffett 81, Rice 133. Well run all; the team score totals 320. Excellent. We are near the S.L.H. representative and ask, “How have you fared?” 285. Well, we are proud of our 320. The scores are being checked now. Birchfield are home again with 94 points, Hallamshire are 101, Tipton are third with 166, Sheffield 266, South London H., 285, are fifth and then—Belgrave 6th. Of 37 Clubs entered only 5 have beaten us. Birchfield, the holders, and Midland Champions; Hallamshire, the Northern Champions; Tipton, second best in the Midlands; Sheffield, second best in the North; and South London H., the Southern Champions. What more could we expect? This is easily our best Our previous record is, of course, not inspiring, but here now is a performance to live up to, and we hope, to surpass. All credit, then to those who have participated. Time is short and we have to get back to the train quickly. We make the long journey back in fine spirit and almost expect to find a welcome at the station. Perhaps that will come later. The brief result follows with details of previous performances. W.H.H. items.label: April 1930
items.sum: History of the R.W.A. 20 miles walking championship from 1908 and of Belgrave's part in it, from third in 1922 to four team wins between 1924 and 1929, with the walkers expected to defend the title next month.
items.s: THE R.W.A. NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP. History of the R.W.A. 20 miles walking championship from 1908 and of Belgrave's part in it, from third in 1922 to four team wins between 1924 and 1929, with the walkers expected to defend the title next month. The R.W.A. 20 miles Championship has not always been a National affair, for it was not until 1912 that the race, previously known as the Southern Road Walking Championship, was thrown open to all. The first race of the series was held in 1908 at Ruislip, when H. L. V. Ross was the winner, and it is interesting to note that he won on no fewer that five subsequent occasions, his last win being as recently as 1920, twelve years after his first success. Even two years later than that, he was still good enough to be placed third. Ross was not alone in enjoying so lengthy a period of prominence in the walking world, for B. C. Brown, who was second in 1908, was still capable of getting 7th in the 1925 Championship, and a number of similar cases could be quoted. Until 1914, Surrey Walking Club appeared to have the monopoly of winning the team event, for except in 1911, when they were beaten by the narrow margin of 2 points, they won every race. Belgrave teams or individuals were certainly not placed during this period, but whether they competed or not I am unable to say. The first race subsequent to the Great War was in 1920, and in this and the following year the team placings were Herne Hill Harriers 1st, Surrey A.C. 2nd, and Surrey Walking Club 3rd, but still no Belgrave in the first three. In 1922 it was decided to hold the championship in Richmond Park, and evidently the Belgrave thought that since this was more or less on their own training ground, they would show what they were capable of, and as a result of this effort and no doubt inspired by “Bob” Ricketts, they finished third in the team event with Surrey W.C. once more securing premier honours. Naturally, we were not content with this, so the next year, 1923, at Leicester, in what was then a record field of 126, they made a still greater effort and, finishing their scoring four in 17, deadheated for second place, the team on this occasion consisting of E. L. Reeve 8th, A. P. Spendlove 11th, W. J. Hawker 14th, and J. Belchamber 17th. None of these men are active walkers now, but E. G. Cooper, who is still one of our mainstays, was the 6th man to finish, but he had not then joined us. Windsor Park was the venue of the next race, and here we made our debut as National Champions. The race was very exciting, for at seven miles we were fifth with 85 points, but at half distance we had knocked off 21 points and were fourth. In the next five miles our team walked into second place, being led by Surrey W. Club, who were a dozen points ahead. During the last mile or two, Allen and Harry Hare, after much persuasion from the “Bels.” supporters, gained a number of places, and at the finish we had secured a 9 point advantage and so won our first Championship. No members of the team which had been placed the year before at Leicester were in this scoring four, so it was all the more creditable to gain such a fine victory with a new team, which consisted of R. D. McMullen 6th, J. H. Allen 7th, W. H. Hare 11th, and J. Miles 14th. Eliminating individuals, their places were 5, 6, 9 and 12, totalling 32 points George Cooper was walking as an individual Belgrave and was fourth. Other of our clubmates to finish well up were E. A. Wall 16th, J. Rathbone 23rd, J. B. Belchamber 28th, and W. J. Hawker 29th, thus we had as many as nine men in the first 29. It was indeed a very fine performance. A record entry was received for the 1925 race and we had to travel to Derby to defend our title, and with the assistance of our old friend Bob Ricketts, a “B” team man, who managed to beat Surrey Walking Club’s fourth man, we just scraped home with a score of 28 to their 29 points. Harry Hare was the only one of the previous winning team to score again on this occasion. Further details of the race will be found elsewhere in this magazine. Owing to the Coal Dispute, no Championship race was held in 1926, and this omission seemed to lose our twenty-milers their winnings ways, for in 1927 we could get no nearer than fourth. Tommy Green, walking as an individual, was fourth and Harold King ,in his maiden effort over 20 miles finished 7th, two very fine performances. Our other men all seemed to have an “off” day and were well back, but we came away determined to regain our lost laurels at the next opportunity. Only seven “Bels.” started at Leicester in 1928, a very poor show compared with foregoing years, but if we lacked quantity, we had quality, as the result showed. MacMullen was our “star” turn on this occasion. for after walking with fine judgment he finished up in fourth place, while Rickards, after making a great effort in the last five miles was 7th with E. G. Cooper 14th and Tommy Green, who had been with the leaders for thirteen miles, 16th; their united efforts giving the club their third win, this time with twenty points to spare. H. F. King and J. Rathbone both walked well to finish 21st and 32nd respectively. Last year’s Championship was held at Hayes (Kent), and early in the race we lost Cooper through disqualification, and F. Rickards, another of the 1928 winning team, who had barely recovered from a serious illness, was compelled to drop out at half distance. Fortunately we had good men to fill the breach, and as is usual with the Belgrave they made up a lot of ground over the last few miles, so with Tommy Green finishing 6th, the evergreen McMullen 11th, J. Rathbone 15th, and Ben Knifton, 19th, we recorded our fourth success in the last five races. From the foregoing it will be seen that although we were not prominent until 1922 we have since then won premier honours four times and been 2nd, 3rd and 4th on the other three occasions, but we have been unable to get any individuals nearer than fourth, although we have had four men in this position, these being E. G. Cooper in 1924, F. Rickards in 1925, T. W. Green in 1927, and R. D. McMullen in 1928. Next month we have again to defend our title and we feel confident that with such men as the four just mentioned, who are still far from being spent forces, together with other proved men such as Harold King, J. Rathbone, B. J. Knifton and S. A. Manning, plus the “young school,” which includes such promising men as J. C. Bidgood, F. H. Elson, E. Saunders, J. E. Field and P. Khlopin, we can hold our own against all-comers. H. L. V. Ross H. L. V. Ross won the first race in 1908 at Ruislip and five more times, last in 1920; third in 1922 Ross Ross B. C. Brown B. C. items.label: April 1930
items.sum: Recollection of Belgrave's 1925 R.W.A. National walking championship win by 1 point at Derby, where this year's race is to be held, with a look at the team's prospects.
items.s: SOME DERBY BRIGHT(S) HOPES. Recollection of Belgrave's 1925 R.W.A. National walking championship win by 1 point at Derby, where this year's race is to be held, with a look at the team's prospects. Now that it has been decided to hold this year’s National Championship at Derby, it may not be out of place to remind the old members, and at the same time for the encouragement of the younger members, recapitulate the glorious victory achieved by the Club in 1925 at Derby. Two of our members who took part in the race are lost to us, viz., W. Griffin and the then President, Bob Ricketts; the former by his vocal encouragement, and Bob by his wonderful walking over the last mile. Derby is a great place to hold a race of this description. It has fine wide roads and the course, which is a ten miles one, is splendidly situated amidst some fine scenery. Another great factor towards the success of the race is that the best-known man in Derby is at the head of the arrangements. Put Jack Britton in charge and you can rest assured that the best of things will be forthcoming. Will our members ever forget the Ford car that Jack kindly lent us to follow the race? If ever a car did yeoman service that one did, and it had a lot to do with the Club retaining the title of Walking Champions. At one part of the race I counted ten occupants, and also viewed the exit of Bill Griffin over the back of the car in his excitement of urging on some of our men. The team that won in 1925 was: Rickards (2), Cooper (3), Wall (11), Hare (12). These figures are arrived at after eliminating the individual walkers. Actually Rickards finished fourth in the race. The team did not actually come into position until after fourteen miles had been covered, and McMullen was then well placed but developing foot trouble, he fell back considerably. Still we were well-placed, but the Surrey W.C. had also come along and were challenging us for first place. As the race progressed, so did the excitement grow. Every man was looked after and given vocal assistance—some of them something a little stronger. The finish in the Market Place was a great sight, thousands of people watching the walkers finish. A bandstand had been erected in the centre and the Town Band obliged with a programme of popular music to liven up the competitors. F. Poynton of the Derby W.C. was the first man home and, of course, that delighted the residents, followed by Goodwin of the S.W.C. First blood to the S.W.C. Our four men were soon in and on a count up of our points and taking into consideration the possibilities of the S.W.C. position, it was made out that a probable result would be a dead heat. A hasty consultation, and it was decided to send the car down the road and find our fifth man. That car did some fast work! The man we wanted turned out to be our Bob. He was strolling along admiring the scenery, and with a mysterious bottle under his arm. The position was hastily explained to him, and that he had to pass a Surrey man before reaching the winning post. A speedy wash and brush up with a generous drink out of the aforesaid bottle, he started off to do or die. Helped along by members (in the car), the Surrey man was viewed in the distance, and Bob, despite the placing of him in the "B" team, going all out, passed his man, and we won by 1 point. It was a near thing. Bob did many good performances for his Club, but of all of them, I think this one must take precedence over all the rest. I am reminded of several other items of interest in this race. As I have mentioned, they do things in great style in Derby. We had two armoured cars to clear the road for the start, and they acted as pilots over the course. We also had 150 Boy Scouts on duty acting as guides and directing the walkers, and also as food attendants. That is another thing they do well, the feeding arrangements are of the best. I remember Speechley praising the refreshments, and when he is satisfied, nothing more need be said. I did hear that he wanted to do another lap to get some more of the Derby good cheer. I would like to write a few words on our prospects; I lay no claim to forecasting the result, as I can never get anywhere near correct forecast results. We shall have Rickards, Cooper and McMullen still on the active list, and they look good for another hard 20 miles. They are backed up by Green, H. F. King, Knifton, and Rathbone. Green has a good chance for individual, as well as Team honours, and I hope Knifton will soon settle down to serious training. These names look on paper good enough to win for us our fifth victory. There still remains the arduous task of strict training for this event, and no unfit man can possibly score in this race, as the competition grows keener every year, and it is the knowledge that every man is in the best of condition that encourages team work. items.sum: Social notes on the season's last dance at Wandsworth Town Hall, thanks to the ticket sellers, and a call to book for the club Dinner.
items.s: THE LIGHTER SIDE OF THE CLUB. Social notes on the season's last dance at Wandsworth Town Hall, thanks to the ticket sellers, and a call to book for the club Dinner. Our last dance of the season, held at Wandsworth Town Hall, on February 28th, came up to expectations and was a decided success, proving that this hall is by far the most popular of our venues for dances. Efforts will be made to ensure that the whole series of dances next season are held there. Before leaving this subject, I should like to mention in particular the efforts made by a few members who regularly dispose of a large number of tickets, thus lightening considerably the work entailed in these affairs. They are Messrs. Chantler, Cook, McKay, McLean, Poulter, Powell, Redgrave, Rollins and J. S. Williams. I thank them. Now a little more about the Dinner. The venue, date and price of tickets are displayed on another page. Arrangements are being made for a first-rate concert afterwards and a band is also contemplated. It is difficult to understand the feeling of awe with which a number of members regard the Dinner. Why it should be associated with the Club's liveliest function of the year I really don't know. So now book the date and make it a real Belgrave dinner. We want to see the same faces present that the Handicappers dream about; and the lesser lights, to hear what the Club has done during the Winter, and what it intends doing during the Summer. Your presence will assure you of a rattling good time. W. A. RICE. W. A. Rice W. A. RICE. W. A. items.label: April 1930
items.sum: Letter from W. H. Hare replying to the suggestion that a club history be serialised in the "Gazette", doubting a serial would work.
items.s: CORRESPONDENCE. Letter from W. H. Hare replying to the suggestion that a club history be serialised in the "Gazette", doubting a serial would work. 2 Sutherland Place, S.W.1. Dear Mr. Editor, Ken O'Kell's letters are always welcome reading. If one feels a little dis-spirited they act as a tonic and if everything is O.K. then we feel tempted to give ourselves several more pats on the back and proudly think what a good Club is Belgrave. Not that we have any doubts on the matter, of course! My object in writing is in reference to his suggestion that Club history should be compiled in serial form in the "Gazette." Although I have myself broached the subject of a history, I am glad that I am not included in those to whom he has appealed. As a matter of fact, I have endeavoured for some years to gather together some tangible records, but there are sad gaps of many years' duration, and nothing very definite. The undertaking is vastly more extensive than first thought, and I am afraid that any serial effort would be terribly disjointed; the more so as a month must elapse between each contribution. However, that is not for me to decide. I have at times endeavoured to bring in some historical matter in the few reports of races that I have submitted. That of the last 7 miles Cross-country Championship in the January issue will convey my meaning. Even so, one cannot be quite sure of one's detail, as witness the correction in the placings in the 1921 race, which information was forwarded to the Editor. However, it served a purpose, for otherwise those concerned would not have troubled to produce the facts. I trust that I have not trespassed on your valuable space, and would say in conclusion that the "Gazette" is now our history book and that possibly, after all, our greater concern is to make history and not its recording. Yours sincerely, W. H. HARE. W. H. Hare W. H. HARE. address in the issue W. H. HARE Ken O'Kell Ken O'Kell his letters in the Gazette; suggested a serial Club history

items.s: THE FIVE MILES ROAD RACE. Report of the Club 5 mile road race and handicap at Wimbledon, won by S. H. Warboys, with H. J. Fletcher winning the handicap. Brilliant weather attended the holding of the Club 5 mile Road Race at Wimbledon on the 22nd. A field, extremely good for this time of the season, of 33 faced the starter, our worthy President, E. Gordon. They went off at a good pace with Warboys showing in front, and at the end of the 2 laps of the Common he was still leading with Footer on his heels followed by Penny, Allum, Rice and J. E. Flower in a bunch. Then came, a few yards behind, T. J. Flower, Duffett and W. G. Webb. These nine had drawn well away from the rest of the field and, as some people thought, our team for the Brighton Relay looked like picking itself, bringing in of course W. S. Mitchell ,who was unable to compete owing to foot trouble. The leading positions were maintained till the finish, Warboys beating Footer by about 15 yards in the splendid time of 29 min. 46 sec. When one remembers last year's time, namely, 31 min. 27 sec., and then realizes that the first eight this year were inside that, it will be granted that we are justified in our high hopes for he race on April 12th. The handicap held in ocnjunction with the run resulted in a win for H. J. Fletcher, whose first race this was as he had previously been a member of our walking section. In finishing tenth in the actual race he displayed fine form and must be considered a "find." J. items.sum: Report of Belgrave's team win in the Bishop of Birmingham's Cup walk, with the results, plus the Surrey and Middlesex county walking championships held the same day.
items.s: THE BISHOP OF BIRMINGHAM'S CUP RACE. Report of Belgrave's team win in the Bishop of Birmingham's Cup walk, with the results, plus the Surrey and Middlesex county walking championships held the same day. In 1921 a Belgrave team of walkers visited Birmingham and returned with the trophy. This year we entered a team for the second time and again had the satisfaction of bringing the Cup back to London. On this occasion our six entrants finished in the first ten places and our team of four scored 17 pts to the 34 of Derby W.C. and 39 of Birmingham W.C. Harold King (3rd) was our first man to finish, followed by F. Rickards (4th), T. W. Green (6th), Joe King (not yet qualified as a team man, 7th), J. Rathbone (9th) and J. C. Bidgood (10th). The last-named was placed third in the sealed handicap, which was won by F. Rickards. This win encourages us to think that we shall retain the National title and in addition win the shield for the first team to finish its eight men. RESULT. TEAM PLACINGS. On the same day the County Walking Championships took place. The Surrey race was held from the Surrey W.C. quarters and the Club champion, Len Fletcher, won the individual title in the very good time of 78 min. 16 sec. McMullen was sixth, but the backward positions of the next two men prevented the team from gaining a better position than third. The team result is appended:— F. H. Elson (4th) and E. Saunders (10th) were members of the Metropolitan W.C. team that was placed second in the Middlesex championship, and C. H. Speechley was included in the Polytechnic H. team, placed third. items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. The Hon. Running Secretary's notes on coming running fixtures: the Brighton Relay, the match with the London Athletic Club replacing the Open Meeting, handicaps, the Inter-Club Relays and the Kinnaird Trophy. Will all readers concerned kindly note my change of address, as under, and oblige? April 12th, Brighton Relay Day, and one which we hope will cover Belgrave with glory. We have the best team ever at our command and should be up with the leaders all the way this year. On the 19th I would like to see as many of the track members as possible out training at Battersea Park in preparation for our match with the London Athletic Club on the following Saturday. The long jumpers and javelin men should also be getting into trim for this meeting. Our annual Open Meeting, always fixed for the last Saturday in April, has now been discontinued and in its place this year we have arranged a series of match events versus the London Athletic Club. A notice giving the list of events is on the back page of this issue ,and with regard to these race I should like to mention that with the exception of the team race, the scoring will be on the basis of 4, 3, 2, 1 points for the first four places in each event. Three men will compete for their respective clubs and the team race will be the usual 4 to run, 3 to score. Make a note of the date, the 26th, and turn up and witness a fine sporting match. For the benefit of Club members we are holding several Handicaps (see notice) and I trust these will be well supported as I am sure our new Handicapper will be delighted with plenty of work even if they don't mean fourpences to him. Entries close first post on the 21st. I should like to add that I hope our members will avoid that last-minute entry habit and send them along in good time. After all, it only means a penny post-card, and you save several people extra work by obliging in this manner. The next Club meeting will be on May 14th and includes the usual Inter-Club Relays with Croydon H., Epsom, and Mitcham A.C. There will also be Handicaps at 220yds., 880yds., and the Javelin. In view of the fact that the Committee have now placed a 220 yds. Championship on our record book, I shall expect an increased interest to be taken in races over this distance. Don't forget "Kinnaird Trophy" day, May 31st, at Stamford Bridge. We are in need of Field Event men, Shot Putt, Long Jump, Hurdles, High Jump, for this meeting and I shall be glad to hear from anyone who wishes to compete. Also at this meeting is the Junior (under 19) Relay race. We have proved the victors for the past two years and it is up to our Juniors to see that we make a treble of it this time. All those who are eligible to compete, that is, under 19 years of age on day of race, should get in touch with me with a view to selecting teams. The distances are the usual, 880, 220, 220, 440 yds. All enquiries to E. A. DUFFETT, Hon. Running Sec., 1 Raymead Avenue, Thornton Heath, Surrey. E. A. Duffett E. A. DUFFETT Hon. items.label: May 1930
items.sum: Editorial notes: death of Vice-President Mr. Benison, marriages of J. Cooper Clark and Alec Robertshaw, the Brighton Relay team's fourth place, Tommy Green's walking wins, new members elected in April and May, and a request for outstanding subscriptions.
items.s: Editorial notes: death of Vice-President Mr. Benison, marriages of J. Cooper Clark and Alec Robertshaw, the Brighton Relay team's fourth place, Tommy Green's walking wins, new members elected in April and May, and a request for outstanding subscriptions. We regret to have to announce the death of Mr. Benison, one of the Club's Vice-Presidents, and a regular supporter at Wimbledon and Battersea Park. Mr. Benison was born 47 years ago at Plymouth, and was the son of a soldier. Always a keen follower of all branches of sport, a knowledge of his physical limitations compelled him to refrain from active participation in strenuous exercises. Bowls, of which he was no mean player, claimed much of his spare time throughout the entire season. As an accomplished baritone he rendered valuable service at many social functions, among which were Belgrave ones, where his efforts were much appreciated. He was always ready to help the Club, and only a few months ago provided the first prize for the novice walk promoted by the Club. By his death we lose a very good friend. He leaves a widow and one son, who is a Club member, and to them we extend our deepest sympathy. * * * * * Congratulations to J. Cooper Clark, our former quarter-mile champion, and Alec Robertshaw, a member of our winning South of the Thames team, upon their recent marriages. Cooper Clark has left England to seek fame and fortune in Canada, and he takes with him our best wishes for his success. * * * * * Our very best congratulations are due to the Brighton Relay team upon their forward running. Of many fine performances, Arthur Allum's stands out as a superlative one, for he not only gained three places for us, but also recorded fastest time over his stage—a feat of which he can well be proud. The finish found the Northern, Midland (and National) and Southern champions in front of us, but it is when we study the clubs finishing behind us that the merit of our position becomes more apparent. This race is yet another manifestation of the Club's continued improvement, for in 1927 we were 17th; 1928, 12th; 1929, 7th; and this year, fourth. A continuance of progress at this rate will render all things possible—will place all championships within our reach—and see the Northern and Midland clubs playing second fiddle to the South, represented by Belgrave. * * * * * Our usual monthly congratulations are due to Tommy Green upon his wins in the North London Walk and Sunderland—Darlington Walk, in which he set up a new record. * * * * * At the April Meeting of the Committee the following were elected to membership : H. J. Bignall (the International, and first-claim Highgate Harriers' runner), H. G. Francis, S. E. Hodgson, H. E. Jackman, J. F. Owen, G. H. Pamment, H. E. Randall, M. Smith, C. J. Wadham, R. A. Coles, D. C. Fretwell, W. Fox. At the May meeting the following names were passed : A. J. F. Valentine, C. H. Brodie, A. W. Birnie, R. E. L. Richardson, H. K. Harris, A. Kench, E. E. J. Trundell, R. Macpherson, D. C. L. Gratte. We wish all these new members many successes in the Club colours and we extend to them all a very hearty welcome. * * * * * The Hon. Treasurer and Hon. Editor would be pleased to receive all outstanding amounts at the earliest possible moment. It is only possible to carry on in a manner worthy of the Club if they are given the co-operation of every member and it is hoped that you will not fail to do your part. items.label: May 1930
items.sum: Report of the London to Brighton road relay, in which Belgrave finished fourth, 5 minutes 50 seconds behind winners Birchfield, with a stage-by-stage table, the order of finish, and extracts from the South London Harriers' Gazette and a letter from organiser Joe Binks.
items.s: THE BRIGHTON RELAY. Report of the London to Brighton road relay, in which Belgrave finished fourth, 5 minutes 50 seconds behind winners Birchfield, with a stage-by-stage table, the order of finish, and extracts from the South London Harriers' Gazette and a letter from organiser Joe Binks. The Brighton Relay seems to attract more attention from the general public than any other race, which may be due to the fact that it is run over the London—Brighton Road, which in the past has been the scene of so many sporting events, or it may be that the team spirit which dominates this type of race more than any other rouses their interest. Whatever the public think about it, we of the Belgrave are mostly concerned with showing what we can do against the pick of the country, for the entry includes Birchfield Harriers, the National Champions; Hallamshire H. and Tipton H., who were second and third in the same race; South London H, the Southern Champions; and practically every other team of note. In spite of a doubtful weather outlook, a large number of supporters accompanied our runners on the 'bus which had been chartered by the Club, and although two of the selected team, W. Mitchell and W. G. Webb, were unable to turn out owing to injuries, the reserves so ably filled the breach that we had the satisfaction of seeing the Club eclipse all their previous performances. Jack Flower ran the first stage for us and when he handed over he was lying fifth, but only 22 secs. behind S.L.H., who were leading. Our next man, T. J. Flower, was unable to reproduce his last year's form, when he returned second fastest time, for this year eight others recorded better times, while the Club's position dropped to 8th, but only little more than a minute and a quarter separated us from Hallamshire, who were now in the lead, closely followed by Birchfield. Ernie Duffett now took over and succeeded in pegging back the Poly. Harrier, thus bringing the Club into 7th place. On arrival at Purley our runners had covered 14 miles 1,208 yards in 1 hr. 21 mins. 8 secs., which was 1 min. 24 secs. slower than our team recorded in 1929. The following stage was covered by Arthur Allum, who showed us some exceptionally fine running, for he returned fastest time over his stretch and took us up into fourth place. Hallamshire and Birchfield were disputing the lead at this point, while Highgate Harriers were 3rd; less than half a minute in front of us. Our next man, Syd Warboys, was a new-comer to the team, but remembering his performances over the country during the winter, we were confident that he would hold his own, and when he handed over at Horley (which is approximately half-way to Brighton) he had passed Bignall, the Highgate runner, and Hallamshire were only 42 seconds ahead, while he was only five seconds slower over this stage than J. E. Webster, the Birchfielder, who had returned fastest time. Bill Rice now carried on the good work and he managed to hang on to third position, although S.L.H. were gradually coming up, having beaten Highgate for fourth place. Birchfield, who retained the lead for the remainder of the race, were less than two and half minutes ahead of us, whereas in 1929 nearly four minutes divided us and the leading club, and on all occasions the difference had been over ten minutes. For the relay between Crawley and Handcross, A. E. Smith was put on, and though he had been selected to run at the eleventh hour, and had not done much training during the preceding weeks, he ran a very plucky race and the only one to pass him was the S.L.H. representative, but Aldershot Command and Highgate were on his heels by the time he had completed his stage. Hopes ran high, for we still had some good men to come, and over the next stretch A. Penny, by running only 15 seconds slower than the fastest man, took us to within 31 seconds of South London H., and over a minute away from the fifth team, which position was now held by the Polytechnic H. The ninth stage, finishing at the top of Dale Hill, is considered by many to be the hardest one of all, so we put on one of our toughest runners, to wit, one Bert Footer, who had run this part of the journey for us on three previous occasions. Much to his disgust he saw the South London Harrier running away from him, and even when it was later disclosed that the aforesaid athlete had beaten the record for the leg by 43 seconds, Bert was still displeased with himself, and yet he had run 16 seconds better than he had ever done before over this portion of the road! Frank Webb now took over to run the last 6½ miles, but from our point of view the race was now over, for although no team was more than 3½ minutes ahead, yet South London Harriers, who were third, had one and a half minutes start off us, so we could not expect Webb to catch up those in front, especially as they were running such men as J. Beman, Birchfield; E. Harper, Hallamshire; and A. C. Stansbury, S.L.H.; while the nearest team in our rear was the "Poly," and they were nearly 2½ minutes behind. In this order we finished, and we have much to congratulate our team on, for in making comparisons of times we have to take into account that the weather was very unfavourable, for heavy rain fell most of the time and a very cold biting wind swept across the runners' course for the greater part of the journey. Despite this disadvantage the team succeeded in knocking off 2 minutes 31 seconds from their previous best, recorded in 1928, and were only 5 minutes 50 seconds behind the winners, whereas before we had never been within 7 mins. 15 secs. of them. Of our return to London quite an amusing account could be written, but it is sufficient to say here that the self-appointed "Captain of the Bus," "Doug" Sloper, kept us in a merry mood all the way home, but in spite of his vigilance we nearly left our old friend, Charlie Cook, stranded on the road, after the bus had stopped at Handcross, to enable us to refresh ourselves. The runners in their order of stages, with actual times and each man's placing, found by comparing times with all the other runners over each stage, are given below. With regard to Club records, the first two stages were altered this year, so no fair comparison can be made with previous years. C.R.—Club Record. (deadheat) ORDER OF FINISH. * * * * * Here follows an extract from the current issue of "The South London Harriers' Gazette," from which we may derive a mead of satisfaction :— "We did not win the Brighton Relay, but we did well enough to justify our optimism with regard to the future. Indeed, this year's race gives us to think that in the near future, instead of clubs competing for third place to Birchfield and Hallamshire, Birchfield and Hallamshire will compete for third place to S.L.H. and Belgrave." * * * * * An extract from a letter received from Joe Binks, of the "News of the World," and the organiser of the London—Brighton Relay, follows. We hope to justify his optimism next year :— ......I would like to offer the boys my most sincere congratulations upon their great race on Saturday last in the London—Brighton Relay. It is certainly the Club's greatest running effort and I am hoping to see next year the great improvement maintained sufficiently to see you win the race. At full strength and with some more improvement you will do it yet. The South are gradually getting nearer the two leaders and it will be a great thing when one gets its head in front. items.label: May 1930
items.sum: Report by J. B. Belchamber of the Club's 20 Miles walking championship for the "R. W. Ricketts" Shield at Wimbledon on April 19th, won by T. W. Green, with the result and a list of earlier Shield results from 1923 to 1929.
items.s: THE TWENTY MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP. Report by J. B. Belchamber of the Club's 20 Miles walking championship for the "R. W. Ricketts" Shield at Wimbledon on April 19th, won by T. W. Green, with the result and a list of earlier Shield results from 1923 to 1929. Blackthorn Winter came to Wimbledon in its playfullest and spitefullest mood on April 19th to have its sport at the expense of the 14 sturdy fellows who faced the starter in the race for 20 Miles Club Championship and the "R. W. Ricketts" Shield. Dull at the start, with a cold wind blowing, they were treated first to a short, cold shower, then to bright sunshine for an hour and a half, and finally to a violent and trying hailstorm. The number of starters was satisfactory for a race of this description, the only notable absentees being Jack Rathbone (on duty!), E. G. Cooper and S. A. Manning. Right from the start, H. F. King, Fred Rickards and T. W. Green set a warm pace and opened a gap between themselves and a group which was comprised of R. D. McMullen, Paul Khlopin, J. E. Field, J. G. Scamell, J. F. King and J. C. Bidgood. Saunders and Knifton both started very steadily. At 5 miles the order was almost the same, Bidgood alone having fallen back through too fast a start, but the gap set up by the three leaders was larger. At 10 miles the three, walking abreast, were still in the lead; but McMullen, closely followed by Khlopin, had drawn a little nearer to them. However, they had done so only by making an effort that was obviously too costly at this stage of the race. The first of the leading trio to show signs of flagging was Harold King, but this was not until 11¾ miles had been covered. The times here were : F. Rickards; 99m. 58s.; T. W. Green, 99m. 59s.; H. F. King, 100m. 5s. Next came R. D. McMullen, who was now clear of Khlopin, and these were followed at fair intervals by J. E. Field, J. G. Scamell, and E. Saunders. Knifton was some way behind, but was now travelling very well. When they came round again the stiff climb from Raynes Park had been negotiated for the second and last time, and on this Green had tested Rickards but had found him to be in fine fettle, finer, perhaps, then he has ever shown, excepting when he made a record over our old course in the 1926 Championship. At the top of the hill (14½ miles), nevertheless, Tommy led by 7 seconds, Harold King being now 1 minute behind. Shortly afterwards the hailstorm came on. Moreover, it turned bitterly cold towards the end of the race and this played havoc with the walkers. Tommy Green alone was unaffected by it. He just hurried home to get out of it, and arrived full of walking, 3 mins. 10 secs. ahead of Fred Rickards, who had been almost with him 2½ miles from the end. RESULT. The new course chosen this year was 21 miles in length, and this was certainly unfortunate for Paul Khlopin and Fred Rickards, as both were only just beaten by Tommy Green in the handicap. Of those who did not complete the journey, Harold King walked splendidly for 15 miles, J. E. Field for 14 miles, and E. Saunders for about 15 miles. J. C. Bidgood fell out at 15 miles, but he started too quickly; while A. H. Field seriously threatened to win the handicap for about 18½ miles. Joe King was up from Brighton for the race and started well, but was obliged to retire at 12 miles through cramp, which attacked him after the 7th mile. That so large a percentage failed to finish is scarcely satisfactory, but it must be borne in mind that an individual fight such as the Club Championship is looked upon by our faithful team men as a day out. Especially is this so in the case of Harold King. He simply loves a fight. The Belgrave Championship is so well worth the winning that no self-punishment he can inflict is too severe if only it may have the effect of breaking up the opposition. This he does not underrate. If Tommy Green and Fred Rickards are allowed to settle down, he knows how well they will race all through, and he is just a joyous battler out to break or be broken. Thus our Championships wax as hot and hectic as did the Battle of Chevy Chase sung of by the old balladist, and the slaughter is even on the same scale. On May 10th, however, our men will fight together as a team against all comers; and we have confidence, founded gratefully upon the knowledge of trust-worthy service rendered in former championships, the every man carrying the Belgrave colours will fight warily and well, and will finish the course. Everyone in the Club has his heart set upon winning not only the National Championship, but also the "Nijmegen Shield," and as this latter goes to the team whose 8th man finishes first, there will be no thoughts of falling out. Neither must there be the slightest risk of disqualification in the Belgrave ranks. As reports of all the earlier contests for the "Ricketts" Shield have not appeared in the "Belgravian," their results are given below for the sake of our many members who have latterly evinced so keen an interest in the Club's history. The course used from 1923 to 1928 is no longer available. E. G. Cooper finished first in 1923, but was not then a first-claim member. The place medals won by R. W. Ricketts in 1923 and 1926 were passed on to the next man to finish, Bob being the donor of the Shield. Before closing we would like to heartily thank Mr. W. F. May, of the London Vidarians and Road Walking Association, who has judged this race for many years, and also Capt. W. H. Ellison and Mr. Benjamin, for the use of their cars. This year, too, we were happy in welcoming our past President, Dick Murphy, as a judge. J. B. BELCHAMBER. Pos'n Name Start Actual Time H'cap Time Pos'n in H'cap 1. T. W. items.s: THE METROPOLITAN W.C. OPEN WALK. Report and results of the Metropolitan W.C. open walk, won by C. W. Hyde of Enfield, with a weakened Belgrave team second in both the scratch and handicap team races. We were poorly represented in this race, for several of those whose efforts had earned the Club many successes during the past few months were preparing for a much more important event—the National Championship. In the circumstances our friends and rivals, Enfield A.C., made a clean sweep of all the first prizes and so gained a little consolation for the "Junior" defeat. Harley. The three last-named gained their first team awards, thus showing that next season our handicap teams should again be scoring. RESULTS. TEAM RESULTS. 1. C. W. Hyde, Enfield A.C. 57 39 5. F. e: Belgrave H. v. Old Emmanuel A.C.
items.s: BELGRAVE H. v. OLD EMMANUEL A.C. Report and results of Belgrave's first summer match, against Old Emmanuel A.C. at the Emmanuel School Ground, Wandsworth Common, won by Belgrave 25 points to 17. On April 24th we contested our first match of the Summer Season, v. Old Emmanuel A.C. on the Emmanuel School Ground at Wandsworth Common. W. G. Gould, one of our members and an old Emmanuel scholar, was instrumental in arranging this very pleasant fixture, and W. F. Roberts, who was placed in our quarter-mile championship two or three seasons back, was also a member of the home team. The first event, the mile, in which we were represented by E. A. Duffett, A. Penny, and F. G. Ford, was won by an Emmanuel runner of great promise, A. Kench, in 4 mins. 46 secs. Kench has since joined us, and we have every hope that he will develop into a first-class runner. The next event, the long jump, was won by B. W. Fleming, with a leap of 19ft. 10ins., 1½ inches better than F. W. Norris, the Emmanuel jumper. The taking-off board had not been white-washed and could not be seen clearly from the run-up. For this reason J. W. Clemens was "no jumped" three times and so prevented us from placing first and second. The two sprints both ended in wins for our man, T. J. Purdy, whilst J. R. McKay showed a return to form by being placed in both events. The 440 yards race ended in W. F. Roberts beating Harold Titherley and giving a glimpse of the form which gained him Surrey County colours a season or two ago. The high jump gave E. A. Saward a win without displacing the bar, and J. E. Tosh led all the way in the half-mile to win in 2min. 7 1-5secs. On a 3, 2, 1 points basis we won this match by 25 points to 17. The match was a very sporting event, and it is to be hoped that it will find a permanent place in our Summer fixture list. RESULTS. 100 Yards—1, T. J. Purdy, B.H.; 2, F. W. Norris, O.E.; 3, J. R. items.sum: Report and results of the match against London A.C. at Battersea Park Track, won by the L.A.C. 41 points to 29, with the Club handicaps.
items.s: BELGRAVE H. v. LONDON A.C. Report and results of the match against London A.C. at Battersea Park Track, won by the L.A.C. 41 points to 29, with the Club handicaps. This thoroughly sporting fixture which took place on April 26th at Battersea Park Track was witnessed by a large gathering of spectators. Our visitors, as last year, again brought a strong team along containing several University athletes, and Tommy Hampson, the International runner, and a member of our Club. Victory went to the L.A.C. by 41 points to our 29, scoring on a 4, 3, 2, 1 basis. Their superiority lay in the sprints and field events, whereas our successes were gained in the distance events. The fixture proved a very enjoyable one, and with the Club handicaps, formed an excellent programme, and one which for sportsmanship and keen racing it would be hard to beat. The 100 yards, which started the programme, and later, the 440 yards, provided our visitors with runaway victories, for in both cases they had the first three men home. In extenuation, we must point out that neither Odell nor Dunckley, the Club Champions at these distances, were available to run. The half-mile proved to be a very close race. Jim Tosh seemed determined to win and after the first few yards until within five yards of the tape he was leading. Here Tom Hampson came up with a burst of speed and won by a yard with Tom Scrimshaw slowing down, third. Time : 2 min. 0 3-5 secs. Considering that Hampson was a member of the England team v. Germany last year, and toured America with the Universities team and is, moreover, five or six years the senior of our runners, our repre-sentatives must be congratulated upon their good showing. The mile was another close race, Jack Flower beating Bill Rice by a yard, with Sargant, L.A.C., another yard in the rear. Well run, Belgrave! The two-miles saw Bert Cook, after being behind for the greater part of the race, take the lead in the last 200 yards and gallop away with Arthur Allum in close attendance. The Cambridge University runners, Cowburn and Wilson, followed thirty yards behind. The time recorded, 9 min. 50 3-5 secs., showed Cook's run to be a very fine performance. In the long jump our man, Clemens (who also won the Club handicap) jumped 21 ft. 3 ins., but was beaten by an inch by J. Simpson, the Manchester University and L.A.C. athlete. Fleming was also beaten by an inch for third place, and L. G. Snow, L.A.C., took first place in the Javelin, with an exceptionally fine throw, little short of the British Native record. The Club handicaps were keenly contested and showed a vast amount of maturing talent. Purdy was successful in the "100" in a close finish, and another very close finish in the half-mile gave Tom Pritchard a win from A. Chubb and T. C. Jones, two promising junior runners. The mile went to F. G. Ford in easy fashion, with Coleman gaining his usual place prize. H. J. Mann, a newcomer, won the 300 yards from a mark he will never see again, with Jim Tosh a yard away. Jim ran well to get so close from the 12 yards mark, considering his strenuous half-mile earlier in the afternoon. The entry for the Walk was on the small side, but W. Clarke won his race in convincing fashion and in good style. R. F. Elson continues to improve and Len Fletcher must be well satisfied with his 14 mins. 20 secs. from scratch, giving him fifth place so early in the season. RESULTS. Match Events. 100 Yards—L. F. items.label: May 1930
items.sum: Report of the Club's Annual Dinner, with Mrs. Ricketts as guest and speeches reviewing a successful season.
items.s: THE DINNER. Report of the Club's Annual Dinner, with Mrs. Ricketts as guest and speeches reviewing a successful season. The Annual Dinner turned out to be a great success. Over a hundred were present and it was really a Belgrave gathering. In a letter from Mr. W. J. Pepper, he remarked that it was the best supported Club Dinner he had attended and he was surprised at the number of active members present. This, however, is typical of all our Social fixtures, but it is very pleasing to have our visitors notice it. Our guest of the evening was, of course, Mrs. Ricketts, and it was quite evident that she was very pleased to be among us once again, and to see us carrying on the good work. Other visitors included representatives from Mitcham A.C., Croydon H. and Epsom H., Mr. Summerfield, of the Surrey Walking Club, Mr. W. J. Pepper and Mr. Joe Binks. After the toast of the "The King" had been given, our Chairman and President, Mr. E. Gordon, proposed the toast of "The Club." He thanked the officials for the way they had supported him during the past season. Especially he thanked Mr. Fish and Mr. Redgrave. The Club, he said, had had a very successful season, both cross-country and on the road, and the social side had been a bigger success than ever. (Applause). Mr. W. L. Bayliss, who responded, said the season had been one of the most successful they had had. The Club had been second in the South of the Thames Championship, first in the Surrey County Championship, third in the Southern Counties Championship, sixth in the National Championship, and fourth in the Brighton relay. On the road they had retained the National Championship and won the Bishop of Birmingham's cup and the R.W.A. Junior Championship. The Club members were a good and happy crowd. (Applause). Mr. F. G. Thomson, submitting the toast of "The Visitors," said the Club prided itself on the number of friends it made. They welcomed them to their dinner. He coupled with the toast the name of Mr. Summerfield, of the Surrey Walking Club. That evening they offered Mr. Summerfield the velvet glove of friendship, but in a fortnight's time they would show him the mailed fist. Mr. Thomson also referred to the presence of Mr. W. Pepper, Mr. J. Binks and Mrs. Ricketts. In reply, Mr. Summerfield said that in a fortnight's time his club hoped to beat the Belgrave Harriers, but if they did not they would be the first to congratulate the Belgrave men. Mr. Binks said he did not consider himself a visitor, as he had been repeatedly with the Club for 30 years. In the present days the Belgrave Harriers were much in the limelight, but it had not always been so. Now was the time to introduce new blood into the Club, so that they might follow in the footsteps of the good men they had. (Applause). Mr. Pepper, on behalf of Mrs. Ricketts, said she was happy to see the great strides the Belgrave Harriers were making. Contributors to an enjoyable concert were Mr. Lew Castle, Mr. Rex. Lenfesty, Mr. Billy Morton, Miss Kitty Keys, and Miss P. J. Matthews. The singing of "Auld Lang Syne" concluded a very pleasant evening. W. J. Pepper W. J. items.sum: Sports jottings column by "Observer" on neat dress and the Club vest, the Southern Amateur Athletic League fixtures, and three promising young members.
items.s: SPORTS JOTTINGS Sports jottings column by "Observer" on neat dress and the Club vest, the Southern Amateur Athletic League fixtures, and three promising young members. I was greatly interested in a recent advertisement of a Sports meeting at Liverpool. Under the heading of Special Prizes came the following awards: Neatest Dressed Competitor (Men and Youths), £3 3s. Neatest Dressed Competitor (Ladies), £2 2s. One is inclined to ask whether this was a sports meeting or a mannequin parade. A cynic might say that this is only to be expected once women took a prominent part in athletics! Yet perhaps the promoters are to be commended on their attempt to try and get competitors to take a little more care and interest in their running garb. I must say, with all fairness, that while some of them look very neat in their Club colours, others are just the reverse. It behoves everyone to turn out in clean running togs, as by so doing you are bringing credit on yourself and what is more important, your Club. Always wear your Club vest. You should be proud of the "Claret and Gold," and if you are in need of one, I am sure our Treasurer will be pleased to supply you on receipt of a postcard. The dates of the meetings staging the Southern Amateur Athletic League (1st Div.) events have now been arranged as under :— 4 x 220 yds. Relay—Saturday, May 31st, at Poly. Marathon meeting, Stamford Bridge. 3 miles Team race—Whit Monday, June 9th, at "News of the World" meeting, Stamford Bridge. 4 x 440 yds. Relay— do. do. do. do 1 mile Team race—Saturday, June 14th, at Civil Service A.A. meeting, Stamford Bridge. 4 x 880 yds. Relay—Saturday, July 19th, at Printing Trades meeting, Herne Hill Track. Medley Relay (440 x 220 x 220 x 880)—Saturday, July 26th, at Fire Brigade Sports meeting, Stamford Bridge. Our readers will remember that last year we finished third in the League and we naturally hope to improve upon this performance. Points are scored as follows: six for 1st place and so on down to one point for sixth. The six clubs in the First Division are: Polytechnic H., South London H., Herne Hill H., Surrey A.C., Highgate H., and ourselves. Four men aside compete in each event, and in the team races all four will score. My next three Club members are typical examples of the youthful promise with which our Club is so well endowed, and which leads us to believe that we are the coming Club so far as the realm of Southern athletics is concerned. (Why qualify this by the use of the word "Southern"?—Ed.). S. R. Chorley, one of the most promising young men in our running section. Sid has shown great improvement over the country during this last season, his best performance, to my mind, being in the Club "7." Should do well on the track this summer, does not want to be too easily discouraged but to keep on persevering and he will reap his reward in the end. A. E. Miller, a comparative newcomer to the competitive side of the Club, but has shown in this, his first season over the country, that he will be a help to our teams, particularly in the earlier races of next cross-country season. Has also a liking for hurdling and might turn out a useful man at this event if he took it up seriously. R. F. Elson, a younger brother of the Club "Junior" Champion. Met with fair amount of success in Club handicaps on the track last year and should naturally improve on these performances this summer. Is of much the same build as his brother and we hope he will one day go one place better than Frank and so become the R.W.A. Junior Champion. S. R. Chorley S. R. items.sum: Hon. Running Secretary's guide to forthcoming fixtures from May 24th to June 28th, 1930, with training-night notes for new members.
items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. Hon. Running Secretary's guide to forthcoming fixtures from May 24th to June 28th, 1930, with training-night notes for new members. On Saturday, May 24th, at the L.A.C. meeting at Stamford Bridge, will be staged an interesting event, namely, Birchfield Harriers v. The Rest, 10 x 1 mile Relay. I do not know the composition of the Rest team, but certainly think we have a few members worthy of consideration. Wednesday, May 28th, we have a Club Handicap meeting at Battersea Park. There are events for Juniors, Veterans, and others at all distances. Entries (1/- each event) close first post 23rd instant. There is also an Open 100 yds. scratch race for Unattached Novices, and I would esteem it a favour if any members who know of Novices wishing to enter will kindly send their names along to me; there is no entry fee, and Medals will be awarded. Saturday, May 31st, the Poly Marathon meeting at the Bridge. Included in a lengthy programme are the "Kinnaird Trophy" events, to which we have received an invitation, also the 1 Mile Relay for Juniors under 19 years of age. We hope to enter 3 teams in the latter event, and trust that one of them will pull it off and so keep up our sequence of wins in this race. Also at this meeting is the S.A.A.L. 4 x 220 yds. Relay and we hope to make an auspicious start in the League. Monday, June 2nd, we have a Junior (under 19) Inter-Club contest with Fitzroy Lodge A.C., Mitcham A.C. and Mary Ward A.C., at Battersea Park. Saturday, June 7th, sees the Middlesex County Championships at Stamford Bridge. With so many of our members holding this county's qualifications we naturally hope to see the Club name well to the fore. Whit-Monday, June 9th. The British Games at the Bridge. A mammoth programme and one which will provide entertainment for thousands of Londoners. At this meeting will be staged the following S.A.A.L. events. namely, 4 x 440 yds. Relay and the 3 miles Team race, 4 to run and count. I hope the members concerned will bear these events in mind when making their Whitsuntide arrangements. True, it is a day spent in London, but what a meeting! Germans, French, and the pick of English athletes. Wednesday, June 11th, we have the second meeting of the Inter-Club Relay Shield competition. This will be at Epsom, and I trust we shall have a better turn-out than in the past. Saturday, June 14th. First and foremost, the Surrey County Championships at Battersea Park. Here it is on our own door-step and I hope our members will avail themselves of this opportunity. I shall be pleased to supply Entry Forms and particulars of any event. On the same day, rather unfortunately, there will be held in conjunction with the Civil Service meeting at Stamford Bridge, the S.A.A.L. 1 Mile Team race, 4 to run and count. In these circumstances our team will have to be composed of Middlesex members, which will, however, not greatly affect our team strength. Tuesday, June 17th, we have an Inter-Club contest versus the Old Gaytonians and Leigh-on-Sea Harriers on the former's fine ground at Harrow. Incidentally, the Leigh-on-Sea Harriers have invited us to a match on their ground any Saturday in August. I am holding the acceptance in abeyance until I can get sufficient men to make the journey and therefore will be pleased to hear from anyone who wishes to make a trip to Leigh-on-Sea. On Wednesday, June 25th, at Battersea Park, will be held the "Doris Shield" Inter-Club Competition versus our old friends Ashcombe A.C. and Thames Valley Harriers. There will be the usual Handicaps open to members of each Club. Tuesday, June 26th, at the Polytechnic's meeting at Paddington Track will be the S.A.A.L. Inter-Club Putting the Shot contest. Saturday, June 28th, is rather an important day. At Stamford Bridge will be the A.A.A. 1 Mile (4 x 440 yds.) Relay Championship, also the Ravensbourne Club are staging a Grand Inter-Club contest, to which we have received an invitation. We shall have teams at both places and I trust members will give me their co-operation in fielding teams of the required strength. Perhaps it might be as well to mention that with regard to the mid-week evening meetings, these start at 7 p.m. Any new members who come to Battersea Park to train—Tuesdays and Thursdays are the Club nights—and are perhaps at a loss as to whom to train with or what distance, etc., if they will get in touch with me there, I will do my best to assist them. items.sum: Late news that Belgrave lost the National Road Walking Championship title at Derby to Birmingham W.C., with T. W. Green third and F. Rickards fourth.
items.s: LATE NEWS. Late news that Belgrave lost the National Road Walking Championship title at Derby to Birmingham W.C., with T. W. Green third and F. Rickards fourth. Despite the fine walking of T. W. Green and F. Rickards, who finished third and fourth respectively, we were beaten in the National Road Walking Championship at Derby by Birmingham W.C. (49 pts.) and Derby W.C. (53 pts.). Our score was 60 pts. and so we had to relinquish the title to the Birmingham walkers, who are the first provincial winners. In congratulating them we would assure them that they have the Shield on short lease only, and we look forward to resuming possession next May. T. W. Green T. W. Green 3rd, National Road Walking Championship, Derby F. Rickards F. Rickards 4th, National Road Walking Championship, Derby National Road Walking Championship Derby Birmingham W.C. Derby W.C.
