items.h: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES JUNIOR RACE.
items.sum: Report of the South of the Thames Junior Race at Epsom Downs on November 15th, where Belgrave's three teams all closed in and the first team was 4th, with Carter 8th on his debut.
e: South of the Thames Junior Cross-Country
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES JUNIOR RACE. Report of the South of the Thames Junior Race at Epsom Downs on November 15th, where Belgrave's three teams all closed in and the first team was 4th, with Carter 8th on his debut. THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES JUNIOR RACE. The South of the Thames Junior Race (Surrey and Berks.) took place at Epsom Downs on November 15th, the weather behaving itself until after the race, when most of us had to swim back to the Town. Our Club had three teams entered and although one or two of the selected men failed to put in an appearance, we managed to start the three teams and, what is more, all closed in. A large number faced the starter and at his signal all were well away, with Tolley, Epsom, leading and Humphris (S.L.H.) closely following. After waiting some little time they could be seen in the distance and, on reaching me, they had covered about half the way, with Tolley still leading the way. Our first man to arrive at this point was Carter, 9th, and Dewberry, looking very distressed, 11th, but where were our next men? Runners passed by until Fletcher came along, 30th, and Canard, 37th; Chorley and Coleman were still further behind, and as Mitcham and Reading's fourth man had already passed it did not look any too rosy for the Bels. However, over the last mile or so, when it was practically all over, they had improved a little. Carter was now 8th, and Dewberry 9th, which positions they kept till the end; Fletcher moved up to 21st place and Chorley, having now passed Canard to finish 35th to complete the scoring team, so that we finished our four men in 35, but it was not good enough to get placed, as Mitcham, Reading and S.L.H. had done better. So the "Bels" had to be content with 4th place. However, they must not get downhearted, but start now and get that extra bit of stamina which is essential. Of the three teams the "B" and "C" teams ran well, but the "A" team did not run up to expectation. From the start of the race they hung too far back, instead of getting away with the leaders, which they are quite capable of doing, and consequently paid the penalty. A word of congratulation must be said of Carter, a new member, on his fine performance in finishing 8th in the race and being the first Belgrave man home, on his first appearance in a Championship race. With a little more experience he will do even better. Fletcher also did well at his first attempt; Dewberry ran as expected; but Chorley, Morrell, Canard and Coleman all disappointed. However, after the race we forgot all our disappointments and had a most enjoyable tea in Town, after which several members finished up the evening at a dance. Tolley Tolley led early Humphris Humphris Carter Carter 8th, first Belgrave man home, new member, first Championship race Dewberry Dewberry 9th Fletcher Fletcher 21st, first attempt Canard Canard Chorley Chorley 35th, completed the scoring team Coleman Coleman Morrell Morrell South of the Thames Junior Cross-Country Epsom Downs Epsom S.L.H. items.s: SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8th, AT WIMBLEDON. Report and results of the second Inter-Club race, at Wimbledon on November 8th with Ashcombe A.C. and T.V.H., won by Arthur Penny, with Belgrave winning the team race (184 pts.) and R. Freestone the club handicap. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 8th, AT WIMBLEDON. To-day's event was the second of the Inter-Club races, with Ashcombe A.C. and T.V.H., with the usual sealed handicap in conjunction. As last year, the afternoon was bright and nippy and although a lot of rain had fallen during the week the going did not appear so heavy as it might have been. A good start was made, all getting away well, with Joe Flower and Arthur Allum slightly in the lead. Harry Parker, I noticed, was trying to hold the first turning-point all alone and it was a wonder the poor chap wasn't killed for the mob was just like stampede of elephants (I haven't heard one of these, but I believe elephants can make a noise). So round the corner of the field and out over the golf links, lost to the view of the spectators who had gathered to see the start. Eventually the runners reappeared. Arthur Penny was the first in sight, with a very substantial lead, with Cohen after him, slowly decreasing the lead and, wonder of wonders, Penny even had energy enough to run wide at the last turn (or perhaps he couldn't see) but anyway, Cohen did the same. Arthur won by eleven seconds from Cohen and then came A. Allum, W. G. Webb and H. S. Cook (all Belgrave) followed by two Thames Valley runners. We gained our usual easy win in the team race, placing our fourteen men in the first 25 positions. Our handicap, in conjunction, was won by Reg. Freestone, with the youthful L. J. Coleman second, and Vice-Captain Dick Savage third. J.E.T. RESULTS. Posn. Name Actual Time Start H'cap Time Pos'n in H'cap 1. A. W. Penny B.H. 28 43 scr. 28 43 14† 2. L. J. items.s: THE MATCH v. ST. GEORGE'S SERVICES S.C Report and result of the 5-mile race at Mitcham on December 6th against St. George's Services, won individually by C. T. Carter but lost by Belgrave 37 points to 41. THE MATCH v. ST. GEORGE'S SERVICES S.C At Mitcham, on December 6th, we were the guests of St. George's Services in their 5 mile Championship and inter-club race. St. George's mustered eight, while we turned out ten and of these Carter and Frank Webb were expected to do well. The day was dull and inclined to be foggy and very wet under foot. The start was in a rough field near the old house of Bishopford and then down various muddy lanes across the fields towards Sutton. In the rush for the lead, Webb just led Carter and Butler, of St. George's, from the field. Butler gained the advantage at the mile and maintained it, until, at four miles, Webb again went in the lead but had the misfortune to tap his ankle on a large stone, which left Butler and Carter to fight it out. Carter made a dash at five hundred yards to go and beat Butler by a dozen yards or so, with Webb a score of yards in his rear. Then came two St. George's boys, Young and Tame; after these Dewberry, followed by another St. George's fellow, Warren. Eighth place saw Tom Cotton finding some form, while Fletcher, eleventh, and Rollins, twelfth, completed the Belgrave team. Still, we had to admit defeat, as after totalling up we found St. George's scored 37 to the Bels' 41 points, counting six a side. RESULT. 1. C. T. Carter B.H. 30 53 2. W. F. Butler S.G. 30 55 3. F. items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. The Hon. Running Secretary's notice of fixture additions and coming events, including the club 7 miles championship, the Boxing Day meeting, social runs and the Surrey senior championship. FORTHCOMING EVENTS. Important ! Will members kindly note the following additions to our fixture list, as under :— January 24th. 5 miles Surrey County Juniors (18 to 21) Cross Country Championship at Imber Court. This is an innovation on the part of the County Committee, who are evidently out to encourage the Junior talent in Clubs. Will any member who is eligible and would like to compete kindly get in touch with me, with a view to team selection. March 14th. 5 miles race v. Old Emanuel A.C., at Wimbledon. Those who remember the enjoyable match on the track last summer will not doubt welcome this opportunity of meeting them again over the country. Prominent among their runners is A. Kench, who is also a member of our own Club. March 21st. We have a fixture, at Wimbledon, with a very old and famous club, namely, the Godiva Harriers, of Coventry. We are unfortunately unable to make a trip to their headquarters at Coventry this season but perhaps will be able to arrange this for next year. Their boys are coming a long way to run against us, so I hope we shall have a bumper turn-out to welcome them. Will members interested please make a note of the above dates on their fixture cards for future reference. We come now to current fixtures, first among which is the Club 7 miles C.C. Championship for the "Blackstaffe" Shield (Holder, H. E. Footer) which will be held on December 20th. Bert. will not, I am afraid, be fit enough to defend his title this year, so we should see a fine race for honour of being the new holder. A Sealed Handicap will be run in conjunction with the race, as usual. The 26th, our Boxing Day meeting at Battersea Park, commences at 11 a.m. Handicaps at 120 yards and 2 miles will be available for our running members, and please enter at once (1/- each event) to me at the undermentioned address. Our headquarters will be open as usual on the 27th for anyone who wishes to go out for a training spin. January 3rd, we have a Social run with Epsom H., Croydon H. and Mitcham A.C., from the Grandstand, Epsom. This is a fine run over the Downs and all members are invited to turn out. January 10th is the day of the Surrey County's Senior C.C. Championship, this time at a new venue, namely, Imber Court, from the headquarters of the Metropolitan Police A.A. The course will be one of 7 miles and our team will have some serious opposition from the S.L.H. for possession of the "Pickett" Cup, which we now hold. Our champion and last year's individual winner, Bert Footer, is a very doubtful starter, so it behoves all our team men to buck into it and show the S.L.H. that there is, at any rate, one race in which we can give them an annual licking. On the 17th we are visiting Mitcham for a Social run with our friends, Croydon H., Epsom H. and the home club. This run will be followed by a Social evening to which all friends are invited and which is on a par with our own Socials at Wimbledon, which speaks for itself. Don't forget the Boxing Day entries; let me know at once if you intend to run; only those on the programme will be allowed to compete. Don't say you told me during the Summer, etc., I am afraid my memory will not hold good all that time, unless it's a "Bob" you owe me, which is, of course, quite a different matter! All entries and enquiries to E. A. DUFFETT, Hon. Running Sec., 1, Raymead Avenue, Thornton Heath. A. Kench A. Kench runs for Old Emanuel A.C. and is also a Belgrave member H. E. Footer H. E. e: Surrey W.C. v Belgrave Harriers match
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. THE "OPEN" RACES. Walking notes: Belgrave won the scratch team race in all four open walks so far, but were heavily beaten by Surrey Walking Club over the Banstead and back course; also new members, Tommy Green's win in the International Walk at Milan, and a Brighton Road dinner. WITH THE WALKERS. THE "OPEN" RACES. Four open races promoted by the Road Walking Association, Enfield A.C., Highgate H. and ourselves, have been held this season and on each occasion we have been successful in the scratch team race. This is very gratifying, particularly as we have won by a good margin in each race and, in addition, our scoring four have been closely followed home by other Belgrave walkers ready to take their place in the scoring team should any of the leaders fail. We have every hope of continuing in the winning way—and such is the keenness and ability of our walkers that we should have little difficulty in doing so. * * * * * In contradistinction to our "Open" scratch race wins came the severe defeat inflicted upon us by the Surrey Walking Club over the Banstead and back course. This formidable journey measures 11¾ miles but is generally considered the equivalent of any other fifteen miles course. We have never yet emerged from this match as victors, but last year we supplied the first man home in Tommy Green. Although present, he was unable to take part on this occasion, owing to a slight injury sustained when racing in Italy, which demanded rest. Our men held prominent positions at the half-distance, but then the arduous course began to tell and the fact that our men were only "seven-miles-fit" manifested itself. Places were dropped; Thorn was disqualified; Elson when favourably placed had to give up owing to leg weariness, and as the race progressed our position became worse and worse, finally ending as the result shows below. And so once again we congratulate our Surrey Walking Club friends on their win; and the failure of our own walkers over the course makes us all the most appreciative of the "Swastika" walkers' efforts. Well done ! TEAM RESULTS. Surrey W.C.—1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 12 ... ... ... 49 pts. Belgrave H.—8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 ... ... 122 pts. * * * * * A feature of our Open Walk was the fine showing our members made. We actually finished ten men in the first thirty positions before any other club finished their fourth man. F. W. Blackmore, the Surrey W.C. captain, was the fourth man for his club and finished 35th. They were the second club to finish four men, but Herne Hill H., whose fourth man was 46th, take second position when the points scored are determined. * * * * * In last month's issue I commented on the need for more new members; novices who would in time succeed our present cracks, and referred to the almost accidental way in which Frank Elson became one of us. In due course his brother became a member and a very promising walker, and these two have since been responsible for introducing other members. Thus an accidental meeting has had a snowball effect and benefitted the Club considerably. And so once again I would like to stress the point that new members are always welcome and that present members can help the Club by bringing along outsiders interested in the sport. We are doing well at present and must ensure that we continue to uphold Belgrave prestige. Tommy Green did exceptionally well to win the International Walk at Milan over a 100 kilos (62½ miles) course, for he was still suffering from the effects of an exceedingly rough Channel crossing. However, he won by a margin of about ten minutes and there was a gap of twenty minutes between the second and third men. Tommy endeared himself to the Italian public and among his awards are a handsome gold medal and a swinging clock—a fine example of Italian craftsmanship. * * * * * T. W. Green, with H. V. L. Ross, the present and past holders of the London to Brighton Walk Record, were the guests of honour at a dinner given by the newly-formed "Fellowship of the Brighton Road." m. s. 1. J. H. OPEN" Report and results of the Road Walking Association open walk at Greenwich, where Belgrave regained the "Berman" Cup for the scratch team race with Tommy Green third; Herne Hill's printed positions add to 80, not the 70 printed. "THE R.W.A. OPEN" The Open Race promoted by the Road Walking Association always attracts a good entry and about 200 competitors assembled at Greenwich for the first important walk of the season. We were represented by 21 individuals, comprising two teams, and were successful in regaining the "Berman" Cup for the first scratch team. Our first man to finish was Tommy Green, third, and the ovation he received when called upon to accept the Cup on behalf of the Club afforded ample testimony of the popularity enjoyed both by "Tommy" and the Club among the walkers themselves. Our teams were placed fifth (B) and seventh (A) in the team handicap, which gave promise of successes to come—a promise which was amply fulfilled at Enfield a fortnight later, and since, in our own "Open" Race at Wimbledon. items.s: SURREY YOUTHS' RACE. Report and results of the Surrey County Youths' 3 miles cross-country championship on Wimbledon Common, won by Belgrave's S. Garland with the club second in the team race; the text says A. A. G. Thorne finished 11th while the result list prints him 6th. SURREY YOUTHS' RACE. The Surrey County Youths' 3 Miles Cross-Country Championship was held from St. John's Hall on December 6th. The course was laid over Wimbledon Common and consisted of fairly easy going. Seven teams had entered and a field of 40 faced the starter. After a lap of the starting field they were well strung out with S. Garland, of our own club, showing up in a little bunch at the head of affairs. These kept together going out to the Windmill, where they turned for home and then three detached themselves from the rest. A Mitcham, Epsom and Belgrave lad made up this trio and our boy, who was Garland, showed them his heels when it came to the finishing straight. He ran a very well-judged race and reaped the reward of some steady training. A. A. G. Thorne, who was next home for the Club also ran very well indeed, seeing that this was his first appearance this season, he finished 11th, so it is obvious that if he were to train regularly he would go near winning. F. H. C. White, our youthful half-miler, was our third man, while L. C. Clapham completed our scoring team, who were placed second in the team race. Clapham is another instance of perseverance, as when he ran in the corresponding race in 1927 he finished last, yet he now secures a place in our placed team. This speaks very well for our Juniors and we can look forward in confidence to the time when they are ready to compete in our Senior teams. items.s: THE ENFIELD A.C. "OPEN." Report and results of the Enfield A.C. open walk, where Belgrave's A team won the scratch team race and the B team the handicap team race, with Len Fletcher second. THE ENFIELD A.C. "OPEN." There were over 160 starters in the Enfield A.C. Walk and we again started two teams, with a very happy result. Our "A" team won the scratch team race and the "B" team won the handicap team race. items.s: THE HIGHGATE H. "OPEN." Report and results of the first Highgate Harriers open walk, run partly in darkness, where Belgrave won the scratch team race with Len Fletcher second and second-claim member J. H. Graygoss won on handicap; Polytechnic's scratch points total is only partly legible (8 and a broken second digit). THE HIGHGATE H. "OPEN." This event was promoted for the first time this season and the entry was on the small side, just over a hundred starting. Conditions were very trying and a late start, due to a breakdown in the arrangements, did not improve matters for competitors had to finish under a street lamp after walking the last two or three miles in the darkness. However, Len Fletcher again followed Hyde home, and led our team to their third scratch team win. Frank Thorn showed a return to form in finishing fifth and was our second man home. Our others to score were F. H. Elson and Fred Rickards, who has been showing up well over the seven miles courses. Owing to the absence of programmes the handicap results were announced later in the week and the individual winner proved to be J. H. Graygoss, one of our second-claim members. Our teams were fourth and fifth in the handicap team race a few seconds out. TEAM RESULTS. Scratch—1, Belgrave H. items.s: OUR "OPEN." Report and results of Belgrave's own open walk (221 entries), won by Len Fletcher after Hyde's disqualification, with Belgrave taking the scratch team race and fifteen of the twenty-two awards. OUR "OPEN." After a week of almost continuous rain we were fortunate to have a few hours of comparatively good weather for our "Open" race, which proved to be as popular as ever. 221 entries were received and this exceeded that received by the Road Walking Association for their Open race by about twenty. Our fine entry must be regarded as a high compliment to the Club from walkers in general and we were particularly pleased to receive the support of the provincial clubs, Leicester W.C. and Luton Utd. H. Our old friends, Surrey Walking Club, sent along two teams and we entered five teams—much to the surprise of some clubs who had difficulty in fielding a full team The same course as last year was used and Hyde, Fletcher and Pope took the lead in turn. They were still together with Fletcher, if anything, a yard in front, when Hyde suffered disqualification for the second year in succession. Thereafter Fletcher increased his lead and won fairly easily, accomplishing excellent time over the difficult course, which is a little in excess of seven miles. Meanwhile Green had made third position secure, and with Elson seventh, and Thorn tenth, we again proved easy scratch team winners. In addition, this team were placed second in the team handicap and our "C" team were third. A. H. Rayner, Cambridge H., won the individual handicap and so helped his club to win the handicap team race. Len Fletcher's fine walking deservedly gained for him third prize in the handicap, with 40 seconds start. Thus Belgrave walkers gained fifteen of the twenty-two awards, Fletcher's share being four prizes—a unique performance. J. E. Field gained the prize awarded to the first Belgrave Harrier not gaining any other award. Altogether, a very successful walk, especially when surveyed through Belgravian spectacles ! TEAM RESULTS. items.sum: Social notes on a record Social evening at Wimbledon and the first Dance of the season at Wandsworth Town Hall, with a plea for members to sell more dance tickets.
items.s: THE LIGHTER SIDE OF THE CLUB. Social notes on a record Social evening at Wimbledon and the first Dance of the season at Wandsworth Town Hall, with a plea for members to sell more dance tickets. THE LIGHTER SIDE OF THE CLUB. The past month was a very busy one for the Social side, as we ran our second Social evening of the season at Wimbledon, on Saturday, November 22nd, and followed this up with out first Dance of the season at Wandsworth Town Hall on November 26th. Both, we are pleased to report, were highly successful. The Social at Wimbledon beat all previous records, as there were over 140 at tea alone. Certainly, we had various other Clubs as guests, but I must say a great proportion, both female and male, were "Bels." I do hope this will be understood. The greater part of the evening was given over to dancing, which appears to be very popular. We had two vocalists—Billy Williams and a friend of Tom Cotton who came along and sung two old favourites with great success. Then, on with the dance again and there was general regret when eleven o'clock arrived and ended the most successful Social held at Wimbledon. Now for our next and last one. We shall have the Metropolitan Police A.A. and Herne Hill Harriers as visitors, and I trust everyone will come along and get on the right side of the Law. Note the date, January 24th, 1931. The Dance was equally successful in point of numbers, but there is still room for improvement in the sale of tickets by members. At present it is left to the same people every time. On going through the books I find six members sell between them nearly a hundred tickets. Only 195 were sold, all told, for our last dance, so " 'nuff said." If every member took one ticket we should have no need to take money on the door, which would be a great advantage in many ways. Our next dance is on Friday, January 16th, so make up your mind to be there, and let us see the tickets a little more evenly distributed this time. W. A. RICE, 36 Ascalon Street, W.8. W. A. Rice W. items.s: WORDS OF WISDOM. The convalescent cross-country vice-captain criticises poor member turnout for the social run with South London Harriers at Coulsdon and the St. George's match at Mitcham. WORDS OF WISDOM. BY H. E. FOOTER. (Our Cross-Country Vice-Captain, now happily convalescent and, we hope, soon to resume training, has taken up the pen and now expresses his opinions). A few words of wisdom to the Cross-Country section of our members. It should be the honest endeavour of all our fellows interested in the Club's welfare to support all fixtures arranged for them by our Committee, whether for dances, races or social fixtures. The Committee arranges these attractive social runs and inter-club races not for themselves, but for you to support and enjoy to the best of your ability. Up to the present season this had has gratifying results; so much so, that the present Committee went a step farther by fixing a social run with our strong southern rivals, and present Southern Champions, South London Harriers. And what result have we? The enormous crowd of 8 Belgravians to carry the Claret and Gold amongst our mighty host. Eight athletes out of a so-called membership of 600 rallied at Coulsdon. Was it the fare? Was it the distance? Or were they frightened of the mud? One of these three reasons must have been responsible for the destruction of our hopes of future fixtures with our genial rivals. Then again, October 25th saw us put out a fair muster of 37 members to race Thames Valley H. and Ashcombe A.C. at Hounslow. But now, Saturday, December 6th, for our match versus St. George's Sports Club, only 10 of that 37 can afford to travel to Mitcham to support the Bels ! Result : we are beaten because men who should have been in the team are idling away their time trying to gain hints from our Youths' Section, or training over our home course in anticipation of a victory individually by so-called specialised training. Such is the Club-spirit shown by these members that I fail to see of what use these men will be to our teams in future championships, as all we shall hear will be, "I can't stomach the plough, anyhow," when they don't even try to accustom their bodies to any heavy going. Others of our members appear to like the proverbial apron-strings too much to attempt to go further afield than Wimbledon, and thus our Club's progress must remain in the hands of that gallant few who always rally to the call and do not think of individual gain in preference to good comradeship. H.E.F. H. E. Footer H. E. FOOTER Cross-Country Vice-Captain; convalescent H.E.F. H.E.F. sign-off Coulsdon Hounslow Mitcham Wimbledon South London Harriers Thames Valley H. Ashcombe A.C. items.s: Club notes: W. A. Rice's marriage, four newly elected members, congratulations on the Surrey Cross-country Championship team win, Penny's and Allum's county wins and walking successes, regret at the death of patron Sir Joseph Hood, and late news of Allum's London Business Houses win and walking wins at Eltham. Congratulations to W. A. Rice, our popular Social Hon. Secretary and mile champion, upon his recent marriage. His clubmates wish him many years of happiness, and a presentation will be made to Mr. and Mrs. Rice during our Social Evening at Wimbledon on the 24th. * * * * * The following members were elected at the last Committee meeting: C. Grainger, E. W. Suttle, J. E. Read and E. Elmslie. We accord them a hearty welcome and hope we shall get to know them very well. * * * * * The Club's congratulations have been merited during the past month by the following :— Messrs. Penny, Cook, Wills, Carter, Bignall and Smith upon winning the Surrey Cross-country Championship. Arthur Penny and Arthur Allum upon being the first men home in the Surrey and Middlesex Cross-country Championships, respectively. A. L. Fletcher for winning the London Business Houses' Seven Miles Walking Championship. Messrs. T. W. Green, J. F. King and E. Saunders upon finishing first, second and twelfth in the Godstone and back Walk, thus gaining first team honours. * * * * * We share in the general regret at the news of the death of Sir Joseph Hood, Bart., Mayor of Wimbledon, for he had been a Patron of the Club for many years, and had taken an interest in the Club's activities for some time past. * * * * * As we go to press there comes the news of Arthur Allum's win in the London Business Houses Championship, and of Len Fletcher's eclipse of C. W. Hyde at Eltham. Also of the dual win in scratch and handicap team races at the Eltham Walk. Congratulations ! W. A. Rice W. A. Rice Social Hon. Footer's report of the last of three inter-club cross-country races between Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and Belgrave at Richmond Park on December 13th, won individually by Cohen of Ashcombe from Allum, with Belgrave taking the team race with nine in the first dozen; result list of placed runners included.
e: Inter-club race (Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and Belgrave)
items.s: THE FINAL INTER-CLUB RACE (DEC. 13th). H. E. Footer's report of the last of three inter-club cross-country races between Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and Belgrave at Richmond Park on December 13th, won individually by Cohen of Ashcombe from Allum, with Belgrave taking the team race with nine in the first dozen; result list of placed runners included. THE FINAL INTER-CLUB RACE (DEC. 13th). East Sheen was the venue for the last of the three inter-club races held this season between Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and ourselves. Only fifty-nine runners faced the starter and this must be put down to the close proximity of the festive season, when all the young bloods are inspired by admiring females to gaze earnestly into shop windows to see the decorations and other things. While the he-men wallow through the muck and slime these poor deluded youths think they are getting off lightly, but little do they know the female mind ! Well, to get to the sterner stuff, the 59 runners consisted of 24 "Bels.," 20 Ashcombe and 15 Thames Valley Harriers. The competitors undressed at "The Hare and Hounds" and then had rather a long walk uphill to the Sheen Gate of Richmond Park, where they were to start and finish. The start was a good one in which Cohen (Ashcombe A.C.), Joe Flower and Dewberry showed to advantage, then over half a mile of parkland and encircling the Deer Enclosure with the runners in the following order: Cohen, Allum, Penny, Jack Flower, Frank Webb, Nuti (T.V.H.), Carter, Dewberry, Morrell, Robertshaw, Smith and Joe Flower. Thus at a mile and a quarter Belgrave had practically settled the team question and it only remained to see who would gain individual honours. Skirting Pen Ponds and rounding Spanker's Hill Wood found many of the runners complaining of pains, a not unknown thing among athletes, I am afraid, so that the order changed slightly, though not among the leaders. After leaving White Lodge and crossing the bridge near Roehampton Gate, Cohen was gradually leaving the field and Arthur Allum, now seventy-five yards away, had to increase his efforts to hold the leader. Fletcher and Robertshaw, who had started slowly were now gaining much ground and many places. Nearing the finishing post, Cohen led Allum by fifty yards and Arthur made a desperate spurt to try and gain the tape but was beaten by half-a-dozen yards or so, with Penny a hundred yards in the rear, followed by Jack Flower. Then came Warboys, Nuti, of the "Valley," Robertshaw, Dewberry, Carter, with a sprained ankle, Fletcher, who passed six in the last mile, Browning (Ashcombe), Smith, at last finding a bit of form, and Joe Flower. So Belgrave scored a hollow victory with nine in the first dozen. RESULT. m. s. 1. L. J. Cohen A.A.C. 29 9 2. A. Allum B.H. 29 12 3. A. W. Penny ,, 29 47 4. J. E. Flower ,, 30 4 5. S. H. items.sum: H.E.F.'s report of the club Seven Miles Cross-country Championship for the "Blackstaffe" Shield, won by Arthur Allum in 39 min. 3 sec. from Penny and Jack Flower, with Allum also taking the handicap from Tom Cotton and Dick Savage, followed by a plea for more members to train for the team races; full result of 30 finishers with handicap times.
e: Belgrave Seven Miles Cross-Country Championship (Blackstaffe Shield)
items.s: THE SEVEN MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. H.E.F.'s report of the club Seven Miles Cross-country Championship for the "Blackstaffe" Shield, won by Arthur Allum in 39 min. 3 sec. from Penny and Jack Flower, with Allum also taking the handicap from Tom Cotton and Dick Savage, followed by a plea for more members to train for the team races; full result of 30 finishers with handicap times. THE SEVEN MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Once again, another murky day for the "Blackstaffe" Shield race. Dull, damp, misty weather greeted the thirty-two runners as they faced Mr. Gordon, our President, for the start. This was the nineteenth race for this particular trophy, presented as far back as 1910 by Mr. H. T. Blackstaffe, the Olympic Sculling Champion of 1908, and for which competition among our cross-country men to have the honour of being its guardian for each ensuing year has become more and more keen as time goes on. Now only the very fittest can hope to survive and be in at the finish. This year was no exception to the rule and after a fast start the race developed into a gruelling struggle between those two well-known county athletes, Arthur Allum (Middlesex) and Arthur Penny (Surrey) while Allum is also our three miles Champion. In the breakaway two things were very noticeable, the lead gained by Joe Flower over the rest of the field, and the waiting tactics adopted by Sid Warboys. Both, I think, carried a little to excess their ideas to be of any great use to them. The field, after crossing the road by the Village, soon closed on Flower, and Allum went to the front only to be headed by Jack Flower when crossing the Golf Links. Down Gravelly Hill Allum let out a link and made the pace a "corker." First Jack, then Penny, and afterwards Harold Wills, our second-claim member from Herne Hill Harriers, tried to dispute the lead with Allum, between the bottom of the hill and Beverley Brook, but gave it up in disgust. When coming over the short rise by the cemetery, Allum was just ahead of Penny, and going up that short, stiff climb to the flagstaff they were practically together with Jack Flower about thirty yards behind. After him came Wills, then Warboys grunting like some over-fed bulldog and reminded me of another old Belgravian with his Birchell bellow. Dewberry stomped by me next, and in his wake came Frank Webb. Then came our old friend and International runner, Bignall, of Highgate Harriers, with Ernie Duffett, a former holder of this Belgrave Championship, in close company. Next we have Bert Smith at last prepared to "do or die," with "Nobby" Fletcher at his heels. Hello! here comes the "three starred nap," Tom Cotton, in quite a hurry. He must be after something very urgent to be dashing about like this. Hush! did somebody mention a handicap? Never let it be said that men are only running to-day for such paltry things. Look! what's that, Shell? No, only Robertshaw, with Bill Webb loping along after him, looking as though it was "too much fag" even to run. At this point about two miles from the start, the issue seemed already to be between the two in the lead, with Jack Flower standing an outside chance of getting on terms. But this Jack found impossible as the farther they went the faster the pace became in front. At the end of the first circuit, with another lap to go, Allum began to force the pace over the Golf Links, and Penny was hard put to hang on. Jack Flower by now had dropped back further still, and found when turning at the Village that he had a leeway of nearly a hundred yards to make up. Of the others, Warboys and Bill Webb had gained much ground, while Wills and Joe Flower were losing their positions. After descending Gravelly Hill again, crossing the brook near Robin Hood Gate, climbing the horse-ride to the Flagstaff, the leaders were next seen near the Windmill, where Penny looked to be trying to take the lead. Jack Flower in third place seemed to be the same distance away as before, but Warboys was coming along fast. Apparently his previous efforts were to get up steam, and not, as I thought, a warning for people to get out of the way. Now came Bignall, who had gained three places on this lap; and Dewberry, with Frank Webb trying to get on terms. Bill Webb must have given himself a shake, for here he comes looking very fresh. Robertshaw with machine-like action and Duffett pounding along behind passed quickly, then Wills—wishing somebody had rolled out that last hill. Bert Smith pattered along just in front of Fletcher. Then came Joe Flower, finding the distance not to his liking, and after a short interval, Tom Cotton loomed from the mist, hoping his foot would hold out to the finish. Next, running together, Michael and Eastman, and after them, with brief gaps, the rest of the field with the two veterans, Dick Savage and George Still amongst them. At last, with the passing of our "champion heavy-weight," Charlie Poulter, and the gathering dusk, I thought it time to hasten to the winning post. Allum, I found had won by nearly two hundred yards in the very fast time of 39 min. 3 sec., or just a minute and a few seconds better than last year. Penny, I heard, had to contend with stomach trouble over that last mile and explains why he fell away so at the finish. Jack Flower ran in third, still about the same distance away from Penny as before, while Warboys was only a short distance behind him. Bignall occupied fifth place, with Bill Webb next, having passed his brother, Frank, and Dewberry in that burst across the common between the Windmill and Village. Looking through results the following men: Allum, Warboys, Bignall and Bill Webb must have put in some sterling work over the last three miles. Sufficient it is to say the handicap fell to our new Champion, Arthur Allum, while Tom Cotton had to be satisfied with second place, a few seconds to the good of Vice-Captain Dick Savage. The result, as a whole, shows improvement on recent years as regards team-work, as the runners were closer together than of yore, though numerically the turn-out leaves much to be desired. Surely there are amongst the five hundred odd members, men who, if they would only turn up and train, would walk into the team for such races as the Surrey County, South of Thames and other district races, while our Southern and National team can be improved by new blood, to infuse greater enthusiasm in the present men by their backing. There is plenty of room for your talent in any of these teams, so why not try and get fit instead of standing about watching, with your nose on somebody's shoulder and your toes under somebody's boots? items.sum: Report and results of the club's rain-affected Boxing Day Meeting: a 120 yards handicap won by P. A. Pelcot, a two miles handicap won by new member J. W. Woodley from Allum, and a three miles walk handicap won by R. F. Elson from C. W. Redgrave.
items.s: THE BOXING DAY MEETING. Report and results of the club's rain-affected Boxing Day Meeting: a 120 yards handicap won by P. A. Pelcot, a two miles handicap won by new member J. W. Woodley from Allum, and a three miles walk handicap won by R. F. Elson from C. W. Redgrave. THE BOXING DAY MEETING. Our Boxing Day Meeting was spoiled to some extent by the weather conditions but entries were well up to standard and some good running was seen by the few spectators who braved the pouring rain. There were six heats in the 120yds. Handicap and the fastest up was G. Weston, a newcomer to the Club, and on his showing a decided acquisition to our meagre list of sprinters. Three of the other heat winners were Juniors, off long marks, while Jim Tosh and G. Tutin completed the finalists. T. C. Jones won the fourth heat but as his name was down for the fifth, the judges had no option but to disqualify him. In the final Pelcot, off next to limit, won with Clasby the limit man second, and Weston third. A large field turned out for the 2 miles run with Bert Cook on the post of honour. He was conceding Allum and Jack Flower 5yds., but once the pistol went these two jumped away from him and commenced to forge their way through the field. However, after a couple of laps Woodley, another new member and off a long mark, had taken the lead and the farther he went the bigger his lead became. At the bell he had a huge lead with Eastman second, but round the back straight Allum, running finely, went into second place, but pursuit of the leader was hopeless. Eastman down the straight stalled off a challenge by Jack Flower and so finished third. The time, 9 min. 46 sec., speaks for itself and Woodley is to be congratulated on his good running even allowing for his long mark. Arthur Allum once again showed that Christmas festivities do not affect him and his was a very fine performance considering the large field which competed. A good field started in the Walk and it was soon seen that a close race would ensue between those two young walkers of infinite promise, C. W. Redgrave and R. F. Elson, who started from the same handicap mark. Eventually, Elson gained the advantage and won, but both walked well in again winning handicap awards. They are always doing this sort of thing and won't be happy until they are on the scratch mark. A. L. Fletcher, from scratch, gave a fine exhibition of fast walking despite unfavourable conditions and, passing Harley, Latter and Larman in the last quarter of a mile, finished third. items.sum: Walking notes: the Boxing Day Croydon–Godstone and back team win makes five successive open scratch team wins, match defeats by Surrey W.C. and the Metropolitan Police, a plan to stage a certified track event so Tommy Green can attempt official records, and a call to train for the "Junior" Championship.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes: the Boxing Day Croydon–Godstone and back team win makes five successive open scratch team wins, match defeats by Surrey W.C. and the Metropolitan Police, a plan to stage a certified track event so Tommy Green can attempt official records, and a call to train for the "Junior" Championship. WITH THE WALKERS. The victory of our team on Boxing Day in the Croydon—Godstone and back walk brings our total of successive open scratch team wins to five. We hope to continue in the winning way in the Cambridge H., L.C.C. Tramways S.C., and Ashcombe A.C.'s Open Walks, which rapidly follow one another. To offset our success in the Open races, we have twice been defeated in match events, once by the Surrey W.C. and once by the Metropolitan Police, as described elsewhere. * * * * * Those who have followed Tommy Green's walking feats with interest, and have read Mr. J. B. Belchamber's informative articles which have appeared in our columns from time to time, have long been aware of his ability to get inside record time at the longer distances. Unfortunately, times recorded on road courses cannot be accepted by the Amateur Athletic Association or International Athletics Federation, as there can be no certainty that the distance is exact, and, of course, gradients and road surfaces differ considerably. So a record, to be accepted by the governing bodies, must be accomplished on a certified track, and timed by not less than three approved timekeepers. It is hoped to promote an event during the Summer in which these conditions will be complied with, and so afford Tommy an opportunity of placing his name and that of the Belgrave Harriers upon the record books. Much work has yet to be done, and many details to be settled, before we can say for a certainty that this event will take place. We hope to give our readers further particulars in a later issue. * * * * * The "Junior" Championship is rapidly approaching and all those eligible for this race should now be training seriously with a view to upholding the Club name in this race. Intending competitors should be out at least twice a week (say Saturday and Tuesday) and the merits of strolling as a supplement to the ordinary training cannot be too strongly emphasised. From these efforts it is hoped that a strong team will mature, capable of making opposing teams say fearfully, "What about Belgrave?" and then for our lads to justify the pessimism of the other teams. e: Belgrave v. Metropolitan Police A.A. walking match
items.s: MATCH v. METROPOLITAN POLICE A.A. Report and result of the walking match lost to the Metropolitan Police A.A. at Imber Court on 13 December, scored as M.P.A.A. 132 pts to Belgrave 168 pts as printed (Belgrave's printed positions add to 175), with Belgrave–Police members on the Police side. MATCH v. METROPOLITAN POLICE A.A. On December 13th we visited the splendid quarters of the Metropolitan Police at Imber Court for our walking match. Our party numbered twelve but could not be described as our strongest team for some of our walkers were engaged in preparing for the "Godstone" Walk. Included in the Police team were some of our clubmates in Messrs. Rathbone, Bidgood, Salmon, Mac Donald and Winner, and the first two of this quintet were mainly responsible for our defeat at the hands (or the feet) of the Police. The course consisted of two laps over very level ground and Len Fletcher took the lead right from the starting signal given by our President, Mr. E. Gordon. Thorn kept Len company for a while, but then experienced leg trouble which caused him to stop for a few minutes and lose several places which could not afterwards be regained. Meanwhile, C. W. Redgrave, walking in fine style, had gone into second place, a position which he had to surrender to A. H. Rayner, of the Police, later. A group of four policemen then followed, eventually filling fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh positions, and this packing proved the critical factor and gave our hosts their win. It had been arranged prior to the race to score twelve aside on the University scoring system and the final result appears below. And so we take pleasure in congratulating the M.P.A.A. on their first win in the long series of races between our two clubs. We have long had a very high opinion of the sportsmanship of the police and have had the pleasure of including members of the M.P.A.A. in our ranks and teams. In fact, many of our past wins in the R.W.A. Championships have been largely due to "Belgrave—Police" members. Names such as E. A. Wall, J. Miles, F. Rickards and J. Rathbone occur to one as having figured in our winning teams in the past and it is hoped that this list will be added to in due course. To return to the race, after digressing a little. Len Fletcher gave his usual fine exhibition of walking without having to exert himself unduly, and C. W. Redgrave deserves our congratulations for his very fine effort which, we trust, will soon become commonplace to him. H. S. Latter and E. A. Jackman, this season's newcomers, gave evidence that they will not always be in the second half of the race—far from it. In the Police ranks we were pleased to see Jack Rathbone and Jack Bidgood prominent, for we shall require them both later in the season, the former in the R.W.A. National Championship and the latter in both "Junior" and "Senior" races. RESULT. M.P.A.A.—132pts. Belgrave H.—168pts m. s. 1. A. L. Fletcher B 56 12 2. P-c. Rayner P 56 45 3. C. W. items.s: "HORWOOD CUP" AND 7 MILES JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP. Report, result and winners list of the club's sixth annual Horwood Cup 7 miles junior walk and sealed handicap at Wimbledon on 20 December 1930, won by F. W. Thorn, who also took the handicap. "HORWOOD CUP" AND 7 MILES JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP. At Wimbledon it was rather cold, damp, and dispiriting on the afternoon of December 20th, when twenty of the Club's junior walkers took part in the sixth annual contest for the "Horwood Cup" and the sealed handicap held in conjunction with this race. This trophy was presented to offer additional encouragement to such of our walkers as are eligible for the Road Walking Association's Junior Championships at 10 miles, and the distance of our race was fixed at 7 miles so that our younger members should not have too many races at the longer distance, but should train up to it gradually throughout the Winter Season. As is usual in the year following a success for the Claret and Gold in the Open Junior race our Club "Junior" was of exceptional interest as, with the winning four and Khlopin ineligible, we were all anxious to learn the quality of those who are to carry on for the club in a race in which we have a wonderful record to maintain. The form revealed was certainly gratifying. F. W. Thorn was fancied to win and right from the start it was evident that he was determined to do so as convincingly as possible. Taking the lead immediately he opened a gap of 120 yards in the first mile and this advantage he increased steadily and evenly throughout to win eventually by about 600 yards. For second place the struggle was a very fine one. R. F. Elson made a bold bid for it and in the early stages of the race he got away from C. W. Redgrave and C. H. Speechley, both of whom were expected to be well up. L. Storey was also prominent hereabouts. Charlie Speechley started slowly, but warming up thoroughly at 2 miles, he was a close 4th at the half distance. In the last lap Elson fell away and Redgrave stayed on well to beat Speechley by 17 secs. for second place. In addition to winning the cup Thorn won the handicap. His time was 2 min. 6 sec. faster than that returned by him in the Club's Open Walk over the same course and yet the day was certainly not so favourable. Had he returned this time in the former race he would have been placed 4th, after Fletcher, Pope and Tommy Green. Moreover, his time was 1¾ min. faster than Frank Elson's when winning last year. As the latter was a very close second in the last open Junior Championship, it will be seen that Thorn's chance of an individual win for the Club in this year's race is indeed a rosy one. As regards the strength of our team, it would appear that, despite the fine race between our next three men home, it is not quite equal on present form to the one which represented us successfully last year. However, considering the youthfulness of almost all in this year's team, there is good reason to expect a much greater improvement between now and March 7th than we could have hoped for from last year's more mature team. L. Storey has had only a few races at 5 miles and over, and he should improve vastly in stamina. C. W. Redgrave has walked splendidly in his last three races and Harley finds a little extra speed each week. H. E. Larman walked strongly to gain 2nd place in the handicap, and one of the most pleasing features of the race was the fine walking of H. S. Latter, who is but a boy of slender build and years, yet who maintained a delightful and exemplary style throughout the race despite the stiff hills. RESULT. †Not eligible for Championship. items.s: THE GODSTONE WALK. Report and result of the Surrey Walking Club's Boxing Day Godstone walk, won by T. W. Green from J. F. King, with Belgrave winning the team race on 15 points. THE GODSTONE WALK. This race, promoted annually by the Surrey Walking Club on Boxing Day, was held this year in very trying conditions, hard rain and bitterly cold winds troubling the competitors throughout the 18¾ miles. Tommy Green, who only decided to come at 9 a.m. on the morning of the race, owing to a severe chill which had troubled him during the week, won the race by about a minute and a half from another Belgravian, Joe King. Having the first two men home gave us a great advantage in the team race and our trio was completed by Vice-Captain Saunders, who stuck gamely to his task over the last four miles when the intense cold threatened cramp. Jack Field was forced to retire owing to the severity of the conditions, but his younger brother, A. H. Field, did well to finish the course and be placed fifth in the sealed handicap. And so we must thank Messrs. Green, King and Saunders for winning this race in the Club name—the fifth open scratch team win this season—and trust they will repeat the performance in the National Championship. items.s: A BELGRAVE FLAG DAY. Report of the Surrey cross-country championship at Imber Court, won by Arthur Penny with Belgrave taking the Pickett Cup for the third successive year (61 points to Surrey A.C.'s 73 as printed, though the chart's 7-mile positions of the first six add to 65), with a chart of each Belgrave runner's positions; Arthur Allum's Middlesex title is noted. A BELGRAVE FLAG DAY. The result of last Saturday's County Championships provided Belgrave with two new Champions in Arthur Allum (Middlesex) and Arthur Penny (Surrey) while in the latter case, Penny had the honour of leading the Belgrave team to triumph over our great rivals, South London Harriers and Surrey A.C. for the third successive year. Imber Court, the scene of the Surrey activities and home of the Metropolitan Police A.C., while providing excellent dressing and feasting accommodation, left opposite recollections as regards cross-country running. One circuit of a frost-bound field and three laps of a huge reservoir faced the hundred odd competitors at the start of the 7 miles trek stipulated for this particular race. It proved nothing more than a glorified track-race, with one or two individuals complaining bitterly about not being able to obtain a foot-hold on the frozen surface. Still, as conditions were alike for everybody, the result must stand as current form of each man at the present time. After completing a circle round the starting field the leading positions were held by Belton (Surrey A.C.), Cohen (Ashcombe A.C.), Penny, Cook, Stansbury (Ranelagh), and Wills. Entering the gate to the reservoir Belton led this bunch by a dozen yards or so with Carter in eleventh position and Smith, Bignall, Dewberry and Duffett in the next dozen places. Coming by the gate to start another lap the leadership had passed to Penny, with Cohen and the same little bunch on his heels. Next seen, at about four miles, Penny had an eighty yards lead of Stansbury (Ranelagh) with Cook close behind. Wills was about sixth, Carter still eleventh, running smoothly, but Smith had lost two valuable positions to the S.L.H. boys. Bignall, also, was feeling none too happy, and Dewberry was wheezing along like some punctured tyre with Duffett just behind. Six mile mark found Penny's lead stronger than ever with a hundred yards advantage over Stansbury and Cook. Wills now finding the pace too much was gradually dropping back but still fighting hard. Carter seemed fixed in his position, while Bignall had reclaimed two places. Bert Smith had lost another two but was, nevertheless, running strongly. Dewberry and Duffett were still chasing one another round about the thirtieth position. With four men in the first dozen, and two in the next, it looked very rosy for us, but you can never tell over that last mile when some men always seem to find that little bit extra which counts with team scores. Our fellows, it seemed, were all in, but though they lost a place here and there, not much ground was lost. At the finish Penny ran in victorious by over a hundred and fifty yards, with Stansbury second, and Belton third. Then Cook for us, a little wait, then Wills, with Carter not far away. Some Surrey boys, then Bignall and at last our sixth man, Smith, followed by a crowd of S.L.H. men. Well, with six in twenty, surely we must have won, but we hear that Surrey have six in eighteen. Now comes the news that they have beaten us by a point, then that they have only counted five men, and last, but not least, the official verdict that we are the winners with 61 points to Surrey A.C.'s 73, with S.L.H. third. Hurrah! the "Pickett" Cup is once more ours to hold for the coming season. Now boys! Hats off to our new champions and may they win still higher honours in the struggles to come; and let us back them up with team work. We've beaten S.L.H. before in the Surrey race, so that is no new honour, but have never done so in either the Southern, National or Brighton Relay. With two of the team running so splendidly, now is our chance to accomplish this feat, if only the rest of us provide them with the sound backing needed in these championships. Perseverance in training, and we may add many more new trophies to our festive board next May. Get to it! Below will be found a chart showing positions of each individual at the various distances. items.s: THE MIDDLESEX CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the Middlesex Senior Cross-Country Championship, won by Allum after a duel with Ferris, with nine Belgravians finishing as individual entrants. THE MIDDLESEX CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. A field of 155 started in the Middlesex Senior Cross-Country Championship and of the fifteen individual entrants nine were Belgravians. Although Stubbs, Broadley and Adamthwaite were non-starters the entries were of a high standard and included such men as Ferris, Harman and Elwin. While expecting Allum to be well up we hardly dared to hope that he would beat these three stars. Yet this is what he did, and in winning this Middlesex title undoubtedly put up the finest performance of his athletic career. Warboys led the field for a short time, as he did in last year's National, but he soon relinquished it to Harman, the former International. About the same time Allum and Ferris moved up to second. At half-way they passed Harman, and a fine fight between the famous Marathon runner and Allum ensued. Allum was forcing the pace, but Ferris, blowing in his usual fashion, hung on to him and Allum was unable to shake him off until two miles of the unpleasantly hard ground had been endured. As soon as he did get away from Ferris he went right away to gain a good lead which he held to the end, winning by nearly fifty yards. Warboys had only dropped a few places and succeeded in finishing ninth. Our next two were the brothers Webb, who seem to be inseparable in cross-country races and who finished 32nd and 33rd. Frank Webb did some very fast running in the last two miles for he was hung up for a long time by barbed wire. This misfortune happened to Robertshaw, and J. E. Flower had a bad time, which accounts for their being outside the first forty. T. J. Flower ran his usual steady race and was only a short way behind his brother and Robertshaw. In a race of this standard it is creditable to finish in the first hundred, and Rollins, after starting slowly, succeeded in this. The ninth Belgrave man to finish was L. E. Fletcher. It says a lot for the spirit of the Club that nine men not running for any team awards should all finish this trying course, in spite of various accidents common to cross-country running. Had we been eligible to run as a team, and had Robertshaw and J. E. Flower been running up to form we might have been placed in the team race. In conclusion a tribute should be paid to J. F. Bain, of Ealing Harriers, who was unlucky enough to lose his shoe in the first furlong and then raced seven and a half miles with only one shoe over hard, frozen, uneven ground and through water covered with floating ice. In spite of this he finished sixth. Not many would have put their club first to such an extent. Full times and positions of our men will be in next month's "Belgravian." L.E.F. items.sum: Notice of the club's forthcoming cross-country fixtures for January–March 1931: the Macher Shield 10 miles championship, the South of the Thames, Southern and National championships and inter-club runs.
items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. Notice of the club's forthcoming cross-country fixtures for January–March 1931: the Macher Shield 10 miles championship, the South of the Thames, Southern and National championships and inter-club runs. FORTHCOMING EVENTS. On the 31st we have our 10 Miles Cross Country Championship for the "Macher Shield" (Holder, H. E. Footer) with a Sealed Handicap in conjunction. As the holder has only just commenced training his chances of retaining the Shield are slight, and we must look to our two County Champions to have a battle royal for the honour. February 7th we have a run with Croydon H., Mitcham A.C. and Epsom H. from the former's headquarters at Sanderstead. I have been given to understand that the dressing room here is very small, so will advise our members later as to the advisability of making the journey. The 14th sees the South of the Thames Championship, probably at Windsor Great Park. Judging by the recent Surrey County running our team has a decidedly improved look about it. for of that team Carter, Smith and Dewberry are eligible together with Frank Webb, Joe Flower and Wally Bayliss, the last two having scored in last year's team who were placed second. The reason why the other four members are now barred is that they were in our placed team in the Southern, this being one of the many barring clauses for the South of Thames race. We have, however, other members who should by now be seriously considered when the final reckoning is made. February 21st. We have two fixtures on this day, both away, one at Ealing versus the local club with whom we had an enjoyable run early in the season, and the other with our old friends, the R.A.F., at Kenley. The run with Ealing Harriers will be an all-to-score-affair, but the race with the R.A.F. must be confined to a limited number owing to restricted dressing accommodation. On the 28th we have the race of the year so far as the majority of our boys are concerned. The Southern Counties C.C. Championship will then be held at Shenfield, where the race was held in 1928 and where incidentally some of our boys ran remarkably well. Our team these days is much stronger and with our members achieving so many notable successes it is only natural our thoughts should turn to the possibility of our winning the Southern. That we have a fine chance cannot be denied and the only question seems to be, will our boys be as fit then as they are now? The answer is entirely in their hands; steady training and a careful preparation will do it. Well, we will hope for the best and leave it to the boys to bring one more honour to the "Bels." that of being Southern Champions. On March 14th the National Cross Country Championship will be held in Wickstead Park, Kettering. Last year the Club did excellently in being placed sixth, while Bert Footer ran the race of his life in being 24th in such a class field as this. Among a batch of teams which include England's best we can hardly expect much improvement on last year's placing, but whereas then we were the second Southern club home let us this time take yet another step forward by being the first Southern club to finish and thus add more laurels to our already heavy crown. We have another fixture on this day, a triangular match with the Old Emanuel A.C. and College of St. Mark and S. John A.C. over our 5 miles course at Wimbledon. This will give our members who do not make the journey to Kettering a chance of representing the Club and we shall have to turn out a useful team as some good men are included in the opposition. items.label: January 1931
items.sum: H. E. Footer's advice on cross-country training: train regularly for at least a month, don't chatter, control breathing, and a week-by-week plan.
items.s: TRAINING. Why Do You Fail? H. E. Footer's advice on cross-country training: train regularly for at least a month, don't chatter, control breathing, and a week-by-week plan. TRAINING. Why Do You Fail? By H. E. Footer. Many athletes when essaying cross-country running train spasmodically, and when they do turn out, treat it either as a race or as a schoolgirls' treat. Don't laugh and chatter while running, you can't do such things in a race. The best way to get the utmost out of oneself when racing is to study oneself when training. Notice where you begin to feel that "beat" feeling which comes to everyone between the first mile and a half and the three miles mark, and fight it off. Don't give in as many do; you will soon get over it, and although you are tired you will find that you can continue automatically if you are able to control your breathing. Now, if you talk while training you are throwing a strain on the chest and your breath is not flowing in and out regularly, but in jerks, which causes loss of strength in an effort to maintain pace with the other members of the pack. Many think that they can get fit in a fortnight, or by turning out when they feel like it, but forget that they may not feel like it on the particular day they are asked to race. In my opinion, the minimum time for anyone to get at all fit for a race is a month, and then only by training three times a week, supplemented by walking. I should divide my month's training as follows:— First Saturday. Run over 5 miles course, steady pace but not a crawl, and finish feeling you have expanded your lungs and stretched your leg muscles. If you feel "half-dead," you have gone too fast. Sunday. Stroll 8 miles very easy. Monday. Rest. Tuesday. Run 5 miles at a medium pace, with as much style as can be maintained without strain on any part of the body, as you will probably be feeling tight from Saturday's spin. Wednesday. Stroll 8 miles and have a brisk rub-down and bath afterwards. Thursday. Run 3 miles smartly. Friday. Half-an-hour's stroll before turning in. Second Saturday. You have now settled down, so in this 5 miles run you should pick out the heavy stuff and a hill or two, but after running over these always have an easy. Don't force the pace but finish briskly. Sunday. Stroll 10 miles at a reasonable pace. Bath and change afterwards. Monday. Take things easy. Stroll about 3 miles on the way home from business. Tuesday. Run 5 miles at medium pace, quickening up towards the end, say over the last mile. Wednesday. Stroll 6 miles briskly with rub-down after. Thursday. Run 3 miles easy. Friday. Walk 4 miles easy. Third Saturday. Run a fairly fast 5 miles. Sunday. An easy 10 miles stroll. Monday. Walk 5 miles inside the hour. Tuesday. Run 5 miles medium. Finish fresh, not winded. Wednesday. Stroll 6 miles moderate pace. Thursday. 3 miles run, taking things easy. Friday. Walk 4 miles easy. Fourth Saturday. Run 6 miles, picking out the heavy ground and climbing the hills briskly, but finish gently. Sunday. Stroll 10 miles at a fair even pace. Monday. Just stroll home as before. Tuesday. Run 5 miles fairly fast. Wednesday. Stroll 6 miles, finishing briskly. Thursday. Run 3 miles slowly. Friday. Rest. Fifth Saturday. You should be ready to race. H.E.F. H. E. Footer H. E. Footer H.E.F. items.sum: Translation of an Italian newspaper report of Tommy Green's win in the International 100 kilometres walk at Milan, November 1930, ahead of Olivoni, with the first six in the result.
items.s: THE INTERNATIONAL 100 KILOS WALK. Translation of an Italian newspaper report of Tommy Green's win in the International 100 kilometres walk at Milan, November 1930, ahead of Olivoni, with the first six in the result. THE INTERNATIONAL 100 KILOS WALK. It is with pleasure that we give below a translation of the description of Tommy Green's win in the International Walk at Milan. This article appeared in the Il Mezzogiorno Sportivo and is of particular interest as the accounts appearing in the English newspapers at the time were of a scanty nature and lacked detail. A phrase such as "Green, incomparabile ed instancabile" scarcely requires translation. and such compliments coming from sportsmen on the Continent make us prouder than ever of "our Tommy." Milan, Nov. 9th, 1930. THE ENGLISHMAN GREEN WINS 100 KILOMETRES AFTER AN EXCITING DUEL WITH OLIVONI. The Englishman Green won the 100 kilometre walk organized by the Sporto Gazette. His victory would not have been so easily attained had it been in the days when walking was held in so great esteem in Italy. The race, as a whole, did not attract a strong complement of our best walkers, and to-day, Donato Pavesi, watching Green on his way to certain victory, regretted that he could not go back over the years to the age of his efficiency. For then the race might quite easily have produced a different result. Green's time is notable, and that in itself reflects credit upon some of our walkers in the rear who proved that they will in time be capable of a similar performance. Considering the number of entrants, and the widespread public interest taken in it, the race can be considered a success. The enthusiasm of the crowds for this most popular sport has certainly not waned. The experience gained by the Englishman last time in this most difficult test stood him in good stead. If, at that time, Green committed errors of judgment in overcoming the many difficulties the 100 kilometres presents, by not distributing his energies wisely, to-day he adopted better tactics and won accordingly. The style in which Green won was indisputable, for he was in splendid physical condition and possessed a good morale. Also, he realized how opportune it was, in such an exacting battle, to allow his most feared rivals to set the pace in the preceding kilometres, and so study, in the early stages, their intentions and capabilities. Green adopted this plan to perfection, and when the time came for him to take an active part in the competition, he did so with a strong faith in himself. In that mood he arrived at Saronno and only Olivoni—the new National walker—replied to his attack. From that point it can be said that the 100 kilometres resolved itself into a battle between these two. Green and Olivoni proceeded neck and neck for practically 40 kilometres, both walking with elastic step, neither showing an atom of fatigue. Behind them, fading in the distance, came their adversaries . . . Beaten were the old warriors by the increasing pace—the youths incapable of making any perceptible ground upon the leaders. The hopes of the Italians were all set upon Olivoni, the only one who was able to respond to the faith placed in him and who struggling manfully to rob the stranger of such a valued prize. In this manner the race between Green and Olivoni became the centre of interest in the race, for between these two was being waged an emotion-provoking and keenly contested tussle. Olivoni put all he possessed into his task on hand. He struggled on with his heart in his throat—responding to every fresh attack of the Englishman with ready and spontaneous reaction, even producing, at one time, an extraordinary effort when the Englishman seemed to be tiring. Better comportment of our representative could not be expected, and now, coming to the ultimate result, one has to proffer to Olivoni all due merit for his performance against a man of Green's class. Green, incomparable and untiring, took the upper hand in this emotional duel while we were still hoping. This happened when three-quarters of the course had been covered, when the struggles of the two began to make themselves felt, and the road was beginning to seem interminable to the competitors. At this juncture one had to admire and value Green's resources. Freed of Olivoni's opposition, he did not slacken his pace but proceeded calmly and determinedly, certain of having given of his best. Green quite deservedly won this (the 18th) race, traversing the last quarter of the course amidst the acclamations of the crowds which lined the streets, and which sportingly appraised the champion who had added yet another victory to his illustrious record. Of the Italian participants, we have shown that Olivoni was the best, actually the only one who really defended his national colours. To be placed second in the final classification demonstrates to the utmost what the Milanese could do. In summing up one has to admit that Green's performance was undoubtedly a revelation and befitting a great champion when the time is considered. The doleful note is struck when one realizes the failures of our old and trusted warriors. Giani finished 5th, Pavesi 10th, and Brignoli, Rivolta Biondetti and some others fell by the roadside owing to the fierceness of the battle. In these our hopes were chiefly placed. A serene day, a moderate temperature, a good road—all were elements favourable for them to give of their best, and yet the result was negative. Only the youths were able to give us some satisfaction, even if not victorious. Next to Olivoni, one cites Guidotti—the first of the juniors, tenacious and eager; then also Casalli, who came fourth. He was courageous, but not capable of keeping the pace which was set by the others. RESULT. h. m. s. 1. T. W. Green, Belgrave H. 10 30 24 2. Olivoni, S.C. Italia 10 40 4 3. items.s: Club notes: ten new members including ex-Air Force and Middlesex champion F. W. Turner, congratulations to Arthur Allum on third in the Southern and fifth in the National Cross-country Championships (earning an England place), Past-President W. H. Hare's marriage, and a Committee decision to engrave championship medals at Club expense. Since our last Gazette was published we have enrolled J. Noah, C. Lancaster, R. Fowles, F. W. Turner, R. Marshall, H. G. Thompson, E. F. J. E. Marshall, R. W. T. Tungay, L. L. Hyde and C. H. E. Penny as members, and we wish them every success in our colours. Turner is the well-known ex-Air Force and Middlesex champion, and we hope to enjoy his assistance for a long while to come. * * * * * Arthur Allum merits the congratulations of all upon his splendid running in the Southern Cross-country Championship. He is the first Belgrave man to finish in the first three of this race, and it should not be long before he improves, even upon this. Another season and we may have a real Southern (perhaps even National) champion among us. Well run, Arthur ! We look forward to seeing you lead the Belgrave team to their first Southern win next year. * * * * * Since writing the above Arthur has very nearly exhausted our supply of superlatives by finishing fifth in the National Championship, and so earned a place in the English team. The Club's best wishes go with Arthur to Ireland, and, meanwhile : Jolly well run, Sir ! * * * * * The Club's heartiest congratulations to our Past-President, W. H. Hare, upon his recent marriage. Harry has served the Club well as President, Hon. Secretary, Hon. Treasurer, Hon. Editor, and in many other ways in the past, and if he is only half as successful a husband as he has been (and is) a Club official, he may well be described as "The Ideal Husband." We wish Mr. and Mrs. Hare a long course, and every happiness. * * * * * It has been decided by the Committee that, in future, medals won in Championships when competing in the Club name shall be engraved at the Club expense. items.s: THE TEN MILES CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the Club Ten Miles Championship for the "Macher" Shield over Wimbledon Common on January 31st, won by Allum with the double of scratch and handicap from Penny and Warboys, followed by mock comments on the race attributed to famous people. Printed result of 20 finishers (27 started); Penny's printed time 61 36 less 0 15 start does not match his printed handicap time 61 23. Saturday, January 31st, was the day chosen for 27 enthusiastic Club members to contest the possession of the "Macher" Shield over the usual 10 miles course round Wimbledon Common. The conditions were fairly good—though the ground was sodden after heavy rains and the runners had to face a steady wind as they came in from the Kingsmere. Bert Footer, the title holder, having had further trouble with his leg, was an enforced but enthusiastic onlooker, so the big struggle lay between our two County Champions. At the start, Dewberry, Warboys and Allum sprang into the lead and were joined by Jack Flower before reaching the "village"; Allum, however, soon moved into first position and maintained it the whole way, gradually but steadily increasing the lead. At the Kingsmere, Penny had come up to second place, about 70 yards behind; at the end of the first lap, the gap was enlarged to 150 yards; at 7 miles 250 and at the finish some 500 yards. Allum ran with that determination to win that is the secret of success in every race and it is evident that he has acquired the "winning habit." The handicapper's endeavour to restrain him from carrying off the handicap prize as well, again failed, and thus to have achieved within the space of a few weeks a double scratch and handicap win in Club championships is in itself an exceptional distinction. Penny was followed home closely by Warboys, who took third handicap prize, and Frank Webb, who failed only by a yard or two to catch his brother, received the second. The two Webbs were followed in by a couple of Flowers; Joe having made a slightly slower start which brought him 10th at 4 miles, when his brother was third. At 7 miles Jack was lying fifth, with Joe ninth, and they finished sixth and seventh. Carter, who came next, ran a good steady race, but dropped a couple of places in the second lap, which Fletcher picked up and finished close behind. Chorley ran well to finish 11th and Rollins and Eastman had a rare "dust up" down the straight, Rollins winning on the post. Dewberry, Duffett and Bayliss, with several others, thought that once round the course was enough and so were not included in the final reckoning. A rumour was heard in the dressing-room that the handicapper had got lost, but this of course was not so. Handicappers don't do that sort of thing ! From this race it is evident that the two Arthurs are going to set a fine example to our teams in the coming big races, and we trust they will be ably supported by their "Knights of the Round Table." * * * * * The following comments on the race by well-known people have been received :— Al Capone (on being told the result by Transatlantic 'phone) : "Gee ! Your boys sure are the slick goods and if they care to come over and join my racket, it's a darned sure thing nobody will get within 1760 yards of putting them 'on the spot.' " Sir Josiah Stamp (the eminent economist) says : "The sterling qualities of the Belgrave Harriers are clearly based on the right use of the Penny." Mr. Cherry Kearton, F.Z.S. : "After watching the antics of the deer in Richmond Park, I was amazed at the beauty in the motion of Allum's legs." Miss Amy Johnson : "I think Arthur is a dear." Mr. Alexander (Hon. Sec. Birchfield H.) : "The fine performances of Allum and the Belgrave Harriers leave us in SUSPENSE regarding the result of the 'National' and 'Brighton Relay.' " S.D. items.s: THE SOUTH OF THAMES CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the South of Thames Cross Country Championship at Windsor Great Park on February 14th: a weak Belgrave display, 10th team, with Frank Webb (36th) and H. J. Fletcher (45th) first home; individual winner W. A. Townsend (Swindon A.C.), team winners Herne Hill H. The South of Thames Cross Country Championship was held on February 14th at Windsor Great Park. It was a brilliant day, and conditions were more or less ideal for running. Yet in spite of this our team gave a lamentably weak display and greatly disappointed the supporters who made the journey. So far as watching the race was concerned it was hopeless as the runners disappeared from sight and unless one was prepared to trudge a mile and a half up the Long Walk one did not see them again until the finish. Even at the half-distance our boys were hopelessly placed and it speaks well for Frank Webb and H. J. Fletcher that they finished where they eventually did. Another to run well was R. G. Michael, one of our Juniors, who incidentally was only put in the team at the last moment. Of the others, well, they all appeared to be trying hard enough and so we must just put it down to temporary loss of form. RESULTS. 22 teams finished. 221 runners. m. s. 1. W. A.
