items.label: October 1931
items.sum: Humorous account of the club Social evening of 3 October 1931, at which four members in disguise performed as a troupe of dancing girls.
items.s: SH ! ! Humorous account of the club Social evening of 3 October 1931, at which four members in disguise performed as a troupe of dancing girls. On the evening of October 3rd, after the customary running and walking handicaps had been decided, we sat down to tea, which was to be followed by one of our very popular Social evenings. Tea finished, dancing held sway until the pièce de resistance was announced. For weeks it had been rumoured that we were to be entertained by one of the fairest troupes of feminine dancers that had ever embraced the Terpsichorean art—that we were to be charmed as Belgrave Harriers had never been charmed before—that it was a show we should remember years after senility had claimed us—a memory to cherish when one's grandchildren left one alone to ponder over the past. The "secret" had been whispered from ear to ear until it seemed everyone's sole desire to have a front seat and a good view. Our Social Hon. Secretary, with a laudable desire to prevent untoward incidents in the presence of such a talented collection of artistes, had, during the preceding week, extracted a promise from one of our more exuberant members, not to applaud too vociferously during the presentation ! And so it was with a keen sense of anticipation, and in a mood of suppressed excitement, that we heard the formal announcement : "The Nonsuch Girls will now entertain you." Six figures with Egyptian-styled head-dresses and shrouded in blankets, entered the Hall; and it was soon obvious that only two of the party were "genuine ladies," the other four being Tom Scrimshaw, Frank Webb, Len Rollins and Bert Footer ! The "real ladies," our friends the Misses Parsons, of the L.O.'s, tried valiantly to instil some idea of grace into the "Neverwere Girls," but their's was an impossible task ! Our four could have given Nervo and Knox a start and a beating, and for unrestrained irresponsibility they could not have been excelled. They were about about as graceful as a herd of elephants stampeding before a jungle fire; and as a spectacle—well ! Epstein should have been there to perpetuate it in stone, to be called "Girls Dancing" or "Souls in Torment"—whichever way you happen to view his art. And so this acrobatic orgy—this frenzy of anything but dancing—continued. If the grace and delicacy usually associated with dancing were missing, the "Neverwillbee Girls" made up for its absence by their realism and strength of purpose. The realistic way in which one of the four appeared to grind the face of Bertina (née Footer) into the flooring created a great impression, which was obvious on Bert's forehead for many days afterwards ! Rounds of applause greeted the final act; while strong men wept in silent mirth, and an encore was demanded. "Ben-Hur" was announced, and in came Footer, stripped to the waist (not looking in the least like a girl), borne by a human chariot. The chariot had not progressed very far before Footer decided to change his character, and emulated "Humpty-Dumpty" and "had a great fall" ! More applause ! Eventually it was possible to continue with real dancing, to the strains of the band which had been engaged; and later to listen to the excellent entertainment of the Brothers Gay and Billy Williams. It was very pleasing to see so many of our new members and their friends entering into the spirit of these Club Socials, which do so much to engender the Club spirit among our members. At 11 o'clock this very successful Social had to be brought to a close and the number of enquiries as to the next date was sufficient guarantee that all had enjoyed themselves to the utmost. * * * * * By the way, I had almost forgotten to give the cream of the joke ! The previously-mentioned member who, with a look of sweet innocence, had promised our Social Hon. Secretary to be on his best behaviour during the performance of the dancing girls, proved to be one of the "Nonsuch Girls" himself ! Imagine the feelings of our worthy Social organiser, who had even engaged a special dressing-room for the use of "the dancers from London," when familiar friends in unfamiliar garb presented themselves ! Who would be a Belgrave Hon. Secretary? And now a word to our four unrepentant masqueraders, who had been at great pains to blacken their eyelids and carmine their lips to give a voluptuous appearance. Next time, if there is one, spend a little time in moulding the leg muscles to accord with feminine fashion, and invest a little money in peroxide, or one of the proprietary articles which shout from the newspaper columns that they are able to remove superfluous hair in a few seconds ! items.sum: Report and result of the Ilford Relay on the road, 17 October 1931, won by Belgrave Harriers in a course record of 3hrs. 15min. 51sec.; the first-stage runner is printed T. C. Carter in the report and C. T. Carter in the table.
items.s: THE ILFORD RELAY RACE. Report and result of the Ilford Relay on the road, 17 October 1931, won by Belgrave Harriers in a course record of 3hrs. 15min. 51sec.; the first-stage runner is printed T. C. Carter in the report and C. T. Carter in the table. On Saturday, October 17th, we had a team entered for the Ilford Relay Race on the road, the course comprising 10 laps of about 3¾ miles, around an area known as Gordon Fields. There was an entry of eight teams, and the "Bels" proved to be the ultimate winners, beating the course record held by Ilford A.C. by nearly 7 minutes ! The day was somewhat dull and inclined to rain, with a troublesome wind, which was noticed when the runners came to the new arterial road, where there was open land on either side. The first stage was taken by T. C. Carter, for the "Bels," who ran a good race; handing over second, behind Burridge (Poly.), who clocked 19 min., Carter doing 19 min. 17 sec. Frank Webb took the next relay and kept us in second position despite a fine effort of Griffiths (North London H.) half a mile from home. With a fine run of 19 min. 18 sec. Sid. Warboys took us into first place, this distance being shorter than Sid. usually likes. From this relay to the end the Club were supreme, going further ahead at each stage; Dewberry, Joe and Jack Flower and Robertshaw, in the order, all running their course in fine style, Jack Flower doing third fastest time for us. W. H. Gross's (Ilford) record of 18 min. 50 sec. was all but broken by Footer who, with a grand effort of 19 min., equalled Burridges' (Poly. H.) time. The ninth relay was taken by Penny, who also ran a good stage in 19 min. 1 sec. Oh ! that second ! Arthur Allum took tenth relay for us and it was pleasing to see that his ankle trouble had improved to the extent of his doing 19 min. 31sec. He said later in the dressing room, "Gee ! only 19 min. 31 sec.; blooming slow !" That's the worst of these Internationals, they can't go slow ! The brighter side came when the boys were assembled (complete with self-appointed trainers) to be filmed for the Astoria Circuit Cinemas. So, not content with being the best runners, they now aspire to be leading men to Greta Garbo ! Altogether a great day and our congratulations are due to the team for its good work, the times shown being very good when we consider that our men had to make all their own running, except, perhaps, over the first two stages. items.sum: Announcement of the formation of The Bells Amateur Athletic Club, open only to first-claim Belgrave members with a Middlesex qualification, so that they can enter Middlesex County team championships.
items.s: THE NEW CLUB. Announcement of the formation of The Bells Amateur Athletic Club, open only to first-claim Belgrave members with a Middlesex qualification, so that they can enter Middlesex County team championships. The anomalous position in which those members of the Club with a Middlesex qualification have found themselves on the day of the County Team Championships—that of onlooker, or competitor for individual honours—has in the past been somewhat ironical, inasmuch that amongst those individual competitors and onlookers there has been the nucleus of a team capable, it has been thought, of putting up a creditable performance in any County Championship. Past performances by individual members, in the cross-country championships particularly, have not only warranted this thought but have enlivened the thoughts and activities of observant club officials (not exclusively our own) to almost unlimited hopes and possibilities. This, perhaps, is not to be wondered at, since to a club whose team is just missing honours, possibly because of its tail being too weak to wag, the sight of a number of individual entrants from a club which is precluded from affiliation to the Middlesex County must appear somewhat galling; especially when it is remembered that those individual entrants might have been helping that club to victory by virtue of second-claim membership. Whatever may be pros. and cons. of second-claim membership, the opinions of the Middlesex members may be reflected in the fact that they have, hitherto, generally elected to run as individuals. This order of things, we learn, may now be changed, and in the forthcoming County Championships we shall, in all probability, see the Middlesex members of the club represented in their county event as a team. This change has come about by the formation of a club registered in the name of "The Bells Amateur Athletic Club." Founded specifically for the purpose of enabling members of the Belgrave Harriers, with a Middlesex County qualification, to compete in Middlesex County team championships (running and walking), membership of the club is open to such members only. That is to say, an applicant for membership must have a Middlesex County qualification and must be a first-claim member of the Belgrave Harriers. The Club will participate in Middlesex County team championships only; and, we learn, it will be considered contrary to the spirit of the rules of the club for any member of the club to compete in any open or individual event other than in the name of his first-claim club. The formation of such a club such as is now founded has been, on and off, the topic of discussion within the club over recent years; but for divers reasons it has not until now matured. Now that it is in being, we sincerely wish it every success and trust that in the sphere of its activities it will honour well the name which it bears, the significance of which cannot fail to be appreciated in the present world of athletics. All enquiries to the Hon. Secretary, W. G. Webb, 11 Birchwood Road, S.W.17. W. G. Webb W. G. Webb Hon. items.label: October 1931
items.sum: K. B. O'Kell explains the new Belgrave points scheme, which awards points towards prizes for 4th, 5th and 6th places in club handicaps, with its rules, grouping of events and worked examples.
items.s: THE "BELGRAVE" POINTS SCHEME. K. B. O'Kell explains the new Belgrave points scheme, which awards points towards prizes for 4th, 5th and 6th places in club handicaps, with its rules, grouping of events and worked examples. Introduced September 24th, 1931. Adopted by Belgrave Harriers Committee on October 1st, 1931, and put into operation by Belgrave Harriers on October 3rd, 1931. Before giving all details of the above scheme, there are two observations I should like to make. During the period the scheme was in process of construction, I was anticipating it being put into practice next May. However, your Committee, seeing extra benefits and attractions to members, decided to put it into operation at once, and so Cross-Country Runners and Road Walkers are now competing for the extra facilities available. The second concerns my friend, David Bramley, to whom I am very much indebted for his suggestions and figures, which contributed to make the scheme so comprehensive. Object Of Scheme. The Club's chief interest is the encouragement of Athletics, and it is to our young promising members that we look for our future success and fame. Therefore, we desire to attract and interest our persevering novices and offer them a little reward should they not have the good fortune to get amongst the first three prize winners during the season. Equally so will all those members who continually enter in Club events and fail to "get up," derive the same consolation. To attain this object the Club are awarding points to the men who finish in the 4th, 5th and 6th position in Club handicaps. The present prize arrangements will not be affected. Prizes won under the additional scheme will be presented at the end of the season. Rules Of The Scheme. 1. Scheme applicable to Club Handicaps only. 2. A prize winner (1st three in Club handicaps) is immediately disqualified. 3. A member cannot win two prizes under this scheme—one prize only. 4. Races will be "grouped" and points can only be scored in own group. Different Group scores cannot be amalgamated. 5. Club Championship placings do not count in scheme, or disqualify. 6. Prizes awarded as follows :— 1st prize Value if runner scores ... 240 pts. 2nd ,, ,, ,, ,, ... 120 pts. 3rd ,, ,, ,, ,, ... 60 pts. How The Scheme Works. The Committee are allocating 420 points for competition to each group. After much experimenting on various figures and percentage basis, we found the figures 240 our most satisfactory "constant" to base the points for competition. Now refer to rule 4. In grouping races we will count all the 100's and 75 yards Group "A," all 220, 300 and 440 yards Group "B," 880 yards Group "C," Field Events Group "D," Miles Group "E," Walks Group "F." To determine the points necessary for each group we divide the number of race in each Group into 240. Example : If there are six races in a group during the season, your result is 40. That gives the points for 4th position. Now, we reduce in the same ration as awards, viz., 4—2—1. So for your 5th position the points will be 20 and for the 6th position 10. In cases where a decimal result is found, we make the number up to even figures, as in the case of 7 events in a group. Here your actual points are 34.28, 17.14 and 8.57. Ratio the same, but we make these 36, 18 and 9 to eliminate decimals. You will see, if a man gets 4th in all the events in his group, he scores 240 points; if he gets 5th, 120 points, and if he ran 6th in each race he would score 60 points. Details (Example : Group of 6 races). Under the scheme it is possible in each group for three different combinations to succeed. As above, three men would win all the points and prizes. Alternatives are 3 at 120 points and 1 at 60 points, or 7 at 60 points. For your own interest, write down 6 columns of figures : 40, 20, 10 and cross out, as imaginary positions are won in a race, and you will get the above combinations. In cases where the group number of races is not 6, the points may not all be absorbed in these combinations. These revert to the Club. If a man gets 4th, 5th and 6th he will score 90 points, and the next race he wins. Under rule 2 he is eliminated and forfeits his points. So you see the scheme is practically an insurance against not winning a prize—one of its may attractions. The points forfeited are presented back to the club, as they cannot be allocated to anyone else. It is possible for nearly all the points in each group to be won and then forfeited by men who run up into the first three positions during the season. One of the attractive points of the scheme is the "flexibility" of the scoring. It is governed entirely by the men themselves. With perseverance and a moderate amount of pluck in racing, a man will find himself among the scoring fairly consistently. Also, the Club are "competitors" for the points. To put the scheme in a nutshell, the Club says, "Here are 420 points for each group; take what you can, and what you leave we receive back with many thanks." It will be seen that the scheme will call for more intense competition, because once a man has scored he will naturally endeavour to increase his total; it is also anticipated that increased entries will materialise and members be encouraged to keep in training right up to the end of season. General Comments. Points scored will not incur any handicap penalty. Prizes will be the same value as awarded in our Club events. Points scored at each Club meeting, and totals as accumulated, will be published in the "Gazette" each month. During the winter season there are 6 running and 5 walking events. For the runs the points are 40, 20 and 10, and for the walks 48, 24 and 12 for 4th, 5th and 6th positions respectively. In the opening walk 2 members who were 4th and 5th, viz. : J. N. Thomas and C. H. Speechley, are typical examples of Club stalwarts who are recompensed by the scheme. If Thomas gets 6th in the next handicap he will score 60 points and be assured of at least a 3rd prize and have three more opportunities of increasing his total. If you have a friend who thinks he cannot run or throw a javelin, tell him about the Belgrave scheme, which may encourage him! Very few organisations cater for their members as Belgrave do and we claim to be the first Club in England to make awards to the first six men in our competitions; therefore induce your pal to join Belgrave. The scheme, being very original, will only be proved after a season's trial, when adjustments or an increase of awards may be advantageous. Any comments, criticisms or suggestions for improving the scheme will be very welcome and receive the immediate attention of the Committee. Any questions of particular interest will be published and answered in the next issue of the "Gazette." K. B. O'Kell K. B. items.label: October 1931
items.sum: Walking notes correcting last issue's record of President J. B. Belchamber in the Brighton Walk, listing Belgrave finishers in the 1931 London to Brighton Walk (won by T. W. Green), and announcing the walking points events and the Twelfth Annual Open Walk on November 28th.
e: London to Brighton and Back Walk
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes correcting last issue's record of President J. B. Belchamber in the Brighton Walk, listing Belgrave finishers in the 1931 London to Brighton Walk (won by T. W. Green), and announcing the walking points events and the Twelfth Annual Open Walk on November 28th. In our last issue some incorrect information was given regarding the past performances of our worthy President, Mr. J. B. Belchamber, and we now hasten to rectify this, and also enlarge upon other details given in our last number. Jimmy was second in the London to Brighton and back (104 miles) race in 1921 (not 1926, as stated last month) and the winner of the race was E. C. Horton, the 12 hours' record holder. Only two of our President's performances in the Brighton Walk were quoted in our previous issue, and we now append a full list of his placings in this historic event, which illustrate his wonderful consistency :— September, 1920—3rd. September, 1922—4th. May, 1923—4th. September, 1923—5th. September, 1924—4th. This is indeed a very fine record, and Jimmy also found time to be placed third in the A.A.A. 7 Miles Championship of 1920; and to win the first Sussex Road Walking Championship in 1923. It will be seen that our President has set a very high standard for us to live up to and we should all be glad to attain the same level of consistency and performance. * * * * * It is now possible to give the placings and times of all our men to finish in the London—Brighton Walk, on September 12th. They are as follows :— * * * * * We are very glad to see Bob McMullen out again and hope he will soon attain some of his former skill, which caused him to be looked upon as one of the best walkers in the country. It is very gratifying to see so many new faces in the walking ranks, many of whom show distinct promise. The novices of to-day are the champions of a few years hence and we can never have too many. Any reader having a friend thinking of taking up walking as a sport would be well advised to persuade him to start now, when we have such a fine crowd of beginners. * * * * * The five events to form the Walking Group in "The Belgrave Points Scheme," as explained elsewhere, are as follows :— Oct. 3—5 Miles Handicap (already decided). Nov. 28—Belgrave Open 7 Miles Race. Dec. 26—3 Miles Handicap. Jan. 30—Sealed Handicap in 10 Miles Championship. April 23—Sealed Handicap in 20 Miles Championship. Points will be awarded to the 4th, 5th and 6th men in the above events, with the exception of our Club Open event (Nov. 28th), when the points will be allocated to the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Club men on handicap time, irrespective of any team or individual award which might be gained in the Open race. * * * * * Our Twelfth Annual Open Walk, over the usual 7 miles course, will be held on November 28th, when it is hoped that every active walker will enter. Last season our event attracted the largest entry of any race in the country, with the possible exception of Championship events, and we are eager to surpass even this. Five Belgrave teams competed last year (probably another record for an Open event) and it would be a fine achievement to improve upon this. Belgrave men are asked to let the Hon. Secretary have their entries before the official closing date, in order to facilitate matters. A large crowd of Belgrave supporters would also be very welcome on November 28th, so make a note of the date. All enquiries to A. A. Harley, 39 Roxburgh Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. h. m. s. 1. T. W. items.sum: Belgrave's walking fixtures for November and December 1931, including the club Open Walk, a race with the Surrey Walking Club, a match with the Metropolitan Police A.A., the Junior Seven Miles Championship and the Boxing Day handicap.
items.s: FUTURE WALKING FIXTURES. Belgrave's walking fixtures for November and December 1931, including the club Open Walk, a race with the Surrey Walking Club, a match with the Metropolitan Police A.A., the Junior Seven Miles Championship and the Boxing Day handicap. November 14th. Enfield A.C. Open Walk. We shall be represented in this event and hope to meet with our usual amount of success therein. November 28th. Our own Open Walk at Wimbledon. Some comments on this walk are included in our Walking Notes, but I should like to reiterate two points : (1) It is hoped every active Belgravian walker will enter; (2) Send in your entries a few days before the official closing date and so help the poor Secretary. The usual special prize will be awarded to the first Belgrave Harrier not gaining any other award, and readers are reminded that this is one of the events included in the "Belgrave Points Scheme," details of which appear elsewhere. December 5th. As the date fixed by the Surrey Walking Club for their annual Banstead Walk clashed with that chosen by Enfield A.C. for their Open event, we have had to arrange an alternative fixture with the ""Swastika" bearers this year. It will take place on the above date from "The Blue Anchor," South Croydon, and take the form of a race over their Croydon to Wickham and back course, approximately nine miles. It is hoped that all our walkers will support this fixture as it is on an "all-to-score" basis. December 12th. The same comment applies to this date when we meet the Metropolitan Police A.A. over their course at Imber Court. Our runners also have a fixture at Imber Court on this day, and it is hoped that a good number will stop to tea and the dance which follows in the M.P.A.A.'s well-appointed quarters. December 19th. The Junior Seven Miles Championship for the "O. Horwood" Cup (Holder, F. W. Thorn) will be held on this day at Wimbledon, with the usual sealed handicap in conjunction. A good race should be witnessed this year to see who shall hold the trophy for the ensuing year, and the minor placings should also be keenly contested, and give us an idea of our Junior prospects. December 26th. Boxing Day. The usual Three Miles Handicap will take place in Battersea Park. Our distance men will be tackling the "Godstone" course (18¾ miles) with, it is hoped, the same success as last year. All enquiries, entries, or requests for further information should be addressed to the Walking Hon. Secretary. F. W. Thorn F. W. Thorn holder of the "O. items.label: October 1931
items.sum: The Running Hon. Secretary previews the November and December 1931 cross-country fixtures, including the South of Thames Junior race, inter-club races, away fixtures at Hanwell and Cobham, and the Surrey Youths race.
items.s: FORTHCOMING FIXTURES. The Running Hon. Secretary previews the November and December 1931 cross-country fixtures, including the South of Thames Junior race, inter-club races, away fixtures at Hanwell and Cobham, and the Surrey Youths race. The Cross Country season is now getting into its stride, and so far the attendances at Wimbledon have been well up to standard. I only hope that our away fixtures will be as well supported. A pleasing feature has been the numbers and also the promise of our Junior members, and on the form displayed it looks as if we are in for a good season. Keep it up, boys, and I can see us even yet winning the Southern, a task which bristles with difficulties in view of the formidable opposition which we have to encounter. On November 7th we entertain our old friends and rivals, namely, Croydon Harriers, Mitcham A.C. and Epsom Harriers, to a social run, followed by a still more social evening. November 14th sees the first of the Open Cross Country races in which our Club is interested. This is the South of Thames "Junior" race, which will held at Epsom Downs, as in previous years. The term Junior applies only to ability and not to age, and we hope to enter as many teams as possible. Teams are composed of eight men to run, with four to score. On November 21st we have, at Wimbledon, the second of the Inter-Club races, over 5 miles, between Thames Valley H., Ashcombe A.C. and ourselves. A Sealed Handicap open to all Club members will be decided in conjunction with this race, and entries should be handed or sent to me at once. The 28th is the day of the Club Open Walk to be held at Wimbledon, and in consequence of the large entry received and our restricted dressing accommodation, I should like it to be understood that no runners will be allowed out from St. John's Hall on this day. We have instead arranged for two away fixtures to be held and the members can please themselves which of the two they can best support. One is a 5 miles race with our friends the Ealing Harriers, at Hanwell, and I may say that all members can be sure of a good time after the race with our sporting opponents. The other fixture is with the Cobham A.C. at Cobham, and in view of the limited strength of this club, I should like if possible for most of our Junior members to support this fixture. Both of the above venues are easily accessible and I trust we shall have a good muster of the "Bels." at each one. In view of the Surrey Youths 3 miles Cross Country race which is to be held at Wimbledon on December 5th, our Juniors under 18 years of age, and with a Surrey qualification, could not do better than have a run at Cobham, where they will meet opponents of their own ability and age. Anyone who is eligible for this race and would like to run, if they will kindly hand me their name for the purpose of making up our team, I shall be greatly obliged. All entries and enquiries to E. items.s: OUR "OPEN." Report and result of Belgrave's Twelfth Annual Open Walk, won by C. W. Hyde of Enfield A.C. from T. W. Green, with the individual handicap won by H. A. Borrett of Essex Beagles. The entry for our Twelfth Annual Open Walk was a little disappointing when compared with that received in the past few years, but there is little doubt that the industrial situation is affecting Sport, and causing many athletes to limit their racing activities on the score of expense. Our actual entry was 157, the largest yet received for an Open Walk this season, and of these 35 were Belgrave walkers. Eighteen teams were nominated, including four of our own and three of the Surrey Walking Club. The race was started by our President, Mr. J. B. Belchamber, and the three walkers with starts of less than a minute were soon in the lead. They were Hyde (Enfield A.C., scratch), and our own Fletcher (20 secs.) and Green (30 secs.). Fletcher suffered disqualification before a mile had been covered, and the fight for individual honours resolved itself into a "ding-dong" struggle, with the "Bel." eventually having to take second place after a very fine effort. Joe King walked probably his best "seven" yet and finished fourth, but our team again had to take second place to Enfield A.C. The performance of Harry Churcher, one of our individual entrants, in finishing sixth was very creditable, and he will assuredly be a tower of strength to our team in due course. A glace at the scratch result is very heartening from our point of view. We had five in 10, 15 in 42, and 30 of the 122 to finish.—something to be proud of. Our "Juniors" show continued improvement and should be prominent when the Championship is decided next March. The individual Handicap resulted as follows :— 1.—H. A. Borrett (Essex Beagles ) all 8m. 20s., 52m. 29s. 2.—S. M. Pauley (Poole W. & A.C.) all 7m., 53m. 28s. 3.—L. Barrett (Enfield A.C.) all 3m. 20s., 53m. 33s. One of our promising young walkers, H. Latter, with 8m. 30s. allowance, finished fourth, and Tommy Green was sixth. Our "D" team (Redgrave, A. H. Field, Larman and Harley) were third in the team handicap. Other placings, etc., appear below. We are glad to be able to express, through these columns, our appreciation of the efforts of the Officials in helping to ensure a successful race; and to the competitors for their much-appreciated support. items.label: December 1931
items.sum: Walking notes praising Enfield A.C.'s improvement while showing that Belgrave's walkers had not declined, with entry figures and the club make-up of the first 42 in Belgrave's Open Walk at Wimbledon.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes praising Enfield A.C.'s improvement while showing that Belgrave's walkers had not declined, with entry figures and the club make-up of the first 42 in Belgrave's Open Walk at Wimbledon. The outstanding feature of this Season's Walks has been the wonderful improvement of the Enfield A.C. On three occasions we have narrowly suffered defeat at their hands, and they have undoubtedly, a team of which they may well be proud. We take pleasure in congratulating Hyde and Co. upon their recent wins. During past years they have been placed second to us on many occasions; and it is only meet that they should have their share of success—the reward of perseverance. On each occasion our men have extended the Enfield walkers to the utmost and every time they meet us they can be assured of a stern, sporting struggle. In view of our recent defeats, many members, in the "leg-pulling" mood which seems inseparable from the Belgrave character, have asked me : "What's the matter with our walkers?" The answer is, of course, "Nothing!" Our team has not deteriorated one iota, in fact, it has shown improvement, as the following details prove. When winning the "Berman Cup" last year we scored 31 points. This year we scored 28 points, an improvement of three points, but were placed second. Again, in the Enfield A.C. Open of last year, we had an easy win with 31 points. This year we scored one point less and were narrowly beaten. Obviously, therefore, our men are as good as ever, and in point of fact show a slight improvement. * * * * * It is when we look a little farther than the first four men that our wealth of talent displays itself. This is, of course, the true strength of any club. Its numbers, enthusiasm, sportsmanship and standard of ability are the true index to a club's pre-eminence; and we need have no misgivings on these points. * * * * * 23 of the 138 entries received by the Highgate H. came from the Belgrave Harriers; and we had 21 men (of 148) in the Enfield Open Event. These figures testify to our strength of numbers, when many clubs have difficulty in fielding a full team of eight men. * * * * * 35 of our members (comprising four teams) entered our own Open Walk at Wimbledon, out of a total entry of 157. A remarkable feature of the result is that, despite the fact that we had three "A" team men ruled out, there were no less than 15 Belgrave walkers in the first 42 positions, a proportion of something better than one in three! This clearly indicates a high general standard among our men. * * * * * It will probably interest our readers to know the composition of the first 42 referred to above. They are as follows :— Belgrave Harriers 15 Enfield A.C. 6 Highgate H. 5 Surrey W.C. 4 Polytechnic H. 3 Cambridge H. and Essex Beagles 2 each. items.s: BELGRAVE HARRIERS v. METROPOLITAN POLICE A.C. Report of the cross-country match against the Metropolitan Police A.C. over a shortened 5-mile course on October 24th, won easily by a mainly Junior Belgrave team though W. F. Butler of the Police finished first. The printed Police team score includes positions 15 and 16, which the result gives to Belgrave men. On October 24th we entertained the Metropolitan Police A.C. to a race over our 5 miles course. In view of circumstances over which we had no control, it was decided to omit the crossing of Beverley Brook and so the course was shortened accordingly. The "Bels" team was, with two exceptions, composed of our Junior men and they proved easy winners over the men in blue. The Police had, however, some consolation in providing the first man home, W. F. Butler, who was closely followed by Frank Tame. The latter is exhibiting excellent form in his first season over the country with our Club. F. J. Summerfield and A. F. Mitchell also showed fine form and seeing that Mitchell is an absolute newcomer to the game he should, if he decides to stick to it, prove a worthy member of the "Bels" teams. m. s. 1. W. F. The first Inter-Club race versus Thames Valley H. and Ashcombe A.C. was held at T.V.H.'s new headquarters at Cranford on October 31st. A course of 5 miles had been laid over some sporty country, although it included a large amount of obstacles. From the word "Go," Arthur Penny made every post a winning one, and although Bert Footer tried hard to get on terms, he just failed to do so. Arthur Allum also showed he is getting back to form, and our three men did well in beating Vic Harman of Slough A.C., who was running for the T.V.H. The team race resulted in an easy win for the "Bels." and after the race, a Tea and Social evening was held which our boys greatly appreciated. m. s. 1. A. W. Penny B 29 45 2. H. E. Footer B 30 00 3. items.s: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES "JUNIOR." Report and result of the Junior South of the Thames Cross-country Team Race at Epsom on November 14th, where Belgrave's "A" Team finished 4th behind Portsmouth R.N. and R.M., Mitcham A.C. and Reading A.C. On Saturday, November 14th, the Junior South of the Thames Cross-country Team Race was held at Epsom in good weather for a change, the course also being in good condition. Our Teams got away to a good start, but after the first lap we realised it was not Belgrave's day. Our "A" Team eventually finished 4th, the same position as last year. Our first man home finished in the 9th position, which is quite a good performance, but we all know Norman is capable of doing better. Probably he is saving it for the Senior! A. F. Mitchell raised our hopes in the first lap when he was right with the leaders, but it was his unlucky day, for he had a bad attack of stitch which put him right back in the field. Two newcomers scored in our "A" Team, namely, Summerfield and Taylor. They have very quickly settled down to cross-country racing and will undoubtedly prove a big asset to the Club in the near future. An old friend and stalwart, "Doug." Sloper, has shown a vast improvement in his racing this year, the result, I understand, of regular training. All our teams finished and have assuredly benefited by the experience gained in this race, and if all members follow Sloper's lead and train regularly we shall have a good crowd of reserves to back up our Seniors and do credit to the Club in the future. items.s: INTER-CLUB RACE v. THAMES VALLEY H. AND ASHCOMBE A.C. Report and result of the second inter-club race against Thames Valley H. and Ashcombe A.C. at Wimbledon on November 21st, won by Arthur Allum, with a Sealed Handicap won by Doug. Sloper; the printed Belgrave score of 54 pts. equals its first nine placings (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12), not ten. The second of the series of inter-club races was held on November 21st—the date also fixed for the North of the Thames Race. As Thames Valley H. had two teams competing in this race, their team at Wimbledon was below full strength, while Ashcombe A.C. have often put much stronger teams in the field. This being so, our runners, despite the absence of Footer and Penny, gained a ludicrously easy win, as the appended result shows. Arthur Allum proved that he is getting back to the form which gained him International honours, by winning this race in very easy fashion. Our Sealed Handicap in conjunction resulted in a popular win for "Doug." Sloper—his first prize. The younger Coleman was placed second and R. G. Goldsworthy, an improving young runner, third. Pos. items.s: MATCH v. COBHAM A.C. Report and result of a cross-country match against Cobham A.C. at Cobham, which Belgrave won 31 pts. to 51, led home by Carter and Robertshaw. The team met at Clapham Junction and a merry party travelled by luxury coach to Cobham—which was just as well, as the quarters of our hosts are situated at some distance from the station. We received a warm welcome and found Cobham A.C. to consist of a group of fine young sportsmen, who, we trust, will have every success. Carter and Robertshaw soon took the lead, which they retained to the finish. The course proved to be a sporting one with plenty of mud and water, and we managed to run out winners. After the race we soaked the mud off, bought out the village store, and devoured our supplies on the way home. C.W.L. m. s. 1. C. T. Carter 33 3 2. A. Robertshaw 33 26 3. W. Ranger 33 32 4. A. J. items.s: RACE v. EALING HARRIERS. Report and result of a cross-country fixture at Ealing, where J. E. Flower, S. H. Warboys and F. R. Webb tied for first but Ealing Harriers won on team packing, 145 pts. to 163. Once again we had the pleasure of being visitors to Ealing, this occasion for a Cross-Country fixture. We had 16 men supporting this fixture and after taking our other attractions into consideration, this number was quite satisfactory, the home club turning out 19 men. The course consisted of two laps of the cinder track and then out into the country. J. E. Flower and S. H. Warboys soon jumped into the lead and the remainder of the team seemed to be backing them up fairly well. Several of our men ran in rubber shoes and after a stretch of country had been covered they encountered a very slippery and muddy path. Many of our chaps came to grief and someone remarked that they looked like a troupe of trapeze artistes walking along a tight-rope. J. E. Flower (after losing the trail several times) appeared in sight with S. H. Warboys and F. R. Webb, which was certainly very encouraging. Then followed C. Penny, no doubt with strict instructions from his brother, Arthur, to uphold the family prestige. Well run, C. Penny! But this is where Ealing stepped in. They took command of the middle of the race and with good team packing kept our boys out. We must therefore heartily congratulate Ealing on a very fine run and extend to them our best wishes for further successes and good luck. m. s. 1. S. H. Warboys 28 54 J. E. Flower 28 54 F. R. items.label: December 1931
items.sum: Running section fixture notes for December 1931 and January 1932: the Boxing Day meeting, social runs, the Surrey Championships, the Surrey Junior Championship and the Club 10 miles Championship for the Macher Shield.
items.s: FORTHCOMING FIXTURES. Running section fixture notes for December 1931 and January 1932: the Boxing Day meeting, social runs, the Surrey Championships, the Surrey Junior Championship and the Club 10 miles Championship for the Macher Shield. The results of our various Inter-Club races during the past month have been very encouraging, and a great feature has been the improved form shown by some of our new members. The old school have also proved themselves to be in fine fettle and the only doubt is whether they can maintain this form until next February. As the song says, "Time alone will tell," but there is every indication that we are causing a little heart fluttering in the opposition camps, which at least is something to be proud of. December 26th, we have our annual Boxing Day meeting at Battersea Park Track. Handicaps, open to all Club members, will be held at the following distances: 120 yards, 2 Miles Run and 3 Miles Walk. This has always been a popular meeting, giving as it does a chance for our track members to make an appearance, and also providing a spot of speed work for our distance men. Points, in connection with the Club Points scheme, will count for the 4th, 5th and 6th places in each of the above events. Entries (1/- each event) should be sent in at once to the Section Hon. Sec., and new members will help the Handicapper by sending along a form showing their last performances. Kindly note that entries positively close on December 22nd. On January 2nd we have a social run at Epsom Downs with the Epsom H., Croydon H. and Mitcham A.C. Dressing room will be in the Grandstand, and in view of the fact that the Surrey Championship will be held here a week afterwards, all prospective team men will do well to turn up and have a run over the surrounding country. January 9th is County Championship Day, and so far as the Club is concerned the Surrey race over 7 miles at Epsom Downs is the one which claims our attention. We have held the trophy for the past three years and with our men at present displaying fine form, should place our name on the Cup once again. Arthur Penny was the individual winner last year, and after his great win at Cambridge should once more lead the field home. We should like to see plenty of supporters present. Epsom is not a long way out, and vocal encouragement can go a long way towards making a successful team, as many clubs can testify. On the 16th we are visiting Mitcham A.C.'s headquarters at Peacock Farm, Morden, for a social run with the local club, Epsom H. and Croydon H. A Tea and Social evening will follow the run, and I trust our members will turn up in good numbers. January 23rd is a busy day for both competitors and officials. On the active side we have a social run with the Herne Hill H. and 2nd Bn. Grenadier Guards at Wimbledon. We have also a race fixture at Coventry to which we hope to send a strong team, and in addition there is the Surrey County 5 miles Junior Championship at Imber Court, Thames Ditton. The Junior race is open to members with a Surrey qualification and who are over 18 and under 21 years of age on the day of the race. Will members who would like to run for the Club kindly let me have their names as soon as possible. On January 30th we have the Club 10 miles C.C. Championship for the Macher Shield (Holder, A. Allum). A Sealed Handicap will be held in conjunction with this race and points will be scored as usual for the first three, outside the placed men, in the handicap. As this is the last Club race before the Open Championships all members who wish to be considered for inclusion in the Club teams should turn out in this event. As in previous years a fine race will be seen, and with our men all fit and well it would be a plucky man who would forecast the winner of this race. All entries and enquiries to E. A. items.label: December 1931
items.sum: Humorous club gossip notes by "Unique" on Ken O'Kell's prize-scheme, the record-breaking Round Ilford Relay team and Tommy Green's walking pace.
items.s: ODDS AND ENDS. Humorous club gossip notes by "Unique" on Ken O'Kell's prize-scheme, the record-breaking Round Ilford Relay team and Tommy Green's walking pace. "Up the Bels!"—over 600, all tolled. * * * * * Doubtless most of those members present at the A.G.M. fully understood Ken O'Kell's proposed prize-scheme for triers. I should like to suggest that he completes all arrangements by writing a fitting song, something after this style:— "There ought to be a Belgrave Saving Time, So I could save those points of mine, Until the pound's worth more in foreign clime ——" Enough said! Let us hope that all of our prizes are of British Manufacture. * * * * * No doubt most of you read of our team's splendid victory in the Round Ilford Relay Race, when we beat the record by 6 mins. 35 secs. I take this opportunity of congratulating those who formed the team, for each man "pulled his weight" and proved himself to be a Teddy Brown ——. Sorry! I meant to say "a good all-round performer." * * * * * An enthusiastic member of our Club ventured to suggest that we make an application to exhibit our hero, Tommy Green, in the Lord Mayor's Show of 1932! This is all very well in theory, but I am afraid that Tommy would catch cold if he walked at the pace of the procession; on the other hand, if he walked at his own pace, he might cover the course two or three times while the Lord Mayor and guests partake of lunch. Doubtless, here is a chance for some of our budding inventors to shine. What we want is a stand, or shall we call it an exhibition platform on wheels, which travels against Tommy's walking at the rate of about 7 miles per hour. items.label: December 1931
items.sum: Humorous piece on bathing after runs at the Wimbledon Common headquarters, with a mock-serious tale of Mr. F——'s bucket and a closing verse.
items.s: OUR BATHS. Humorous piece on bathing after runs at the Wimbledon Common headquarters, with a mock-serious tale of Mr. F——'s bucket and a closing verse. Let us consider for a moment this question of bathing. Opinion would seem to be sharply divided as to the desirability of the habit. On the one hand, we have those ardent hygienists who bath themselves immediately on rising, after breakfast, before lunch, after lunch, before tea, after tea and two or three times more during the course of the night, and on the other we have that school of thought which declares that only dirty people wash. Be this as it may, however, it is certain that he who would be a runner must, loathsome as the prospect may seem, splash himself with a little water at least once a year—say Good Friday, for on that day it behoves us all to be good and Fridays are proverbially unlucky. Moreover, nothing is more detrimental to one's social status to exude an aroma of stale oil and sweat which, to put it kindly, compares unfavourably with the more nauseating denizens of the Zoological Society's Gardens. Since a bath, then, is so necessary to the sensitive runner, let us consider the plight of the perspiring Belgravian who, taking his weekly trot over the Common, and having, perhaps, stopped now and then to admire the beauties of nature, arrives back late to find that about 500 screaming club-mates have been collecting little bits of Wimbledon Common, removing them reverently and placing them in the baths provided for the purpose. If he is wise he will have brought a shovel, with which he will then be able to make a hole large enough to extract a little water, sufficient to give him a pleasantly damp sensation. The composition of the water, again, gives rise to a certain amount of ribald speculation among our more unseemly members. While there is a possibility of its being collected weekly from the Brook (so deservedly unpopular among the die-hard once-a-year onlys), it can be stated authoritatively that there are no grounds for the widespread belief that it is made up solely from the remains of last week's tea. We take the opportunity here of relating the following sad incident which we are informed actually occurred recently after a mid-week run. Too much reliance, however, cannot be placed on our informant's veracity, and everyone knows how the atmosphere of Chelsea stimulates the imagination of the artistic story-teller. It appears that Mr. F——, who, of course, is not a big man, is in the habit of bathing in a bucket. In order to gratify this whim he takes his own bucket with him wherever he goes, and we believe that on his annual visit to Margate they are inseparable. On the evening in question, then, Mr. F—— returned from his run full of lively expectations of a pleasant swim, only to find that Mr. C—— was using his (Mr. F——'s) unusual bath. Incensed with rage at the insult to his property, Mr. F—— peremptorily ordered Mr. C—— to get out. Mr. C——'s reply was regrettable. Then Mr. F—— trembled so much with anger that he fell from the bench into a bath in which there was at least six inches of the liquid previously referred to. His sudden disappearance was not noticed and he would undoubtedly have drowned had not another Belgravian, in searching for his soap, washed him up on a small islet. We are glad to learn, however, that peace has now been restored by Mr. C—— promising to present Mr. F—— with a brand-new marble bucket for Christmas, while Mr. F——, not to be outdone in expressions of good-will, has promised in return a supply of Antipon. * * * * * And so, you see, everything ended O.K. But, nevertheless, I would like just to say, That little Bert Footer was kissing Tom Cotton, While Tom murmured, "Bert dear, the past is forgotten." * * * * * And that will be all for the present. items.sum: Club notes congratulating Tommy Green, Arthur Allum and Len Fletcher, regretting the loss of the Surrey cross-country title, welcoming new members and discussing the Surrey Inter-Counties selections.
e: London Business Houses 7 Miles Walk Championship
items.s: Club notes congratulating Tommy Green, Arthur Allum and Len Fletcher, regretting the loss of the Surrey cross-country title, welcoming new members and discussing the Surrey Inter-Counties selections. Congratulations to Tommy Green upon his second win in the historic "Godstone" Walk; and to the team which secured premier honours. * * * * * Also to Arthur Allum upon retaining the Middlesex Cross-country Championship, which was held at Northolt. Arthur appears to have regained the form which placed him among the best half-dozen men in the Country last season, and this year he seems destined for further honours. * * * * * Also to Len Fletcher on winning the London Business Houses 7 Miles Walk Championship for the third year in succession. * * * * * The Surrey Cross-Country Championship was wrested from us this year by Surrey A.C., our team finishing second. It was unfortunate that we were handicapped by the absence of the County Champion, Arthur Penny, who had the misfortune to strain his leg the previous week, and by the indisposition of H. E. Footer, the Champion of 1930, which prevented him giving of his very best. The regaining of this Championship must be the first item to be inserted in the Club's 1933 diary for accomplishment! * * * * * We welcome the following new friends this month : K. W. Beddall, A. R. Shaw, W. Rentell, L. F. Wakeling. We extend to them our usual hearty welcome and wish them every success in our colours. * * * * * We must congratulate C. T. Carter and E. A. Duffett upon being selected to represent Surrey in the Inter-Counties Race to be held at Chingford on January 30th. It is unfortunate that the Inter-Counties Union decided to hold their Championship upon this day, which has been traditionally regarded among Southern Clubs as "10 Miles Championship Day" for decades past. Arthur Allum, the Middlesex champion, and J. E. Flower, who was seventh in the recent championship, have decided to decline their County's invitation, and to run in the Club Championship, which is held by Allum. items.s: THE SURREY YOUTHS' RACE. Report and result of the Surrey County A.A. youths' race from the club's Wimbledon headquarters, won by Belgrave's team by one point. As reported in our last issue, our team won the race promoted by the Surrey County A.A., and held from our headquarters at Wimbledon, and we have much pleasure in congratulating these young wearers of the "Claret and Gold." The victory was only a narrow one—one point to be exact—but the knowledge that the issue was a close one spurred our runners on and on, giving of their best, and ending with the reward of a win in the Club name, and a gold medal apiece. items.s: AT IMBER COURT. Report and results of the December 12th five-mile cross-country match and walk against the Metropolitan Police A.A. at Imber Court; Belgrave won the run but lost the walk by 26 points. On December 12th, both runners and walkers visited the Metropolitan Police A.A.'s quarters at Imber Court. The runners engaged in a five miles cross-country match and won rather easily, while the walkers were defeated by the M.P.A.A. men after a very close tussle. Right from the commencement of the run it was obvious that our boys were certain winners of the match, but the duel between Arthur Allum and Jack Flower for first place caused great interest. The issue was in doubt to within a few yards of the finish, when Arthur managed to gain a couple of yards lead and keep it. The full result appears below and it will be seen that we had nine home in the first ten; Dyke, the Police champion, who finished third, being the only M.P.A.A. man to trouble our runners. Our walkers were not at full strength, but this factor helped to make this fixture one of the most exciting we have yet had. It had been agreed to score 16 aside, and so even was the form shown throughout the race by the 34 competitors, that almost every Belgrave man was battling with an M.P.A.A. walker for the whole of the course. This occasioned some very fine finishing tussles and when the aggregate scores were determined it was found that our Police friends had won by 26 points. From the start Len Fletcher had led, followed by P.S. Caffrey and A. A. Harley and these positions were retained to the end. The full result of this very even and sporting match is appended. After the races the majority of the "Bels" stayed to tea and the dance which followed and thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Ask "Nobby" ! m. s. 1. A. Allum B.H. 26 55 2. J. E. Flower B.H. 26 56 3. A. items.h: THE 7 MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP FOR THE "BLACKSTAFFE SHIELD."
items.sum: Report and result of the Club's 7 Miles Cross-country Championship and handicap for the Blackstaffe Shield on December 19th, won by Arthur Allum, with H. Roy winning the handicap.
items.s: THE 7 MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP FOR THE "BLACKSTAFFE SHIELD." Report and result of the Club's 7 Miles Cross-country Championship and handicap for the Blackstaffe Shield on December 19th, won by Arthur Allum, with H. Roy winning the handicap. The Club's 7 Miles Cross-country Championship for the "Backstaffe" Shield was held on December 19th. A field of 32 faced the starter and Arthur Allum at once jumped to the front, accompanied by Jack Flower. These two ran right away from the rest of the field and Carter led a small bunch who were intent on the third place. At half-way, Allum had drawn away from Flower a little, who in turn was well ahead of the next man. The positions remained unaltered when the finishing post was reached, and third place was gained by C. T. Carter, who drew away from Alec Robertshaw on the level run home from the Windmill. We were pleased to see W. S. Mitchell out with us once again and he ran well considering the limited training he had had. C. H. Penny also ran extremely well and deservedly gained second place in the Handicap. The winner of this was H. Roy, who received 8 minutes start, while third place was taken by H. W. Shields, who is a promising newcomer to our ranks. The race was to some extent spoilt by the absence of Arthur Penny and Bert Footer, both of whom were nursing injuries, but Arthur Allum ran a good race and Jack Flower certainly kept him at it all the time. items.sum: Report and results of the club's Boxing Day meeting: a 120 yards sprint handicap won by G. Pamment, a 3 miles walk won by L. S. Fairman and a 2 miles run won by Jack Flower.
items.s: THE BOXING DAY MEETING. Report and results of the club's Boxing Day meeting: a 120 yards sprint handicap won by G. Pamment, a 3 miles walk won by L. S. Fairman and a 2 miles run won by Jack Flower. We were treated to a fine morning for our exertions after the Christmas festivities, and a large crowd assembled to watch the racing and exchange compliments. In fact, as someone remarked, this annual meeting is rapidly becoming one of our most important social events ! We were pleased to see an old President, in "Dick" Murphy, present. His thoughts are always with us, but it is not often that he is able to attend the Club engagements. The racing commenced with the Sprint Handicap heats. The final, decided later, was won by a promising junior member, G. H. Pamment. His future will be watched with interest, for he his undoubted possibilities. A. H. Green as second, Farrington third; and our 220 yards champion, George Basford, fourth. Victory in the Walk went to the youngest competitor, L. S. Fairman, who thus reaped the reward for perseverance in training. J. G. Coleman followed up his place prize in the Club Junior Championship sealed handicap, by gaining another one in this event and he promises to become as great a "menace" to the Walking Handicapper as he was to the Running Handicapper a year or so back. Redgrave, who seems to like this event year by year, finished third, walking in excellent style throughout. Three Internationals were included in the entry for the Two Miles Running Handicap, but Tommy Hampson did not turn out. Jack Flower (15 yds.) jumped into his stride from the commencement and with about half a mile to go, took the lead ! Although not extended from this point, he recorded 9 min. 40 secs.—an excellent performance. In June and July we hope to see something of the 9 min. 20 secs. order from him ! Carter ran well and in good style to take second place, and Cole, running with determination, did well to finish third, with two Club champions chasing him down the straight. items.sum: Report (signed A.E.M.) and result of the Surrey County cross-country championship at Epsom Downs on January 9th, won by L. H. Weatherill of S.L.H., with Belgrave second to Surrey A.C. in the team race.
items.s: THE SURREY COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report (signed A.E.M.) and result of the Surrey County cross-country championship at Epsom Downs on January 9th, won by L. H. Weatherill of S.L.H., with Belgrave second to Surrey A.C. in the team race. Held at Epsom Downs on Saturday, January 9th, this race provided the small gathering of spectators with few thrills. The "Bels" were represented by a very good 12, but unfortunately were without last year's champion, A. W. Penny. The "field" of just under 100 were away to a good start (although it appeared a slow one), C. T. Carter being up in the front, with Weatherill and Tebbutt of S.L.H. At the first lap Weatherill was "out on his own" and, politely inquiring how far he was in front, seemed to draw further ahead; but it was very gratifying to see a "Claret and Gold" in second place, carried by Carter, with Tebbutt at his shoulder. Going out into the country past the Grand-stand for the second time, the "Bels" were all well up; Footer, Mitchell, Wills, Penny (C.) and Cook (H. S.) all running strongly in a bunch; then came Duffett, Dewberry, O'Kell, Summerfield and Walker, also going well. The very bleak wind seemed to trouble quite a lot of the competitors, although they could not complain about the "going," which was really light. After the runners had gone away for the second time, I thought the prospect of the "Bels" winning a very good one, but some fine running by the Surrey A.C., who had Belton and Newton second and third respectively, backed up by their tail men, secured them first team honours. Carter ran a splendid race to finish sixth and be first Club man home; a word of praise also is due to "Old Man" Duffett for his fine second lap running and finishing 10th. Truly a good performance, with little training and a fine pointer to our younger members, who think it can't be done ! The "Bels" had their 12 in the first 40—a very good effort—and with Arthur Penny running in the team, we should have undoubtedly retained the Championship. A real "tear up" down the straight to the finish gave the onlookers a glimpse of the fighting finishes of the "Bels" and must have reminded them that there is a "to-morrow" and next year we hope to once more put the trophy back on our Club sideboard A word on the running of Weatherill, our worthy foe, who simply swamped all opposition and won as he liked. A runaway win, surely, has not been seen like that before, even by the check-waistcoated gents. on Derby Day ! Nevertheless, Belgravians, we still have the South of the Thames, Southern Counties and the National. What about it? Shall we see the Claret and Gold foremost. Remember our Hon. items.s: MATCH v. SURREY WALKING CLUB. Report and result of the walking match against the Surrey Walking Club over the Wickham and back course (9¾ miles), won by Len Fletcher but lost by Belgrave 56 points to 80. We derive much pleasure in visiting the Surrey Walking Club each winter season and in engaging in a match with them over one of their courses. In previous years we have raced over the Banstead and back course (11½ miles), but on this occasion we tried conclusions over the Wickham and back course (9¾ miles) and found it to be of a testing nature. Unfortunately, circumstances prevented us from fielding our best representation, and the news that Tommy Green had sustained a slight foot injury sufficient to prevent him from being with us, although happily not a serious one, was sorrowfully received by Surrey men and "Bels" alike. Len Fletcher took the lead from the start, and walking in fine style throughout, finished an easy winner. Then followed Kemp and Galloway, of S.W.C., with Ted Saunders fourth. Final scores appear below, and it will be seen that our hosts were winners by 56 points to 80. We congratulate them upon their win, and must make amends when the Championships come along. h. m. s. 1. items.label: January 1932
items.h: THE HORWOOD CUP. 7 MILES JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP.
items.sum: Report of the Club's 7 miles junior walking championship for the Horwood Cup at Wimbledon on December 19th, won by H. G. Churcher, with the handicap to A. A. Harley, by J. B. Belchamber.
items.s: THE HORWOOD CUP. 7 MILES JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the Club's 7 miles junior walking championship for the Horwood Cup at Wimbledon on December 19th, won by H. G. Churcher, with the handicap to A. A. Harley, by J. B. Belchamber. The afternoon was dull and grey on December 19th, when 18 of our walkers raced for the Horwood Cup and the Club's Junior Championship, over our stiff 7 miles course at Wimbledon. Rain threatened, but only fell lightly for a short while and, as it was not too cold, conditions could be reckoned as normal for the time of the year. F. W. Thorn, the holder, had a chill and did not start. This robbed the fight for the trophy of a good deal of interest, as although Harry Churcher had been walking brilliantly during the past few months and had beaten Thorn, he had not shewn time quite equal to the latter's in last year's race. Then Thorn won in 56 min. 58 sec. Harry Churcher's time in the Belgrave Open this year was 57 min. 48 sec. and although he covered the Highgate Harriers' course in 55 min. 59 sec., their's is quite a minute easier than our's, as a comparison of other members' performances will shew. It was Churcher's first appearance in a Belgrave Championship and it was one that he will surely be pleased to remember. Before a mile had been covered he had set up a lead of about 30 yards from A. A. Harley, who was out to fight his utmost all the way, and who, in turn, had gained a slight lead from C. W. Redgrave. After a short interval a bunch of competitors followed. Going down Coombe Lane the gaps remained about the same, but once on level ground the leader piled on the pace and, fighting grandly up the stiff climb that followed, he had set up a winning lead by the time one half of the course had been covered. Charley Redgrave and Alf Harley were still only a few yards apart, whilst Charley Speechley, who had started more slowly than usual, was now gaining slightly on both. Redgrave made a great effort in the final lap, and reduced Churcher's lead considerably, eventually finishing about 90 yards behind him. Charley Speechley, the veteran Junior of this race, walked quite as fast as he was capable of doing 10 years ago, and just outlasted Harley to finish third. It was the handicapper's lucky day, 29 seconds covering the first seven handicap times. Alf Harley walked two minutes faster than in our Open to win this from D. E. Brown, who also shewed great improvement. J. G. Coleman walked 2½ minutes faster to get third. As regards our prospects in the Road Walking Association's Junior Championship this year, the race revealed that we have a sound team and one that is, moreover, improving. Harry Churcher is not yet qualified to walk for the Club, but he certainly has a good chance of gaining the individual honour. Frank Thorn has already been placed third in the race and at his best is capable of surpassing this achievement. Then Redgrave and Harley are improving vastly and Charley Speechley, who has always been unlucky in the Junior Championship, has only to produce the form he readily finds on other occasions, in order to make our team a formidable one. R. F. Elson, who finished fifth, was below form, but he has only to reproduce that shewn in the Enfield Walk to be up with Charley Redgrave. Last year our team walked disappointingly at Luton, but the day was exceptionally cold, the course a severe one, and the conditions were all against youth. The extra year's experience and added stamina should make a deal of difference Then. Larman is steadily improving and Reg Hillier will one day shew that he can walk a good 10 miles. D. E. Brown, E. A. Jackman and J. G. Coleman give promise of first-class performances in another year. RESULT. We were glad to have Oscar Horwood with us to present the Cup and W. C. items.s: THE "GODSTONE" WALK. Report of the Boxing Day Croydon to Godstone and back walk, won by Tommy Green, with Belgrave beating Surrey W.C. by one point in the team race; the team scores give Belgrave's scorers as 1, 6, 9 while the result lists them 1st, 7th and 10th. The annual Boxing Day fixture over the Croydon to Godstone and back course of 18¾ miles found us well represented, and our team was successful by the narrow margin of one point. Tommy Green, as last year, again led our team to victory. He led at the half-distance, but later was caught by Galloway, of the Surrey W.C., and passed. Tommy eventually won quite comfortably, however, beating his last year's time by 19 seconds, and retaining possession of the "Edward C. J. Webb" Challenge Cup. Meanwhile a very stern struggle was taking place between our boys and the S.W.C. walkers. Over the last mile, Amer, a Surrey stalwart, made a gallant attempt to catch and pass Joe King. This would have given our Surrey friends victory by one point; but Joe, with an equally fine effort, held his position and in the final stages of the race was even getting away from his rival. This race brought out the best of both Clubs and showed us team racing at its best. Our thanks and congratulations are extended to T. W. Green, J. F. King and J. E. Field, who formed our winning team. A. H. Field again showed promise as a distance walker, while Ring and East did well at their first attempt over this distance. Times, etc., appear below :— RESULT. items.s: THE CAMBRIDGE HARRIERS' OPEN WALK. Report of the Cambridge Harriers' Open Walk at Eltham, won by T. W. Green, with Belgrave taking the scratch team race, the first two handicap team places and the individual handicap through A. H. Field. This event was supported by 23 entries from our walkers, a notable absentee being Len Fletcher, who had not fully recovered from an attack of influenza. It has been our custom over a number of years to bring away a good proportion of the awards offered, and this year was no exception. T. W. Green walked a splendid race in beating Hyde, while Harry Churcher (4th), Jack Field (5th) and Frank Elson (7th), also gave our colours prominence. Churcher was an individual entrant, and our team was completed by Ted Saunders, and gained a narrow two-point victory over our Enfield rivals. We also had the pleasure of supplying the individual handicap winner in A. H. Field, who walked his best "seven" yet. H. G. Churcher was placed third in the handicap, beating A. A. Harley by one second for the position. With two in the first four of the handicap the handicap team awards went to our "B" team, capable backing coming from H. Latter and H. E. Larman. Thus the 10 first prizes awarded by the promoters left Eltham in Belgrave hands! All our walkers may be said to have done well, but a special word of praise must go to W. Holman for his very fine showing in his first race. RESULT. TEAM SCORES. Pos. Name Act. Time All'ce H'cap Time 1. T. W. Green A 52 11 0 30 51 41 4. H. G. Churcher Ind. 53 29 3 10 50 19 5. J. E. items.sum: Walking notes on recent team wins, coming championship dates, the Annual Dinner date, the Business Houses Walk and the Belgrave Points Scheme scores.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes on recent team wins, coming championship dates, the Annual Dinner date, the Business Houses Walk and the Belgrave Points Scheme scores. Our walkers have now broken the ice and scored two scratch team race wins in the "Godstone" Race and the Cambridge H. Open Race, and it is hoped that this habit, now happily re-acquired, will continue. * * * * * The Championship season is now rapidly approaching, and it is hoped that all our men are holding themselves ready to give of their very best, and re-establish our old position of "Junior" and "Senior" Champions. The "Junior" will be held at Regent's Park on March 5th. Our walkers, eligible for this event, show every promise of doing well and should worthily uphold the Club's prestige in this event. * * * * * All those interested should note that the National 20 Miles Championship will take place on May 7th (NOT May 14th, as in our fixture list), and will be held from Fort Dunlop, Birmingham. The date has been brought forward a week owing to the fact that May 14th is Whitsuntide. * * * * * Our Annual Dinner has, therefore, also been brought forward a week (i.e., to April 30th), to enable all our loyal Club men to attend this most important Club function. * * * * * Whilst writing of fixtures, our distance walkers may be glad to know that the R.W.A. 50 Kilometres Championship will take place from Leicester on June 25th. The result of this race will probably determine who is to go to the Olympic Games at Los Angeles (D.V.), so all Belgrave aspirants should make a note of the date! * * * * * As mentioned elsewhere, Len Fletcher, walking in the Victoria A.A. colours, again won the Business Houses Walk. We were also pleased to see that D. E. Brown and H. Latter, walking for the same Business House, did well, and were placed second and third respectively in the Sealed Handicap held in conjunction. * * * * * The following walkers have scored points in the Belgrave Points Scheme : J. N. Thomas 48, C. H. Speechley 24, D. E. Brown 24, H. Latter 48, T. W. Green 24, J. F. King 12, E. C. Heather 48, A. A. Harley 24. The remaining events in this group are the handicaps in connection with our 10 miles and 20 miles Championships. * * * * * And, finally, a word of congratulation and praise to the much-maligned person, the Hon. items.s: FUTURE EVENTS. Walking fixtures for February and March 1932, including the Club 10 Miles Championship for the R. Murphy Shield and the R.W.A. Junior Championship at Regent's Park. February 6th. Club 10 Miles Championship for "The R. Murphy Shield" and sealed handicap in conjunction. The holder of this championship is A. L. Fletcher and no doubt a stirring struggle will be witnessed between him and Green to decide who shall be holder for 1932. This race is of particular interest to our "Juniors," for our teams in the R.W.A. Championship, to be held on March 5th, will be largely selected upon the form shown. February 20th. Ashcombe A.C. Open 10 Miles Walk. This race is now the only Open event held over 10 miles, and we shall be well represented, as usual. The course is mainly in Richmond Park and will provide a last race before the "Junior" for those eligible. March 5th. The "Junior" R.W.A. Championship. We hope to have a large crowd of supporters present at this race, and our walkers should perform creditably. A more central venue than Regent's Park cannot be imagined, and it is hoped that all who can will come along and give our men a cheer. March 19th. items.label: January 1932
items.sum: Cross-country notes on the Surrey County C.C. Championship, the Middlesex club question and coming February fixtures, urging members to support the team at Beaconsfield on February 27th.
e: South of Thames 7 Miles C.C. Championships
items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. Cross-country notes on the Surrey County C.C. Championship, the Middlesex club question and coming February fixtures, urging members to support the team at Beaconsfield on February 27th. I should like to make a few comments on our team's running in the recent Surrey County C.C. Championship. The papers said "Shock for Belgrave," but so far as I was concerned the only shock was the fact that Surrey A.C. deprived us of our title and not South London H., who I still think should have won this race. Our team, while stronger as regards the 12 to run (the fact that they all finished in the first 40 proves that), was very much weakened by the absence of A. W. Penny, the individual winner last year, H. J. Bignall, who also scored for us last season, and Bert Footer's recent illness. In fact, only two of last year's six scored again this time. One point which seemed to please many people was that our six was composed of all first-claim members, but in saying this don't think I am slighting our second-claim members. I know all of them to be true Belgrave men at heart, and think I am right in saying that they are interested in the "Bels" just as much as their first-claim club. It is the fine Club feeling which pervades the Belgrave members that prompted our members with Middlesex qualification to start a small club of their own. They did not want to join another Club and so do somebody out of a place in that team. Surely this is the quintessence of good sportsmanship. However, it seems that the powers that be have frowned on the whole thing, at all events, up to the present; and these men have been denied the pleasure of running as team mates, which is, after all, the highest expression of sportsmanship in Athletics. Those concerned have hopes that their point of view will be eventually regarded as the only sane one; and that those fellows who are pals in training, real good chums in their leisure hours, and loyal friends always, will be allowed to carry the same admirable spirit into their racing, and run (or walk) shoulder to shoulder, one dependent upon another, and so give expression to the noblest ideal in Athletics—Team Spirit. Now, having cleared that out of my system, I will say a few words about our forthcoming events. On February 6th we have a Social run with the Croydon H., Epsom H. and Mitcham A.C., to be held from Croydon's place at Sanderstead. I hear they have some very good country down that way, so trust our members will take this opportunity of sampling it. On the 13th we have the South of Thames 7 Miles C.C. Championships, venue, Foots Cray Place, Sidcup, and we hope our team will do their best to secure a place in this event. It is within their compass if the team men will buckle down to serious training, and keep pegging away during the race. For the 20th we have a fixture at Wimbledon with the College of S. Mark and S. John, Cobham A.C. and the Tooting Bec Hospital team. This will take the form of a 5 Miles Race and will give those men who just miss a place in our Championship teams, a chance of representing the Club. FEBRUARY 27th. The great day, and really it is beginning to be a great day for us. A few seasons back it was perhaps just another race fixture, although each year we used to conjure up what proved to be false hopes. Now, however, times and teams have changed and we look forward to this race as a chance of justifying ourselves as a Club to be reckoned with in the running world. We have, to a certain extent, to rely upon last year's team, although Carter for one has shown great improvement this season. If only Arthur Penny and Bert Footer can report fit on the 27th, then "everything in the garden will be lovely." Another point which I should like to labour, and this concerns, not the team, but the Club members who are not in the team. TURN UP at BEACONSFELD on the 27th, and give our team your vocal support. When we see how other Clubs' supporters turn out and what effect it has on their teams' running, I guarantee that if all our members, active or inactive, turn up on the 27th, then the result will be a foregone conclusion. You can bring your rattles along, Chelsea won't miss them for one Saturday, and having been to Beaconsfield I can vouch for the fact that it is an ideal course, from the spectators' point of view. As to the actual race there is no possible doubt that with the class of runners there will be competing you will receive ample value for your money in the race you will witness. Book the date, FEBRUARY 27th; trains will be advised later. Drop me a card if you want any particulars and I shall be only too pleased to assist you. All entries and enquiries to E. A.
