items.label: January 1932
items.sum: Letter from the Hon. Treasurer, W. H. Hare, proposing that members save halfpennies to fund a Club-house of the Club's own.
items.s: CORRESPONDENCE. Letter from the Hon. Treasurer, W. H. Hare, proposing that members save halfpennies to fund a Club-house of the Club's own. 16a Albert Bridge Road, S.W.11. Dear Mr. Editor, I trust that the following is sufficiently interesting to warrant inclusion in the "Belgravian." It has been prompted by a direct question raised at a recent Committee meeting, that some effort be made to secure our own Club-house. I need not dwell on the desirability of such an attainment. The matter has been in the minds of a number of members for many years. Up to the present, however, it has been a dream, and the very thought of the capital required has deferred really serious consideration. It has, of course, been suggested that possibly some philanthropist would present us with the necessary funds; or allow us to rent at a nominal figure of one shilling per annum; such as the Duke of Westminster has done for the National Playing Fields Association. Sitting down and waiting for a favourable opportunity to secure our requirements so easily is, I am afraid, futile. In the same way, hoping and trusting for a balance of income over expenditure each year until the necessary assets are realized will be far too slow. We are, without doubt, obliged to rely upon our own efforts and the effort must be shared by every member of the Club. The effort must not be heavy, but necessarily must be sustained. How, then, can we hope to attain our objective? Well, here is my idea, which need not cost members a penny. Strange, but I hope true! Has anyone realised the insignificance and yet the power of the humble halfpenny, or as it is more commonly termed, "a'penny"? But surely, you are beginning to think, the man must be mad if he is thinking to build a Club-house with "a'pennies." That, however, is precisely what I am considering. First let me tell you that for just over three years I have not spent a halfpenny. This is not in its general meaning, but that actually every coin of that denomination that has come into my possession has not been again expended but very carefully retained. Sometimes, of course, I go for days without receiving one. Sometimes I receive 7 or 8 or more in one day. Whatever the number, they never leave me, with the result that I have now a total of 1,080, representing a sum of £2 - 5 - 0 gathered, as I have already stated, in three years. Now, I am one of approximately 600 members of the Club, and if I can collect 240 or more halfpennies in 12 months, then surely 300 members can do likewise. You will have observed that 240 is less than my average yearly collection and that 300 members represent only one-half of our total. I have allowed generously for disinterested members and also that fact that possibly my average rate of collection is rather high. Personally, I don't think that it is. However, 300 members each collecting 240 coins of small value (but equal to to 10/- in bulk) each year will amount to £150. In three years, exclusive of a small sum in interest, this will amount to £450. We would then be in a position to consider seriously our Club premises. For illustration, say suitable premises can be found valued at £2,000. Any Building Society will accept £400 as a first deposit. This leaves £1,600 on mortgage. Spread over 20 years, repayments at £8 - 15 - 0 per month for each £100 borrowed equal £140 per annum. Now, our income from our "a'pennies" must continue. This has already been estimated at £150 per annum, so we shall have a balance in hand each year of £10 and also £50 on our deposit, which will go towards legal expenses, rates and renovations. These latter items are difficulties to be considered but, I think, to be satisfactorily overcome. I have but briefly outlined the scheme that is in my mind. Whether it is fantastic or not is for others to decide. Criticism would be welcomed, either direct or through the columns of the "Belgravian." Helpful suggestions would be doubly welcomed. In conclusion, I would ask all members to try an experiment. From to-day do not spend a halfpenny. Be fair with yourself and put every one that comes to your hand aside! any small receptacle will do to hold your stock. Then at the end of four weeks count them up and advise me of the result. We will then develop the scheme. It is worth a trial? Yes, surely it is! Don't you think so? Faithfully yours, W. H. HARE, Hon. Treasurer. W. H. Hare W. H. HARE Hon. Treasurer; wrote the letter; address in the issue National Playing Fields Association

items.sum: Club notes congratulating J. R. McKay and L. E. Fletcher on their marriages, welcoming new members, praising H. E. Footer's Southern run, reviewing the winter season, and announcing club ties and the team trophies won.
items.s: Club notes congratulating J. R. McKay and L. E. Fletcher on their marriages, welcoming new members, praising H. E. Footer's Southern run, reviewing the winter season, and announcing club ties and the team trophies won. We heartily congratulate J. R. McKay and L. E. Fletcher upon their recent marriages. Both have served us well for a number of years as Committeemen. “Jock” has been a conscientious Hon. Treasurer, and more recently a painstaking Hon. Auditor. “L.E.F.” is also deserving of the foregoing adjectives in connection with his duties as our Running Hon. Handicapper and as a member of our Finance Sub-Committee. We hope to have the loyal services of these two gentlemen for many years to come; and wish Mr. and Mrs. McKay, and Mr. and Mrs. Fletcher long and happy married lives. * * * * * We welcome D. G. Randall, A. H. Doerr, W. F. Cobbett, H. H. Taylor, W. A. Burrows to membership and trust they will soon come into prominence. * * * * * We must devote a special paragraph to congratulating H. E. Footer upon his very fine running in the “Southern.” Bert has been the mainstay of our team for many years past and it is very pleasing to find him maintaining, and even improving upon, his form now that we have others to give the support which was lacking a few years back. He has been described as a “24 carat” team man and we hope that next year he will lead our team to victory in the “Southern” and realize his ambition and gain an “International” vest. * * * * * The past month has seen the decision of most of the important championships of the Winter season, the only remaining one being the Senior Walk Championship at Fort Dunlop on May 7th. Of course, we still have the Brighton Relay before us and this is rapidly approaching championship status. A glance at the past month’s results shows no brilliant performances, no flashes of extraordinary merit, but they are characterized by a high standard of all-round excellence. Third in the “South of the Thames”; fourth in the “Southern”; tenth in the “National”; and fourth in the R.W.A. “Junior” Walk are not phenomenal performances, but they possess an inherent soundness and create confidence in our ability to rise higher. This season has been one of consolidation, and next season should witness the brilliance which we know to be present in embryo. * * * * * How many halfpennies have you sent along to our Hon. Treasurer? He will be glad to hear from you. * * * * * Every Club man should make a point of wearing a Club tie on Brighton Relay Day. They may be had from A. A. Harley, 39 Roxborough Avenue, Isleworth, Mx., at a cost of 2/6 each, by post 2/9. * * * * * A word of congratulation to the members of the teams which won the “Sir J. Colman” Cup in the South of the Thames Race, and the “Odling-Smee” Cup in the Southern. In some respects, these trophies, awarded for the complete team of 12 men, may be considered even more important that the Championship which goes to the best scoring team of six. Well done! J. R. items.label: February 1932
items.sum: Report and result of the club ten miles walking championship on February 5th, won by Len Fletcher for his third successive R. Murphy Shield, with Redgrave third and J. McCarthy first on handicap.
items.s: THE TEN MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the club ten miles walking championship on February 5th, won by Len Fletcher for his third successive R. Murphy Shield, with Redgrave third and J. McCarthy first on handicap. This race was held on February 5th and attracted 24 entrants. Unfortunately, Tommy Green, whose unavailing but closely fought races with Len Fletcher in the last two races for the Club title at this distance are so well remembered, was unable to compete owing to an attack of influenza. The course used covered the same ground as that in use last year, but a slight re-arrangement was made, adding to the distance and making it a full 10 miles. Len Fletcher quickly took the lead, closely followed by Harold King—we were very glad to see him at Wimbledon again—and these two were never headed. Fletcher gradually drew away and walking in fine style and well within himself, finished an easy winner. Meanwhile, Redgrave gave further evidence of his continued improvement and he is to be warmly congratulated upon gaining third place in the championship, which also earned for him second prize in the sealed handicap. The first handicap prize went to J. McCarthy, our champion hand-shaker and ever-smiling heavyweight, and we were all glad to see him take his first prize for walking. Our heartiest congratulations to Fletcher upon winning the “R. Murphy” Shield for the third time in succession—no mean feat in a Club such as ours! Actual Time Allce. H'cap Time H'cap Pos. 1. A. L. items.sum: Report and result of the R.W.A. Junior Championship walk from St. Dunstan's Institute, Regent's Park, won by Sheffield United Harriers, with Belgrave fourth by two points and A. A. Harley first club man home in 15th.
items.s: “THE JUNIOR.” Report and result of the R.W.A. Junior Championship walk from St. Dunstan's Institute, Regent's Park, won by Sheffield United Harriers, with Belgrave fourth by two points and A. A. Harley first club man home in 15th. It was decided to hold this year’s R.W.A. Junior Championship from St. Dunstan’s Institute, in Regent’s Park, and the course chosen was probably one of the fastest ever used for the particular race. A record entry of 38 teams, representing 31 clubs, had been received, and of these three teams were ours. We had high hopes of being placed, but eventually suffered disappointment, losing third position by two points. The start, as was only to be expected, was very fast, but Harry Churcher, an individual entrant from our Club, was soon in the lead. At six miles, when still leading, he suffered disqualification, leaving the eventual winner, F. J. Redman, of the Metropolitan W.C., to take premier place. At the half-distance Surrey Walking Club were leading, but in the latter stages of the race the Sheffield United Harriers team came through strongly and won for the third time in their history. Surrey W.C. held to second place and Highgate H. narrowly beat us for the third set of medals. As last year, our Walking Hon. Secretary, A. A. Harley, had the distinction of being the first Club man to finish, his position being 15th. Don Brown, the first of the “B” team to complete the course, walked splendidly and next year should do remarkably well. Incidentally our “B” team succeeded in beating all the other “B” teams entered. Holman also did well, and Bentley showed a glimpse of what he can do. Charles Churches, our second man to finish, should, with his brother, greatly strengthen next year’s team, and enable us to record our fourth win in this series of races. m. s. 1. F. J. Redman Met. items.s: COMING WALKING FIXTURES. Notice of the club 20 miles walking championship for the R. W. Ricketts Shield at Wimbledon on April 23rd and the Senior Championship at Fort Dunlop a fortnight later. All our gallant army of twenty-milers should now be well on the way towards the pinnacle of fitness. Our Club Championship for the “R. W. Ricketts Shield” and sealed handicap in conjunction, will be held at Wimbledon on April 23rd. The Senior Championship takes place a fortnight later at Fort Dunlop, Birmingham, and the arrangements being made there are a guarantee of a perfectly organised race. items.sum: Social notes thanking dance supporters and announcing a tea and social evening on April 2nd and the Club Annual Dinner at Carr's Restaurant, Victoria, on April 30th.
items.s: SOCIAL. Social notes thanking dance supporters and announcing a tea and social evening on April 2nd and the Club Annual Dinner at Carr's Restaurant, Victoria, on April 30th. I should like to take this opportunity of thanking those who have contributed towards the success of our Dances. The attendances have been satisfactory and the proportion of Club members present very gratifying. Our next Social fixture is a Tea and Social Evening on April 2nd, following the runners’ 5 miles Handicap and walker’s training spin. This is the last of the Socials at Wimbledon for the year, and we expect a large gathering. On Saturday, April 30th, the Club Annual Dinner will be held at Carr’s Restaurant, Victoria. The menu has been chosen to suit you and we have been at great pains to engage first-class artistes to entertain you. A more convenient or accessible venue from the travelling standpoint cannot be found. All that remains, then, is for you to honour your Club and our President by signifying your intention to be present. Ladies are particularly welcome. Tickets (5/- each) may be had from W. A. items.s: FIELD EVENTS. Field events captain's notes calling members to training, announcing the May 7th track programme and Southern Amateur Athletic League contests, and inviting suggestions for scoring the Harry Wright Shield. The Summer Season is almost upon us and I should be glad to see those members interested in Field Events out training again, together with any others who intend giving this branch of the Club’s activities a trial. Our first Track programme, to be held on May 7th, includes a Long Jump Handicap for Club members, and in addition, men will be required to represent the Club in the Long Jump and Javelin matches which form part of the Inter-Club meeting v. London Athletic Club on the same day. The Southern Amateur Athletic League Field Events section is being carried on again this year and two contests will be held of each event. I look to our men for their co-operation to assure that we are worthily represented in these fixtures. There have been several discussions as to the need for revising the conditions and/or method of scoring points for the “Harry Wright” Shield; and I should welcome suggestions regarding this trophy. If anyone is able to devise a scheme which will encourage our sport, I shall be glad to have it. At the moment, four events are taken into account in the competition for the Shield, viz., Long Jump, High Jump, Javelin and Shot Putt. This may easily prove unsatisfactory, as if a member is compelled to miss one of the four events, his chances of winning the Shield are remote. I should like to see all four events decided in one evening. What are the views of others? I should be glad to have suggestions and trust that this season our Fields Events men will give of their best and that we shall be able to claim supremacy at this branch of Athletics, at any rate, in the South. items.h: THE SURREY COUNTY FIVE MILES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP.
items.sum: Report and result of the Surrey County Junior cross-country championship at Imber Court on January 23rd, won by R. Herbert of Epsom H. and by Surrey A.C. as a team, with Belgrave fourth and R. G. Michael sixth.
items.s: THE SURREY COUNTY FIVE MILES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the Surrey County Junior cross-country championship at Imber Court on January 23rd, won by R. Herbert of Epsom H. and by Surrey A.C. as a team, with Belgrave fourth and R. G. Michael sixth. The Surrey County Junior C.C. Championship was held on January 23rd, from the headquarters of the Metropolitan Police A.C. at Imber Court. There was quite a good entry, 10 teams comprising over 60 runners faced the Starter, and after half a mile had been covered, P.C. Gittings, of S.L.H., had a good lead from Herbert, of Epsom H., and R. G. Michael, of our own Club. After one lap of the Reservoir, Gittings still led, although complaining of a damaged ankle. Michael had fallen back a bit and was now lying 5th although the leaders were pretty well bunched together. After another lap round, Pringle, of Surrey A.C., was leading with Herbert at his shoulder; Collet, of Mitcham A.C., lay third, with Gittings pluckily battling along in fourth place. In the run in, Herbert found a fine burst of speed and won a good race (this was his first time out over the country), Pringle was a good second and, moreover, had run the last two miles with only one shoe. Michael ran very well to finish 6th, while Canard made a welcome re-appearance and was second man home for us. Martin was just behind him, and then came Goldsworthy to complete our scoring four. The team packed too far back to do well, but the surprise of the race, from the team point of view, was the win of Surrey A.C. They only started four men and they finished 2, 5, 8, 13, which was certainly splendid running. The course was very muddy in parts, the appearance of some of the competitors afterwards testified to this, and it proved a strong test to the Junior runners. The pluck of Gittings and Pringle, who though both dogged by misfortune, kept going to the finish, proves that the Juniors are made of the right kind of stuff, and they will no doubt be a great help to their Senior teams in a few years to come. m. s. 1. items.sum: Report of the club's 10 miles cross-country championship for the Macher Shield on January 30th, won by A. Allum, with Alec Robertshaw winning the sealed handicap, and the full result.
items.s: THE TEN MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP FOR THE “MACHER” SHIELD. Report of the club's 10 miles cross-country championship for the Macher Shield on January 30th, won by A. Allum, with Alec Robertshaw winning the sealed handicap, and the full result. January 30th, the day of our 10 miles Championship, turned out to be rather misty, not too cold, with the going fairly light underfoot. Thirty-two faced the starter, some with that “do-or-die” look; others as if it was the most natural thing in the world to run 10 miles. Allum and J. E. Flower were in the lead after half a mile, followed by the “one-and-only” Footer and Mitchell. The rest of the field were bunched—a sure indication of a slow (or not too fast) start. At four miles Arthur Allum led Jack Flower by 25 yards, with Footer third some distance behind. At six miles Jack had moved up to Arthur's shoulder and the other positions remained as before. Warboys passed me as if he had only just started. The last mile showed Allum holding a hundred yards lead, with Flower and Footer fighting for second place. Alec Robertshaw is to be congratulated upon finishing fourth and deservedly winning the sealed handicap. Dewberry, C. Penny and Taylor also ran well, particularly the last two named, who were attempting ten miles for the first time. A word of praise also to our Captain! A.W.P. items.label: February 1932
items.h: THE SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP.
items.sum: Report of the South of Thames senior cross-country championship, where a weakened Belgrave team placed third and won the Sir Jeremiah Colman Cup by finishing all 12 men in the first half of 203 runners; won by L.-Cpl. G. W. Ward.
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the South of Thames senior cross-country championship, where a weakened Belgrave team placed third and won the Sir Jeremiah Colman Cup by finishing all 12 men in the first half of 203 runners; won by L.-Cpl. G. W. Ward. As most of our readers are aware, owing to so many different clauses, nearly all our “acknowledged” senior men were unable to compete in this race, but this did not deter our team from “having a go” and a jolly good “go” they had, as you will see by the result appended. The race was a very interesting one to watch and from the spectators' point of view, a better venue could not have been wished for. The “Bels” made a good start and with Mains early in the lead, closely followed by Carter, things looked quite rosy. At the end of the first circuit, three-quarters of a mile, we must have had all our 12 in the first 50 places. Naturally, this state of affairs did not last, but it made all our supporters extra keen. On the second lap, one and a half miles, Carter had just taken the lead with Mains (who had probably made too fast a start) falling back. Our other men had also dropped, but even so it looked all Belgrave. The runners then went out in the country for a three miles stretch and when they came in sight again Carter had had a bad time and had dropped back into the 25th position. Mains, however, was “coming again” and was in the 10th place, and our other men running very strongly were round about the fifties. So off they went again for the last lap of three miles and we were hoping that they would peg back a few places to gain a place in the team race. Sure enough, when they came round again every one of our men was running strongly. Carter had improved to 15th place, Mains had dropped back to the 20th (this was due to a slight recurrence of the trouble he had in our ten miles championship) and with Dewberry, F. Webb (showing a welcome return to form), Taylor and Shields coming in close together inside the first 56 positions, we gained third place in the race. Our other men, full of fight, kept going to the end and ultimately we had the pleasure of finishing our 12 men in the first half of a field of 203 runners, and so won the “Sir Jeremiah Colman” Cup. This was really a splendid performance. Two newcomers this season, namely Taylor and Shields, are to be warmly congratulated on their splendid performances and undoubtedly have a good running future before them. L.-Cpl. G. W. Ward, the winner of the race, was a surprise, but to those who saw him he is a real champion and with average luck should gain many more laurels. T.J.F. RESULT. TEAM SCORES. m. s. 1. L.-Cpl. G. W. items.label: February 1932
items.sum: Report of the Southern Counties 10 miles senior and 5 miles junior cross-country championships at Beaconsfield on February 27th, where Belgrave were 4th in the senior race (winning the Odling-Smee Cup) and 16th in the junior, with results and team scores.
items.s: THE “SOUTHERN.” Report of the Southern Counties 10 miles senior and 5 miles junior cross-country championships at Beaconsfield on February 27th, where Belgrave were 4th in the senior race (winning the Odling-Smee Cup) and 16th in the junior, with results and team scores. The Southern Counties 10 Miles Senior and 5 Miles Junior Cross Country Championships were held at Beaconsfield on February 27th. It was a glorious day and the course was very firm underfoot, just as well perhaps, because given a wet day it would have been decidedly heavy over the plough. The course included many obstacles and gates which had to be opened each time round, otherwise it was quite easy going. In the Junior race were 32 teams, but so far as the individual race went it was a walk-over for Pte. Archer, of the 2nd R.W. Kents. Archer has been running for the Aldershot Command hitherto, and is as yet unbeaten over the country. H. W. Shields was our first man home, and in finishing 29th did very well, as also did R. G. Michael, who was 45th. It must be remembered that the standard of this race is very high for Juniors, so that our team was not disgraced in being placed 16th. For the Senior race 30 teams turned out, comprising just on 300 runners, and it was a magnificent sight to see the field come along. Jack Flower had the temerity to take the lead early on, but was soon desposed by L. H. Weatherill, of S.L.H., and hereafter everyone had a good view of Weatherill's back. Bert Footer ran what must have been the best and also pluckiest race of his career. When you remember that only a short time ago Bert was on the sick-list, it certainly speaks volumes for his pluck and ability for him to finish where he did. I make bold to say that only a Footer, as we know him, could have done it. Jack Flower also gave his best performance over the country and in finishing 11th Jack shewed what conscientious training can do. Arthur Allum was another hero. All that week he had been suffering from the 'flu, but pluckily turned out to help the team and we admire him for his pluck and team spirit. Alec Robertshaw also ran extremely well and it was indeed unfortunate that on the day that Alec shewed his true form, the team was unluckily beaten out of a place. I say unluckily in all sincerity, for no one will disagree, I am sure, that given any other day, Allum would have assuredly been up with Jack Flower. The fact that Harman and Dockerill, whom Arthur has already beaten this season, finished 5th and 6th respectively, proves what I say. To think it was a question of a mere 10 points, and the irony of it was the fact that the next team had 310 point.s Still, we heartily congratulate Enfield A.C. on their first placing in this race. Their boys have run consistently well all the season and they deserve all the honours they get. We once again won the “Odling-Smee” Cup, awarded to the first Surrey Club to finish its complete team of 12 men, and in this respect we have yet another hero, Cecil Mains, who ran the last 2 miles minus his shoes. It just shows you the fine sporting spirit which pervades our members and we extend our best thanks to the whole team for their splendid effort on the Club's behalf. The critics may have considered we failed in only finishing 4th, but why worry, our team is a young one (excuse this, Bill, old boy!) and we shall be only too eager for next year's race to come round, so that we may have yet another try to break South London Harriers' fine sequence of wins. 10 MILES SENIOR CHAMPIONSHIP. items.label: February 1932
items.sum: The Hon. Running Secretary's notes on his change of address, a Southern Counties ruling on open races, and coming fixtures: the 5 miles road race at Wimbledon, the Brighton Relay, the S.A.A.L. and the first club track meeting.
items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. The Hon. Running Secretary's notes on his change of address, a Southern Counties ruling on open races, and coming fixtures: the 5 miles road race at Wimbledon, the Brighton Relay, the S.A.A.L. and the first club track meeting. Silence, please! Will all and sundry please take note that I have once again changed my address? I expect I shall now be flooded with abusive postcards. On the last occasion I had one which read, “Dear Sir, Why don't you live in a caravan?” However, I think my present place of abode, namely, 307 Morland Road, Croydon, will be my address for many years to come, at least bar earthquakes, family increases, etc., I see no reason why it should not. Before I come to the last few fixtures of the Winter Season, I would like to say a few words on a decision of the Southern Counties C.C. Assn., that a County race is not an Open race. Well, I ask you! If you follow that to its logical conclusion, the “South of Thames” and even the “Southern” are not Open races. I understand, however, that the A.A.A. are to give a decision on this point, but really, the way the rules are “mucked abart,” I honestly don't see the use of having any. On April 2nd we have our last Club fixture of the season at Wimbledon. This will be a 5 miles Road Running race, with a Handicap in conjunction. I don't know whether the Handicapper will have returned from his honeymoon, but I hope so. The form shown in this race will help our Committee when selecting our team for the Brighton Relay race. With the Handicap also being held there should be a good entry, for this will be the last chance to obtain points, so far as the Winter races go, for the Belgrave Points Scheme. Entries (1/-) should be sent to me at once. A Social Evening will be held after the race—see notice elsewhere. April 16th, Brighton Relay Day. On the stroke of 11 from Big Ben the race from London to Brighton, in 10 stages, will start. As in past years, we shall have a Club 'bus for our team and supporters, only this year we are going to have an up-to-date covered top one. Seats can now be booked (5/- return) and names, together with the money, should be handed to H. L. Rollins, who will be in charge of the 'bus arrangements. I advise you to book early, as there is every indication of a record crowd going down to cheer our team along. Our 'bus will leave Westminster at 10-30 a.m. sharp, which please note. Nobody will be waited for, as it is essential for our next runner to be at his stage in time to take over. We come then to the Track Season, and a momentous one it promises to be, with the vision of Los Angeles in the background. We have already arranged our usual Inter-Club fixtures and have also fixed other dates with new opponents. It looks as if our fixture list will be a pretty full one, and so I trust our members will co-operate with me in the matter of turning out teams in the various events. After all, unless we can turn out teams of fair strength in these fixtures, it is useless our arranging them. We are once again competing in the 1st Division of the Southern Amateur Athletic League, and this year are in Section 1 of the S.A.A.L. Field Events Competition. The same events as last year will be held in regard to the latter, only this time there will be two of each, and so the venues are fairly well strung out. George Powell, I know, will do his best to turn out men for each event, but the members must assist him by doing their bit. They have moaned in the past about lack of Field events, so here is their chance of doing something. On April 20th, at Battersea Park Track, will be held the first fixture in this competition, namely, the High Jump, and members who wish to compete for the Club (2 men may compete for each Club) are asked to give their names to George Powell at once. On May 7th we have our first Club Track meeting at Battersea Park, a match versus the London Athletic Club, some Club Handicaps, and also a 1 Mile Scratch run for Unattached Novices only. See next Club Gazette for full list of events, etc. I think our members will find plenty of competition awaiting them and I trust they all have a very enjoyable and successful season on the track. items.s: BELGRAVE BUILDING FUND. Unsigned notice announcing that the Committee has sanctioned a Building Fund for a club house, financed by members saving halfpennies, with the fund at 2,514 halfpennies (£5 4s. 9d.) so far. Since my letter to the Editor was published in the last issue of “The Belgravian,” the Committee, to whom I had previously explained the details of my scheme for providing our own Club quarters by subscriptions of “ 'a'pennies,” have sanctioned the institution of a Building Fund. The full details have yet to be definitely drawn up and approved, but for the present the following are being acted upon. An account is being opened with a Building Society in the name of the Belgrave Harriers. This will form our Building Fund and all accounts will be kept distinctly separate from the ordinary Club funds. Subscription cards will be issued to all members participating and a record retained of all contributions. A Balance Sheet will be issued annually. As outlined in my letter, the idea is for every member not to spend a “ 'a'penny” (this will not cost you a penny!) but to retain every coin of that denomination that comes into your possession. You will not miss them if they are put aside in some suitable receptacle. Any old cigarette tin, etc., will do. Then, from time to time, forward them to the Hon. Treasurer, who will enter up the amount to your name and pay into the Building Society. With 300 members carrying out this practice we shall soon be in a position to seriously consider the Club House. Many points have yet to be settled, but for the time being carry on and do not spend a “ 'a'penny.” If desired, a box can be provided for you on application, and one point that is definitely settled is that in the event of the scheme falling through, all contributions will be returned to the members in accordance with the amount they have paid in. It is hoped however that this will not be necessary, and that the scheme will eventually mature. At the time of going to press the fund totals 2,514 “ 'a'pennies,” representing a sum of £5 - 4 - 9. Apart from my original collection, I am indebted to Messrs. J. B. Belchamber, W. L. Bayliss, W. G. Webb, F. R. Webb, H. L. Rollins, A. Robertshaw, A. A. Harley and V. J. items.s: Club notes congratulating the London-Brighton relay team, F. G. Thomson and A. L. Fletcher, welcoming nine new members, and announcing medals, vests, ties and the Hospital Savings Association. Our heartiest congratulations to the team which carried our colours so prominently in the London—Brighton Relay Race. Theirs is a performance which will be long remembered; and has brought congratulatory messages from many quarters. Congratulations also to F. G. Thomson upon his recent election to the Southern Committee of the A.A.A., where we are sure his hard work for, and experience of, Athletics, will be as much appreciated as it is in our own Club. A. L. Fletcher also merits our congratulations upon regaining the Surrey Road Walking Championship. We hope Len will add a National title to his other distinctions before long. Our cordial welcome is extended to the following new members this month, and we trust they will enjoy many successes in our colours. They are F. Vaticas, A. J. Mitchell, B. Rainford, F. Haly, J. O. Whitehouse, A. O. Tookey, J. Mansfield, J. Holder and D. Sargent. In accordance with the usual policy of the Club, when a trophy has been won on the Club's behalf and there are no individual awards accompanying it, the Committee have sanctioned the award of Club silver medals to the teams responsible for the winning of the "Sir J. Colman" Cup and the "Odling-Smee" Cup. We heartily congratulate one of our popular figures, J. Grimwood, upon his recent marriage and wish his wife and himself every happiness. Our Hon. Treasurer has long-sleeved, short-sleeved and sleeveless Club vests for sale, price 3/6 each. When writing him (for address see page 1) don't forget to specify the kind you require, and to give your chest measurement. Badges are also available. The Hon. Treasurer would also be glad to receive outstanding subscriptions; or halfpennies on behalf of the Belgrave Building Fund. Club ties are obtainable from A. A. Harley, 39 Roxborough Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. Price 2/6 each, by post 2/9. Many of us are aware of the good work accomplished, and the benefits offered by the Hospital Savings Association to its members. If any Belgravians who are not already members of a branch of the organisation at their place of employment, are interested, Mr. C. items.sum: Report and results of the 1932 National Cross Country Championship at Wolverton, won by J. A. Burns, with Belgrave tenth team.
items.s: THE NATIONAL CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and results of the 1932 National Cross Country Championship at Wolverton, won by J. A. Burns, with Belgrave tenth team. The National Cross Country Championship was held over a 10 miles course at Wolverton on March 12th. The weather was fine and the course, consisting of three laps, dry and made for fast running. A field of 289 faced the starter, and Bailey, of Salford, made the pace a hot one, with Burns and Holden in close attendance. Bailey led until half-way round the finishing field and then Burns came by him with a great burst to win a magnificent race. Jack Flower ran exceptionally well to finish where he did, but Bert Footer was, I think, a little disappointed at his own showing. It has long been one of Bert's ambitions to gain an English vest, and so we trust he will gain his reward next year. The other members of our team, omitting Allum and Robertshaw, both of whom retired through indisposition, packed much too far back for a forward position to be gained, but even so we were the third Southern club to finish and reversed our placings with Enfield A.C. I disregard Aldershot Command, as no one seems to know whether they are a club, unit, regiment or what! RESULT. TEAM RESULT. 29 teams closed in m. s. 1. J. A. Burns E.H. 53 22 2. G. W. items.s: THE 5 MILES ROAD RUNNING HANDICAP. Report and full result of the club's 5 miles road running handicap at Wimbledon on 2 April 1932, won on handicap by Nick Carter, with Arthur Allum fastest. Our 5 Miles Road Running Handicap was held at Wimbledon on April 2nd. The form shewn in the level race was to be used as an indicator to our Brighton team and so we had a full muster. The only two absentees were Penny and Mains, both of whom were suffering from leg injuries. Arthur Allum took the lead from the start and Jack Flower never got on terms with him again. Allen, of Highgate, who was having a run with our lads, was always up near the leaders, although he was, of course, officially not in the race. There was quite a little bunch of "hopefuls" fighting round about the seventh place and the hills on the return home duly told their tale. On the run home round the triangle, the positions remained unchanged and the result was as follows. The handicap resulted in a popular win for Nick Carter, with H. J. Bignall, our Highgate member, second, and "Nobby" Fletcher third. The result proved that we have a very useful team for the Brighton race and, moreover, have several useful reserves; which, in the case of withdrawals, is a most important factor. † Dead Heat. Pos. items.label: April 1932
items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of Belgrave's third place in the London to Brighton Relay on 16 April 1932, the first Southern club to finish; the full result prints Surrey A.C. (6.) above South London H. (5.).
items.s: ON THE BRIGHTON ROAD—APRIL 16th, 1932. Stage-by-stage report of Belgrave's third place in the London to Brighton Relay on 16 April 1932, the first Southern club to finish; the full result prints Surrey A.C. (6.) above South London H. (5.). This date—April 16th, 1932—will remain memorable in Belgravian history as the day when one of the most impressive achievements by our runners was recorded. To finish third in London to Brighton Relay with the keenest possible competition—it would be impossible to secure a stronger field without going outside the British Isles, if it could be found even then—is something of which we may feel justifiably proud. It was also an honour, of which we are deeply sensible, to be the first Southern club to finish the course. We have, indeed, set ourselves a very high standard to maintain in the future, but we are supremely confident of our ability to live up to, and even surpass, this year's very fine performance. To come to the details. Our combined Grandstand and Dressing Room, in the shape of a modern double-decked 'bus, arrived at Westminster about 10-30 a.m. and nine team men, three reserves and the full complement of loyal supporters soon took their places, and we were off to the first change-over point at Clapham Common. "Nick" Carter had been entrusted with the first stage, and that our trust was not misplaced was soon evident. Our man was in the first flight right from the stroke of eleven from Big Ben, which started the race. In fact, passing over Chelsea Bridge, Carter was forcing the pace, oblivious of the distinguished company in which he was running. However, Nick has never stood on ceremony, and at the conclusion of his stage of 4 miles 176 yards, we were delighted to find him handing over fourth, a few yards in the rear of R. R. Sutherland, the well-known Birchfield Harrier. Carter, with the three men who had preceded him, had broken the course record for this stretch. A good start! The leaders at this point were :— Jack Flower was our representative over the next section, extending to Mitcham, a distance of 5 miles 176 yards. He overtook the Highgate and S.L.H. runners and these Clubs were destined not to trouble us again throughout the race, but he had to yield places to Tipton H., whose International, J. T. Holden, broke the existing record, and to Cwmbran H., the Welsh Champions. Aldershot Command A.C. were on our heels at this point and the position were now :— Jack had acquitted himself well, now our colours were carried on by Alec Robertshaw, over the 5 miles 856 yards stretch to Purley Knoll. Positions altered a little here and the Army runner turned his one second deficit into a one second lead, so pushing us back one place, but this was of little moment, for was not our International, Arthur Allum, going next? Alec's sterling run was followed by a similar effort from Arthur Allum, who, it will be remembered, injured his ankle in last year's race, when overhauling the leaders and had to limp in. Arthur's stretch extended to "The Feathers," Merstham, and by the time this point was reached we were again in front of the Army team. Salford H. had now come up through the agency of a record-breaking run by H. Platt, whilst Cwmbran had fallen back. Allum caught the International, T. Kay, of Tipton, only to have to let him go again in the last few yards, but now we were fourth again and within three seconds of the third position. Well run, Arthur! The fifth stage (6 miles 342 yards) finishing at "The Chequers," Horley, as usual, attracted many of the best-known athletes in the country, for it is rightly regarded by the Clubs as being of the utmost importance. Our choice was Syd Warboys, and he was passed by Corporal Wilson, of the Command, who is one of the fastest men in the country. Syd had served us well and so at the conclusion of the fifth stage (26 miles 1032 yards, approximately half-way) we were in fifth position, and well within striking distance of the leaders. We now called upon Jack Fletcher, one of our younger school of runners, and he more than justified his inclusion in the team. He quickly drew further away from the Polytechnic H. representative, and passed the Tipton Harrier who appeared to be having muscle trouble. On strode "Nobby," gaining a few seconds on the Army runner in front of him, and so on to "The George," at Crawley, where Ernie Duffett, our popular Running Hon. Secretary, was waiting to carry on with the good work. Well run, Nobby! You'll be breaking records over this course for us before long! Duffett was soon off on the 4 miles 704 yards stage, finishing at "The Red Lion," Handcross, and he maintained our position, cutting well into the Club Record for this stretch in the process. Positions now were :— It was now Arthur Penny's turn. Unfortunately, an injured leg has denied us Arthur's services during the cross-country season, but now it is well again and he helped to consolidate our position. Well done Arthur! And next—Vice-Captain H. E. Footer. We have come to expect big things from this little fellow and on this occasion he surpassed himself. By virtue of a really wonderful run, Bert brought us up to third position. What excitement now prevailed! Could we hold our lead and show our supremacy among Southern clubs? The answer, appropriately enough, depended upon our Captain, W. G. Webb, and he soon showed that the answer to the question was an emphatic "Yes." Bill will probably remember this run all his life, for he rose to the occasion, as we had confidently anticipated, and played a true Captain's part in leading our team to their best performance yet. We are proud of our Captain and have no doubt he is equally proud of his team! Actually, Bill increased our lead over Aldershot Command A.C. by over 6 seconds! Meanwhile, as the above positions at the end of the various stages indicate, an exciting struggle for first place had been taking place between Birchfield H. and Salford H., with the Manchester club eventually taking first place on the last stage. Here is the full result :— Our supporters shouted themselves hoarse as the race neared its end. Throughout the race they were busy encouraging our men, and exchanging banter with the members of other clubs. Many of our party must have run well over five miles at different times during the progress of the race! In short, our 'bus once again proved a huge success. We always arrived at the change-over points long before the runners, and there was never the slightest suggestion of any interference with the race by our conveyance. In fact, we were able to be of assistance to several runners of other Clubs, who otherwise would have experienced difficulties. It was our privilege to extend the hospitality of our dressing accommodation to Laurie Pool, the South London Harriers' captain, who had missed his 'bus. Two Polytechnic Harriers were also given "lifts" and we were also glad to be of service to several other athletes. To resume after this digression. At the Tea and Distribution of Awards by the Mayor of Brighton, which followed the race, Joe Binks spoke of some of outstanding performances of the race. The announcement that two men only had ever beaten 28 minutes for the ninth stage, and that one of them was H. E. Footer, whose time that day had been 27 min. 55 sec., was drowned in cheers, which testified to Bert's popularity among athletes. A little later Bill Webb had the honour of leading our team up for their medals, amidst hearty applause. * * * * * Our time in this race was 4 hrs. 44 mins. It is interesting to note that, apart from this year, this time has only been beaten twice previously over the present course, i.e., by Birchfield H. and Hallamshire H. in 1928. Our time this year would have won the race in 1929, 1930 and last year! Of course, weather conditions affect the times recorded, but this year's conditions were far from perfect. Another interesting point is the even running, the soundness, of our men, with each individual pulling his weight. This is shown by the fact that we were never farther back than fifth, never farther forward than third! We did not rely upon record-breakers to make up for the ground lost by others. This is a sign of strength and indicative of the team spirit which is carrying us to success. We heartily congratulate our team upon their showing, and also thank our reserves who trained on. It is a further sign of strength that if we had been forced through unforseen circumstances to introduce reserves into our team, it is very doubtful whether we should have been weakened, such is the high standard of our men over a large number. If it were possible to have a 100 miles relay with 20 men a side, Belgrave would take some beating! And now, what of the future? Can we improve five minutes and lead the field home? Is it possible? To a Club such as ours, which has risen from 17th position in 1927 to third in 1932, it is not a possibility—it is a certainty! This year, a week before the race, we read in the Press that our team had deteriorated, that we should not be in the first bunch. If this is true, and we were able to finish third, we may expect to be winners when the Press forecast is a little more hopeful! Below you will find a table giving the times of our men over the various stages and it will be noticed that in every instance a new Club Record was created. Ten new Club Records on ten stages! This is a testimony in itself to the ability of the team. And so we look forward to the day when a representative of the Club, which had its origin in Westminster and ran its earliest races along the Embankment over the ground now included in the first stage of the Relay, has the pleasure of handing the Lord Mayor's message to the Mayor of Brighton. The day will surely come when the Claret and Gold will be pre-eminent. Will it be in 1933? * * * * * Our 'bus started on the return journey from Brighton at 6-30 p.m. and it was soon evident that our fellows were pleased with the day's performance. And how they killed Cock Robin, observed silver linings and traversed long, long trails, and how ——. Eventually London was reached and all made their way home, registering a mental vow that if they could not be in the team next year, they would certainly be on the road to cheer our men on—on to victory or something very near it. m. s. 1. items.s: With the Walkers Walking notes welcoming two new walkers, reporting Len Fletcher's Surrey Road Walking Championship win, the Middlesex Championship at Enfield (Belgrave members walking as Cadogan A.C.), Tommy Green's return to form, and the walkers' fixtures. WITH THE WALKERS. We welcome to the walking ranks this month A. O. Tookey and A. J. Mitchell. Tookey is a first-claim Polytechnic Harrier, their Walking Captain, and Mitchell is a keen young novice who should do well. * * * * * Len Fletcher regained his individual title in the Surrey Road Walking Championship, held over a 10 miles course on Mitcham Common; but the team title eluded us once again. We have never yet been able to secure this championship, but must make a determined effort next year, when our team will be considerably strengthened. RESULT. TEAM RESULT. Brown did well to be our second man home and Holman seems to gain a little more speed at each outing. * * * * * On the same afternoon several of our walkers were interested in the Middlesex Championship held at Enfield. A most exciting struggle for third place ensued between the Polytechnic Harriers and four of our members walking as Cadogan A.C. representatives. The second Poly. man, A. A. Webb, beat the second Cadogan walker, C. W. Redgrave, in the last stride of the race and thus secured the third medals for his team. Had Charlie been able to beat his rival by inches, instead of the other way round, the result for third place would have been an equal number of points each, and our members would have taken the awards on lowest time aggregate. Charlie Speechley was a member of the Polytechnic Harriers' scoring team. RESULT. TEAM RESULT. It is very good to see Tommy Green back in his old form again. In February he was confined to bed for a fortnight with a severe attack of influenza, but that he has now shaken off the after-effects is evident by his very fine walking in the "Bishop of Birmingham's Cup" race, when he was placed second to H. Taylor, of Derby W.C.; and in "The Leicester Mercury" race, when he won from his old rival, T. Lloyd-Johnson. Both races were at 20 miles, and we anticipate a good performance from Tommy in the "National" on May 7th. * * * * * All members have now received their fixture cards and it will be seen that an excellent programme has been arranged for the walkers—in fact, there is not another Club in the country which provides its walkers with the same opportunities for competition. In order to relieve the monotony of the customary two miles handicaps, it has been decided to include one handicap at three miles and one at four miles in this season's fixtures, and these will take place on June 29th and May 18th respectively. There will be two miles handicaps on May 7th, June 1st, June 15th, July 13th and August 17th, and the Club Championship on July 30th. * * * * * We have received an invitation to participate in a Two Miles team walk, included in the Polytechnic H. Marathon Meeting, to be held at Stamford Bridge on May 28th. This has been accepted and we hope to turn out our strongest representation. * * * * * All entries for Club handicaps, enquiries for information, etc., to A. A. items.label: April 1932
items.sum: Track season preview: the opening match v. London Athletic Club at Battersea Park, club handicaps, the Ealing match at Drayton Green, S.A.A.L. relays, the Inter-Club Relay Shield and the Kinnaird Trophy.
items.s: Forthcoming Events Track season preview: the opening match v. London Athletic Club at Battersea Park, club handicaps, the Ealing match at Drayton Green, S.A.A.L. relays, the Inter-Club Relay Shield and the Kinnaird Trophy. FORTHCOMING EVENTS. The last event of the Winter Season, namely, the London to Brighton Relay, having come and gone, leaving behind it pleasant memories for many of us, we look forward with great interest to our first track meeting. This will be held at Battersea Park Track on May 7th, at 3 p.m., and our visitors will be the London Athletic Club, a very famous body, who include in their ranks runners of International class. The events in the match will be: 100 yards, 220 yards, 440 yards, 1 mile, Long Jump and Javelin. We hope to have Tom Scrimshaw and Jim Tosh assisting us, also our Southern Long Jump champion, J. W. Clemens. A. Kench, our youthful mile champion, is also likely to make his first appearance this season, and we are looking forward to great things from him. In addition to the match we shall have the honour of staging the S.A.A.L. 3 miles Team race, in which many famous runners will be competing. We hope to have a stronger team than last year and trust we shall make a good start in the league table. Club Handicaps will also be held at the following distances: 100 yards, 220 yards, 880 yards, 1 mile, 2 miles Walk and Long Jump. A 1 Mile Scratch Open event for Unattached Novices only will be held, and if members know of anyone wishing to compete, will they please send names to me at once. Please note there is NO entry fee and medals will be awarded. Entries for this meeting should be in my hands by April 30th latest, and please note that no late entries will be accepted. New members entering a Club event for the first time will be well advised to fill in an A.A.A. form, so that the Handicapper can treat you at your true value. On May 14th we have a renewal of our enjoyable meeting at Drayton Green Track, West Ealing, with the Ealing H., Slough H. and Ashcombe A.C. The match will consist of scratch and team events, and our team men will be advised in due course. Anyone who wishes to witness a real sporty contest will do well to come along on this afternoon. On May 21st we have two S.A.A.L. fixtures to be held at Stamford Bridge, in connection with the L.A.C. meeting there. These will be the 4 x 440 yards and 4 x 880 yards contests and we hope to field two very formidable teams in each. May 18th. To-day we have the first of the Inter-Club Relay Shield contests between Croydon H., Mitcham A.C., Epsom H. and ourselves, to be held at Battersea park at 7 p.m. The Shield events are: 4 x 100 yards, 4 x 300 yards, 4 x 880 yards, 1 mile Team race (4 to run, 3 to score). We had great difficulty in retaining possession of this Shield last year and expect our members to make sure of our supremacy by turning out in these events. I know we have members who are eager to run, but you must realise that the opposition, although not so strong in the distance races, is worthy of the best we have at our disposal. In addition to the above we are holding the following Club handicaps: 220 yards (under 19), 4 miles Walk and Javelin Throw. Please note our new Field Events Handicapper is K. B. O'Kell, to whom entries and monies should be given. If Ken gets to work with some of his charts I can see a Chartered Accountant having to be called in to decide the results. At any rate, you can rest assured you have a man who will give his whole interest to the job on hand, and bar any unknowns upsetting the book, the handicaps should work our remarkably well. On May 28th we have the Kinnaird Trophy meeting at Stamford Bridge, and we hope to see our boys well to the fore. We realise that up against opposition such as the Achilles, who, you must remember, are a specially fine trained body of athletes, it is extremely difficult for a club such as ours to make headway, but we are gradually developing class performers and trust that one day we shall be able to make a decent fight of it. At present a point or two has to satisfy us, but there again the events which would appeal to us "civilian" clubs are not put on, such as a Walk and Javelin Throw, and we are continually striving against men who have been trained at the Universities to specialize in certain events. At this meeting will also be held the S.A.A.L. 4 x 220 yards Relay, and if our team repeat their performance of last year, then we shall be well satisfied. We have always looked upon ourselves as being rather weak in the sprinting line, but with men like Basford, Read, Jarvis, Wilcock, not forgetting our veteran Morrie Odell, we are likely to shew some improvement in this department. We certainly started the season very well at Gravesend (even if the S.L.H. did "slip up" over their teams (we have memories of a similar happening at Chislehurst; ask Bert Footer!), and we are sorry that Bruce Hayman, who did the "double" there, is leaving us in the near future. His family is moving down to the West Country and although Bruce will still remain a member, we shall not be able to call on his services very often. However, we wish him all the very best and trust he will shake the locals up down that way. Our membership continues to increase and with old and new members pulling together, we should very soon be in a position that will prove beyond doubt our claim to be the Premier Club in the South. items.sum: Anecdote of an A.A.A. official at the mental hospitals' cross-country championship at Claybury who suspected Bert Footer of being an inmate.
items.s: Concerning "Our Bert." Anecdote of an A.A.A. official at the mental hospitals' cross-country championship at Claybury who suspected Bert Footer of being an inmate. CONCERNING "OUR BERT." A well-known A.A.A. Official was recently judging the Annual Cross-Country Championship organised for attendants of Mental Hospitals. The race was held in the grounds surrounding Claybury Mental Hospital, Essex. After the race he was surprised to find "Our Bert" Footer walking in the grounds and he became suspicious when Bert asked for the result of the race. The official was then reminded that at the same race two years ago at Bexley Heath, he had the following experience:— He was leaving for tea and it was snowing hard, when a man walking in the grounds stated that he was from the press. With his usual courtesy, the official started giving the enquirer the details he required. However, the Chairman of the Committee asked the man to go and have tea. When the official stated the man had said he was from the press, he was told, "Oh, that's all right; the man is an inmate of the Asylum!" Well, with that in his mind, the official wondered whether "Our Bert" had been found out at last. After a few questions he was relieved to find that "Our Bert" had only come down to cheer the Tooting Bec boys into third place. items.sum: Notice of the club's summer outing to Earlswood Common on 19 June, with a request to settle outstanding Dinner and Dance accounts.
items.s: THE SUMMER OUTING. Notice of the club's summer outing to Earlswood Common on 19 June, with a request to settle outstanding Dinner and Dance accounts. It has been decided to hold our annual jaunt into the country on Sunday, June 19th, and we shall go to Earlswood Common, near Redhill, as last year. This place has many attractions. Cricket may be played and swimming indulged in if the weather is kind. At all events, a jolly time is assured by the number of "bright sparks" in the Club who have already notified their intention of being present. I should welcome any offer of cricket gear, and a Belgrave versus Cadogan match, if it can be arranged, should prove popular. The usual catering arrangements will prevail, i.e., an al fresco lunch in the open air, and a set tea at 1/3 per head in "The Railway Inn." Should the weather be unkind this place is available for an impromptu dance, etc., so don't be deferred should the sky be cloudy. Travelling details are as follows :— Meet at Clapham Junction at 11 a.m. Cheap day fare is 2/10 return. Train leaves at 11-25 a.m. I should be glad if those who intend going would let me know, so that I can arrange for tea. * * * * * And now for another matter. There are still a number of outstanding accounts for Dinner and Dance tickets and I should be obliged if those members owing would settle at once. It is impossible for me to present a complete account of our Social activities to the Committee until these debts are settled, and I should be glad to have the co-operation of those concerned. W. A. Rice, 36 Ascalon Street, S.W.8. W. A. Rice W. A. Rice social organiser; address in the issue Earlswood Common Redhill Clapham Junction Cadogan

items.s: THE "R. W. RICKETTS" SHIELD RACE. Report of the club 20 miles walking championship on 23 April, won by Len Fletcher from Fred Rickards, with intermediate positions and the result with handicap. This year our 20 Miles Walking Championship, held on April 23rd, promised to be one of the most successful we have had with its 18 entries; but it must be confessed that the eventual result did not justify our optimism; nor was it of much assistance in the selection of our teams. This race was notable for the fact that Len Fletcher was essaying his first attempt at 20 miles. We have come to regard him as the best man over 10 miles in the country; and now eagerly awaited his performance over the longer distance, in view of the National Championship a fortnight later. Our President started the race and Tommy Green, the holder; Fred Rickards, a past holder; Harold King, and Len Fletcher were soon in the lead closely followed by Ted Saunders. Very little alteration had taken place at the eight miles mark, but before the 11 miles point was reached, J. E. Field and R. G. Hillier had retired. The positions were now (at approximately 10¾ miles) :— Rickards was forcing the pace at this point; and shortly afterwards Harold King retired owing to blistered feet. At 15 miles Tommy Green was attacked by cramp and, in view of the fact that the R.WA.. Championship was only a fortnight away, decided to retire rather than carry on and risk the reaction which such an effort would entail. Rickards and Fletcher were still together and it was only in the last 100 yards that Len drew away to win by a few yards. Fletcher had obviously had enough, but Fred Rickards finished looking as fresh as when he started. Ted Saunders walked well to finish third, and A. H. Field's fourth position in the Championship gained him first place in the sealed handicap. Fletcher is deserving of our heartiest congratulations in adding the Club 20 miles title to the Club Championships at two miles and 10 miles, which he already holds. Len has also been holder of the "Horwood" Cup (7 miles Junior Championship) in the past and so has held four of the six trophies the Club has to offer for walking—a record which will take a lot a equalling. And, of course, he still has plenty of time yet to gain the remaining two—the "Bayliss" Cup awarded to the first Club man to finish in the National Championship, and the "Belgrave" Cup awarded for the Long Distance Club Championship over the London to Brighton course! items.label: May 1932
items.sum: Report of the National 20 Miles walking championship at Fort Dunlop, Birmingham, on 7 May: T. W. Green 2nd and F. Rickards 4th behind A. E. Plumb, Belgrave 4th team, with full results and intermediate times.
items.s: THE NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the National 20 Miles walking championship at Fort Dunlop, Birmingham, on 7 May: T. W. Green 2nd and F. Rickards 4th behind A. E. Plumb, Belgrave 4th team, with full results and intermediate times. Two teams had been entered in the National 20 Miles Championship to be held at Fort Dunlop, Birmingham, on May 7th, and we went to the Midlands feeling confident that our walkers would make a good show, even though we were handicapped by the absence of several of our stalwarts. J. F. King, E. Saunders, J. C. Bidgood, A. H. Field and C. H. Speechley were unable to make the journey owing to business reasons, etc., and so we started one full team of eight walkers and three individuals. From the start our men assumed prominent positions and at five miles our placings were very satisfactory. At 10 miles our team was leading, scoring 53 points to the 60 of Derby W.C.; but shortly after this misfortunte overtook us. Harold King began to drop places and eventually retired with leg trouble. At 12 miles, approximately, our men were placed as follows :— 3 ... T. W. Green. 7 ... A. L. Fletcher. 16 ... F. Rickards. 31 ... F. E. Bentley. 41 ... H. F. King. A rough calculation showed Derby to be leading with 50 pts. We now had 57 pts, Surrey Walking Club 64 pts. and Birmingham W.C. 82 pts. At 15 miles Len Fletcher had lost some places; but Fred Rickards was gaining, as we had anticipated, and showed form which may help to gain him Olympic honours. Unfortunately, Fletcher had to retire from the race at 17 miles and our team prospects were gone. It was a case of the spirit being willing but the flesh weak. It is to be hoped that next time his legs will not go back on him, and that he will be responsible for a performance worthy of one who has competed with so much distinction at the shorter distances. This retirement caused Bentley to become our third man. He had been walking a very even race and shown excellent judgement in his first attempt at 20 miles. Meanwhile, Green, walking as well as he has ever done, was in second place without any chance of catching the North London Harrier, A. E. Plumb, who is clearly without superior at the National Championship distance. Rickards had overhauled many rivals and after a terrific tussle with Archibald, of the Surrey W.C., had to allow him to take third place, with Fred a few yards behind, fourth. As previously mentioned, Bentley, who did extremely well to finish inside three hours, was our third man to finish; and our team was completed by J. Rathbone, a member of our winning team in 1929. This secured fourth team position for us and must be considered a very creditable performance in a field of 23 teams. Our recovery of the Championship must be left until next year. In Tommy Green and Fred we have two of the world's best walkers at 20 miles, and we must strain every effort to support them in 1933. A special word of commendation must be given to W. Holman, who, in his first season of walking, finished 59th in 3 hrs. 6 min. 48 sec.—an excellent performance. We await his further progress with keen interest. 19 teams closed in. Position Ind. items.label: May 1932
items.sum: Explanation of the Belgrave points scheme rewarding 4th to 6th places in club handicaps, with the summer track groups, points values and prize thresholds.
items.s: THE BELGRAVE POINTS SCHEME. Explanation of the Belgrave points scheme rewarding 4th to 6th places in club handicaps, with the summer track groups, points values and prize thresholds. To our new members this may be a novelty but, actually, the scheme has been in operation since last October. The objects are to supply a means of reward to the man who runs, walks, throws or jumps consistently well, and yet is not fortunate enough to get amongst the first three prize winners during the season. Briefly, the rules are these :— 1. The scheme applies to Club Handicaps Only. 2. A prize-winner in above is immediately eliminated from the scheme, and forfeits any points won. 3. Points may be scored in one group only. Full details of how the scheme works were published in the October—November issue of the "Belgravian" (1931), which members may be able to borrow from other Club members. Points are awarded to the men who fill the fourth, fifth and sixth positions in Club Handicaps. The groups and points for the summer track season are as follows :— Group "A." All sprints and one 440 yards (June 29th)—10 races, points value is 24, 12 and 6. Group "B." 880 yards (4) and one 440 yards (August 17th)—5 races, points value 48, 24 and 12. Note—The 880 yards handicap on July 30th has been transferred to Group C. Group "C." 880 yards (July 30), ¾ mile, 1 mile and 2 miles—5 races, points value 48, 24 and 12. Group "D." Walks—7 races, points value 36, 18 and 9. Group "E." Field Events—6 events (including 120 yards hurdles)—points value 40, 20 and 10. Special Note. Veterans and Junior Races are not included in this scheme. These members are requested to enter Group "A" and thus participate. The differences in values are due to the number of races—the more races the less points, but an increased chance of scoring, and the reverse in small groups. I will keep the points scored at every Meeting and they will be published in the Gazette regularly. I will also be pleased to supply information any time when at Battersea Park track. The number of points to be scored to qualify for prizes is :— 240 points win a 1st prize. 120 " " 2nd prize. 60 " " 3rd prize. These prizes are of the same value as awarded in all our races, and will be presented at the end of the season, the probable date being the Annual General Meeting in September. K. B. O'Kell. K. B. O'Kell K. B. O'Kell keeps the points scheme records Club Handicaps Battersea Park

items.label: May 1932
items.sum: Article explaining the new efficiency-based conditions for the Harry Wright Shield (Field Events Champion), with the Belgrave 100 per cent. standards and the four championship meetings.
items.s: THE "HARRY WRIGHT" SHIELD. Article explaining the new efficiency-based conditions for the Harry Wright Shield (Field Events Champion), with the Belgrave 100 per cent. standards and the four championship meetings. Until 1924 Belgrave had never won a Senior Championship, but this year the great achievement was accomplished. We need not dwell on the further numerous honours which have been won by the Club. Now our minds are set on the few remaining events that have so far proved elusive to our men. Our runners and walkers are now reputed all over Britain,—and abroad also—as competitors warranting great respect, and the Committee hope that within a very short time our Field Events section will also obtain the same degree of success and publicity. The first move to this end has been the alteration of conditions for competition for the shield mentioned above, presented by our loyal supporter, Mr. Harry Wright. The Committee have agreed that the numerical strength of the section does not, at present, warrant the institution of Club Championships for the events we cater for, and I think that all our members will endorse the wisdom of this decision. To meet the needs of the section in the meantime, the Shield will carry with it the status of Field Events Champion, and this will be decided on an efficiency basis. In the past, men were compelled to compete in four events to score points—High Jump, Long Jump, Javelin and Shot Putt. Last year this condition was relaxed, but the competition still favoured the man who found it possible to compete in all four events, and the specialist at one particular field event was at a disadvantage. Under the new scheme it is quite optional how many events a man competes in—if he likes he can "have a go" at all four, but if he prefers to specialise, then he is quite in order doing so. I am indebted to our genial Hon. Editor, Alf. Harley, for the basic idea of the new scheme. Alf told me he attributes his lack of success in not winning a R.W.A. title to the fact that when in a race he does not concentrate enough as his brain is too busy trying to improve the conditions of the Field Events Section. Personally, I do not believe this—my reason for his backward performances is due to the fact that the officials will not allow him to take his umbrella and bowler hat with him. However, at a Committee Meeting Alf. mentioned a 100 per cent. scheme, so we have built up on this. To set a standard to work on, the winning performances in the A.A.A. Championships for 20 years, or as near as possible, have been averaged, and Belgrave 100 per cent. standard are :— To determine the Championship we are allocating four Meetings, and these will take place as follows :— Regarding the S.A.A.L.—even if a member is not chosen to represent the Club, I will arrange for members to have their event when the League competition is over, so make sure you send your entry in, and turn up on the evening stated. The performances only which are achieved on the evening stated will count for the Efficiency Scheme, even if a better performance is put up before or after that date. These are Field Events Club Championship Meetings, so members are reminded to note the dates and train accordingly. Next year we will probably have the events on Club Championship Saturday, but the scheme for this year was not finished before the fixtures were made. The usual handicaps will be held in conjunction. The efficiency is decided by the performance which is nearest to the above standards : for instance, in E. R. Turner can throw the Javelin 180 feet he achieves 93.26 per cent. of the standard. To equal or beat this the High Jumpers must clear 5 ft. 7in., or the Long Jumpers must leap 21 ft. 8½ in., or Shot Putters must get really annoyed and sling that cannon ball 40 ft. 1¼ in. It will thus be seen that a man can score efficiencies in more than one event, should he care to do so, although the highest percentage only will be recognised. It will be seen that the Javelin exponents have best chance at present, but it will be appreciated that we cannot lower our standard to suit our undeveloped talent—this would be very unfair to the "class" performers who are the rightful challengers of a Belgrave Club Championship. In concluding, I appeal to all our members to seriously consider trying their strength and skill in the Field event handicaps. I intend to frame the handicaps as handicaps, so you are assured of a generous allowance. I will also ignore your previous handicap and give you allowance on what you can do, and not what you ought to do. I don't intend to fiddle about in feet and inches in the Javelin event. If Bert Footer enters, I'll allow him the distance to the new Gasometer; if Harry Hare enters I'll allow him the distance of one Belgrave Building Brick, full of half-pennies, put side by side, and so on. So my lads, try a shilling's worth, even if you have not tried before—you will get a good start, and you will also develop that symmetrical figure which will cause pangs of envy from the other chaps, and gain the admiration of the charming ladies who grace our Meetings. For the convenience of members (And "the charming ladies," etc.?—Ed.) my address is :— 127 Oakhill Road, Putney, S.W.15. Gifts of cigarettes, chocolates, theatre tickets, etc., will not be accepted, and I have also a special book for entering names which were not bestowed upon me on my christening day (Asbestos leaves, I hope.—Ed.).
