items.label: January 1933
items.sum: Instructional article on hurdling by F. R. Gaby, five times A.A.A. champion: physical qualifications, the run-up and clearance, four gymnasium exercises and training advice, reprinted by permission of the Civil Service Sports Council.
items.s: HURDLING. Instructional article on hurdling by F. R. Gaby, five times A.A.A. champion: physical qualifications, the run-up and clearance, four gymnasium exercises and training advice, reprinted by permission of the Civil Service Sports Council. [The famous hurdler, who was five times A.A.A. Open Champion (1922-3-5-6-7), a member of the British Olympic team (1924-8), and British Empire team (1930)]. First of all let us deal with the physical qualifications that go to make the hurdler: height, length of leg, flexibility or looseness around the hips and a fair speed are the main essentials if one is to excel, and of these, the last two may, if not already possessed by the athlete, be developed by careful training and exercising. Phlegmatic temperament is also extremely useful in order to stand him in good stead against the many setbacks which may be his lot during the early days of training. The foregoing qualifications are for the ideal type of hurdler, the combination of which go towards making the champion. There are many, no doubt, who would like to take up this fascinating sport, but who are prevented by the thought that they do not possess the above. However, this should not deter them, because it is only given to one or two in any sport to be champions, and if every one who takes up sport of any kind stops to consider what chance they have of becoming top dog—where would we be? I venture to say that sport would soon be dead if it were not for the vast majority who enter sport for the love of it and with no thought of becoming champions. All this may sound rather strange after opening this article with qualifications for a champion hurdler, and although my later remarks may seem as though I am still on the same subject, I wish it to be understood they are general and directed to help the merest novice, as well as the athlete who has already had hurdling experience. It should be fairly evident that the budding hurdler, right from his early days, needs a coach to look after him, who will correct his faults and give him every encouragement, so that he may gain confidence in himself. We come now to the description of the event. The start, the run up and the take-off may be dealt with together, as they all depend on each other. It is usual to take seven, eight or nine strides to the first hurdle, but the actual number taken will be decided by the length of stride, which leg is used to lead over the hurdle and also by which leg comes out of the holes first at the start. This very important part of the race will have to be found by practice. The taking off point is approximately 7½ ft. from the hurdle, and if the hurdler finds that seven strides (the number usually taken) does not bring him to this position, then he must shorten his strides and try nine. If on the other hand nine strides takes him too near, then he must compromise by taking eight, and in this case alter the leading leg or reverse the starting leg. The writer was one of the few who found nine strides suited him best. Too great an emphasis cannot be laid on the importance of thoroughly mastering the run-up, for on this depends the speed which will be generated over the hurdles. Let a man get away badly and if he is not very experienced he will at once struggle and overstride, which usually proves fatal, for in all probability he will crash a hurdle and come down. Form must maintained at all costs. The hurdle clearance should be 11½ to 12 ft., which is split up by approximately 7½ ft., from the take-off to the hurdle and inside 4½ ft. to the landing point, and action is thus: As the hurdler arrives at the taking off point, the leading leg is lifted and kicked out towards the top bar, the opposite arm is thrust forward in a line with the leading leg and at the same time the body is bent sharply from the waist to meet the upward life of the leading leg. This body dip is very important and should be such that the knee practically touches the chest. Now as the leading leg reaches the top of the hurdle, the rear leg, which has been left hanging loose and idle, commences to come up. The leading leg is now snapped down and and the body is given an upward lift, this, although primarily used for a quick and close landing, automatically helps to lift the rear leg upward and enables it to be in a position on landing to follow through for a full first stride, which is a most important point. As the leading leg approaches the ground, the very forward lean of the body now gives way to the more straightened or running angle and the hurdler must land on the ball and not on the flat of the foot. At this moment the rear leg should be still very high and started on its follow through stride assisted by the reverse arm being thrust forward. This stride is no mere passive movement, but a real live and vigorous action, because on it depends whether the following two strides to the next hurdle are stretched or taken in a nice easy running action. Under no circumstances must the first stride be chopped. This is the whole action of high hurdle clearance and there now remains the other nine hurdles to be cleared in the same unbroken manner and the final sprint to the tape. The hurdler must keep his eye on the immediate hurdle to be cleared, and as he clears the last of these the tape flashes across his vision for the first time. Here the value of good technique is found by the athlete being, automatically in the correct running position to sprint the final fifteen yards to the tape without having, so to speak, to gather his arms and legs to him for this last effort. This, often, is a deciding factor in a close race. Exercises and Training. (1) This is an exercise which teaches and corresponds with the take-off action and which helps to strengthen the under muscles of the leading leg, also the abdominal and back muscles. Fling up leading leg sharply, simultaneously bending the body from the waist to meet this leg, at the same time throw out the opposite arm and keep the other bent, in the running action, to the body. It is essentially a vigorous action and must be carried out in one movement. It may be attempted walking or standing still and treated as an indoor or outdoor exercise. (2) This is an exercise which teaches hurdle clearance. Take a 3-ft. hurdle and stand about 1½ to 2 ft. in front, lift the leading leg over hurdle, bend the body from the waist down to the leg, throw out the opposite arm, keeping the other arm close into the body and drop over hurdle as though in act of clearing, not forgetting to bring the rear leg round and take a full stride forward. A fine exercise for the winter in the gymnasium for gaining style, as the different movements may be done slowly and faults more easily corrected under the supervision of a coach. It may also be varied by walking up to the hurdle and clearing it in the above manner; this will call for a good control of the body if the hurdler is to clear in good style. It may also be tried over a 2-ft. 6-in. hurdle. (3) This exercise will teach the hurdler to swing his rear leg and help to develop the hip muscles. Take a 3-ft. hurdle (to commence with), stand at one side and lift the rear leg into its flexed position of crossing the hurdle and let it rest on the top, now bend the body forward, swing the leg over and round, taking the full stride forward, not forgetting to use the arms in unison. This may later be attempted over the 3-ft. 6in. hurdle in one movement without the preliminary rest on the top, but only when the hurdler has strenghtened, loosened and accustomed the hip muscles to action. (4) This exercise, which helps tremendously, is quite a difficult ones to carry out. Sit on the floor (if indoors, on a mat, as there is a fair amount of pressure on the knee and ankle) in the position of crossing the hurdle: leading leg outstretched, rear leg flexed and arms in position, now try and raise and lower oneself without the arms or hands touching the floor. In the raised position one is resting on the heel of the leading leg and the side of the rear foot. It places a great strain on the under muscles of the whole of the leading leg and the hip of the flexed leg. This should be attempted very carefully at first as a strain or pulled muscle may result, but although it is very difficult it is probably the most beneficial of the series. In addition, one can strengthen the back and abdominal muscles whilst in this flexed position on the ground by bending the body from the waist so that the shoulder touches the knee, at the same time flinging out the opposite arm in a line with the leading leg. All the exercises described may be attempted in the gymnasium during the winter, and if the hurdler will practice the whole of them assidously he will find that it is half the battle. Providing there is sufficient room for a full run-up and a fair space in which to pull up, there is nothing to stop a little fast work in the gymnasium, but it is advisable to have a loose stick or cane for the top bar of the hurdle as this will give confidence to the hurdler. A long heavy cocoanut mat for landing is necessary and should be long enough to take up the first stride after landing, the fact that it is long and heavy will prevent it from slipping. Due allowance must be made in the run-up for the difference between turf and a wood floor. I have personally carried out all the above exercises in the Polytechnic gymnasium during winter time, using the items named: mat, loose stick, etc. When the time arrives for practice or training in the open, the exercise described may be carried out as in the gymnasium, but a preliminary warming up process is necessary, otherwise a strained or pulled muscle may be the result. More than one hurdle may now be attempted and these also should have loose tops, so that some fast work may be accomplished without loss of confidence to the hurdler. A knee or ankle pad may be worn at this stage. Careful measuring of the run-up, take-off, landing and the three strides between hurdles must be gone into. Pieces of paper may be used as a guide to this, and when on cinders, brushing before each run will help by enabling fresh measurements to be taken of the actual strides, take-off and landing. Correct one fault at a time and keep at it until the particular point is mastered. Some athletes are gifted with the ability to do the correct thing after only a little practice, others may take quite a long time, but they must peg away until it is second nature to do it as it should be done. When the athlete has mastered some of the technique of hurdling he may then practice starts out of the holes with the sprinters, and do some bursts of fifty to seventy-five yards, with an occasional run of 200 yards at three-quarter speed, the latter will help to develop stamina to last out 120 yards over a flight of hurdles. When in real training for competition one rarely runs over a full flight, between five and seven hurdles being enough, with plenty of slow running, doing five strides between hurdles and a couple of fast runs doing three strides, is usually sufficient. The reason for the slow running five strides is that it enables one to do a considerable amount of hurdle practice without unduly tiring oneself. But please remember this slow running five strides between hurdles should not be practised until one has mastered the three strides. This may sound rather puzzling, but five strides is useless for competition, and therefore the three strides must be concentrated on first. (The above article is reprinted by kind permission of the Civil Service Sports Council; and by courtesy of Mr. F. R. Gaby, whose efforts over the hurdles have given us all many thrills and moments of pleasure). F. R. Gaby F. R. Gaby five times A.A.A. Open Champion (1922-3-5-6-7), British Olympic team (1924-8), British Empire team (1930) F. R. GABY Mr. F. R. items.s: FIELD EVENTS. Field events notes looking ahead to the 1933 season, the Southern Amateur Athletic League and London Athletic Club match and Club handicaps, with W. H. J. Sutton as the contact. With Christmas over and the New Year here, the majority of us will be looking forward to the opening track fixture and getting down to strict training. I should like to see all the Field Events men start to polish up their technique and be ready for the Southern Amateur Athletic League events, the London Athletic Club match, and Club handicaps. We must seek to raise our standard, and ensure that the Club Field Events representatives in match events will be a credit to the Club and pull (or putt!) their weight. Entries for the Club jumping events were a little disappointing last year and it is hoped that some of our newcomers will apply themselves to these events. The Shot Putt handicaps were very successful—the extra event held on Championship Day providing a record entry. In conclusion, I would like to end on a personal note, by warning the Javelin throwers that I am not a dart-board! Let's hope 1933 will prove a very successful year for the Club in general and the Field Events section in particular! Enquiries, etc., to W. H. J. Sutton, 33 Tintern Street, Ferndale Road, S.W.4. W. items.sum: Short report noting that no detailed result was received for the third Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and Belgrave match at Sheen on December 10th, which Belgrave won as a team.
items.s: WITH THE RUNNERS. Short report noting that no detailed result was received for the third Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and Belgrave match at Sheen on December 10th, which Belgrave won as a team. In which we make the most of a bad job! It is unfortunate that the first fixture which should have been recorded, described, analysed and duly placed before our readers in these columns has passed—and we have no detailed result to offer! The race referred to was the third of the series between Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H. and ourselves, held over the course of the first-named club from their quarters at Sheen, on December 10th. We hear that Belgrave gained their usual easy team win, that Tom Carter was the first man to finish, and that Bill Rice and Harry Shields were prominent on our behalf. Also that Arthur Penny was the unfortunate victim of bad pointing, and went off the course when leading by a large margin, and was eventually placed 16th. However the team race was already won; and as we appear to have said all we have to say it is as well to pass to the next item. items.label: January 1933
items.sum: K. B. O'Kell's account of the Club 7 mile cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield, won by Arthur Penny.
e: Belgrave Harriers 7 Mile Cross-country Championship (Blackstaffe Shield)
items.s: “THE BLACKSTAFFE SHIELD.” K. B. O'Kell's account of the Club 7 mile cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield, won by Arthur Penny. K. B. O'Kell, a former Club Champion and holder of the "Blackstaffe Shield," now finds the pen mightier than the running pump and contributes Every year, during the Cross-country season, it is generally the cherished desire of all our gallant winter members to be the proud possessors of the above prize. That it has evaded the grasp of many worthy contenders cannot be denied, but this year this cannot be said. As an impartial critic, I venture to say that the winner, Arthur Penny, would have beaten all the previous holders, had they been in action, as in their hey-day, on this particular occasion. This is with all due respect to such brilliant runners as A. Allum and H. E. Footer. Penny ran like an animal; strong, fit as a fiddle and superbly trained. There were no men good enough to push him, and it is to Arthur's credit that he ran every inch of the distance, as his figures prove, apart from the fine physical display he gave. The "field" lined up minus a lot of very familiar faces—rather a pity, as some of the spicy "tear-ups" between various antagonists are very enjoyable to all concerned. However, we are all controlled by our own particular circumstances. Conditions were ideal; no wind, just a nice nip in the air, when our worthy "Father"—Teddy Gordon—told the 25 Belgravians to "Go," and they all set off to see who would be back first and hailed as the Club 7 Mile Cross-country Champion. The watches were ticking away, Harry Parker was having a very anxious time getting smokes from other chaps and squeezing into photographs, when Penny came along. At approximately half-way he led "Nick" Carter by 23 sec.—roughly 115 yards—quite a lead to create over a man of Carter's ability. Mains was on Carter's shoulder, then came our "second Footer"—Harry Shields—nearly a minute behind Penny! Cook, Rice, Shaw and Walker were in a string after this. Mention should be made of Shaw, who was in very experienced company. All the above boys were clocked, and we made off for the finish. In a very short time Penny came into sight and finished as fit as anyone could wish for. Carter came next, full out—a very game finish and only 37 seconds behind the winner. Next was Mains, 39 sec. behind. Shields 4th—great running by such a young "colt." Rice beat Shaw by 2 sec.—Bill always could raise a spurt. After this came all the "field" at intervals. My early remarks on Penny need not be added to. Carter deserves every praise for some very fine running, and also a lot of sympathy in not having a chance to have his name inscribed on the shield. He is in an era of super-runners—quite a different state of affairs from 1924—1926. Mains is a stout-hearted Belgravian, and has a knack of always running very well when the Club needs endeavour most. Shields was 4th; if he looks after himself and takes advice, he will win this trophy one day. Bill Rice is great, as consistent as the moon, and as varying; sometimes brilliant, sometimes clouded over, but always there. Of Shaw, I do not know much owing to business ties. However, I hear great reports of his promise, and sincerely trust he will mature to this anticipated success. To get sixth in a Belgravian Championship is a very good performance. I cannot dwell on all the members who made the race interesting, but Bill Webb might have chosen a more appropriate place than 13th! Bill is no chicken, but a fine Captain, and consequently a great asset to the Belgrave Harriers. The figures to be given will clearly show the credit and ability of all the various competitors. The handicap seems to have gone to the deserving fellows who put in some hard running. Perhaps our handicapper, Ernie Duffett, deserves a small medal for a good handicap. Four seconds between 3rd and 4th men—extremely accurate over seven miles and with a cunning horde of fellows! In conclusion, I extend my best wishes to all in the forthcoming Championships, and trust they will see that we have a good supply of the familiar headlines: "Belgrave Triumph Again." Arthur Penny should reserve a place in his cabinet for the "Southern" Honours, and have a needle and cotton prepared to sew a Red Rose badge on to his vest. As Belgravians, we all sincerely trust he will not disappoint the Club, himself and all his fellow-members. Arthur Allum and the croaking Footer were out again, and I also hope these two will contradict my earlier comments, with a reservation: that Allum does not overdo it, on top of his recent serious operation. However, their wonderful team spirit is to be greatly admired, and with the backing available we look forward to the big events with great optimism. Set a hot pace you fellows, and give our competitors a first-class view of your elegant shoulders, which house some stout hearts and spirits. The dawn of our greatest victories has broken—let us look back at the end of 1933 with quiet pride and whisper modestly: "I told you so, Belgrave Harriers!" Pos. Name Act. First position was shared by two of our promising younger runners—both eligible for the South of the Thames Senior event—in "Bert" Mitchell and "Nobby" Fletcher. items.label: January 1933
items.sum: "Captain" Webb's account of the New Year's Eve cross-country match at Cobham, won by Belgrave 13 points to 33 with C. T. Carter and H. W. Shields first, with results and team scores.
items.s: “DOWN COBHAM WAY.” "Captain" Webb's account of the New Year's Eve cross-country match at Cobham, won by Belgrave 13 points to 33 with C. T. Carter and H. W. Shields first, with results and team scores. "Captain" Webb crosses some verbal channels and takes us with him. It was New Year's Eve, though 'twas hard to believe so, for the countryside was bathed in beautiful sunshine as we sped luxuriantly to the field of honour comfortably seated in a superbly upholstered 20-seater. Who wouldn't go to Cobham? Having stormed the Village Hall, only to find that Cobham A.C. had long since moved their quarters elsewhere, we eventually reached our hosts, who gave us a very warm welcome, though their numbers were sadly depleted, possibly on account of the nearness of the fixture to the season's festivities. When we stripped for action there was a nippiness in the air that made one eager for work, and as the signal for the start of the race was given the teams plunged forward to their first objective, a gap in the hedge some 200 yards away, with the intervening whole a soft, sticky mass of newly-ploughed soil. A veritable cross-country man's joy! "What does he know of Wimbledon, Who only Wimbledon knows?" Two Cobham boys, Osborne and Hoar, were the first to drag their limbs across this stretch, closely followed by Carter, Michael and Shields. From here the course consisted of a short stretch of lane and two left-handed circuits of roughly 2½ miles of soft grass land and plough, interspersed by several obstacles; and then a final spurt home across the plough, from whence we started, making in all roughly 5½ miles. Half-a-mile out Osborne (Cobham) and Michael dropped back and Dench (Cobham) went up to the front with Carter and Shields. Thus remained the leaders until the end; Carter and Shields leading and Dench in close attendance. Carter always appeared to have the best of the other two, though there was a critical few minutes when Dench gained a temporary advantage of 25 yards, due to our boys missing the turn point. C. Tame was our next man home, having taken things steadily in the early part of the race he put in some sterling running in the last 2½ miles which took him near the front. W. W. Mitchell came next, though not at his best, followed by Saunders and R. G. Michael who had been having a great duel with Osborne. The result of the race was never in doubt with Cobham's 4th man trailing in the rear. The excellent running of the Juniors is worthy of comment. Shields should have many more good performances to his credit ere he reaches his majority. Michael is obviously improving and A. T. Jordan was seen doing tricks with the Captain on a parallel bar 2 miles out with Chantler and Martin close behind. E. Saunders made a very welcome re-appearance and performed very creditably. On the whole this was a very enjoyable outing, the change of going being a great contrast to that at Wimbledon, but beneficial for all that. I am sure all those who ran thoroughly appreciated the little things Dick Savage did for our comfort. The tea he brought from Cobham's hospitable quarters was good—and the arranging of the 'bus can be sometimes a much more irksome task than that of riding in it. The advantage of a coach on such an occasion cannot be gainsaid and maybe one day we shall learn to use them more often, but, I trust, in a more economical way. 1. Carter, C. T. B 32 47 2. items.sum: Len Rollins' report of the Surrey County Cross-Country Championship at Epsom on 14th January 1933, won by Arthur Penny with Belgrave team champions on 63 points, with an editor's note on H. Mitchell, and results; the text places Cook 13th, Robertshaw 14th, Carter 18th and Walker 19th whereas the table gives 16, 18, 22 and 20, and Walker's printed time 43 20 is out of sequence.
items.s: SURREY COUNTY CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Len Rollins' report of the Surrey County Cross-Country Championship at Epsom on 14th January 1933, won by Arthur Penny with Belgrave team champions on 63 points, with an editor's note on H. E. Footer giving his medal to A. F. Mitchell, and results; the text places Cook 13th, Robertshaw 14th, Carter 18th and Walker 19th whereas the table gives 16, 18, 22 and 20, and Walker's printed time 43 20 is out of sequence. Len Rollins discourses on the winning of the Individual and Team Championships of Surrey, as follows:— Held at Epsom, 14th January, 1933. What a day! Bill Rice and Tommy Carter, both suffering from the effects of the 'flu. But that did not deter us. A record entry lined up at the start, and our boys were anxious to get away. "They're off!" the bookies shouted. Sorry! thought I was at the Derby, being on the course, and standing next to Charlie Cook with a big, fat cigar (somebody remarked, "Lord Lonsdale!"). After the field had covered 1½ miles two Ranelagh men were making the pace, closely followed by Penny and Footer. Carter, Robertshaw and others were well up. Out into the country and Arthur Penny thought it was time to get going, so he went into the lead unchallenged. At three miles Penny loomed into sight 30 yards ahead of K. C. Allen, then our little "Bert" chasing Allen. Carter, undoubtedly feeling the effects of the 'flu, was 13th with the remainder of our team hanging on. This looked good and almost a certain Team Championship. After covering 5 miles Penny had left Allen by 200 yards and Bert fighting, as usual, was running 5 yards behind Penny (1st and 2nd). Robertshaw, Mitchell, A. F. (running as an individual), Carter and Cook were going great guns, occupying 13th, 14th, 15th and 17th positions and Mickey Walker holding 19th place. Tommy Carter collapsed but managed to pick himself up and eventually finished. Penny and Footer ran together until the last 100 yards, when Arthur Penny went away and won a glorious race by 10 yards. Congratulations, Arthur, upon running such a fine race and winning for the second time the Surrey County Championship. "Bert," although down with 'flu only a few weeks ago, ran a great race, and more will be heard of him in the big races. H. S. H. Cook, who finished 13th, ran well and once again was in our scoring six. Alec Robertshaw, whom we unfortunately do not see very much of these days, ran splendidly and scored in the 14th position. Keep it up, Alec, we shall want to see more of you in the Southern! Mickey Walker deserves special praise. Only in his second cross-country season, and if I may say so, only a moderate runner (yet), but what a fighter! He is an example to all members. Strenuous training has reaped its reward. Tommy Carter occupied 18th position and after a very hard race deserves a special pat on the back. Right from the start it was a terrific fight for him and only goes to prove his fine team spirit in running for the Club as he did. It would have been interesting to have seen what Carter would have accomplished if he had been fit. He has already this year beaten Dench, of Cobham A.C., who finished fifth. Would the Bels. have had 1, 2, 3? However, we were content with our win. Our six men scored 63 points as against Ranelagh's 130 and Surrey A.C.'s 150. We had the pleasure of taking the Cup from the latter Club. Of the remainder of the team, hard luck for Charlie Tame, who finished 21st and 7th for the Club. Our Captain, W. G. Webb, taking things very easily, completed the course and in company with Bill Rice and Nobby Fletcher, finished 37th, 38th and 41st respectively, closely followed home by W. W. S. Mitchell, 53rd. Perhaps the most unfortunate man was A. F. Mitchell, who arrived late and was entered as an individual. He ran splendidly, particularly after taking into consideration that he is unable to train, and only had two hours' sleep the previous night, owing to his work, and yet finished 15th. Congratulations, Mitchell! [Hon. Editor's Note—It is our pleasure to pay tribute to an act of sportsmanship on the part of H. E. Footer, and this is most easily done by quoting an extract from a letter to the Hon. Editor from A. F. Mitchell. " . . . . Owing to my work, I was a few minutes late at Epsom and so was not included in the team for the Surrey County Championship. I ran as an individual and finished 15th, and although as an individual my position didn't count in team race, Bert insisted that I should take his medal as a souvenir of the race. I accepted it in the spirit in which it was offered and it will be, I am sure, one of my most treasured possessions. This demonstrates the fine sporting spirit of the Belgrave Harriers. Yours etc. (signed), A. F. Mitchell. Comment on the above is quite unnecessary, and we will content ourselves with "Well run, Bert! Well done, Bert!] Position m. s. 1 1 A. Penny 40 54 2 2 H. E. e: South of the Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: H.L.R. ON THE AIR. H. L. Rollins, the new Assistant Hon. Secretary, introduces himself and looks ahead to the championship season. Hullo, everybody, this is H. L. Rollins calling, and I thank our Hon. Editor for his kind words in introducing me as your new Assistant Hon. Secretary. I fully realise the task I have taken upon myself, and also appreciate the enormous amount of work E. A. Duffett did when he was Running Hon. Secretary. However, I shall give of the best of my ability to serve the Club and in all fairness to myself I ask you members to co-operate with me and do your share when the time is opportune, in turning out to support the fixtures the Committee arrange for you. We are now in the "Championship season" and our chances do appear to be good. There is our 10 miles Championship to be held at Wimbledon on the 28th and form shown in this race will help the Selection Committee to choose the team for "The South of the Thames Senior" to be held at Epsom on 11th February. With Carter, Shields, Shaw, Mains, Rice, Mitchell (A.F.), Walker, Fletcher and others our team looks good. Also the "Sir Jeremiah Colman" Cup for the first team to finish 12 men (which we hold) must be retained. So come on, "The Bels," and put in some sterling training for this event. The Southern Counties race is being held at Chingford, but as this race is some weeks ahead I will deal with this later. In conclusion, I should like to see more members supporting the fixtures than have been in the past, particularly the Social runs arranged by the Committee. Usually a tea and social follows the run, and it is up to all members to participate. I should be glad to hear from any new members desiring information, and shall do all in my power to help them enjoy the benefits of Club membership to the full. Enquiries to H. L. items.s: OUR BOXING DAY MEETING. Report and results of the club's Boxing Day handicap meeting at Battersea Park: 120 yards sprint, two miles and three miles walk. As usual, a good crowd gathered at Battersea Park to witness our Boxing Day programme of handicaps. The entry for the Two Miles Run was excellent; that for the Sprint good for the time of year; but the number competing in the Walk was disappointing, although it must be remembered that we had teams competing in two distance events on the same day. R. W. Jordan showed excellent form in easily winning the Two Miles Handicap, and it is a great pity that business claims prevent him from turning out for us on Saturdays. Arthur Penny, in finishing second from the scratch mark, was responsible for a very fine performance, and was only slightly slower than Jack Flower in the corresponding race last year. The 120 yards Sprint final was a very close affair, victory going to F. W. Pritchard with Mewes and Pamment only inches away. The Walk provided Don Brown with another chance to show his great improvement, which is rapidly taking him into the highest class. RESULTS. 120 Yards.—1, F. W. Pritchard (12); 2, A. Mewes (15); 3, A. items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes: coming walking fixtures up to the R.W.A. Junior Championship at Birmingham, new walkers, Don Brown's improvement, and the R.W.A. 20 miles championship to be held in the Dulwich area. Our racing activities have not followed one another quite so frequently during the last week or two; but the weeks to follow will provide everyone with all the competition they desire. To set out our coming fixtures in tabulated form:— Jan. 28—Club 10 Miles Championship ("R. Murphy" Shield). Feb. 4—L.C.C. Trams S.C. Open 7 Miles Race. Feb. 18—Ashcombe A.C. Open 10 Miles Race. Mar. 4—R.W.A. JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP (10 MILES) AT BIRMINGHAM. Is it again our turn to win the "Junior"? Our first team of eight walkers will all be doing their utmost, and it would take a super-optimist to predict our first four to finish. This is all to the good, and if only our men can avoid the very prevalent illness which is striking so many down at the moment, we need fear no team. One of our newcomers this season, F. W. Chandler, is showing gradual improvement; and is joined this month by three others, L. Jones, D. J. Heath and H. W. Clemow, who, we trust, will soon settle down and become valuable members of our Walking Section. One of the most pleasing features of this season's activities has been the phenomenal improvement of Don Brown. Following upon an excellent walk v. Surrey W.C. over their West Wickham sourse, he took second place in the Club Junior Championship; and has since finished third in the London Business Houses Championship. In this latter event he also won the sealed handicap held in conjunction. Congratulations! Brown should be well to the fore when the R.W.A. "Junior" is decided. It has been decided to hold the R.W.A. National Championship (20 miles) which takes place on May 13th, in the Dulwich area. The race will start and finish on the Crystal Palace Parade and will consist of three laps (two of 7¼ miles, and a smaller one to complete the distance) in the Dulwich and Herne Hill districts. It is hoped that when the time comes we shall have a large crowd of supporters around the course to encourage our walkers. Further details will follow in later issues. F. W. Chandler F. W. items.s: MATCH v. SURREY WALKING CLUB. Report and results of the walking match against Surrey Walking Club over 9¾ miles from West Wickham, won by Surrey W.C. 93 pts. to 117; the printed Belgrave team score (3, 4, 5, 6, 12, 13, 17, 18, 19, 20) does not match the B/S marks in the result list, kept as printed. We travelled to Croydon on December 10th to meet our old rivals, Surrey W.C., over their West Wickham and back course, 9¾ miles to testing roads. Harold King took the lead from the start, closely followed by Archibald and Kemp, of the S.W.C., with Brown, A. H. Field and Harley not far away. Field dropped away later, and at about four miles Archibald took the lead from King and retained it to the end. Shortly afterwards, Kemp suffered disqualification, and with Brown walking strongly and Saunders coming through the field at a fast pace, our chance of a team win looked very rosy. At about six miles, however, W. F. Amer, one of the Surrey stalwarts, entered the first half-dozen places and eventually finished second. Thus Surrey W.C. had the first two men, followed by four of ours, but the superior packing of our hosts in the later positions gave them a team win. Of our walkers, we were pleased to see King again in action; and Brown's forward walking gave general pleasure and was in advance of anything he had previously shown. His style and turn of speed were very impressive; and we look to him for many fine performances in the future. RESULTS. TEAM SCORES. 1. items.label: January 1933
items.sum: Report and results of the Club Junior walking championship for the Horwood Cup at Wimbledon on 17th December 1932, won by Harry Churcher with C. H. Speechley winning the handicap, with a table comparing times over the course in 1930–32, signed J.B.B.
e: Belgrave Harriers Junior Walk Championship (Horwood Cup)
items.s: THE "HORWOOD CUP" RACE. Report and results of the Club Junior walking championship for the Horwood Cup at Wimbledon on 17th December 1932, won by Harry Churcher with C. H. Speechley winning the handicap, with a table comparing times over the course in 1930–32, signed J.B.B. There were 15 starters in the race held on 17th December, 1932, at Wimbledon, over our usual seven-miles course for the Club Junior Championship and the "Horwood" Cup. F. W. Thorn, a former winner, and C. W. Redgrave, second last year, were notable absentees, both having been unable to train this season. C. E. Churcher and J. G. Coleman, who have been scoring for the Club in open handicaps this year, were prevented from racing by colds; but otherwise the field was well representative of our Junior strength. A most interesting race ensued. Harry Churcher, the holder, cut out a fast pace at the start, but D. E. Brown, who improves every time out, would not be shaken off, and for four miles the pair raced neck and neck. In the second lap, however, Brown tired and eventually lost second place to Charlie Speechley, whilst Harry Churcher went on to win by about 270 yards in the exceptionally fast time of 56 min. 53 sec.—the fastest yet recorded over the course by any walker qualified to take part in the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship. Speechley improved on his last year's time by 1 min. to win the handicap by 3 sec. from D. E. Brown. Bert Field, despite a pull for second prize in the preceding Club handicap, took the third handicap prize. RESULTS. Since last the Belgrave Harriers won the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship in March, 1930, the three races for the Club Junior Championship have been held over the course used in the race described above, and as several of this year's team have taken part in two or more of these races, the following table throws light upon the improvements made. The continued improvement made by Charlie Speechley is the most remarkable feature to be noted, as he is already a veteran. D. E. Brown has only been racing 16 months and promises to develop into a champion. Bert Field gets minutes faster in seven-miles races each after each "50 Kilos" or "Brighton" race that he essays. The Eastleigh Town S.C. decided to promote an Open Walk on Boxing Day, the course being from Eastleigh to Southampton and back, a distance of 12 miles. The purpose of the race was to encourage the sport in the locality with a view to strengthening the promoting club; and, possibly, lead to the formation of other clubs in the district. The entry was not a large one, but interest in Tommy Green's home town was tremendous and large crowds turned out for the start and finish. Green, as expected, was the winner, being followed home by Sykes, Cooper and Watts, all of Eastleigh. Then came Harley and Bidgood, of ours, and as scoring was three aside, the home team won by 9 pts. to 12pts. items.s: HONOURS BADGES. The Committee's new Honours Badge for members reaching a high standard, with the conditions of award and the qualifying standards in each branch of the sport. The Committee have decided to institute an Honours Badge which will be awarded to those members reaching a certain standard of ability. The standard of attainment to secure one of these badges has been kept high in order that it shall be an "Honours Badge" in every sense of the word, and to ensure that it shall be considered a real honour to have one's name added to the list of those entitled to bear the Badge. The form the badge will take has not yet been definitely decided, but will probably consist of the Club badge combined with a laurel wreath, and will be worn on the vest. It is, of course, impossible to make these awards retrospective, and the following conditions have been drawn up to govern the award of Honours Badges:— (1). No badge to be awarded without the consent of the General Committee and the names of winners to be recorded on the Club Minute Book. (2). Only first-claim members shall be eligible, and only performances when entered in the Club name shall be considered. (3). Only one badge may be awarded to any member. (4). The Committee is empowered to consider any performances not otherwise provided for such recommendation under this clause to be confirmed by the Annual General Meeting. The following are the qualifications necessary to secure an Honours Badge:— Cross-Country Running. Anyone finishing in the first 25 individual positions of the National Cross-Country Championship: or in the first six individual positions in the Southern Cross-Country Championship. Track Running. Anyone attaining First Class A.A.A. standard in the A.A.A. Championships, or finishing in the first four positions of the 100 yards A.A.A. Championships. Field Events. Anyone attaining A.A.A. First Class standard in Championships. Track Walking. Anyone attaining First Class standard in the A.A.A. Chamships. Road Walking. Anyone finishing in the first 12 individual positions in the R.W.A. National Championships; or in the first three individual positions in the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship. items.sum: A year's progress report on the Building Fund for club headquarters, including a dropped offer of a house in Lauriston Road, Wimbledon, and the fund's present state of £56 7s. 8½d.
items.s: BELGRAVE BUILDING FUND. A year's progress report on the Building Fund for club headquarters, including a dropped offer of a house in Lauriston Road, Wimbledon, and the fund's present state of £56 7s. 8½d. A period of 12 months has now elapsed since the Building Fund was instituted, and if the amount of cash now standing to its credit does not reach the optimistic figure that was at first anticipated, there remains a satisfactory feeling that progress has been made and that the fulfilment of the objective will eventually mature. For the information of any member who may not be aware of the scheme, the following brief details are repeated:— 1. To provide suitable headquarters with all facilities for training and recreation for the exclusive use of Belgrave Harriers. 2. Subscriptions to fund to be regular and purely voluntary. 3. As an easy method it is suggested that you do not spend a halfpenny and that every coin of that denomination be placed aside for the benefit of the Fund. A box for that purpose will be provided if required. 4. In the event of the scheme being abandoned, each member's actual contribution will be returned. It will be of interest to all to know that the Committee recently considered an offer for sale of a large house situated in Lauriston Road, Wimbledon, midway between St. John's Hall and the Common. The premises would have been well suited to the Club as Headquarters. The amount required was in the region of £2,500, and after careful consideration, lack of capital and difficulties in raising sufficient income to repay mortgage and working costs caused the matter to be dropped. And yet if every reader would enter whole-heartedly into the halfpenny scheme we could tackle the matter with a light heart. However, it was not anticipated that our Headquarters would be obtained quite so quickly; whilst the information obtained by the Committee will be of service in the future. The present state of the fund is as follows:— The fund is growing weekly. May we have your support to hasten the growth? Any details will be given by Hon. Treasurer. items.label: February 1933
items.sum: Editorial celebrating second place in the Southern cross-country (H. E. Footer winning), the R.W.A. junior walk team win and first-time placing in the National, with the death of sprinter Albert H. Shannon.
e: Road Walking Association Ten Miles Junior Championship
items.s: Editorial celebrating second place in the Southern cross-country (H. E. Footer winning), the R.W.A. junior walk team win and first-time placing in the National, with the death of sprinter Albert H. Shannon. The three successive Saturdays, February 25th, March 4th and March 11th—brought with them three performances of outstanding merit which focussed the eyes of all the athletic world upon Belgrave and more than ever fortified our right to be considered the greatest all-round athletic club in the country. These three successive knocks upon the door of Fame have drawn universal attention to our Club, and congratulatory messages have been received from all directions. Great things have been done, great things remain to be done, and we are confident in the knowledge that we have the men to do them. The cumulative wave of success must not stop with March 11th, 1933, but carry on, and on . . . . always preserving the spirit of comradeship, honest endeavour and Club loyalty which has raised us to our present position. * * * * * And now let us deal chronologically wlth the above-mentioned exploits. With February 25th came the “Southern” our best team position yet—second; and an individual win for H. E. Footer with A. W. Penny third. All honour to Bert upon his wonderful success! It would be difficult indeed to mention anyone in our Club—or in athletics generally, for that matter—who is more deserving of the high honours which have now come his way. They have not come easily, and are probably appreciated all the more because of that. Bert’s enthusiastic perseverance throughout a dozen or more years’ running holds a moral for all of us, as does also his conscientious, systematic training. It is very fitting that one who has done so much for the Club, who has imbued his club-mates with confidence and has been largely responsible for bringing our team to its present state of excellence, should be the first to receive the Club Honours Badge—even if Arthur Penny earned his one minute later! On March 4th “that remarkable club Belgrave” —we quote the Sheffield Sports Echo—won the Road Walking Association Ten Miles Junior Championship at Birmingham and so once again became proud holders of the “Garnet” Cup. This is our fourth win—a record superior to that of any other club in the country—and was an example of good team work. The score of 26 points is the second lowest ever recorded in the history of this competition, and the best Belgrave score yet. * * * * * Further honours came on March 11th, when for the first time in our Club history we were placed in the National Cross-country Championship; and had two men in the first five home, so securing International selection. Our heartiest congratulations go out to Bert Footer and Arthur Penny upon their well-deserved honour. We trust it will become an annual affair for them, and that in future years there will be other Belgravians to accompany them. * * * * * Truly, a wonderful sequence of meritorious achievements and the Club’s thanks and congratulations are extended to all who participated in these three successes. Successful as the past month has been, we can look to an even more successful future for we have a wealth of young talent rapidly maturing, whilst our tried and experienced athletes should be active on our behalf for many years to come. * * * * * It is with very deep regret that we have to announce the death of one of our young sprinters, Albert H. Shannon. He had been a member of the Club for many years past and had shown considerable promise. Immediately before his death, the International cross-country results were read to him, and he died whilst expressing his appreciation of Footer’s running. We extend our profound sympathy to Albert’s parents and friends. * * * * * Club vests, badges, ties, etc., may be obtained from the Hon. Treasurer, who would also be glad to receive any outstanding subscriptions and donations towards the Belgrave Building Fund. H. E. Footer H. E. Footer won the Southern cross-country championship; first to receive the Club Honours Badge A. W. Penny A. W. items.s: SOCIAL. Report on the club's social evening at Wimbledon and dance at the Queensberry Hall, South Kensington, with notice of the Club Dinner at Carr's Restaurant, Victoria, on May 6th. Since our last issue appeared, we have held a successful social evening at Wimbledon; and a dance at the Queensberry Hall, South Kensington, which exceeded even our most sanguine expectations. A fine crowd assembled here and everyone appeared to enjoy themselves immensely. We shall certainly have to consider holding several Saturday evening dances at this venue next season. The proceedings were crowned by the arrival of our “National” team from Alderley Edge, bringing with them the trophy awarded to the first Southern Club. Our next social function is the Club Dinner at Carr’s Restaurant, Victoria, on Saturday, May 6th, which it is hoped every loyal Clubman will make a special effort to attend. The entertainment promises to be of a novel character and the venue is easily accessible from all parts of London, so note the date and write for your tickets (5/- each) to : W. A. items.s: THE OPEN WALKS. Report on Belgrave walkers' showing in three open walks promoted by Cambridge H., L.C.C. Tramways A. & S.C. and Ashcombe A.C., including Green's disqualification. Since our last issue appeared we have participated in three open events promoted by the Cambridge H., L.C.C. Tramways A. & S.C., and Ashcombe A.C. The first of these, a seven miles race, provided us with a shock, for Green was disqualified with 100 yards to go. Even Olympic Champions have their lapses! This robbed us of scratch honours, but first handicap team prizes came the way of A. H. Field, Harley, Speechley and Elson. A peculiarity of the handicap was that four men dead-heated for third place in the handicap, two of them, Field and Harley, coming from our own Club. If this happens very frequently promoting clubs will be crying out for a new Handicapper, to save them additional expense. In the L.C.C. event, owing to considerably shorter handicap marks, our men were unable to shine, although they recuperated somewhat to take third prizes in the Ashcombe A.C. 10 miles race a fortnight later. This is now the only 10 miles race in the South before the Junior and is looked upon as as a final test before the Championship, We cannot be said to have come out of this test too well compared with our Surrey W.C. rivals, but we were confident of doing better things a fortnight later, and so it proved. items.sum: Report and results of the club ten miles walking and cross-country championships on January 28th on a frozen Common, won by Tommy Green (walk) and Bert Footer (run); the text says J. E. Field was disqualified while the table lists A. H. Field 8th, and R. F. Elson's printed handicap time (79 54) does not match his actual time less start.
items.s: THE CLUB TEN MILES CHAMPIONSHIPS. Report and results of the club ten miles walking and cross-country championships on January 28th on a frozen Common, won by Tommy Green (walk) and Bert Footer (run); the text says J. E. Field was disqualified while the table lists A. H. Field 8th, and R. F. Elson's printed handicap time (79 54) does not match his actual time less start. January 28th was the day fixed for the decision of the Club Ten Miles Walking and Cross-country Championships, and what a day it was! Winter’s icy hand had taken hold of the days preceding our championships and snow and persistent frost caused fears that our events might have to be postponed. However, the Saturday proved to be clear of snow, although still intensely cold, with the Kingsmere and other lakes covered with several inches of ice. Hundreds of skaters thronged the ice, and thousands of spectators gathered—whether to watch the sport, or in the expectation of a crack in the ice is a matter for speculation. It is peculiar that so many people surge to the Common when the ponds are ice-covered, and yet ignore its delights in winter on the many other occasions when the conditions are of a more temperate nature. However, to come to our racing. The walkers were first away in quest of the “R. Murphy” Shield. Green, J. E. Field, Brown and Harley, walking together, made the pace for the first two miles, when the last-named began to drop. Half-a-mile later Brown allowed the leaders to get away and so positions remained until the half-way mark. Shortly after this Field suffered disqualificaton and Saunders and Speechley passed Harley. R. F. Elson came through strongly in the last two miles, to dispossess Speechley of fourth place. Tommy Green had an easy win and one missed the customary struggle between him and A. L. Fletcher, winner in the previous two years, who was a non-starter on this occasion. Second place was taken by Don Brown, still improving and likely to improve still further into the very top class; and Ted Saunders, always persevering and likely to be a valuable aid to the Club at twenty miles, took the third medal. Jack Bidgood, showing a return to his form of a few years back, took the handicap prize, with Reg. Elson and ditto Hillier filling the minor placings. And now for the run. For weeks there had been much friendly argument as to the merits of Footer and Penny and the prospects of one beating the other. If anything, it is possible that there was the slightest balance in favour of Penny, the Club Seven Miles champion, but all were agreed that an interesting race was certain. Owing to the possible danger to ankles it was decided to omit Beverley Brook, now frozen over; and to substitute a lap of the field at the start to compensate for the distance so lost. The competitors were greatly hampered and hindered by the hundreds of cars and multitudes of people who had assembled for skating and sight-seeing. Not only was this difficulty of forcing one’s way through crowds encountered in the starting field, but also at the Kingsmere, which serves as the furthermost point of our course. This lap had to be run twice and so our runners’ task was anything but enviable. However, with all its difficulties our men managed to carry on. Footer and Penny were together for six miles but then Bert managed to open up a gap and eventually won by over a minute, so winning the “Macher” Shield—not for the first time. Third came Arthur Allum, showing that he is rapidly recovering from his operation and that next year we may expect him to be in International class again. Jack Flower was unlucky in that he was forced to retire from the race at four miles owing to a nail working through his shoe into the foot. Continuance in the race with this handicap might well have led to a serious injury, to the detriment of the Club’s team prospects in future races and so he did well to retire. Owing to the alteration in the course, it is impossible to compare Bert’s time with that of previous years, but undoubtedly it was of a very high order. This running won for Bert the sealed handicap, with Arthur Penny second, and Cecil Mains third. Alf. Taylor ran well and was a little unfortunate to be squeezed out of the sealed handicap places. e: Road Walking Association Ten Miles Junior Championship
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking column on the club's record fourth R.W.A. Junior ten miles win, prospects for the R.W.A. National 20 miles on a Crystal Palace course, the R.W.A. Handbook and "Nijmegen" Shield, and forthcoming walking fixtures. Well, the “Junior” is over and won; and we take particular pride in this fourth win of ours which places us above all other clubs in the number of wins recorded. Out nearest rivals are Sheffield United Harriers, who gained their third win last year. Our juniors must always strive to be at least one win ahead of our nearest rivals. Our win this year was particularly gratifying, as our team recorded the lowest score ever made by a Belgrave team and the second lowest in the series of 19 races. Another feature of our success was the good team work which received the commendation of many outside critics. At eight miles our four were one behind the other within a distance of 100 yards or so, and no other walkers intervening. From this point onwards Harry Churcher, who was very unlucky not to gain his Honours badge, drew away from the others, but less than 30 seconds covered Brown, Field and Harley at the finish. Most clubs expect to have a lean year in this particular race, following upon a win, but there is certainly no reason why we should not be prominent again next year with men such as C. E. Churcher, R. F. Elson, C. H. Speechley, J. C. Bidgood, C. W. Redgrave, H. Latter, R. C. Hillier, E. A. Jackman and many others to call upon. Let's quote from The Sheffield Sports Echo of March 11th: "The Ten Miles Junior Walking Championship at Fort Dunlop was won by that remarkable club, Belgrave, who, although not so strong in walking as Birchfield are in running, can claim to be the most consistent club in the country." There's something for our walkers to live up to! Meanwhile, our principal aim must be to regain the Senior R.W.A. 20 miles championship and so complete a glorious treble—Brighton Team. "Junior" Team, "Senior" Team. It would be a wonderful feat if we could add a National Walk win to the runners placed team in the National cross-country championship, and so be the first Club in the country to be placed in both National championships in one season! Our prospects are quite bright with both T. W. Green and F. Rickards eager to improve upon even last years' very fine performances, and strong backing will be forthcoming from J. F. King, H. F. King, F. E. Bentley, E. Saunders, A. H. Field, J. C. Bidgood, R. C. Hillier, C. H. Speechley, W. Holman and others. As previously announced, the race will start and finish on the Crystal Palace Parade, and the course will be via Sydenham Hill, Lordship Lane, Court Lane, Dulwich Village, Red Post Hill, Herne Hill, Half Moon Lane, Burbage Road, Gallery Road, Alleyn Park, The Avenue, Farquar Road. This circuit (7¼ miles) will be walked twice and a smaller lap once. It is hoped that we shall have some hundreds of supporters around the course on May 13th to encourage our representatives and cheer them on to what we hope will be our fifth National Championship. The Road Walking Association have recently published their annual Handbook giving details of past championship performances, details of records, rules, and other information of immense interest to all walkers. Copies (6d. each, by post 7d.) may be had from the Walking Hon. Secretary, address below. In addition to the Shield awarded to the winning team in the National 20 miles Championship, the "Nijmegen" Shield is also up for competition and goes to the Club first finishing their complete team of eight. Sheffield United Harriers are the holders of this trophy at the moment, and it is to be hoped that the "Nijmegen" Shield will follow the "Garnet" Cup from Sheffield to London into Belgrave possession. Meanwhile, the track season is fast approaching and our walkers will again have plenty of opportunity of competition. The first Club handicap is on Saturday, May 6th; and our Inter-Club races at 1, 2, 3 and 5 miles will take place on Monday, June 19th. FORTHCOMING FIXTURES. April 22—Wimbledon—Club 20 Miles Championship for "R. W. Ricketts" Shield (Holder, A. L. Fletcher), and Sealed Handicap. May 6th—Battersea Park—Club 2 Miles Handicap. May 13th—Crystal Palace Parade—R.W.A. National 20 Miles Championship. All enquiries, etc., should be addressed to the Walking Hon. Secretary. A. A. Harley, 39 Roxburgh Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. items.sum: J. B. Belchamber's report of Belgrave's win in the R.W.A. Junior ten miles walk at Fort Dunlop on 4th March, with individual result and team placings; it compares the score with the Surrey W.C. win of 1919 but then refers to Surrey's fourth man 'in 1929'.
items.s: THE "JUNIOR." J. B. Belchamber's report of Belgrave's win in the R.W.A. Junior ten miles walk at Fort Dunlop on 4th March, with individual result and team placings; it compares the score with the Surrey W.C. win of 1919 but then refers to Surrey's fourth man 'in 1929'. It was a happy and hopeful party of Belgraves that made the journey to Birmingham on 4th March to contest the R.W.A. Junior Championship over 10 miles. Realization of the strength of the opposition was not lacking, but our boys were quietly confident that they would win. Arrived at Birmingham we proceeded by tram to Fort Dunlop, where we were delighted to notice that the flags and pennons profusely decorating the tramway standard were claret and gold, or so nearly so that no other club competing could claim them as their's. This was strange! The Dunlop Walking Club's colours are white, amber and black! Was it a happy chance, or was our victory confidently anticipated? Presumably the latter, as the arrangements when a race is held at Fort Dunlop are so complete and all-embracing, and such forethought is exercised, that a successful forecast of the winners and appropriate celebration would only be in keeping with all that is done for us. The day was a very fine one, and conditions were favourable until the leaders had about a mile to go. Then there was a very heavy rainstorm. The wind blew violently, whilst the rain was icy cold and keenly penetrating. The race for individual honours was an exceptionally fine one. W. Treacher (North London Harriers) led for about 9 miles, but L. P. Hancock (Surrey Walking Club) and W. J. Hogan (Southgate and Wood Green A.C.) were always within striking distance. At 9 miles Hancock closed on Treacher, and for two-thirds of a mile there ensued a tremendous tussle, with Hancock shewing as the likely winner. Treacher was then dropped, but Hogan came up with a fine burst and beat Hancock by about 30 yards. Our boys walked well right from the commencement of the race. At three miles, four of ours were right up and we were leading on points. At five and six miles we were substantially ahead. The Surrey Walking Club men have a habit of producing their best walking soon after six miles, but although Hake and Burt walked very strongly over the last part of the journey and picked up many valuable points, they could not get up to our leaders. Hake's effort was a particularly fine one. RESULT. TEAM PLACINGS. Thirty teams competed and the field numbered 211. On only one occasion has this championship been won with a lower score, viz., in 1919, when the Surrey Walking Club, represented by Blackmore, Amer, Chilton and Archibald, scored 22 points only. On that occasion, however, only 21 teams were in the field, whilst the starters numbered 143. So proportionally our score was phenomenally low. Surrey's fourth man in 1929 finished 4 mins. 5 secs behind the winner, whereas Alf. Harley was this year only 3 mins. 14 sec. behind Hogan. Accordingly we have ample reason to be proud of our juniors. Aiming at a win for the Club, Harry Churcher walked with scrupulous care and finished fourth in the race, giving a display the fairness of which was unquestionable. Young Don Brown did all that we hoped, and showed that he must be looked upon as a potential champion. Bert Field walked the race of his life, and Alf. Harley fought the Surrey boys in a style that thoroughly earned a place in the winning team. Charley Speechley is still, by the irony of fate, a junior, and C. E. Churcher, our fifth man to finish, also lives to walk another day as a junior. A pleasing feature of the race was the revival of walking strength shewn by the Polytechnic team. In the days of Billy Sturgess, Jack Butler and J. J. Lynch, the Poly. walkers were a power in the land, but for some years past they have been only a shadow of their former selves. A. O. Tookey, whom we all know as a second-claim member of our own club, has unearthed a great number of novices this year and has performed Trojan service in whipping them into shape and style. That they should walk into third place against such opposition after so short a novitiate must indeed be gratifying to him. It was a success that was thoroughly deserved, and we are heartily pleased to compliment him and his club-mates. J. B. BELCHAMBER. m. s. 1. W. J. Hogan Southgate and Wood Green A.C. (Ind.) 79 38 2. On this occasion we depart from our usual custom of presenting the various events in chronological order and prefer, instead, to commence with the "high-lights" of the past few weeks. Owing to the space devoted to the three Championship events it becomes impossible to deal, other than in a sketchy manner, with our various engagements, which are summarised at the conclusion of this feature.

e: South of Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: THE "SENIOR" SOUTH OF THAMES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Joe Flower's report of the Senior South of Thames cross-country championship on Epsom Downs, where Belgrave, led by Tom Carter in ninth, were second to Surrey A.C. and retained the "Sir Jeremiah Colman Cup", with result and team scores. Joe Flower blossoms out and discourses on:— Held on Epsom Downs, the above race was decided on a bitterly cold day, the wind cutting right through one. Our team, thanks to the "flu" which was then at its worst, were not quite as fit as we had hoped. Tom Carter had had a bad attack of "flu" and with only a bare week's training ran superbly to lead our boys home finishing in the ninth position. The race was started against the wind and somehow the "Bels" were bottled up at the start, and at the first obstacle, about 400 yards out, not one of our men was in the first fifty places. The team must have put in some marvellous running out in the country, because when they came round for the first time we looked assured of a place. Every man in the team ran well, and if anyone deserves special mention I think probably A. F. Mitchell is the one. He is employed on night work and cannot train, and he only had about two hours' sleep before the race. His position 30th, proves his natural ability and fine team spirit. Another splendid performance, which in my opinion shows the fine team spirit which exists amongst our members, was that of Bill Rice. He was suffering from a very bad throat and should not have run, but as there was no one else to take his place, he did his bit and kept his end up, thereby enabling us to retain the "Sir Jeremiah Colman Cup." These are only two instances of the Belgrave team spirit and whilst this spirit lasts, our teams are bound to improve and reach the highest honours in the near future. Our two Kent members, Mains and Shaw, are proving their worth, and greatly assisted the team to gain second position to the Surrey A.C., our old rivals, whom we all congratulate on their splendid victory. The result is published below, so you will see for yourselves that every man ran well, and that our runners are a credit to the Club. RESULT. TEAM SCORES. Pos. m. s. Pos. m. s. 9 C. T. items.sum: "The Tatler"'s account of the Southern Counties cross-country championship at the Jubilee Retreat, Chingford, won by Bert Footer with Arthur Penny third and Belgrave second to Aldershot Command, plus the Junior 5 miles (dated February 27th, 1933, a day the text calls a Saturday), ending with the team song and the result and team scores.
items.s: THE SOUTHERN COUNTIES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. "The Tatler"'s account of the Southern Counties cross-country championship at the Jubilee Retreat, Chingford, won by Bert Footer with Arthur Penny third and Belgrave second to Aldershot Command, plus the Junior 5 miles (dated February 27th, 1933, a day the text calls a Saturday), ending with the team song and the result and team scores. "The Tatler" tittle-tattles about The dawn of February 27th, 1933, to the majority in this little isle of ours was merely the heralding of another Saturday. But to the Belgrave Harriers it had a special significance, for this day the Southern Counties Championship was to be contested at the Jubilee Retreat, Chingford, and our team had virtually promised a good performance. I left my home with the rain coming down very heavily, but on my arrival at Chingford I found to my great delight that it had ceased, and realised that the "Bels" supporters could now do their supporting in real earnest; which, by the way, brings me to wonder how many supporters of other clubs change into running kit solely to encourage their club-mates in the far distant and outlandish country! The "boys" all looked remarkably fit in the dressing-room and our prospects of a record Club performance seemed very rosy. The start of the race was very brisk and businesslike, the teams getting away in a body and the "Bels" were seen well to the fore. Doing a "traditional short-circle' 'round the golf-links, the runners had to cross the road, and at this point it was gratifying to see Footer, Penny, Allum, Mains and Flower all with the leaders. Here I must award Bill Rice a laurel wreath for tipping the winner, for when the runners had gone into the "country" he remarked to the world at large that it was Footer's day, and certainly "our Bert" had that expression on his face that we in the Club have come to know means "Business only" at the Footer works. He wears it when he cleans up the camp he runs during the summer session! Having taken up a prominent position, we patiently waited for the first arrivals up a beautiful steep hill. I use the expression "beautiful" with due respect to the competitors who, I understood from their phrases after the race, did not consider the hill anything to go into raptures over! We were told that the runners had started the ascent of the aforesaid hill and eventually, to our unrestrained enthusiasm, Bert Footer came leading the field, closely followed by Barnet, of Wycombe, Arthur Penny being very near the Wycombe man and so one by one the competitors breasted the hill until we had counted seven Belgrave "boys" in the first 25. The rest of the team were battling nobly with the very heavy conditions, allied with steep hills to negotiate. Leaving my vantage point I hastened down to below the golf-links to see field go "out" for the second time, and although the leaders had gone away by the time I had got there, it was some consolation to see that Walker and Robertshaw had moved up, after both having experienced a bad patch. It was about this time the Aldershot boys were beginning to pack in their well-known manner and it was only the thought of Footer and Penny's positions that kept my hopes from dropping to below zero! After a very long wait (during which the Belgrave "scouts" were dispatched into the unknown to persuade any of our boys, by vocal noises supplemented with the aid of a bell, to "keep going") the leaders were signalled from the opposite hill and then we saw "Our Bert" tearing down the hill and coming up the one on which we were waiting, with that tireless stride of his that he can maintain for such a long time. Although finding that final part of the race very testing, Bert finished in great style, 37 secs. ahead of Humphris, of South London, who had always been prominent, thus reversing last year's positions, when Humphris was 2nd and Bert 3rd. Arthur Penny maintained his third place 1 minute behind Footer, having run a gallant race all the way. A word of praise is due, I think, to Tom Carter on his 17th position in the race, being third man home for the Club. When one realises that Carter is quite young in running experience, it makes one look forward to his and the Club's future. Jack Flower ran well in view of the fact that undoubtedly he has not trained quite so exactingly this year, and the same applies to Arthur Allum, who also gave us a taste of his prowess, even though short of training. To our boys from the Kent county, Mains and Shaw, I think must also go an extra hearty congratulation for their sterling performance. The remainder of the team ran with spartan-like fortitude (a now recognised trait in the Belgrave Club) and each gave of his utmost under conditions demanding exceptional fitness and bulldog stamina from each competitor. Our sympathy must go out to Alf. Taylor, who ran three parts of the race with a very bad ankle which I understand has turned out rather seriously for him, and is diagnosed as a broken bone in the ankle which requires him to walk with crutches. So to finish 165th I think is a great performance and we can surely say with great feeling, "Well run, sir!" The Club made another step up the ladder of fame in finishing second to Aldershot Command in the team race, and can we say that this is a pointer to the National and Brighton Relay? Who knows—our lads are capable of annexing the greatest honours and I feel sure that there will be no lack of support for them when they go forth to conquer. To Bert Footer, Southern Counties Champion, heartiest wishes; to all other prospective members of future teams, train well and remember, UP THE BELS! In the Junior 5 miles race which preceded the Senior event, our team ran creditably and finished eighth of the 31 teams to close in. Our first man to finish was H. W. Shields (17), and Michael, Martin and Chantler completed our team. All our runners and supporters returned home very pleased with the team's showing, and with Footers' placing. The following song, to the tune of an ancient German marching song learned by some of the boys when away on a Continental tramping holiday was, soon being lustily roared:— "Come my lads and let us sing, Victory! Victory! To the heavens let it ring, Belgrave boys are we! When we walk, and when we run, Our fame is known to everyone. Spread this slogan wide and free, Belgrave boys are we!" Those who know an iambic pentameter from a trochaic hexameter may find fault with its metrical construction, but we venture to think all will be in accord with its sentiment. Anyhow! memorise the words and be prepared to join in next time! RESULT. Pos. m. s. 1 H. E. Footer 60 54 2 L. F. Humphris...S.L.H. 61 31 3 A. W. Penny 61 54 17 C. T. Carter 63 38 25 J. E.
