items.sum: Walking notes: congratulations to Don Brown, prospects for the season and the Junior championship team, coming open walks and the Berman Cup, the Finchley Charter Week open walk result and a win over Polytechnic Harriers.
e: Belgrave Harriers club 2 miles walking championship
Surrey Walking Club v Belgrave Harriers
Eastleigh Town S.C. 12 miles Open Walk
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes: congratulations to Don Brown, prospects for the season and the Junior championship team, coming open walks and the Berman Cup, the Finchley Charter Week open walk result and a win over Polytechnic Harriers. We must congratulate Don Brown upon his win in the Club 2 miles Championship in fast time. This road season should find him well to the fore in the open races, and it should not be long before his growing experience and undoubted ability carry him into championship class. * * * * * As described at length elsewhere, the Brighton team race has again been won, and the long-anticipated 50 miles and 8 hours Track Walk taken place. Now we have to prepare for the Open races and match events, and then, in the New Year, for the Club Championships, the "Junior" and two months later, the "Senior." * * * * * Generally, our prospects for an even more successful season tha last year are quite bright. All last year's men will be available, some undoubtedly showing improved form, and this, with the introduction of some new blood (I am thinking of R. Martin, particularly) should keep us well to the front. * * * * * It is always a difficult task to find a new "Junior" team the year following a win, and this year H. G. Churcher, D. E. Brown, A. H. Field, A. A. Harley and J. C. Bidgood are no longer eligible. However, our remaining material has undoubted possibilities, and with conscientious training we should, at least, be among the placings. Among the men we look to to maintain the Club's splendid record in the "Junior" Championship are C. E. Churcher, J. G. Coleman, R. F. Elson, J. A. Grimwade, E. C. Heather, W. Holman, E. A. Jackman, H. Latter, R. Martin, C. H. Speechley, L. Storey, F. W. Thorn, L. Jones, and very probably there will be others making their claims for inclusion. * * * * * The Highgate Open 7 miles races will probably have taken place before this issue of our journal is published, but the Enfield A.C. Open 7 miles race will take place on November 11th, and we should be well represented. * * * * * Our own Open event is fixed, as usual, for the last Saturday in November, the 25th, and it is hoped that all our active men will rally round as usual, and send their entries in as early as possible. On this occasion the R.W.A. have allocated the "H. Berman" Cup to our race, and this trophy will go to the Club winning the scratch team race. We have held this cup twice in the past, but Enfield A.C. are the present holders. This should make our promotion even more interesting than usual, and every Club member should come along as a spectator, if he is not actively engaged in the race, or supporting the Club's running fixtures on that day. * * * * * On December 2nd we visit the Surrey Walking Club for our annual tussle over the Croydon to West Wickham and back course. We have been unable to win this inter-club event so far, and we should make a determined effort this year to participate at full strength, and turn the tables. The following Saturday (December 9th), Eastleigh Town S.C. are promoting a 12 miles Open Walk, and I should be glad to hear from members desirous of making the trip and supporting our "resident" members, Tommy Green and Joe King, in the team race. Cheap fares have been arranged and I shall be pleased to forward particulars to anyone interested. * * * * * A few of our members supported the first Open race of the season, held in connection with the Finchley Charter Week Celebrations, more in the spirit of friendliness and goodwill rather than with the idea of showing up prominently. October 7th is much too early in the season for serious racing, even at six miles, and the appended result shows that our representatives were not unduly troubling themselves. Green did well, and Bidgood showed that his recent "Brighton" has had a tonic effect and that we may expect to find him in the early placings this year. Willis made a creditable debut in our name and should develop into a very useful walker. RESULT. 138 finished. HANDICAP TEAM RACE. 1. Poly H. ... 173m. 7s. 5. Belgrave H. ... 179m. 49s. Our first match of the season, versus Polytechnic Harriers, over 5 miles, gave us a win by 102 pts. to 231 pts., 12 aside scoring. Len Fletcher led the field of 38 home, and we placed 10 men in the first 12. Our sealed handicap in conjunction was won by A. A. Harley (2 min. 40 sec.) with A. H. Field (2 min. 50 sec.) and L. Jones (4 min. 30 sec.) taking second and third prizes. Full details in our next issue. * * * * * All entries and enquiries to A. A. HARLEY, 39 Roxburgh Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. 1. A. A. items.label: September 1933
items.sum: Review of the field events season: George Powell wins the "Harry Wright" Shield on percentage standards, and Belgrave finish third in the Southern Amateur Athletic League Field Events Competition.
e: Belgrave Harriers Club Field Events Championship
Southern Amateur Athletic League Field Events Competition
items.s: FIELD EVENTS. Review of the field events season: George Powell wins the "Harry Wright" Shield on percentage standards, and Belgrave finish third in the Southern Amateur Athletic League Field Events Competition. The Club has just concluded a successful season as far as Field Events are concerned, having regard to the lack of interest evinced generally in the throwing and jumping events. The Committee of the Club has persistently encouraged this branch of Athletics, and it must be said that its efforts have not been without success, although we should be glad to see greater numbers interesting themselves in the field events. They are interesting, a means of attaining physical fitness, keenly competitive, and often very helpful when the Club has a match comprising varying athletic events. Our two most prominent performers this year have been G. H. Powell (3rd A.A.A. Championship) and J. W. Clemens (2nd Southern Championship). Both have beaten A.A.A. standard and so earned their Club Honours Badges. It is now possible to announce the winner of the "Harry Wright" Shield,for the season. He is George Powell, and to him go our heartiest congratulations. He is probably the member with the longest experience in the Club and might almost be termed the "Father" of the Field Events Section. RESULT. It will be remembered that the Club Field Events Championship, which carries with it the "Harry Wright" Shield and Club gold medal, is determined on a percentage basis, the actual performance of any club member being expressed as a percentage co-efficient of a series of standards which have been drawn up and agreed upon. This year's competition has had a very close finish, only .4 per cent. separating the two men! The institution of the Southern Amateur Athletic League Field Events Competition has done much to focus attention on the sport and afford opportunities of competition. This effect has been even more marked during the past season, now that the events are centralised, and all competitions are held at the Battersea Park Track in connection with the various Club meetings taking place there. We have been represented in practically every Division I event, and in the final table we take a creditable third position. Next season it is hoped that we shall do even better. W. H. Sutton remains Captain of the section, with R. Nowak as Vice-Captain, and with the assistance of enthusiasts like Clemens, Powell, Holder, Henchoz, Ivall, Kelly, Ellis, and others; and the addition of some newcomers, we may be certain that the Field Events men will contribute their share towards the progress the Club continues to make. items.label: September 1933
items.sum: T. H. Scrimshaw recalls his most thrilling race, the 1931 A.A.A. Half-mile Championship at Stamford Bridge, where he went through as fastest loser and finished 4th behind Hampson.
items.s: MY MOST THRILLING RACE ! T. H. Scrimshaw recalls his most thrilling race, the 1931 A.A.A. Half-mile Championship at Stamford Bridge, where he went through as fastest loser and finished 4th behind Hampson. No. 1.—By T. H. SCRIMSHAW. I have been asked to write an account of my most thrilling race, a task which I find far from easy, in view of the difficulty of deciding which of the many races I have had has thrilled me most. After due consideration I have awarded the laurels to the A.A.A.'s Half-mile Championship of 1931. This was the first time I had run in these Championships, so naturally I was very dubious about my performance. I arrived at Stamford Bridge with just the usual nervous feeling which one has before a race, and after studying the programme my nervousness increased slightly, for I found that the main opposition in my heat was Johannessen (Norway), Gutteridge, T. J. Flower, Claydon and Booth. Johannessen, about this time, was accredited with doing something like 1 min. 53 sec. for 800 metres, so I thought, all things taken into consideration, I might get sixth in my heat. There is one particular incident which happened in my heat which I should like to mention, because I feel sure if it had not have been for this I would not have been in the final, and I doubt whether I should have got my triple International that year, because the International teams are chosen on the results of the A.A.A.'s Championships. After the first lap, we were round about the finish of the "hundred," and I was very badly placed, being behind three runners running abreast, and Johannesssen and Gutteridge were in front of these three. Johannessen and Gutteridge were beginning to open up a gap from the three in front of me, when Joe Flower, who happened to be the inside runner of these three, let me through, thus enabling me to get on equal terms with Johannessen, who, at the finish, beat me by about 2 yards in 1 min. 56 sec., the fastest heat of the evening. So I went into the final as the fastest loser! That evening I went to bed early, with the intention of having a good night's rest, but it was about midnight before I slept. About 1 o'clock somebody living opposite me thought it an excellent occasion to have a fire, which meant that my slumber was disturbed until about 6 o'clock next morning. During this time I lay in bed wishing the fireman would go to another fire which I have heard never goes out! On arrival at the 'Bridge next day I was feeling a nervous wreck. The finalists were Hampson, Peltzer, Townend, Powell, Carr and Johannessen, and, I think, the most classical field I have been in. I drew sixth position, with Hampson fifth and Powell seventh. At the gun I lost all nervousness, but got away very badly. Townend was soon in the lead, followed by Carr and Hampson. At the first bend I way lying last behind Johannessen and Peltzer. It was necessary to have wooden borders on the track, owing to the track having been widened for dirt-track racing, and on going round the bend Johannessen struck the wooden border, stumbled, "spiked" Peltzer, who in turn struck me in the side, but only lightly. For the rest of the first lap I contented myself with following behind Powell, who was lying fourth. Coming into the finishing straight for the bell, I moved up past Powell and Carr and followed behind Townend and Hampson, until half-way down the back straight, Hampson took the lead and I followed him. At the 220 yards mark he started his terrific finishing burst. I tried hard to hold him, but half-way round the last bend I found the gap between us was increasing considerably. Coming into the straight Townend and Peltzer caught me; Townend came up on my left and Peltzer on my right and it was neck and neck fight to the finish, Townend drawing away from us about 5 yards from the tape. I shut my eyes and threw my body forward as much as my condition would allow. I was held in suspense until it was announced that Peltzer was 3rd, therefore making me 4th in my first English championship. Hampson won this race by what I consider a "street," his time was 1 min. 54 1-5 sec., and I think the accident which involved Johannessen and Peltzer at the start of the race was a considerable handicap to both men. If it had not occurred, I think I would have been back another position. T. H. Scrimshaw T. H. SCRIMSHAW writes on his most thrilling race, the 1931 A.A.A. items.sum: Editorial notes: New Year wishes, the Building Fund, new members, a representative team v. Cambridge University, cross-country championship prospects and Field Events lectures at the Polytechnic.
items.s: Editorial notes: New Year wishes, the Building Fund, new members, a representative team v. Cambridge University, cross-country championship prospects and Field Events lectures at the Polytechnic. This issue will be too late in your hands to wish you "A Merry Christmas," but it is with all sincerity that we wish all our readers "A Very Prosperous and Successful New Year." 1934 is bound to find our Club still on the upward grade, and with the loyal and enthusiastic endeavours of all our members, we should be in the happy position of being able to look back at the conclusion of the year upon many memorable happenings. And if you want to make an individual New Year resolution, why not make a personal vow to help the Belgrave Building Fund as much as you are able, and as often as you are able? We welcome new members in F. A. Lee, J. G. Weston, R. Burgess, M. E. B. Keller, A. W. Jannaway, F. G. White, G. H. Salter, F. W. B. Gayler, F. C. Gladden, J. H. McCammond, F. J. Abberton, and wish them many successes and a long association with our Club. It was pleasing to see that three of our runners (A. Allum, C. T. Carter and A. W. Penny) were members of a representative team which ran against Cambridge University recently. Arthur Penny led the field home and the visiting team to victory. A word or two as to our cross-country championship prospects. It seems that in the Southern and National championships we shall be definitely stronger than last season, whereas our principal opponents, as far as we can tell, will have to rely upon last year's strength, and in fact in some cases appear to me much weaker. This season we hope to have Arthcr Allum, now fully recovered from his illness, up with his fellow-Internationals, Footer and Penny, with Carter and Flower on their heels, and the others not far away. New talent in the shape of the three brothers Patience will be making its claim for inclusion, and if their form at ten miles is anything like that at five miles, we should be greatly strengthened. It remains for our supporters to do their bit and we hope to have a large Belgravian crowd at the "Southern," and a few at the "National," which is to be held at Dudley, to encourage our men. Items of general interest for our columns would be gladly received by the Hon. Editor. The more authors we have, the greater the scope, and the more interesting the "Belgravian" becomes. Four lectures on Field Events are to be held at the Polytechnic Institute early in the New Year. Further details may be had from our Field Events Captain, W. H. Sutton. The dates are January 19th, February 2nd, March 9th, March 16th and the lectures, which will be illustrated by films, will commence at 6-30 p.m. Admission is free. F. A. Lee F. A. Lee new member J. items.label: November 1933
items.sum: Walking notes: F. G. Thomson's R.W.A. election, plans for the R.W.A. Junior, National 20 miles and 50 km championships, the match v. Polytechnic Harriers, and the Highgate Harriers and Enfield A.C. open walks.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes: F. G. Thomson's R.W.A. election, plans for the R.W.A. Junior, National 20 miles and 50 km championships, the match v. Polytechnic Harriers, and the Highgate Harriers and Enfield A.C. open walks. Congratulations to F. G. Thomson upon his election as Chairman of the Southern Committee of the Road Walking Association. His work for our sport is appreciated in all quarters and we are indeed fortunate to have such a hard, dependable worker in our ranks. The venue of the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship, to be held on March 3rd, has not yet been decided; but it is certain to be within easy reach of the Metropolis. Courses in Richmond Park and North London have been under consideration; but it will be appreciated that it is a very hard task to find the ideal course and quarters for a field of between two and three hundred walkers. Accommodation must be adequate and easily accessible to those coming a long distance; roads must be wide (especially for a start), of good surface, and reasonably free from traffic; and it is generally conceded that the course should contain some rises and falls and not be dead level. In addition, the spectre of Finance raises its head, and the question of receipts and expenditure has to be seriously considered. Altogether, it will be seen that it is no easy matter to satisfy all these conditions; and to find the ideal spot for the decision of this very popular race. However, the R.W.A. may be relied upon to do their best and it should be possible to announce the "Junior" venue before very long. Incidentally, those on whom the honour of representing the the Club in this race will fall should, with the New Year, begin to get serious and devote all their endeavours to be at the peak of fitness and condition on March 3rd. Our excellent record in this event must be maintained; and if eight fit and keen men start on our behalf, we need have no misgivings. Our Seniors have a long journey in May before they have the opportunity of again winning the National Championship. It has been decided to hold this twenty miles race in Sheffield, and no doubt the local club, old rivals, will fancy their chances of finishing in front of Surrey W.C. and ourselves, first and second teams in the last championship. It is a pleasing thought, however, that in the last championship walk held in Sheffield (the "Junior" of 1926) we supplied the first two men to finish in Tommy Green and Len Fletcher. May history repeat itself! It is pleasing to announce also, that the 50 kilos. Championship will be held in connection with the "Guildford" Cup Walk next June from the Surrey Walking Club's quarters at Croydon. In this way we shall avoid the spectacle of two races being held at this distance; either clashing or within a few days of each other, as has sometimes happened in the past. And now let us drift back from future engagements to past fixtures. As briefly mentioned in our last issue, we were successful in our match v. Polytechnic Harriers. There were many Belgrave names in the first dozen placings. The "Poly" are fortunate, however, in having two such promising Juniors in their ranks as Stone and Denyer. Our sealed handicap held in conjunction provided our Walking Hon. Secretary with a "First," with Bert Field second, and L. Jones, continuing in his great promise, third. The Open Race promoted by the Highgate Harriers from De Bohun's Farm, Southgate, found us represented, but unable to claim any of the awards. We were not at full strength, but Don Brown did well to finish in ninth position in a good class field. Bidgood also showed that he intends carrying through with his improved form at the shorter distances. Adequate support was lacking for these two, however, and we finished a few points behind the Polytechnic Harriers in the scratch team race, in third position. Incidentally, we must congratulate the Poly. H. on this win, their first for many moons in open competition; and in particular acknowledge the strenuous efforts our friend and member, A. O. Tookey, has made on their behalf. He has raised his club's numbers and strength from a small and mediocre body, to a large, improving, keen band of walkers, in the course of two years; and it must have been very gratifying to Tookey to see his team successful in a well-supported race. The handicap flowers were not for us to pick (Dunlop W.C. won the handicap race for the third year in succession); but we left feeling that it would not be long before Belgrave would find a place in the team events. We were represented by two teams in the Enfield A.C. Open 7 Miles Walk, and our "A" team took second handicap team prizes, Leicester W.C. being the winning team. Our team consisted of R. Martin, E. C. Heather, J. C. Bidgood and D. E. Brown. Martin again showed that he is a "Junior" to command respect, and Heather gained his first team award in splendid style, which will be taking him up with the leaders in a year or so. In the scratch race a minor sensation was caused by the disqualification of Green when leading downhill in the last mile of the race; and this put us out of the fight for scratch team honours. F. G. items.label: November 1933
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's fourteenth annual open 7 miles walk on 25 November, where Belgrave won the scratch team race and the Berman Cup for the third time and R. Martin won the handicap.
items.s: OUR "OPEN" WALK. Report of Belgrave's fourteenth annual open 7 miles walk on 25 November, where Belgrave won the scratch team race and the Berman Cup for the third time and R. Martin won the handicap. Our Fourteenth Annual 7 miles walk was held on November 25th and, as is usual, the Club's popularity and reputation attracted a very fine entry of 204 individuals, comprising 24 teams. Of these latter, we supplied four, our Surrey W.C. friends three, and the London Vidarians' W.C. and Polytechnic H., two each. Of the other teams, we were particularly glad to welcome two from the Provinces, Eastleigh Tn. S.C. and Dunlop W.C. An added attraction to our race this year was that the Road Walking Association allowed the "Berman" Cup to be awarded to the first team in the scratch race. As Enfield A.C. had won the Cup on the last two occasions, and only required to win it this time to make it their own property, it was only natural that all the other clubs were extra keen to frustrate their endeavours. Our President, J. R. McKay, started the race and before half-a-mile had been covered Johnson, of Enfield, had gained a substantial lead. At the half-distance, however, Green had caught Johnson, with Hurst, of the Cambridge H., a yard in the rear. At this point it seemed that unless something sensational happened in the second lap, we should be the winners of the scratch team event and holders of the "Berman" Cup. Eventually the finish came, Johnson leading Hurst and Green home, and Belgrave winning the scratch team race with 32 pts, Enfield scoring 53, and Surrey W.C. 63 pts. Our second man was Len Fletcher, walking in something like his old form; and third for us came Don Brown—an excellent performance. J. F. King made a welcome re-appearance and completed our team. While discussing scratch performances, it is interesting to note that we finished our fifteenth man in actual 46th position. This included our eight "B" team men, and as a sign of strength we may point out that our "B" team were placed fifth in the scratch team event. Before the decision of the race we were not hopeful about our handicap possibilities, for the Hon. Handicapper had dispensed some ruthless "pulls" on our team which had gained second team awards in the previous Open race. However, one of the greatest sufferers in this respect, R. Martin, rose to the occasion splendidly and won the handicap with an allowance of 5min. 30 sec. He was only one second ahead, on handicap time, of another Belgravian, L. Jones, whose consistent improvement has previously earned comment in our columns. The third man in the handicap was last season's "Junior" winner, W. J. Hogan, with an allowance of 2 min. 10 sec. Hogan must like our course, for he was second in last year's event. With the first two in the individual handicap it was obvious that we should have the winning handicap team, and support came from C. H. Speechley and J. C. Bidgood. Fred Bentley (23rd) won the prize for the first Belgrave Harrier in the scratch race not gaining any other award. It will be seen from the above that the Club enjoyed a large measure of success which prompted the headline, "Belgrave Sweep the Board in Their Open Race," in the Sporting Life. We were particularly gratified in winning for the third time the "Berman" Cup, no other club yet having achieved three successes. We should like to express our gratitude to the Clubs and individuals who again gave us such a splendid entry; and to the Officials who conducted the race in such an efficient manner. J. R. McKay J. items.label: November 1933
items.h: Sergt. Bidgood gives you the "low-down" on the match against the Metropolitan Police—
items.sum: Humorous account of Belgrave's walking match with the Metropolitan Police Walking Club at Wimbledon on 18 November, won by Belgrave 238 to 244, with an Editor's reply and the full result.
e: Belgrave H. v. Metropolitan Police Walking Club match
items.s: Sergt. Bidgood gives you the "low-down" on the match against the Metropolitan Police— Humorous account of Belgrave's walking match with the Metropolitan Police Walking Club at Wimbledon on 18 November, won by Belgrave 238 to 244, with an Editor's reply and the full result. If Dr. Jekyll would be suitable biographer for Mr. Hyde, then I suppose I am a suitable person to supply a few details of Belgrave's little affair with the Metropolitan Police Walking Club at Wimbledon on November 18th. Not that I was alone in my treachery, for there were no less than six other Belgravians in the enemy camp for the day, namely, Freds Rickards and Bentley, R. Martin, Willis, Boddington (a newcomer) and Centurion A. G. White. As a slight offset we found that R. Burgess, a prominent and popular member of the M.P.W.C. before severe knee trouble compelled him to resign from the police last year, had journeyed from the Midlands especially in order to turn out against his old colleagues. The "call-over" promised a close race and to an exciting degree such it proved to be. Scoring fifteen a side the policemen lost by the very narrow margin of six points (238 to 244). A very close thing indeed. Len Fletcher, Don Brown and your very worthy and hard-working Walking Secretary set the pace at the start, with H. Latter in close attendance. R. Martin and the writer, supported by the Police ten mile champion, R. R. Sims, filled the next three positions. Jack Field showed promise of a return to his old form when he moved up to join the leaders in the early stages, but he seemed to lack just that little extra degree of stamina which the course always seems to demand, although by normal standards his time for the full journey must be accounted good. Fletcher was obviously never extended, and Brown, too, seemed to have plenty in hand. How much they had in hand can be gathered from the result table below. Rickards and Bentley came through strongly at the finish, and so deprived the writer of the honour of being first policeman home, but not quite strongly enough to catch Master Alfred. In both time and style Martin's performance came as a firm endorsement of the things we had read of him in the last edition of the "Gazette." After faltering slightly near the half-way mark, H. Latter fought out a fine finish to beat one of the Club's most promising juniors (forgive me, Charlie!)—C. H. Speechley. A former Belgravian, T. W. Salmon, who left the Club on removing to North London a season or two ago, showed good form in finish sixth for the Police, and in time but a few seconds behind Sims, Churcher Senior, and Field Senior. Fourteenth in 61 min. 54 sec., L. Jones showed some of the form which earned him the distinction of being last season's most promising novice. The day, of course, was a triumph for Belgrave, for the four policemen home were enemies for the day only. The writer, must, however, record this one protest: although one could have nothing but admiration for Mr. Secretary Harley's thoroughness in "S.O.S.-ing" second-claim members Tookey, Sutton & Co., surely it was hardly fair to want to bring in non-members? Believe it or not, gentlemen, but I was only just in time to prevent him handing out a number card to a Surrey Walking Club member who had turned up—a week too soon—for the Club "Open"! J.C.B. Hon. Editor's Note.—The above reached me with a covering letter which said, "You challenged me to this, so your blood be on your own head! Publish it verbatim or not at all. (I shouldn't quarrel with an Editor's Note or two, of course)." And so, thanks to our contributor's magnanimity, I am permitted to make a few observations. I freely admit I lack our friend's professional ability to describe things as they are not, and I fear I can never meet him on equal terms in the imaginative sphere. And so I take my stand firmly on the rock of Truth, and plead "Not Guilty" on all counts, and await the acquittal which an enlightened, discerning, erudite Great British Public will undoubtedly award. Police evidence! Ha! ha! That's me scoffing! RESULT. TEAM SCORES. Belgrave H. ..................238 pts. M.P.A.A. ..........................244 pts. m. s. 1. A. L. Fletcher B 57 29 2. D. E. items.s: THE "HORWOOD" CUP RACE. Report and result of the club Junior 7 miles walking championship for the Horwood Cup on 16 December, won by C. H. Speechley at 46. The Annual Club "Junior" 7 miles Championship for the "Horwood" Cup was held on December 16th. Our winning team in the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship of last March, and also J. C. Bidgood, had disqualified themselves since last year's race according to conditions governing the event; and this year's entry was on the small side, only six walkers eventually starting. Many of those who would have turned out in the normal way were prevented from doing so by severe colds and minor injuries, and it is to be hoped that the New Year will see those so affected well again, and training hard for the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship in March. From the start Charlie Speechley led from R. Martin, and this was still the position at the end. L. Jones and R. F. Elson were together for a great part of the distance but Jones shook off his opponent in the last two miles, to finish third. Two of our new friends, D. J. Heath and F. A. Lee, also started, and with perseverance will become useful walkers in due course. Speechley's "Junior" win at the age of forty-six has a paradoxical sound about it, but it is nevertheless a fact that he finds a little more speed each year. His time of 57 mins., without ever being seriously pushed, is excellent, and would have given him tenth position in our "Open"! Let us hope that Charlie's 13th "Junior" Championship next March will find him prominent. Martin also improved upon his "Open" time and with Jones and others should be even better in three months' time. RESULT. No. Name Allce. H'cap Time. H'cap Pos. 1. C. H. Speechley 57 0 0 50 56 10 1 2. items.s: BELGRAVE H. v. ASHCOMBE A.C. AND THAMES VALLEY HARRIERS. Alf Taylor's report and result of the inter-club cross-country race with Ashcombe A.C. and Thames Valley Harriers at Wimbledon on 28 October, won by Belgrave with 77 points, with a sealed handicap won by G. M. Murray; as printed, the handicap times of A. T. Jordan and A. F. Taylor do not match their actual times less allowances (they look transposed). Alf Taylor leads off with his account of A cold wind and drizzling rain greeted the 68 stalwart athletes that represented Ashcombe A.C., T.V.H. and Belgrave H. in the inter-club race at Wimbledon on October 28th. After the usual rush at the start, Carter and Shields were making the pace with several Belgrave and T.V.H. men in close attendance. At Beverley Brook the field had become well strung out and Arthur Allum came through to take the lead and eventually to finish first, with Carter 2nd and Shields 3rd. The next five positions were all filled by Belgrave men, thereby assuring us of an easy victory in the team race. Cohen finished first for Ashcombe, filling the 13th position, and Phipps, the first T.V.H. man, being 9th. Our sealed handicap held in conjuction proved to be an all-junior affair. G. M. Murray ran well to win, and we hope his victory will urge him to greater efforts. A. T. Jordan finished 2nd, and Chantler 3rd, and both the last-mentioned should do big things in the future if they listen to advice and train conscientiously, as they have done up to the present. RESULT. items.s: AT EPSOM. Report and result of a junior cross-country race at Epsom on 11 November in which Belgrave's A team finished second to the Royal Navy and Marines, their best since 1928. November 11th was the day our Juniors had been waiting for—the day on which they were going to show the world at large that they were a force to be reckoned with in the art of running over country. It was a miserable afternoon when our boys lined up with some hundred odd other runners from various clubs. They were not very promising at the start, excepting S. Ring, who was in the twenties. Passing the Grandstand on the first round, the team had improved on their bad start but as far as individual placings were concerned, at this stage we were, unfortunately, not in it. On the second lap a lot of our boys were running with that "Footer" expression and were making havoc of the opposition (no apology needed to Bert!) and we eventually finished second, our best performance since 1928. Well done, Juniors! A performance they can better next year! RESULT. TEAM PLACINGS. 1—Royal Navy and Marines ... ... ... ... ... ... 19 pts. 2—Belgrave H. e: Belgrave H. v. R.A.F. (Uxbridge), Kensington A.C. and Ealing Harriers
items.s: OUR FIXTURE WITH R.A.F. (UXBRIDGE), KENSINGTON A.C. AND EALING HARRIERS AT EALING, NOV. 25th. H.L.R.'s report and result of the cross-country fixture at Ealing on 25 November, which Belgrave won with 57 points despite their leaders taking a wrong turning. H.L.R. on the air, commentating on Hullo, everybody! Once again we were visitors to Ealing Harriers' Headquarters, and our little band of 13 was very warmly welcomed. There were 42 starters. Our men did not fare too well over the first stage; gradually, however, the Bels. settled down, and were soon taking the lead. Jack Flower, D. Patience and Abberton were running 1, 2 and 3, closely followed by Shields, F. R. Webb, Saunders and R. Patience. Scoring seven a side this looked good. The course was not heavy. This suited our fellows, and on the way home the three leaders had decided to run in together. I would mention the trail had been carefully set down, but Jack took the wrong turning (a bad habit of his!) when a mile from home, taking D. Patience (affectionately known as "Spud") and Abberton with him. Harry Shields (having been so well schooled by Capt. Bert Footer and, no doubt, bearing in mind Footer's instructions and commands, never to disobey a Captain's or leader's orders) followed the three strays. Also F. R. Webb, Saunders and R. Patience went off the trail. Having been called back to the right track by the Ealing men, the Bels. set about regaining the lead again. It was a hard task and D. Patience and Jack Flower just failed to catch the Ealing man, Thomas. It was gratifying to see the three brothers Patience running so well, and young J. C. Smith ran well and has the making of a very good team man, with time and experience. Alf Taylor, feeling the effects of a cold, had an off-day, and W. W. Mitchell appeared to be troubled with his shoes. An old member of ours, Canard, ran for the R.A.F. and finished 25th. Crewdson, a former member of Croydon Harriers, also with the airmen, filled 21 position. Ealing Harriers were not concerned because our fellows had been deprived of the lead, but leaving the result of the race according to the order in which the men finished, we won this pleasant fixture. A vote of thanks to "Strube," I mean H. Parker, for his kind work as an official. RESULT. TEAM SCORES. Belgrave H.—2, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12, 14, ... ... ... 57 pts. items.s: THE SURREY COUNTY YOUTHS' RACE. Joe Flower's report and result of the Surrey County Youths' three miles cross-country race at Lower Morden, where Belgrave's team was third behind Mitcham and Caterham. Joe Flower is tempted to relate "When I was young ——" but satisfies himself with describing This race was held over a heavy three miles course at Lower Morden, and was confined to those between the ages of 16—19 years. Our team finished third—quite a good performance for our young runners. Our first man home was Chantler, who was third in the actual race; Martin did well to finish 8th, considering that he had come a nasty cropper in the early stages, when he was well leading the field. Pointer, who has scored in our team previously, was our third man to finish; Merryman, our fourth man home, deserves much praise, as I hear from Dick Savage that he has only been in training a month or so. Altogether, it may be said that our Juniors show great potentialities, and we can say in all sincerity "Well done! Keep it going!" RESULT. TEAM SCORES. 1. items.sum: T. J. Flower's report and result of the 7 miles cross-country match with the 2nd Battalion Scots Guards at Wimbledon on 2 December, won by Belgrave 85 to 125 with C. T. Carter first.
items.s: BELGRAVE H. v. 2nd SCOTS GUARDS. T. J. Flower's report and result of the 7 miles cross-country match with the 2nd Battalion Scots Guards at Wimbledon on 2 December, won by Belgrave 85 to 125 with C. T. Carter first. T. J. Flower discourses on On Saturday, December 2nd, we had a very interesting match with the Scots Guards, from our Headquarters at Wimbledon. The race was decided over our 7 miles course, 10 men aside to score. About 30 runners faced the starter on an ideal day for a cross-country run. At the end of the first half-mile the "Bels" were well to the fore. J. E. Flower was leading, closely followed by Carter, Rice, Taylor and Smith. Coming up the hill about 3 miles out, Carter had taken the lead and, running very strongly with that natural easy style of his, he was gradually dropping the rest of the field. At this point J. E. Flower was 2nd about 50 yards behind, Alf Taylor 3rd another 80 yards further back with "Bill" Rice and J. C. Smith leading a small batch a few yards away. On the second circuit Carter had gained more ground and appeared to be running very comfortably, although he was covering the ground at a very fast rate, as his time at the finish shows. J. E. Flower was second. He also appeared to have had a comfortable race. Alf Taylor, who finished third, was close behind, running very strongly. Then came "Bill" Rice and J. C. Smith, Bill getting the better of Smith over the last mile. Smith is to be congratulated on his very good running. He is making very rapid improvement and undoubtedly will prove a decided asset to the Belgrave teams in the near future. The first Guardsman to finish was Guardsman Knox. He finished in the 6th position. The "Bels" won the match with 40 points to spare, but it is interesting to note that the Guards closed their team in before ours. It was quite a good race to watch, and our opponents were a very sporty and sociable crowd. We hope to meet them again next year. RESULT. Scoring 10 a side. items.sum: Bill Rice's account of the club 7 miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield, run with a match against Cadogan A.C. which Belgrave won 38 pts to 40, with full results; Arthur Penny set a fast time and young Martin won the handicap (Cadogan's printed scorers include a 7th place, though 7th is a Belgrave man and their 8th went unlisted).
items.s: 7 MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP Bill Rice's account of the club 7 miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield, run with a match against Cadogan A.C. which Belgrave won 38 pts to 40, with full results; Arthur Penny set a fast time and young Martin won the handicap (Cadogan's printed scorers include a 7th place, though 7th is a Belgrave man and their 8th went unlisted). Bill Rice on the The "Blackstaffe" Shield Race for 1933 brought together the hottest field for a Club Championship that I can remember. A match with Cadogan A.C. was arranged in conjunction, and the keen rivalry existing between our Surrey and Middlesex members caused all this unusual enthusiasm. The Cadogan crowd were (I nearly said "quietly"—far from that, however!) confident and that they had reasons for this confidence I must admit. Forward running by Saunders, Taylor and Shields, the three very useful soldier brothers, R., E. and D. Patience, Art Allum and Jack Flower were also in good trim, and lastly had they not dug dear old Syd Warboys from his armchair? So being a nice day our Sydney obliged! In the dressing-room Middlesex County vests were being displayed rather prominently with little effect upon us except to comment on the bizarre appearance when one competitor proceeded to place a Belgrave sleeveless vest over the county vest. Jack Flower caused a fluttering in the camp by arriving late, and Harry had cast many anxious eyes at first the clock, then the door, and his relief was very apparent when "J.E." eventually arrived. With Jack Flower ready we got along to the start. There were 26 starters and the start was fairly fast, and automatically Art Penny was in front, with Arthur Allum close up. On the far side of the starting field Syd Warboys found a bit of speed and went through to the front, immediately causing Penny and Allum to draw away from the field. Going across the Golf links the order was Penny, Allum, Carter, J. E. Flower, H. Shields, R. Patience and Warboys. Penny put in some good running down Sandy Hill and got away from Allum, and the others had settled down in practically the same order mentioned previously. Bert Footer came through at this point, but was not in the best of trim, as I managed to hang on to him for well over two miles. The half-way mark was passed with Art Penny well clear of Arthur Allum some 25 seconds up, with Allum a little distance ahead of Carter, Jack Flower being fourth. R. Patience was fifth, remarkably good running for this boy. Shields came next, looking very worried. In fact he stopped shortly afterwards, only to be stirred up by Syd Warboys and Alf Shaw, who were together. Footer was next with the other two Patience brothers and myself on his heels. Dan was not going too good. The hard going had stiffened him up somewhat: Footer, from Sandy Hill onwards, put in some very good work and passed one or two, but otherwise the positions remained very nearly the same. Micky Walker ran a strong second lap to finish twelfth, thereby making a Belgrave win almost a certainty. The scoring was very close, however, as we finish up two points to spare. Bert Footer, in passing Warboys, Shields and R. Patience over the second lap made all the difference. Of the others, young Martin ran exceedingly well, deservedly winning the handicap from two of the Patience brothers. "R" was second, and "E" was third. Alf Taylor disappointed a little over the second lap, but undoubtedly the fast going was the undoing of most of the field as quite a few fell away rather badly in the second lap. One cannot close without mention of the remarkable time set up by Arthur Penny in beating last year's time by well over a minute. In fact, the times shew form that augurs well for the forthcoming Championships and it is possible for us to turn out twelve men good enough to win both the Metropolitan County Championships: Cadogan A.C. "The Middlesex," and Belgrave H. "The Surrey." Anyway, here's to hoping! RESULTS. † Dead Heat. TEAM SCORES. Belgrave H.—1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 12 ... ... ... ... ... 38 pts. e: South of the Thames Cross-Country Championship
items.s: WITH THE RUNNERS. Reminder of the coming cross-country fixtures from December 1933 to February 1934, including the club's first Junior cross-country championship and the ten miles championship. This is a reminder of the forthcoming attractions during the next few weeks. All cross-country members should now be tuning up for the many Championships which follow each other thick and fast during the remainder of the season. Only the teams turning out the fittest men can win, so it is up to all the members to get as fit as possible and so help make this a bumper year for the "Club." I should like to mention that the "Juniors" should get into touch with their Captain and Coach, Mr. R. J. Savage. He is only too willing to help youngsters on as those who have been under his care will substantiate. So get acquainted with your captain and improve your running. 30th December is set aside for our "Junior" Cross-Country Championship (5 miles). This is an event open to all our members who are under 21 years of age on the day of the race. This is the first time the Club has promoted a race of this kind, so it is up to you juniors to send it off with a bang and have a good try at becoming the first Belgrave cross-country champion. Packs will be organised for training runs for the senior members. January 6th.—Social run with the Epsom H., Croydon H. and Mitcham A.C. over the Epsom Downs. This fixture should be well supported as the Surrey County hold their Championship over this country on the following week. January 13th.—County Championship Day. We naturally wish to retain the Surrey C.C.C., and a Team will be entered by the Club with this object in view. At the same time a number of our members will be competing in the Middlesex Championship and we hope for a "double." January 20th.—Surrey County Junior Cross-Country Championship at Imber Court. A Team will be entered by the Club for this event. The Seniors have a fixture with Mitcham, Epsom, and Croydon H., from Mitcham's Headquarters. All cross-country members should be out this week in view of our ten miles Championship next week. January 27th.—Ten Miles Championship Day with the usual sealed handicap in conjunction. This race will have an important bearing on the constitution of our teams in the Championships, so let's see you at your very best on this day. A Social follows the fixture. February 3rd.—Run with Mitcham A.C., Croydon H., and Epsom H. at Croydon. February 10th.—South of the Thames Senior C.C. Championship at Brighton. R. J. Savage R. J. items.label: November 1933
items.h: MY MOST THRILLING RACE. (No. 2—A. W. PENNY).
items.sum: Second in the 'My Most Thrilling Race' series: Arthur Penny describes the National Cross-Country Championship of 11 March 1933 at Alderley Park, where he beat Bert for 4th place.
items.s: MY MOST THRILLING RACE. (No. 2—A. W. PENNY). Second in the 'My Most Thrilling Race' series: Arthur Penny describes the National Cross-Country Championship of 11 March 1933 at Alderley Park, where he beat Bert for 4th place. FOREWORD.—In the last issue of our "Mag.," the "Belgravian," "Tommy" Scrimshaw started us off with a very satisfactory description of his most thrilling race, and very ably described the feelings of a well-trained athlete keyed up for his big race. In this issue Arthur Penny continues with the good work, and has given a description of his feelings is what he considers his most exciting race. However, it is not only the internationals who have these exciting events; practically everybody who participates in athletics gets his "thrill" at some time or other, so be prepared to put pen to paper and write up your experiences, as you may be the next one called upon to contribute to these interesting and entertaining articles. THE NATIONAL CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP, MARCH 11th, 1933. I think that I can safely say that last season's National C.C.C. was my most thrilling race. It was a beautiful day in March, when 340 odd runners lined up in Alderley Park, Cheshire, each with the same idea. Bang! We are off on our ten miles "sprint," and what a start!—each man straining every nerve and sinew to get in front of the next. More by luck that judgment I was well placed in the seventh position, at the end of the first mile, with Bailey (Salford), Holden (Tipton), Evenson (Salford), Webster (Birchfield), Dodd (Wirral A.C.) and Sutherland (Birchfield) in front of me. What a pace they were setting! It really was terrific, and how I managed to go with them I really do not know. For the next six miles I was content to run with "Jock" Sutherland and moved up with him. We were continually passing each other, but never getting far away. During this time "Our Bert" was making a really magnificent fight in catching us and (I say this in all sincerity) to be placed in the "thirties" at the end of two miles, in a race of this description and class, and to grind through like he did was sheer grit. I doubt if anyone else in the race could have done it. At the end of the third lap (7½ miles) Dodd had joined Evenson, Sutherland was 3rd, Holden 4th, myself 5th, and Bert 6th. With that effortless stride of his, Bert passed me, gained ten yards, and then I caught him, and we ran together for the next two miles, with no quarter given. The last half-mile. Bert passes Sutherland for 3rd place, and leaves me standing. Sutherland catches him with a terrific burst, and holds him for nearly 300 yards, eventually going away with another burst. With feelings of relief I see the finishing straight, with Bert a few yards in front of me. I catch him, and beat him by the proverbial yard for 4th place. It is all over! Consistent training has had its reward, and barring accidents I am sure of my colours! A. W. Penny A. W. Penny 4th in the National Cross-Country Championship, March 1933 Arthur Penny Arthur Penny Tommy Scrimshaw "Tommy" Scrimshaw wrote No. 1 of the series in the previous issue Bailey Bailey Holden Holden Evenson Evenson Webster Webster Dodd Dodd Sutherland Sutherland Jock Sutherland "Jock" Sutherland National Cross Country Championships Alderley Park Cheshire Salford Tipton Birchfield Wirral A.C.

items.label: November 1933
items.sum: Account of the club social evening of 4 November 1933 and a dance at the Queensberry Hall, South Kensington, with notice of the next dance and tea and social in January.
items.s: THE SOCIAL SIDE. Account of the club social evening of 4 November 1933 and a dance at the Queensberry Hall, South Kensington, with notice of the next dance and tea and social in January. Our last Social evening, preceded by tea, held on November 4th, sent a large crowd of Belgravians and their friends home at 11-30 p.m. feeling well satisfied; and in the knowledge that it would have been very difficult to obtain an evening's entertainment as enjoyable at ten times the cost elsewhere. The spirit of sociability, the informality, and the feeling of uncertainty as to what the lads will do next, all add to the attractiveness of these evenings; and it is a pity that we cannot have more. But, unfortunately, we are all slaves of the purse, and it is a regrettable but undeniable fact that we usually lose money on these affairs. Our Social Hon. Secretary would be glad to hear of means of remedying this; but meanwhile, make a note of January 27th and come along to tea and the social evening which follows. See something of the Club 10 miles championships in the afternoon and then stay on for tea and the fun. To revert to November 4th. We were happy to have with us Croydon, Epsom and Mitcham athletes and their friends. The band coaxed almost everyone on to the floor, and Tom Cotton's songs were greatly appreciated. The lads performed "Little Nell" with tragic feeling. Carter's entrance as a bewhiskered policeman on a piebald steed, held up the action for some minutes, but eventually it concluded amid thunderous applause. Then, on with the dance, some unofficial acrobatics and floor grovelling by old friends in "Castor" and "Oil"—and on until Time cut short our pleasure. All of which seems a very prosaic account of what transpired, but it is impossible to capture the spirit of the evening for transmission to paper. You must come along yourself! A further dance has been held at "The Queensberry Hall," South Kensington, on November 25th, and attracted a large number of members and friends, all of whom appeared to enjoy themselves to the full. Our next dance at this hall is on January 13th, when we hope to surpass our previous numbers. So make a note of these two Social Events fast approaching:— Jan. 13—Dance. Queensberry Hall. Jan. 27—Tea and Social. Wimbledon. All enquiries to W. A. Rice, 36 Ascalon Road, S.W.8. e: South of the Thames Cross-country Championship
items.s: ONWARD ! Editorial reviewing the club's rise to cross-country success, celebrating the double Surrey and Middlesex championship wins of 13 January 1934 (individual winners A. W. Penny and A. Allum), urging support at the Southern and National, joking about the Captain's training schedule, previewing the R.W.A. Junior walk and giving club notices on honours badges, binding the Belgravian and club books. About the years 1923—1924 we began to consider that we had a chance of annexing the Surrey Cross-country Championship. Up to that time our runners had performed creditably in championship events, without attaining any conspicuous success, and it was necessary to look back to 1904, when the Club was third in the South of the Thames "Senior," for a feat worthy of mention when athletic prowess was discussed. Our walkers were beginning to bring the Club into prominence by their "Junior" Championship wins in 1920 and 1922 and their placings in the "Senior" Championships of 1922 and 1923, culminating in the first Club win in 1924. Our growing number of enthusiastic members, combined with a competent, painstaking set of officials, under the virile leadership of the late "Bob" Ricketts, inspired all connected with the Club with the belief that we should not have long to wait before cross-country honours came our way. And so it proved, for in 1925 came our first win in the Surrey race, and that evening there was joy and enthusiasm, expressive of the attained ideal, in "The King's Head," at Epsom, and the "Pickett" Cup circled the gathering many times. The pristine glory of this first win can never be repeated; and it is no exaggeration to say, without belittling our opponents, or detracting from the merit of our men's performances, that the once eagerly-sought, keenly desired, win in the Surrey race has become common-place, with our seven successes in nine years. Yesterday's dreams, hopes and unattained ideals have become to-day's accepted facts—foundations upon which we hope to build higher—certainties almost, which occasion great surprise should our confidence prove to be ill-founded. This gradual change of attitude, from doubt to certitude, from diffident hope to unbounded confidence, is universal; and, like Alexander of old, we yearn for new worlds to conquer. * * * * * After our initial Surrey Championship, ambition soared, and the passing of the years gave us our first "South of the Thames Senior" win, our placings in "Southern," "National," Brighton Relay, and numerous other events. However, having regard to our peculiar geographical position, we had always speculated upon the chances of our runners securing both Surrey and Middlesex titles in one afternoon. The nebulous ideas of such a double triumph seemed, in those far-off days of 1926 and 1927, fantastic—incapable of fruition. We had our hopes, of course, and the determination to work for these ends, no matter how far away fulfilment seemed to be. And now, once again, the passage of time has brought its reward for past endeavours, and on January 13th, 1934, we had the satisfaction of providing the members of the winning teams in both Surrey and Middlesex championships; and the individual winners of both events, in A. W. Penny and A. Allum respectively. Our congratulations and thanks go out to all who contributed to our dual success! More detailed descriptions appear elsewhere in this issue. * * * * * "Belgrave Harriers Set up County Championship Record"; "Belgrave Show Their Heels"; Unprecedented Feat"; "Belgrave's Four Championships." Such were the headings which appeared in the National Press. It was certainly a heartening sight to see the two trophies—the "Pickett" Cup and the "Daily Telegraph" Cup—on show at the Club Dance on the evening of the Championships; and to find the merit of the performances forcing its way into the columns of the Daily Press, which seems so often (to admittedly prejudiced persons like ourselves) to exist for the purpose of exluding athletic news—so thoroughly do they succeed in doing so. So passes another phase in our history, and fortunately our lads are not content to rest on their laurels; to lay on their oars; but are eager to be on . . . on . . . Eyes are now fixed on the "Southern" and "National" titles, in the same way that once the lesser championships commanded our attention, and provided the incentive to train, and to strive. That our success will be as sure is beyond doubt, given the same will to win and co-operative spirit which have always permeated our activities. That these attributes exist as strongly as ever are apparent to anyone taking a peep into the Club dressing room, and so it remains only for the ordinary Club member to do his share. He can attend the "Southern" Championships at Taplow on February 24th, and possibly the "National" Championship at Himley Park, Dudley, on March 10th, to encourage our men, and play a small part in the creation of the new history which we hope our runners will bring about. Our General Hon. Secretary will be pleased to supply full details of the travelling arrangements when they become available. * * * * We have written of the will-to-win, and the excellent team spirit existing. Does the ability also exist? A prophet must always take risks and so I answer "Yes"—knowing the risk I run of being proved wrong is not a great one. The "National" may elude us this time—our aims have not always been achieved in one year—but we may be assured of a "best yet" performance, with three Internationals in our team striving for their Club and further representative selection, backed by others no less keen. * * * * If "ballyhoo" formed part of Athletics, as it does some less favoured sports, we could weave wonderful tales of the Midget Manager who guides the destinies of our potential team members, from their two glasses of hot water and 120 deep breaths in the morning, to the evening run and bed at 10 p.m. in the evening. We could dilate at length on the Monthly Schedule (copyright) whose appearance is more eagerly awaited than that of the "Belgravian." This is amateur jealousy, of course! We could tell the tale of the young hopeful who quoted the aforesaid Schedule: "No stodgy puddings," etc., in the privacy of his home—and then dodged a pretty saucepan deftly tossed sonwards by an irate mother, unused to such remarks regarding her cooking, and demanding to know, "Who is this Footer person?" If hook or by crook publicity was our objective, we could repeat the ominous rumour that the whole affair has been financed by the undertaking profession, on a commission basis. We could tell of busy B's round the honey-pot (B stands for Belgravian, of course!); of secret elixirs compounded of orange juice and olive oil . . . .but, hush, there are spies at the gates; and many matters more. But it is not our intention to sink to the level of the usual Boxing, Football and Film Fan Gossip (who could imagine a Footer fan Club, or be interested in Harry Shields' size in boots?) and so I'll resist the temptation (between ourselves, I'm rather good at this temptation-resisting business! and conclude by reiterating the injunction to all Club members to go along to the "Southern" and "National" and cheer on our team. * * * * And yet I hardly like to finish without some further mention of the Schedule (copyright) which our Captain has compiled from the wealth of his experience, and committed to paper for the benefit of his club-mates. Undoubtedly the tendency of the average athlete is to undertrain; and to proceed in disjointed fashion rather than progressively, with a definite object in view. Such a schedule as our runners now have should be of great assistance, and the next few weeks should prove its value. Knowing the eagerness with which the appearance of the Monthly Schedule (copyright!) is awaited, and anticipating the success of the training system shortly to be demonstrated (the success, not the system) we have, with considerable business acumen, managed at enormous expense (fabulous to the extent of being unreal!) obtained reproduction rights in Mr. Footer's forthcoming writings. We understand he is at present at work on a treatise entitled "How to Increase Your Height by 6 to 8 Inches in Three Weeks. No Drugs"; to be followed at a later date by another epoch-making journalistic achievement, "Red Noses. How to Abolish Them—by a Sufferer." We contemplate so many expressions of congratulation upon this amazing piece of modern journalistic enterprise, that we are seriously considering requisitioning, for private use, from the same H.E.F.-ty pen, a monograph entitled, "Blushing. Its Cause and Cure." Bye, bye, kiddies. That's all for to-day! * * * * * Incidentally, we would like to make it quite clear that the newspaper heading quoted above—"Unprecedented Feat"—refers to our men generally, and not in particular in Harry Shields. * * * * * Another event worthy of your patronage is the R.W.A. Junior Championship at Southgate, on March 3rd. Further details appear in the Walking Notes. With last year's winning team no longer eligible, we can hardly hope to win again so soon; but undoubtedly our walkers will show up well, and with that little bit of luck which is so essential, might give the "favourites" a shock. Our team should certainly claim a place and withstand the strong challenge that is certain to come from all directions; for a race such as this attracts clubs from all over the country. At our last Social, held on January 27th, the Honours Badges were awarded to those who have qualified since the inception of the scheme. The Club Executive recommend that the badge be worn on the front centre of the Club vest, on the gold band. In this way uniformity will be secured, the badge shown off to the best advantage, and the credit which always comes when a band of athletes are neatly clad, in uniform style, will re-act to the benefit of the Club. * * * * * A member who possesses copies of "The Belgravian" since the first numbers, edited by W. H. Hare, desires to have these suitably bound, and suggests that if there are other members similarly desirous of having the Club journal bound in permanent form, it might me possible to arrange a more attractive price if several get together. If this is of interest to any other members, will they please let the Hon. Editor know? * * * * * The Hon. Editor is still anxiously awaiting news of the various books on Athletics, which are held by various members. Please advise him at once if you have one in your possession. items.label: January 1934
items.sum: Obituary of H. S. ("Jim") Latter, a promising young Belgrave walker who died before the age of 21.
items.s: H. S. LATTER. Obituary of H. S. ("Jim") Latter, a promising young Belgrave walker who died before the age of 21. It is with very great sorrow that we have to record the death of H. S. Latter ("Jim"), one of the most promising walkers we have had in recent years. During his 3½ years with the Club he had made dozens of friends by means of his pleasing personality, his whole-hearted entry into all Club social affairs, and his enthusiastic support of our racing activities, both on road and track. Although not 21 years of age, he had already distinguished himself by winning the "Belgrave" Open Seven Miles handicap, and London Fire Brigade S.C. 2 miles event—two of the most important events held in the South. His fifth position in the Polytechnic H. Invitation Team Walk at the White City last June, comprising the pick of Southern track walkers, is still very fresh in our memories; and his fine performance was largely responsible for the Club's win on that occasion. It is little short of tragic that we should be robbed so prematurely of such a splendid young sportsman; and we extend to our late Club-mate's parents, sisters and friends our very profound sympathy in their sad bereavement. items.s: THE BOXING DAY HANDICAPS. Report of the club's annual Boxing Day handicaps: sprint won by B. L. Bone, two miles won from scratch by Arthur Penny in 9 min. 47 sec., and the three miles walk won by Reg. Elson. Rain tried hard to spoil this annual fixture, but I think it will take an earthquake to upset this meeting of ours. In the sprints it is very pleasing to note how well the Juniors are shaping; they had things pretty well their own way in the final. Tom Scrimshaw, off 4 yards, our half-mile track International, tried a turn of sprinting, and very nearly caught Bennett off 10 yards, a proof that he is keeping himself fit during the close season. In the final, B. L. Bone ran very well to get up off 4 yards to win in 12½ secs. A. Mewes was second off 7, and A. Dyke third off 7 yards. In the two miles event we had our three other Internationals out, and what a fine race this was! Arthur Penny, who from the place of honour, scratch, won in the fast time of 9 min. 47 sec. and put up a marvellous performance. There seems no stopping Arthur nowadays, and good luck to him; May he carry on and win, not only the National, but International as well! Allum, who finished second off 25 yards, seems to be getting right back to his best form. He put in a tremendous effort down the straight, but Penny was running too strongly to be worried by it, and finished about 15 yards to the good. Harry Shields, still a junior in years, was third off 85 yards. Harry is undoubtedly a Champion of the future, he has the right spirit and fights all the way. J. E. Flower was 4th and R. Patience 5th. Patience is to be congratulated on this very good performance, as he had been on Guard duty throughout the preceding night. The Three Miles Walk Handicap resulted in a win for Reg. Elson in good style. Don Brown and E. C. Heather fought out second place down the finishing straight, but as was to be expected the virtual scratch man, Brown, prevailed. items.h: THE SURREY COUNTY CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP AT EPSOM on 13th JAN., 1934.
items.sum: W. L. Bayliss's report of Belgrave's seventh team win in the Surrey County Cross-Country Championship at Epsom, with A. W. Penny first and H. E. Footer second, and the Belgrave finishers' positions and times.
items.s: THE SURREY COUNTY CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP AT EPSOM on 13th JAN., 1934. W. L. Bayliss's report of Belgrave's seventh team win in the Surrey County Cross-Country Championship at Epsom, with A. W. Penny first and H. E. Footer second, and the Belgrave finishers' positions and times. W. L. Bayliss writes of our seventh win in On a glorious day for Cross-country running we set off for Epsom, very hopeful of a further victory, despite the fact that many of our good men have Middlesex qualifications and therefore are not eligible to run in this race. These Middlesex members (banded together under the title of Cadogan A.C.) were competing in the Middlesex County Championship and also hoping to achieve honours. Thus our Cross Country men were divided on this occasion, but you will read of the performance of our Middlesex men elsewhere. I thought Penny the outstanding individual, as he is running right into last year's form, but was not too sure of Footer, who has been troubled with a cold. We all knew, of course, that Bert would put up a fair show, and consequently hoped for the best. The first view I had of the runners was when they had covered the first mile. Penny was in the lead with Weatherill, the South London Harrier, and our hopes were soon raised when we saw Footer lying 6th, followed by Carter 8th, and Abberton 10th. Our other men were at this time not doing too well, for Rice and Walker were in the 30's. They were, however, closely followed by Robertshaw, Mitchell and Cecil Penny. At 3 miles Penny was 100 yards in front of Weatherill, and Footer had come up to 3rd place, about 80 yards behind Weatherill Both Carter and Abberton were running well and each had picked up a place. All the rest of the team had moved up and things looked rosy for us. At 4½ miles Penny was still going as strong as ever and we saw then that Footer was doing his utmost to catch Weatherill. Carter and Abberton were going very well, and Walker and Rice held the 32nd and 33rd position with Robertshaw and W. Mitchell in close attendance. Nothing short of a catastrophe could stop us winning now. Penny won a very fine race, and Footer must have put in some very hard work to have overhauled Weatherill and finish second. Our other scoring men were Carter, Abberton, Rice and Walker, comprising a team that well deserved their victory. ... Perhaps "Footer's Training Schedule" is beginning to bear fruit already! items.label: January 1934
items.sum: Account by "A Cad." of the Belgrave members' win, as Cadogan A.C., in the Middlesex County Cross-Country Championship at Northolt Aerodrome and the Daily Telegraph Cup, Arthur Allum taking the County title for the third time.
items.s: Account by "A Cad." of the Belgrave members' win, as Cadogan A.C., in the Middlesex County Cross-Country Championship at Northolt Aerodrome and the Daily Telegraph Cup, Arthur Allum taking the County title for the third time. Our Hon. Secretary has described the very fine win by our runners in the Surrty Championship. Here follows an account of how our members fared in the Middlesex event—by "A Cad." The Middlesex County authorities had decided to hold their championship once again from the Northolt Aerodrome; and the senior event was preceded by a junior race, for those under 21 years of age, over five miles. Our only runner in this race was F. W. Nash and he finished in the first half of the race and shows promise of development. H. W. Shields, winner of the Junior event last year, and E. Saunders were both eligible for this, but had decided to assist the Senior team in their quest for championship honours. It must be said that we went to Northolt in an optimistic mood; but it would have required a super-optimist to have expected such an easy and convincing win. From the start our lads took up prominent positions, and at the end of the first lap, approximately half-way, we had nine men in the first twenty-five. This, in a field of 181 starters, was wonderful work, and there was no question about the direction in which the championship would go. So the finish came, with our boys following one another in rapid succession. Throughout the race Arthur Allum had been prominent and our International justified our confidence in his return to form by winning the County title for the third time. Barnes, of Enfield, and Hennessey, the Ealing and R.A.F. runner, were with Arthur at the end of three miles, with L. F. Humphris fifty yards in the rear. Over the second lap, however, Humphris managed to reduce the lead and upon entering the finishing field was about twenty yards behind Allum. Arthur slowed when entering the funnel and Humphris came up with a last-minute rush, the official difference being given as one-fifth of a second. There is a moral here for all our runners. Run right through to the narrow part of the funnel where the timekeepers stand, and discs are distributed, or a few valuable places may be lost! Our next man in was last year's Junior champion, Harry Shields, who excelled himself in finishing sixth, and scoring four for team purposes. Grand running, Harry! Two members of other clubs came by, then Jack Flower. Another seven seconds elapse, one stranger passes, and R. J. Patience finishes full of running! Edwards, of Ealing, and Adams, of the Poly., pass by and Alf. Taylor is in, scoring 11 points to the team total. Almost on his heels in Dan Patience, and the team of six is complete. But the splendid running of our men is by no means finished, for A. Patience (17), S. H. Warboys (21), E. Saunders (22) are in faster than the words can be written! Next comes F. R. Webb (42), J. C. Smith (74) and C. E. Brockwell (91) to complete our twelve. When everyone did so well it is difficult to single out individuals for special mention, but common justice compels us to congratulate Allum upon his third Middlesex championship, and Shields upon a really splendid achievement. Alf Taylor showed his best running to date; and the form of our Patience friends impressed everyone present. Warboys ran quite well to find himself only eighth man home, and Ted Saunders showed up very well for one still a junior. Smith and Brockwell completed our twelve in impressive style, our last man being placed 91st of 181 starters! To finish our scoring six in fifteen, and nine men in twenty-two, tells its own tale, and brought forth the congratulations of all present. Perhaps we may sympathise a little with A. Patience, S. H. Warboys and E. Saunders, who ran so well without gaining a place in the team, but they shared in the pleasure of the others, and the joys which team-racing brings. As a further indication of our twelve's running, I should like to point out that our twelve men totalled 314 points, whereas the six men of both Enfield A.C. and St. Mary's H.H. (who tied for 9th place of the 16 competing teams) scored 413 pts. each! It was very gratifying to our boys to win "The Daily Telegraph Cup" at the first time of asking; and if I may be allowed to end on a personal note, as one who took many "kicks" when we first attempted to secure the right to compete as a team, my "kick" forthcoming on this occasion was of a very different sort! May next year's race find our men equally prominent and successful. RESULT. From the times recorded, it would appear the course was short. Act. Pos. Team Pos. m. s. Act. Pos. Team Pos. m. s. 1 1 A. items.s: TEN MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Fred H. White's report of the club Ten Miles Cross-Country Championship for the "Macher" Shield on 27 January, won by Arthur Penny from Bert Footer and Arthur Allum, with Penny also first on the sealed handicap, and the full 22-man result. Fred H. White gives, in black and white, his impressions of the The race on January 27th, for the "Macher" Shield, held by Bert Footer, had been enthusiastically awaited since the Surrey and Middlesex Championships. The afternoon was perfect and 26 runners lined up for the start. On leaving the starting field, the runners were bunched together, with Penny, Flower and Carter making the pace. At the Windmill, however, we had a surprise, for Penny had opened up a gap of 100 yards. He was followed by Allum and Footer together, with Carter, Shields, Flower, Patiences A. and R., and Rice in that order. There was little change as the runners crossed the Golf Links at the start of the second lap, but Alf Taylor and Syd Warboys had moved up slightly. Eventually came the finish, with Arthur Penny recording very fast time. Bert Footer followed, having run his inevitable fast second lap, and Arthur Allum took third place. The sealed handicap showed that the scratch mark need not be an insuperable handicap, for Penny took first prize. Brockwell showed improved form and well deserved second prize, and Alf Taylor again showed some very good running and claimed third position. The result is appended: RESULT. † Dead Heat. Pos.
