items.s: OUR OPEN WALK. Report and results of the club's fifteenth annual 7 miles open walk from Wimbledon on 24 November, won by J. F. Johnson, with the individual handicap to J. E. Rutland and the handicap team race to Surrey W.C. (several printed handicap times, e.g. Churcher, Storey and Asher, do not equal actual time less allowance). OUR OPEN WALK. Our Fifteenth Annual promotion took place on November 24th from our quarters at Wimbledon, and once again walkers generally showed their appreciation of the Club, and the popularity of its Open event. 189 entries were received, comprising 24 teams and some 15 individuals. The Surrey W.C. came along with their usual three teams; Enfield A.C., Highgate H., London Vidarians W.C., Polytechnic H., were each represented by two teams. Single team entries were received from Ashcombe A.C., Cambridge H., Essex Beagles, London Transport (T.C.) S. and A.A., Metropolitan W.C., Southgate and Wood Green A.A., Surrey A.C., Valentine's S.C. and Woodford Green A.C., and we entered four teams. Twenty-seven of our own walkers entered—quite good representation—but several of our men who have given such excellent service in past races were still resting; and circumstances precluded the entry of several others who have added lustre to our teams in the past, and will do so again in the future in all probability. Among those we missed were Tommy Green, Len Fletcher, J. F King, F. Rickards, F. E. Bentley, J. C. Bidgood, R.Martin, H. F. King, A. H. Field, E. Saunders, J. E. Field, F. H. Elson; and in addition, some of the slower men—Jarvis, Snell, Willis, Seddon, Armstrong, and others. One hundred and sixty-three competitors actually started to the signal of our President over our usual seven miles course, and from the start Johnson (Enfield), Cooper (Woodford Green), Redman (Metropolitan), Plumb (Enfield), Stone (Polytechnic) and Treacher, of ours, were prominent. Plumb and Stone suffered disqualification early on, and Johnson soon showed his superiority over the other competitors by opening up a big gap. Meanwhile, the Surrey W.C. walkers came steadily through the field and, packing splendidly, gained scratch team honours from Enfield A.C. and ourselves. The individual handicap went to one of our very promising young walkers, J. E. Rutland, who had an allowance of 8 mins. 30 secs. Rutland, when only 15, won our Novice Track Walk, and now, while still a month or two short of seventeen, showed excellent form to finish 23rd in 60 min. 27 seconds, and annex first prize. His future will be watched with great interest, and given an easy year or so, we should number another first-class walker in our ranks capable of bringing the highest honours to the Club. Second in the handicap was an individual entrant, A. Leveridge (Suffolk R.W.A.), 4 min. 40 sec., with an Ashcombe friend, J. Banfield (9 min.) third. Our Surrey W.C. friends provided the winning handicap team, with our "B" team taking the second set of awards, and the Metropolitan third prizes. Of our men, Treacher showed excellent form in winning the prize for the first Belgrave Harrier not gaining any other award. His fourth place, walking as an individual, was very creditable, and showed that Bill will be of great value to us when qualified in the New Year. Our Captain, Don Brown, had an unfortunate day and retired at the half-distance. Speechley again showed that he is faster than ever, and Charlie Churcher and Redgrave also distinguished themselves. In fact, the performances of the three last-named, all "Juniors," were very encouraging, as were those of Rutland, already mentioned, and Storey. Elson and Boddington still have something in hand, and our younger brigade had valuable experience which should be of great help to them in the future. We cannot conclude without expressing our gratitude to all who contribuited to the success of the event, both competitors and officials. Particularly do we wish to thank the latter gentlemen for their valuable assistance, without which we should be unable to carry on. RESULT. 163 started, 139 finished. SCRATCH TEAM RACE. items.s: THE "HORWOOD CUP" RACE. Report and result of the Horwood Cup club walk for Junior-qualified walkers on 15 December, won by holder Charlie Speechley from Charlie Churcher, with Percy Wright winning the handicap and donor Oscar Horwood judging (L. Seddon's printed handicap time does not equal his actual time less start). THE "HORWOOD CUP" RACE. This annual Club race, open only to those walkers possessing the "Junior" qualification as laid down in R.W.A. Rules, was contested on December 15th. Charlie Speechley, the holder, was favourite, and went to the front from the start, closely followed by Charlie Churcher. It seemed, at the half-distance, that we were to be robbed of the close race which had been promised between these twain, for Speechley had opened up what appeared to be a winning gap and seemed comfortable in his walking. But Churcher had other views and towards the finish came along at a tremendous rate, and all but snatched a dramatic win in the last few yards. The holder managed to prevail, however, and both can take credit in having accomplished extremely fine times over an admittedly difficult course. Len Storey had been in third position practically throughout the race, and he, too, can take pride in his time. If he shows the same ability and determination that featured his racing on this day, in the "Junior" Championship, we shall have another first-rate man in our team. Of the others, Reg Elson, E. Heather and Leo Jones were clearly below form, but have plenty of time to find it before the first Saturday in March. Wright, Earle, Burns and the others in their first year will find that each race brings its modicum of experience, and next year will find them battling with the more experienced. Percy Wright (who threatens to become one of the Club "characters" unless we apply a purgative in the near future), showed some much-improved walking and was a well-deserved winner of the handicap. It was pleasing to see Wright record his first success, particularly as he has proved such a good Clubman, and hard worker for the Club on Brighton Walks, and in the matter of the Building Fund. Len Storey took second prize, with Charlie Churcher third, making the most of a thirty-seconds allowance. We were glad to have the donor of the Cup, Mr. Oscar Horwood, present as a Judge and to award the prizes. Business has taken up much of Oscar's time lately, but we hope he will soon find it possible to become a "regular" once again, as befits one who has done so much for the Club, particularly in the days when athletes, finance and officials were much more scarce than they are to-day. items.s: BOXING DAY. Report and results of the club's traditional Boxing Day meeting: a 120 yards handicap won by E. J. Johns, the 2 miles run won by A. W. Penny from scratch and the 3 miles walk won by D. A. Earle. BOXING DAY. Our traditional Holiday meeting enjoyed fine weather, and a good crowd of Clubmen and their friends came along, if not to compete, then to gain appetites for the Seasonal feastings. The Sprint entry was very disappointing, and makes one wonder whether it is wanted or not. Teddy Johns, a half-miler turned sprinter, was successful with 12 yards allowance, and shows promise of becoming a useful performer at the shorter distances. The Walk gave us an opportunity of seeing Brown at his best, and it was a very fine effort which gained second place for him. Victory went to "Doug" Earle, one of our recent newcomers, and he should repeat this success many times in future races despite shortening marks. The 2 Mile always makes us expect brilliant running and racing, and this year's race fulfilled all our expectations. Arthur Penny showed his best form to win from the scratch mark once again, and Carter and Shaw also displayed excellent running to fill the minor positions. There were the usual repentant few retiring with thoughts of the preceding day very much with them—but it was always thus! RESULT. 120 Yards.—1st, E. J. Johns (12); 2nd, A. M. Dyke (6); 3rd, F. South of the Thames Junior Cross-Country
items.s: An unsigned contribution descriptive of our clash with Thames Valley Harriers and Ashcombe A.C. from the quarters of the last-named club on October 27th. Unsigned report of the cross-country match against Thames Valley Harriers and Ashcombe A.C. at Sheen on 27 October, won easily by Belgrave with Syd Ring first, with full result and team scores. An unsigned contribution descriptive of our clash with Thames Valley Harriers and Ashcombe A.C. from the quarters of the last-named club on October 27th. For our oldest inter-club fixture, 26 of our members visited Sheen and with 25 T.V.H. men and 12 Ashcombe runners, comprised the field. In view of the home club's numbers, it was decided to score ten aside, and the race resulted in the easiest of victories for us. In fact, we had the first ten home, but as Bert Cook is only a second-claim member, he was eliminated from the scoring, and we had our 10 in 12. At the beginning of the race the T.V.H. runners were noticeably prominent—in fact, they held the first dozen places at the end of half-a-mile, but then Harry Shields and Bill Rice decided to move up; Harry led for a while, when Syd Ring ran away cleverly and ultimately finished very fresh 50 yards ahead of Shields, with Tom Carter a similar distance behind. It was very pleasing to have 15 men in 19 places and within two minutes of the winner. Our International trio went out with the object of coaching our "South of the Thames" Juniors, and that they did their self-imposed task well is shown by the fact that three of them finished 1st, 7th and 10th. Dan Patience had the misfortune to go off the course about half-a-mile from home, otherwise he would have finished much nearer the winner. Full result and times are appended. RESULT. items.h: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY RACE.
items.sum: Harry Parker and Frank Webb describe the South of the Thames Junior cross-country race at Gravesend on 10 November, won by D. B. Pell (H.H.H.) with Syd Ring fifth and Belgrave "A" second to Mitcham A.C.; some clogged times in the result are kept as a scan.
e: South of the Thames Junior Cross-Country
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY RACE. Harry Parker and Frank Webb describe the South of the Thames Junior cross-country race at Gravesend on 10 November, won by D. B. Pell (H.H.H.) with Syd Ring fifth and Belgrave "A" second to Mitcham A.C.; some clogged times in the result are kept as a scan. Harry Parker and Frank Webb ("Super Snake") combine to write of THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY RACE. This year's race was held from Henleys' Sports Ground, Gravesend, on Saturday, November 10th. What a day! We, who were deeply ensconced in the motor coach the Club had provided, congratulated ourselves as we ploughed along blindly through the torrential rain and hoped that it would give over before the race. In this we were very fortunate, as it stopped with our arrival. Our driver had quite an experience in finding the venue, as the locals seemed only to have a vague idea as to its location—and after an appeal to "Slow-motion" in yellow oilskins, and a further appeal to the fair sex, we found we were off the road but in lovely country. Tom Eaton took such a fancy to our surroundings that he alighted to get a "close-up" and got left. His cross-country experience, however, did not fail him, for he went "as the crow flies," and on our arrival we found him awaiting us. The supporters had nothing to complain about as regards seeing the race, as the course chosen formed a natural amphitheatre and the race could be seen throughout without leaving the starting place. Our team was not, perhaps, quite at full strength, but was very serviceable, and we had great hopes of finding the individual winner in our ranks. The five mile course of two laps was laid diagonally across a field into a valley, rising to the brow of a hill, which was followed for about ¾ miles, then a left turn across ploughed fields into the valley again. Then up a field-path to the starting field, and the second lap, which was a trifle more extended. The course was one which "old-timers" call a good sporting one, but was perhaps too heavy for Juniors. A good start was made, and when the runners appeared on the hill brow, already well strung out, it could be seen that Syd. Ring was laying on the shoulder of the leader, well away from the rest, and running strongly. Comig back to the starting field after a gruelling climb up the field-path, Waldock (Mitcham) was just leading Ring, wtih Constable (Croydon) third, and the ultimate winner 5th. At this point it appeared that our old friends, Mitcham, had the race well in hand, their colours being well in evidence supporting their leader. Towards the closing stages Syd Ring found the heavy going too much and lost ground to finish 5th, thirty seconds behind the winner. Special mention must be made of Chantler and Martin, both having run splendidly over the last lap to finish 12th and 13th. Actually Martin pulled up from 34th position at half-way! And so we finished four in fifteen places, and Mitcham four in sixteen. Final scores were Mitcham A.C., 40 points; Belgrave, 45 points. Heartiest congratulations to Mitcham! Of our other members, we can only say that they ran remarkably well under such trying conditions, many taking part in their first big race. With a little more experience they will be finishing much higher up the field. RESULT. TEAM SCORES. m. s. m. s. 1 D. B. Pell H.H.H. 28 2 51 A. Patience B. "A" 30 3[illegible] 5 S. T. Ring B. items.s: Tyrian Club fixture Vice-Captain Arthur Penny reports the first fixture against the Tyrian Club at Motspur Park on 10 November, an easy Belgrave win by 22 points to 61, with the result. While Capt. Footer took charge of our "Junior" teams at Gravesend, Vice-Captain Arthur Penny led his men to Motspur Park for our first fixture v. Tyrian Club. Here follow his comments :— About twenty of the "cream of the Club" were entertained by the Tyrian Club at Motspur Park on November 10th. It was an awful day and we are all grateful to Mr. Gordon, Reg. Freestone and last, but not least, Capt. Ellis[illegible]n, for officiating at the race. Due, no doubt, to the fact that our opponents were weakened by the Inter-University fixture at Birmingham, we gained an easy victory. Without disrespect to our rivals, our boys enjoyed a rather hard training run, and came back smothered with mud, but none the less pleased with themselves. We were the guests of the Tyrian Club at tea afterwards, and two of our members showed that rain and mud do not affect their appetites, judging by the amount of cake consumed! RESULT. items.s: Brotherly Love Cecil Penny writes on the match against 2nd Scots Guards at Wimbledon on 17 November, won by Belgrave 96 points to 204 under varsity scoring, with W. G. Webb, F. R. Webb and D. Patience sharing first. Cecil Penny on "Brotherly Love" and, in passing, our match versus 2nd Scots Guards at Wimbledon, on November 17th. Did I hear remarks such as "A snaky piece of work" emerging from the babel of voices after the match versus our ever-welcome visitors? How brotherly! Now, now, fellows! You must hand it to the veterans this time! To be placed first in a race of any description figuring on our fixture list, is a praiseworthy performance, and I believe I am correct in stating that this was Frank's first win in a cross-country race for the club, so, sarcastic youngsters, hold your peace! The race itself was not unduly exciting. Several of our visitors were prominent at the start, but principally due to lack of training, they soon fell back and the race resolved itself into a friendly battle between the brothers Patience (who led for a considerable way) and the Webb brothers, with the result as shown. items.sum: Jack Flower's account of the match against Ealing Harriers and R.A.F. Uxbridge on Ealing's course, won by A. Allum, with Belgrave winning on 108 points (R.A.F. total printed as 462, though its listed places add to 456).
items.s: The onlooker sees most of the game Jack Flower's account of the match against Ealing Harriers and R.A.F. Uxbridge on Ealing's course, won by A. Allum, with Belgrave winning on 108 points (R.A.F. total printed as 462, though its listed places add to 456). "The onlooker sees most of the game." Read Jack Flower's account of the match versus Ealing H. and R.A.F. (Uxbridge) and see if you agree. Once again we had the pleasure of visiting Ealing's course, and amassed a strong team of 25. The race started steadily (or seemed so to me, but I was only an onlooker!) and four Ealing men led the field through a nice muddy lane, for the country. I was silly enough to follow and managed to become covered in mud, all in order to see who was leading at the half-distance. As the tail-end passed me, lo and behold! I saw two R.A.F. lads having a nice hike and discussing family histories! Shortly after they had strolled from the field, the leaders came to view, having done about 2½ miles. Allum and Saunders led, with Edwards (Ealing) 20 yards behind, and C. Penny fourth. When the runners returned to the track for the finish, Carter had joined Allum and Saunders. Then Arthur remembered the hot water and flew down the straight to win from Saunders and Carter! Others followed fast as per result, and it was very pleasing to see men like A. Patience, A. Beavan, Doubleday, A. Smith and Nash, improving each time out, and before long I hope they will be right up with the leaders. In conclusion, I am on safe ground in saying that our boys thoroughly enjoyed the run, and are looking forward to our next meeting with our hosts—probably on the track next May. RESULT. items.s: BELGRAVE H. v. METROPOLITAN POLICE A.A. G. R. Chantler reports the match against the Metropolitan Police A.A. at Imber Court on 1 December, won by C. T. Carter, with Belgrave winning 257 points to 563 under varsity scoring. G. R. Chantler writes of BELGRAVE H. v. METROPOLITAN POLICE A.A. On December 1st a team of 24 made the journey to Imber Court, for our match with the M.P.A.C The Police, fielding a team of 22, Varsity scoring with 20 aside was decided on. The field was smartly away and the Claret and Gold were soon in evidence, about a dozen being packed in good team formation at the head of the field by the time the Reservoir was reached. When the field was sighted, for the turn home, Carter was leading the pack, running comfortably, followed by Ring, Shields, Rice, and J. Flower, with our "South of the Thames" Juniors, Martin, Saunders and Chantler, close on their heels. These positions were held until the finish, Carter crossing the line 20 seconds to the good of Ring. Our team finished 20 men in 26 places—fine packing. Congratulations to J. E. Tosh, who scored for the team on a course which is a stiff trial for a track runner! RESULT. TEAM RESULT (20 aside). (Varsity Scoring). m. s. 1. C. T. Carter B 27 35 2. S. T. Ring B 27 55 3. H. W. items.s: THE "BLACKSTAFFE" SHIELD RACE. Syd King describes the 23rd race for the "Blackstaffe" Shield, the club 7 miles cross-country championship, held in heavy rain on 15 December with a Belgrave v. Cadogan match; Arthur Penny won for a record third time from Bert Footer, with Martin winning the handicap. (The Shield is printed "Backstaffe" once.) Belgrave beat Cadogan A.C. 61 to 75. In the result, W. H. Styles's printed handicap time (40 55) does not equal his actual time less start, and D. Sargent's actual time has a damaged digit read as 49 30 from the arithmetic. Syd King will tell us the story of THE "BLACKSTAFFE" SHIELD RACE. A record field of forty faced the starter on 15th December to compete for the honour of holding the "Blackstaffe" Shield and the title of Club 7 Miles Cross-Country Champion for the ensuing year. Again a match between Belgrave and Cadogan was arranged in conjunction with the Championship, but the interest in this did not appear to be so great as in previous years. It was the 23rd race for the Shield, but although past descriptions of the race mention dark, dismal weather, I think this year it was darker, more dismal, and certainly wetter than any other within my recollection. Large puddles were everywhere, the ground being waterlogged over large stretches of the course. Owing to late-comers, and the usual athletic tendency to take a tremendous time in changing, it was a quarter to four before our President gave the word to go and in heavy rain the runners set off on their uncomfortable journey. By the time they had traversed the first field and were going out on to the Common it was seen that H. S. Cook was making the pace, and he was a few yards ahead with Penny, Allum, Carter and Footer lying next, and a crowd of others close up, while our old veteran, George Still, brought up in the rear. The few, but enthusiastic, spectators now moved to the end of the first lap and soon in the failing light a few runners could be seen struggling along the course, but after frantic efforts to distinguish Penny, Footer or other of the "cracks" it was discovered that, after all, it was only training pack. When the competitors did come along, Penny was nearly hundred yards ahead of Ginty and he in turn was about the same distance in front of a hot little trio consisting of Footer, Allum and Carter, followed a little later by Ring and Shields. Then another gap and along came a half-dozen together, amongst whom could be seen Martin, the ultimate winner of the handicap, Jack Flower, and Bill Rice who, incidentally, was running in this race nine years ago. The running of Ginty was a pleasant surprise to many of us, and enquiries were made as to who he was and where he came from and whether he is eligible to represent us in the forthcoming cross-country championships. Those "in the know" confided to us in a very secretive manner that his previous performances included fourth place in the Army Championship. Whether this is correct or not, his running on this day shows him to be a useful addition to our team. At this point the proximity of the dressing room, combined with the mud and rain, caused six or seven of the runners to retire, and had it not been for the coaxing of the spectators that number would have been much larger, and who could wonder at it under these conditions? Over the second lap Ginty dropped away a bit, and Bert Footer passed him on the hill, whilst Carter and Allum both made on him. By the time the runners arrived at the finish it was so dark that electric torches had to be used for time-keeping, and it was only with difficulty that the competitors' numbers could be distinguished. Arthur Penny was first past the post, thereby creating a record for this race, inasmuch as he is the first one to win the Backstaffe Shield on three occasions, although several have two wins to their credit. Thirteen seconds later Bert Footer appeared out of the darkness, to fill second place for the fourth time, the last occasion being in 1927. In 1929 he was the winner and in 1923 he was third, but I think he must have been too small to run prior to that, for I have seen no record of him appearing until then. There was a good race for third place, for only four seconds separated the next three, Ginty finishing just in front of Allum and Carter. Half a minute later Harry Shields put in an appearance. After waiting another forty seconds or so a crowd rushed at us through the darkness, no less than seven runners finishing in 8 seconds—the same little bunch that had been in company at the half-way point led by King, who had dropped back during the last mile or two. Altogether thirty-three finished and it will no doubt surprise many to see who was last, but I think he must have been whipping in, instead of racing. In the team race Belgrave beat Cadogan fairly comfortably, whereas last year a bare two points separated them. D. Martin won the handicap with two minutes less than he had last year when he also took first prize, and Cecil Penny was runner-up only four seconds behind and Ginty, in his first club race, was placed third, so with a medal and a "pot" he certainly had some encouragement. The Hon. Handicapper put up a good performance also, for a minute covered the first eleven, which we must admit was not too bad. Have a look for yourself :— RESULT. TEAM SCORES. items.label: January 1935
items.h: THE FIVE MILES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP.
items.sum: Joe Flower describes the club Five Miles Junior Cross-Country Championship for the "Savage" Shield, won by G. R. Chantler from D. Martin after a close finish.
items.s: THE FIVE MILES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Joe Flower describes the club Five Miles Junior Cross-Country Championship for the "Savage" Shield, won by G. R. Chantler from D. Martin after a close finish. A dissertation by Joe Flower on THE FIVE MILES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Ten of our junior members turned out to compete in the above championship, and for the honour of holding the "Savage" Shield for the next twelve months. Harry Shields, last year's winner, was no longer eligible, owing to the age limit. However, those who were fortunate enough to witness this event were treated to a tip-top race over a five miles course. G. R. Chantler, the new champion, had a ding-dong battle all the way with D. Martin, and it was only in the finishing straight that Chantler forced himself to the front and victory. Both these juniors are to be congratulated on the fine fighting spirit they showed, and with average luck should gain many further honours for Belgrave. Chantler and Martin cut out a fast pace from the start, closely followed by Clements and Stimpson. Just over a mile out Clements had the misfortune to twist his ankle and had to retire. Very unfortunate for him, for we know him to be a real good runner anxious to carry off the Shield. At the half distance Martin held a slight lead from Chantler, with Stimpson running very strongly about forty yards behind. At the Windmill, about a mile from home, Chantler and Martin were running stride for stride at a very fast pace. With half-a-mile to go Chantler made an effort and started to open up a gap. Martin was not finished with yet, however, and slowly but surely pegged the other man back. On entering the finishing straight these two game lads were level, and only then was Chantler able to force himself to the front to win from a very gallant loser. Stimson, who finished third, also ran splendidly. He has nothing like the experience of the other two, but I like his style and determination, and feel confident he will make a good name for himself as a cross-country runner. Jordan, who was fourth, ran a better second half and finished very strongly. K. N. Wood is another who calls for praise, for he was only 75 seconds behind the leader in his first year of racing. We should like to see larger fields for this event; but meanwhile we can feel very proud of those who treated us to such a fine race as shown in the result below :— m. s. 1. G. R. Chantler 27 35 2. items.sum: Preview of the coming cross-country fixtures: the Club 10 Miles Championship for the "Macher" Shield on 26 January, a quiet day at Wimbledon on 2 February, the South of Thames 7 Miles at Epsom Downs on 9 February, a social run with Herne Hill on 16 February, the Southern at Hassocks on 23 February and the National at Beaconsfield on 9 March.
e: South of Thames Cross Country Championship
items.s: FORTHCOMING CROSS-COUNTRY FIXTURES. Preview of the coming cross-country fixtures: the Club 10 Miles Championship for the "Macher" Shield on 26 January, a quiet day at Wimbledon on 2 February, the South of Thames 7 Miles at Epsom Downs on 9 February, a social run with Herne Hill on 16 February, the Southern at Hassocks on 23 February and the National at Beaconsfield on 9 March. FORTHCOMING CROSS-COUNTRY FIXTURES. I believe that this issue will be in your hands on or before January 26th, which is the day fixed for the Club 10 Miles Cross Country Championship for the "Macher" Shield. Arthur Penny is the present holder, but whether he will be fit enough to compete is open to doubt. In his absence Bert Footer should win readily enough, and even if Arthur does run (we all hope he will) there is no doubt that Bert will make him go all the way, and it seems to be a case of any odds, bar two. There is, however, a Sealed Handicap for this race and this is where the rank and file come in. No matter how far back you may finish, when the handicap is worked out you may have the pleasure of finding yourself in front, on handicap. Another reason why all members should do their best to compete is that the subsequent teams for the "South of Thames," "Southern" and "National" are selected on the form displayed in this race. Previous events are, of course, also taken into account, but to be really sure of your place you should make up your mind to be present at Wimbledon on January 26th. February 2nd. We have a quiet day at Wimbledon and this should give members a chance to have a breather before the big races that are due in week or two's time. Above all, remember to keep behind your pack-leader and also finish with a little bit in reserve. There is plenty of time to go "all out" when the day of the race comes round. On February 9th the South of Thames 7 Miles Cross Country Championship will be held from the Grandstand, Epsom Downs. This is country which should be familiar to all our lads, and with the team which is qualified to run, we ought to stand a sporting chance of winning. Most of our cracks are barred, under the various barring clauses, also our "Service" members, such as Dan and Ron Patience and our new member, Jim Ginty, but we can still turn out a fair team and if they run to form (unfortunately this seems to be a race where some of our members do not reproduce their best!), as stated above, I think we should be there at the finish. In any case there is the "Sir Jeremiah Colman" Cup, awarded to the first club who finish their complete team of 12 men, to be considered, and so everybody is given a chance of helping the Club to success. Being near Town, I hope our supporters will come along and give our boys a cheer. Compared with some clubs we are a little backward in this respect, and it is up to the non-active members to do their best to remedy this. The following Saturday, February 16th, we are again at Epsom Downs, this time for a Social run with our friends, the Herne Hill Harriers. It was thought this would provide a steady foundation for the gruelling test a week hence. All members are invited to come along, for there will be packs to suit all, fast and slow, and it makes a change from our own country at Wimbledon. FEBRUARY 23rd. THE SOUTHERN COUNTIES 10 MILES C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP AT HASSOCKS (SUSSEX). This can be reached by Southern Railway from either Victoria or London Bridge. I have not yet heard whether a "special" is going down, but from Victoria there is the 1-10 and 1-32, and from London Bridge the 12-30, 1-24 and 1-32. These I give for the benefit of members who are not in touch with our mid-week training quarters, but as soon as I hear something definite I shall post full instructions on the notice board at "The Rising Sun." All team men will, of course, be advised, time and place of meeting, etc., as usual. As regards Hassocks, I see it is 43½ miles from London, so it cannot be so very far from Brighton, and those who remember the "Southern" held at the latter place in 1930, the first time the Club was placed in this race, will know what to expect from the surrounding country. Still, we did well at Brighton and with our present team, who are easily over 100 per cent. stronger than in those days, we ought to be able to hold our title of Southern Champions. Funnily enough, a few years back this was a thing to shout about, but nowadays, well! I doubt if some people know who are the holders, which we might put down to Belgrave modesty or the trend of modern conditions. Be that as it may, we are proud of our title and I am sure all our lads will fight to their last ounce to hang on to it. Of our rivals, Surrey A.C. appear the most formidable. True, they were runners-up last year, but on present form their men are running perhaps even better than then ,and although some of the smaller clubs are coming along, I think it is a little early to think of them as possible Southern contenders. The Polytechnic Harriers seem to be improving of late, as regards the country, whereas South London Harriers seem definitely on the down-grade, which is a pity when one considers their past record, but I suppose this comes to all clubs in due coure. Wycombe Phoenix are always great triers and can be relied upon to put up a good fight, but I expect they will miss their old Stalwart, Sam Ferris, who could always be relied upon in a race of this desscription. I hope the above has whetted your appetite and that you will be there on February 23rd, complete with throat lozenges. Instead of going along and booing the "Ref." at Stamford Bridge, come down into the wilds of Sussex and give vent to your feelings by cheering our lads to yet another hard won victory. And don't forget that the "Senior" race is preceded by the "Junior" (under 21) Championship over 5 miles. We have high hopes of winning this for the first time, possessing, as we do, several very fine young runners. So use your voice to shout for a "Belgrave Double Win." A fortnight later, March 9th to wit, there comes the most important test of all, the National 10 Miles C.C. Championship. This will be held at Beaconsfield, which was the venue in 1929, and in those days athough we started a team, only four men closed in. Their positions were 73, 104, 106 and 178, and this only six years ago, mark you, whereas now we expect our whole team of nine men home before 73. I won't mention names, but even one of our Internationals was one of the above, and I bet he enjoyed his run as did another who finished the course, although nearly last. Such was the spirit then, and in my opinion this has largely contributed to our present-day position. We hear the smaller clubs talk of their days of struggling, but on looking at the above we find it is not so long ago that we are not in the same place. It just shows what can be done, not by huge transfer fees as in 'Soccer, but by developing your present members, not forgetting the all-important Junior, who after all is the Senior of to-morrow. If other clubs have the same club spirit as pervades the Belgrave (perhaps they have) they will soon reap their reward and will rise from a place of minor importance into being one of the most powerful clubs in the country to-day, which is the Belgrave position. All entries and enquiries to the Gen. Hon. Sec., W. L. BAYLISS, 71, Ravensbury Road, S.W.18. items.label: January 1935
items.sum: Humorous account of the second Social of the season on 3 November, with its Crazy Cabaret and the "Love in Bloom" ballet, and notice of the next Social on 26 January.
items.s: CRAZY CABARET. Humorous account of the second Social of the season on 3 November, with its Crazy Cabaret and the "Love in Bloom" ballet, and notice of the next Social on 26 January. CRAZY CABARET. The second Social of the season was held on November 3rd, and was well supported by our guests, Croydon H. Epsom H. and Mitcham A.C., supplemented by the ladies who had been running from the Windmill during the afternoon. No doubt the advertised Crazy Cabaret, produced by Tom Cotton and trained by Miss Jo Parsons, was one of the attractions, and accounted for the really fine crowd which assembled. The versatile talent among the Bels. is outstanding! Among the performers were several who have delighted us before, including Tom Cotton, Florrie Footer (once again in the rôle of Princess Charming), and our old friends Castor and Oil, who again left us without a leg to stand on. The curtain rose at 9 p.m. with Miss Gladys Bailey singing "Over My Shoulder," which served to introduce us to "The Seven Belgrave Sisters" (including sylph-like Sidney and Harley, the original Harlequin) in a singing and dancing act which was well received. Then followed Castor and Oil (alias T. Carter and P. Donnelly, or vice versa. Which is vice and vich is versa, I'll leave you to guess). Their act was very moving. Tom, girlishly garbed in a shimmering creation of russet and gold which displayed her form (or that which he used in lieu of) to advantage, and with lovelight in her eyes, although a trifle haughty as becomes such a queenly figure, was soon swept off her feet by the advances of Paddy, all sackcloth and gnashes. Eventually her feminine charm, plus a half-nelson, brought the debonair swain grovelling at her feet, only to be left flat for his pains! Curtain, amidst tremendous applause! Charlie Boud then gave a number dedicated to Capt. Footer, entitled "Belgravian Bertie," although his costume reminded one of the famous advertisement, "1887—and still going strong." The words, written by C. Williams (father of "J.S."), and Charlie's interpretation, gave great pleasure. The most spectacular act of the evening—"Love in Bloom"—was then given with the following cast:— Belgrave Sisters ... S. T. Ring, C. H. Penny, F. R. Webb, F. A. Walker, T. H. Scrimshaw, A. A. Harley. Singer ... Tom Cotton. Castor and Oil ... Irresponsible Equilibrists. Love (in full bloom) ... H. E. Footer. The ballet opened with Tom Cotton singing the theme song, "Love in Bloom," in front of a large representation of a flower-tub, while the Belgrave Sisters entered and with incantations to Sol, gracefully gyrated round the flowery bowery. Then with full pomp and glory, entered Castor and Oil with wheelbarrow, the Heralds of Spring. They joined in the now maddened whirl of pink and flounces, to bestow the first dew of spring and natural fertiliser upon the virgin soil. Then to the words, "You planted a seed," the dancers sowed in dumb show, and soon amidst a thick grey mist of morning glory and on the words, "This is the hour of sweet fulfilment," Love in Bloom appeared from the flower pot in the form of Footer in a blonde wig, garlanded with yellow pansies and little else. Around the Hall he scampered, followed by the corps-de-ballet, spraying the audience with sweet scents and Mitcham Lavender. (If I came from Mitcham, I wouldn't boast of it!). Personally, judging from the sulphurous smell which accompanied the "sweet fulfilment," I should have thought "Little Love" came from the nether regions rather than from Sol! Then exit, and the company re-appeared a few seconds later for the final item—a tableau. If the desire was for laughter, this item may also be said to have well succeeded. Altogether a most successful show! Those who participated, and indeed, all of us, would like to express their appreciation of Miss Jo Parsons' invaluable assistance in rehearsal, and also their gratitude to Miss G. Bailey and Miss L. Smith for their splendid help. The next Social is on January 26th, and offers of entertainment are invited. Don't keep that talent to yourself! Let the Social Committee hear from you. As a matter of fact, I believe they are arranging for a paper-tearing act by Tommy Scrimshaw, so if you want to avoid that, come forward with your suggestions early. Don't forget,—January 26th. items.sum: Gossip column credited to Arthur Penny but written up by A.A.H., who explains he could hardly decipher Penny's pencilled notes on the last "Queensberry" Dance and deleted the personal parts.
items.s: THE GOSSIP COLUMN. Gossip column credited to Arthur Penny but written up by A.A.H., who explains he could hardly decipher Penny's pencilled notes on the last "Queensberry" Dance and deleted the personal parts. THE GOSSIP COLUMN. By Arthur Penny. —Or it would have been, if I had been able to decipher Arthur's pencilled notes commenting on the last "Queensberry" Dance! Amidst a mass of pencilled matter, one typewritten line stands out in stark simplicity—in mute reproach to the past. It reads, "A.W.P. was in at the finish." Whether the word "all" should be interposed between "was" and "in" I am unable to say, but suggest we should give him the benefit of the doubt on this occasion, and offer our congratulations! Our amateur columnist's first paragraph seems to contain a libellous comment which might be taken by some to refer to the Hon. Editor. As the writer is not sure of his rights, as an individual, to sue under the Law of Libel in respect of a comment sanctioned by him as Hon. Editor in a journal published by a Committee of which he is a member—breath—no comment must appear which might prove Penny-wise and pound foolish! A tribute is then paid to the tangoing grace of H.E.F. and F.R.W., and reference made to our contributor's lapsed contract with the House of Guinness. Penitent Penny! He concludes with a statement that he has heard of beetroots growing in dirt, but never of dirt growing on beetroots, and couples with this the initials H.L.R. On the face of it this seems ridiculous (the statement, of course!) and if a fellow, for reasons of his own—possibly very good reasons—decides to disguise himself, is it our concern? Or is it? And if not, why? Arthur adds a personal note giving me permission to delete anything which I consider too personal! I have exercised that permission! A.A.H. items.h: ACHIEVEMENT ! English Cross-Country Champions, 1935 : Belgrave Harriers.
items.sum: Editorial by A.A.H. celebrating Belgrave Harriers' first English Cross-country Championship, won at Beaconsfield in the club's 48th year, with hopes of a treble of National team titles and praise for captain H. E. Footer and the Southern Counties Junior winners.
items.s: ACHIEVEMENT ! English Cross-Country Champions, 1935 : Belgrave Harriers. Editorial by A.A.H. celebrating Belgrave Harriers' first English Cross-country Championship, won at Beaconsfield in the club's 48th year, with hopes of a treble of National team titles and praise for captain H. E. Footer and the Southern Counties Junior winners. To have succeeded where we have so often failed—to have achieved an ambition which once seemed almost beyond hopes of realisation—to have tasted the sweets of victory when we have known the dregs of bitterness and disappointment. To have advanced gradually from the darkness into the dazzling light of publicity that is directed upon a champion club—to have striven and to have toiled; and now to know the feeling of exhilaration which accompanies the fulfilment of aspirations. That is our reward. Hard-won honours are ours. The satisfaction which comes from a win such as ours is all the more real and heart-felt because of the difficulties with which we have had to contend in the past. Every impediment to progress and advancement known to the smallest and poorest club now, has been our lot in the past. We have had to fight for our very existence in the past; but we have won through and in the 48th year of our history assumed the title of English Cross-country Champions. Everyone of us feels that he has helped, in varying degree, towards the success which has attended our efforts, and this is the quintessence of Club-spirit. It is given to few to bring honour and distinction to the Club name, but we are all part of the spirit which has inspired the effort. One of our younger walkers tells the story, against himself, of how he rushed into the street after hearing the news over the radio of our Beaconsfield win and, meeting a friend, shouted excitedly, “We've won the English Cross-country Championship.” To which his astonished friend replied, “Where were you placed?” Upon being told that our young friend was many miles away at the time of the race, and never ran (opportunity for joke! gambit declined) he walked away marvelling at the inexplicability of human nature! Well, at least, we can understand! Congratulations have rolled in from all directions, for which we are very grateful. Our win was certainly a very popular one and it is good to know we stand high in the estimation of our fellow-sportsmen. Well, we are English champions, and next season will find us defending, not challenging. We shall do our utmost to hold the title and our runners will find, as our walkers have found in the past, that they are expected to win, win, win, whatever the opposition. The second or third placing which seemed out of reach a few years ago, and which, only yesteryear, was so greatly prized and gave our Club-members and supporters such intense pleasure, will to-morrow be regarded as failure. A new standard of comparison has arisen, and that our team will do their very best to live up to it is beyond question. We can congratulate ourselves upon being the only club in the history of Athletics to place its name upon three National team trophies. At the moment we hold both the Cross-country 50 kilos. walking team championships. The 20 miles walking title has been ours in 1924, 1925, 1928 and 1929, and we have great hopes of annexing it again in a month's time and so complete a glorious treble. It would be a wonderful finale to the Winter season. And so let us close by heartily, sincerely and gratefully congratulating our Cross-country captain, H. E. Footer, and his team upon the new honours brought to the Club, not forgetting all the hard workers who have laid foundations in the past, and the helpers, reserves and supporters of the present. As to the future, the inspiration has been provided. Our young men will see that it has not been provided in vain! In winning the Southern Counties “Junior” title for the first time, our younger runners have shown they have real talent, and in the years to come we have but little doubt that they will bring more and more credit to the Club to which they belong. A.A.H. A.A.H. A.A.H. H. E. Footer H. E. items.h: THE ENGLISH CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP, BEACONSFIELD, MARCH 9th, 1935.
items.sum: A.A.H.'s report of the English Cross-country Championship at Beaconsfield, 9 March 1935, where Belgrave Harriers packed six men between 11th and 20th to beat Salford by 56 points, with captain Bert Footer receiving the trophies.
items.s: THE ENGLISH CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP, BEACONSFIELD, MARCH 9th, 1935. A.A.H.'s report of the English Cross-country Championship at Beaconsfield, 9 March 1935, where Belgrave Harriers packed six men between 11th and 20th to beat Salford by 56 points, with captain Bert Footer receiving the trophies. Having generalised about our successful tilt at the highest cross-country honours, the time now comes for something more detailed. But how to treat the subject? Is our win to be the occasion for a welter of superlatives, a panegyric of praise, a laudatory outpouring partaking of all that flies fastest to the head in the English language? Or is it to be regarded rather as the inevitable reward of planned progress and persistence, allied to splendid team spirit? Undoubtedly the latter is the truest approach. Knowing the determination to succeed which has permeated our team for some time past, one would have been surprised, upon looking back at some future time, if the English title had not been won. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that there was something of a dramatic suddenness about the manner in which our hopes were realised. A fortnight previously we had surrendered our Southern title to Surrey A.C., and whilst we had plenty of confidence that this result would be reversed, and that Salford would have to yield to us this time, we were not so optimistic as to think that Birchfield, holders for the previous seven years, with eight Internationals entered in the team, would be humbled and forced into fourth position! However, we anticipate. Let's start at the beginning. Two hundred and ninety-five runners thundered from the starting pens, and in the first 50 yards Shaw and Shields had nasty falls over two prostrate Ealing men. They picked themselves up and had all the field before them. The first lap of one mile was soon covered, and then out into the country on the first lap of three miles of fast, undulating park land, with our boys fairly well placed. At four miles we had another view of the runners. Bailey (Salford) led with Close (Reading A.C.) on his shoulder. Jim Ginty was fourth at this point, and our other men all seemed to be weighing up their opponents and running strongly. An attempt to get an idea of the scoring was doomed to failure owing to the speed with which the men passed. We could see, however, that Surrey AC.'s sixth man was behind our eighth. Salford had three men prominent, but where were the others? Birchfield seemed well beaten even here. Currie, the Midland Champion, had retired at 1½ miles, and they had two men in the first bunch, the rest nowhere! However, we have been deceived before by the wearing of white vests and so were not unduly jubilant. At seven miles it was obvious that, bar accidents, victory was ours. Ginty had fallen back a little and was running with Bert Footer, Dan Patience being a few yards in the rear—all in the first 25 places. A few seconds later came a very heartening sight, Alf Taylor, Harry Shields and Tom Carter all running together. Bert Shaw, Arthur Allum and Jack Flower were all running strongly and we rejoiced to find our ninth man in front of Birchfield's sixth. Over the last lap many places were gained, our Taylor-Shields-Carter trio, in particular, pegging back many opponents. Dan Patience was another man to run strongly and looked as if he might even win if the race continued for an extra mile or so! In the last mile our boys gave all they had, and we had the remarkable scoring sequence of 11th, 14th, 15th, 18th, 19th, 20th places. Better packing can never have been seen before, and the scoring epitomises the team spirit existent in our ranks. It was a wonderful sight, shortly after Close had won from Flockhart and Bailey, to see six men in claret and gold passing down the roped “funnel” to hand in their numbered discs to your humble servant It is no easy task acting as recorder, when such splendid team packing exists, I can assure you! Well, we had won! Our remaining three runners were soon in, and we had finished our complete team of nine in 57 scoring positions. The congratulations poured in. Our boys regained their breath and composure, completed their toilets and dressing, had their photograph taken, and adjourned to Burnham Hall for the presentation of awards by the Hon. Mrs. Lawson. Cheers greeted Bert Footer as he accepted the “Frank Wynne” Cup on behalf of the Club. Cheers again as he took the “Finch Wayte” Cup for the first Southern Club. Cheers yet again as Bert was called upon to receive the replica awarded to the first man of the first Southern club to finish. A speech was demanded and Bert obliged in his best film-star manner and called for three cheers for the previous title holders—Birchfield Harriers. Carried away by his enthusiasm, he led the cheering by waving the miniature cup above his head, and the lid dropped the four feet odd to the ground and bounced into the footlights. More cheers! It would be invidious to discriminate when our whole team did so well. We have only to refer you to the result for the superlative merit of the performance to be evident. To use Biblical language, “they were stronger than lions, they were swifter than eagles.” It must have been a proud moment when Bert Footer realised that one of his greatest ambitions had come to pass, and that he had led home a Champion team—not by a narrow, fluky margin—but with 56 points to spare. Same again in 1936, please! A.A.H. A.A.H. A.A.H. items.label: February-March 1935
items.sum: The President's message on the English Cross-country Championship win, the Honours Badges for J. Ginty and D. Patience, the Juniors' Southern Counties title, the Ilford Relay and hopes for the R.W.A. National Championship at Chingford.
items.s: FROM OUR PRESIDENT. The President's message on the English Cross-country Championship win, the Honours Badges for J. Ginty and D. Patience, the Juniors' Southern Counties title, the Ilford Relay and hopes for the R.W.A. National Championship at Chingford. At last we have achieved our greatest ambition and captured premier honours in cross-country running, namely the English Cross-country Championship, and our congratulations are extended to the members who comprised our team. After our amazing set-back in the Southern Championship it came rather as a surprise to find all our team in such fine fettle on March 11th. Perhaps the defeat at Hassocks did our men good; but in any case, the dreadfully muddy condition of the course, which did not suit our team at all, made the result no criterion for a fortnight later. However, that race lost us the backing and support of the Press, and mention of the Belgrave was conspicuous by its absence in the papers. As we have noticed previously, lack of publicity is usually a good omen, and it certainly was in the case of the “National.” Nevertheless, this oversight was quickly remedied after the race, and one paper kindly informed the world of our Building Fund efforts. To revert to the great race, not only was our victory a surprise, but the easy manner in which it was accomplished was astonishing. To “close in” our 6 before the third man of any other club finished was a rare feat. In addition, this happened with A. Penny, our stalwart International, leaning on crutches and looking on as a spectator; and A. Allum, International and one of the mainstays of our team, failing to finish close enough to count in our scoring six. Apart from these six, congratulations are due to the other three men who ran so extremely well that any one could have taken the place of our first man home and still left us with a winning margin! We realize their disappointment in not attaining their championship medal. Allum, Shaw and Flower have all scored for the Club in past National races, but we know their natural disappointment soon turned to joy at the Club's win. However, we hope to emulate the example of the Birchfield Harriers, and make a habit of winning this event and so give futher opportunities to our members of earning these coveted medals. J. Ginty and D. Patience are to be congratulated in winning their “Honours Badge” as a result of the running in this “National.” After the success of our Juniors in winning the Southern Counties Junior Championship, every confidence can be placed in our future chances in all cross-country races. We have chased the “bogey” away and our fear of the Midland and Northern opposition has faded into thin air. The progress of our juniors must be closely watched as our future successes will depend on their efforts; but with R Savage looking after them we have little cause for anxiety. Our success in the Ilford Relay augurs well for our prospects in the London—Brighton Relay, and once again we have shown the Athletic World our strength in team races. Not only did our first team break the record for the course, but only four other clubs could beat our second team. We are all looking forward eagerly to May 11th, for the R.W.A. National Championship at Chingford, as we hope to pull off the “treble” National Championships. That our men have the ability to win there is no doubt, but unfortunately in walking there is more danger of set-backs owing to “lifting.” Our team suffered in that respect in the “Junior” Championship at Birmingham on March 2nd, but this is not likely to happen at Chingford. If we do win this race we shall have set up another record in Athletics. It is to be hoped that all members will support this event and come along to cheer our men along the course. Encouragement in a long race of this kind goes a long way in helping to keep up the spirits of the competitors. As the track season is fast approaching members should be taking advantage of the mild weather and commencing their training rather earlier than usual. The track men have been set an excellent example of the standard expected of the Belgrave nowadays, and the results of the Summer season are being looked forward to with great confidence. J. R. items.sum: Club notes: Smoking Concert and Club Dinner, the team picture credit, Bert Footer's English cap, the Club's championship trophies, Jim Ginty and Dan Patience in the Army championships, Brighton Relay buses and ties, Arthur Penny's injury and the R.W.A. 20 miles team.
e: South of the Thames Cross Country Championships
London Divisional Army Cross Country Championship
items.s: JUST JOTTINGS. Club notes: Smoking Concert and Club Dinner, the team picture credit, Bert Footer's English cap, the Club's championship trophies, Jim Ginty and Dan Patience in the Army championships, Brighton Relay buses and ties, Arthur Penny's injury and the R.W.A. 20 miles team. Should this issue of our Gazette reach you before Saturday, March 30th, don’t forget the Smoking Concert being held on that evening at “The Rising Sun,” Ebury Bridge Road, S.W.1, on behalf of the Belgrave Building Fund. * * * * * The illustration of our winning team in the English Cross-country Championship, appearing on another page, is published by kind permission of the Editor of “Sport and Play” and by the courtesy of the proprietors of this well-known Midlands sporting weekly, Sport and Play (1930) Ltd., Lionel Street, Birmingham. * * * * * Heartiest congratulations to Bert Footer upon his inclusion in the English team for the third year in succession. Bert was not called upon to travel to France, but will receive his colours. * * * * * We now have the satisfaction of knowing that our name appears on the three Team Championship trophies awarded in connection with the National Championships. The “Frank Wynne” Cup (Cross-country) and the “Horlick” Cup (50 kilos. Walk) are at present on the Club sideboard, and we have held the Senior R.W.A. 20 miles Championship Shield on four occasions. Our Club is the only one to have held all three trophies. In addition, in the “limited” championships—which may sound like a contradiction in terms—we have succeeded in winning the R.W.A. “Junior” Walk Championship (1920, 1922, 1930, 1933); the Southern Counties Cross-country title (1934); the “Junior” Southern (1935) : the South of the Thames Championship (1929); the Surrey cross-country title on many occasions; and the Relay in 1931 and 1932. So Belgrave must figure on nearly every championship trophy of any account. Additional to these are Brighton Relay (1934); “Nijmegen” Shield (1933); “Knott Memorial” Shield (Brighton Walk) on many occasions; “Sir J. Colman” Cup (1929); “Odling Smee” Cup several times; and many other trophies awarded for events of lesser importance. We have also headed the First Division of the Southern Amateur Athletic League, for which no award exists, in 1932 and again last track season. * * * * * Jim Ginty recently won the London Divisional Army Cross-country Championship from another of our members, Dan Patience. They were placed third and fifth, respectively, in the Army Championship proper, and are certain to represent the Army in the Inter-Services race. Congratulations! * * * * * It has always been our Cross-country Captain’s ideal to have twelve men running within a minute of one another over ten miles. The “National” result, with 52 seconds covering our scoring six, shows that his ideal is fast becoming a reality! * * * * * Congratulations to our popular Asst. Hon. Secretary and Hon. Handicapper, who has recently been added to the A.A.A. Board of Handicappers. * * * * * In view of this year’s very special success, it is hoped that as many as possible will attend the Club Dinner at Carr’s Restaurant, Victoria, on Saturday, May 4th. Tickets are 5/- each and you are asked to get in touch with Bill Rice as quickly as possible and so allow him to make the necessary arrangements. Ladies are specially invited. Let’s make the Club Dinner a great social success, worthy of the Athletic successes which have come our way. * * * * * The Brighton Relay will soon be upon us and if you have not yet booked your seat on one of the Club’s buses, it is advisable to do so at once, and avoid the risk of disappointment. A limited number of seats only are available. Arrangements will be much the same as in previous years. Our buses will leave Westminster at 10-30 a.m. and proceed by easy stages to Brighton. The Brighton Corporation rules compel us to leave promptly at 6 p.m., and passengers for the return journey will be picked up at a point about a quarter of a mile east of the Palace Pier, on the Lower Marine Drive. This day’s outing is always a memorable and happy one, and eagerly-awaited. So if you propose to come along, write at once (fare 5/-) to the addresses given elsewhere. Brighton Relay Orders : Club ties to be worn. Our quartermaster, W. G. Webb, will be pleased to send you one upon receiving your remittance. His address appears on page 1. * * * * * Arthur Penny’s damaged foot continues to make very slow progress, but we hope that the Spring will find him out and about again. The season has been most disappointing to Arthur, and we have all shared his regret that such a minor fracture should take such a long time to knit together. We hope that future seasons will make up to him, in some measure, for what he has lost this year. * * * * * Our President elsewhere asks all Club supporters to be present at Chingford on Saturday, May 11th, when the R.W.A. 20 miles Championship is to be held from “The Jubilee Retreat.” It would certainly be very pleasing for our representatives in the Walk to have the active support and help of their club-mates. Our probable team is a very strong one and has a wonderfully fine chance of gaining another “National” trophy for the Club. Last year we lost by a bare two points, but on this occasion we expect to have the help of both Tommy Green and Joe King, who were prevented from travelling to Sheffield last year. items.sum: Report of the club 10 miles cross-country championship for the Macher Shield, run in snow and won by H. E. Footer from C. T. Carter, with a handicap result and a Cadogan A.C. win over Belgrave H. in the accompanying match.
e: Club 10 Miles Cross Country Championship (Macher Shield)
items.s: 10 MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP FOR THE MACHER SHIELD. Report of the club 10 miles cross-country championship for the Macher Shield, run in snow and won by H. E. Footer from C. T. Carter, with a handicap result and a Cadogan A.C. win over Belgrave H. in the accompanying match. A record field of 27 lined up for the start in terrible weather, there being a very strong wind blowing, which the runners had to face for a considerable part of their journey. A good start was made, and the hardy group of “he-men” were off on their long trail or trial. A snowstorm commenced which could not have improved their hopes. The runners were soon out of sight and the hardy group of spectators also did a spot of running to the nearest shelter, where the return of the runners on their first lap of 5 miles was keenly awaited. A small group is seen, which as it draws nearer is recognizable as C. T. Carter, J. Ginty and H. E. Footer running in that order. They sweep past to continue the second lap, having shown 29 mins. 27 secs. for the first 5 miles. A. Allum, D. Patience, Jack Flower and H. Shields are well up with the leaders, and a good finish is already assured. W. Rice, A. F. Mitchell, A. E. Taylor, A. Patience, A. Shaw are all running well and evidently going “to have a go.” We, the spectators, are now poor, cold morsels, and some genius sends out for a jug of tea, which was very welcome. Out in the cold, cold snow once more we go to await the finish. A little white dot is seen—someone suggests it is a snowflake—but no! it is our little “H.E.”, running like the champion he is to record a very popular win in the time of 59 mins., which, considering the conditions, was very good going. C. T. Carter is next (“Well run, Carter”), followed by A. Allum and D. Patience, all running well. SHORTS FROM THE RACE. 1.—25 finished the course. 2.—H. E. Footer has won this race five times, the first being in 1925. 3.—Mr. H. Parker and Mr. W. L. Bayliss were responsible for scoring and timing—an unthankful job in such weather. 4.—A match run in conjunction with the race between Belgrave H. and Cadogan A.C. resulted in a win for Cadogan by 58 pts to 78 pts. 5.—Eight finished within three minutes of the winner. 6.—Alec Patience and Dan Patience were rewarded for their good running with first and second prizes in the sealed handicap. 7.—A. F. Mitchell, third in the handicap, was another to do well and D. Martin is deserving of a word of praise on his first attempt at ten miles. A. A. DEACON RESULT. TEAM SCORES. Cadogan A.C. items.s: THE SURREY CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS. Report and Belgrave results of the Surrey Cross-country Championships: the Senior won from Coulsdon with Footer and Carter first and second (Penny fracturing his foot), and the Junior at Imber Court won by South London Harriers with Belgrave third. The Senior Championship held from Coulsdon provided us with a fairly easy win, and we had the pleasure of supplying the first two home in Footer and Carter. There was one crowning misfortune, however, for it was in this race that Penny fractured the bone in his foot which has robbed us of his services since. He completed the course and scored in our team, but has not run since. Mitcham A.C. did well to finish second and their improvement has been one of the features of the season. In the “Junior” race held at Imber Court a week later, the South London Harriers proved the strongest team and we took third place. Chantler and Martin ran well, with Jordan not far away, but we dropped points in our search for a fourth man. RESULTS. SENIOR. The following competed as Individuals:— TEAM SCORES. 1. Contested at Northolt as usual, Junior and Senior races were held on the same day. In the Junior event, E. S. Stimpson, who has been commended for his promise in our columns before, ran exceedingly well to finish in third place. With another year’s strength and experience he should win this event. For the greater part of the Senior event our boys (who ran on behalf of their second-claim club, Cadogan A.C.) were fighting it out with the Polytechnic Harriers. In the last couple of miles, however, they drew away from the opposition and eventually ran out easy winners. e: South of the Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES “SENIOR.” T. C. Jones's report and results of the South of the Thames Senior cross-country at Epsom Downs, won by F. Close (Reading A.C.) with Mitcham first team and Belgrave third; the text gives Reading's score as 168, the table as 162. The “Senior” at Epsom Downs on the 9th February was contested by a large field and our boys, although badly drawn, got away fairly well. When seen at the end of about a mile and a half the field was led by Close (Reading) followed by a bunch including Cohen (Ashcombe) and Pell (Herne Hill). Our first man was Bill Rice 21st, then Patience 26th, followed by Walker, Duffett, Ring, Webb, F. R., Mitchell, A. F., Chantler, Lindsey, Doubleday, and then smiling Syd Warboys. We then indulged in a race of our own to the next vantage point near Tattenham Corner, when we saw that Patience had moved up to 15th Bill Rice 25th, Ring 27th, Martin 32nd, Webb 45th, and then our handicapper 48th (looking as though he was thinking that it might be easier work with a whistle). At this point we seemed to have a good chance of a place. When we saw the field at the end of about five miles, Close was still leading, closely followed by Pell. Patience was still our first man, but had dropped four paces. Bill Rice had gained two, and the others were in more or less the same positions, and our hopes of a place were still justified. We then went to the finishing straight and on counting the positions it seemed that we had at least secured third place, and this proved correct. Once again we must congratulate Mitcham, who scored 127 points, and also secured the “Sir Jeremiah Colman” Cup for the first club to finish 12 men. Reading were second with 168, and ourselves third with 192. We last won the South of Thames Senior in 1929, and it seems that several years must elapse before we are again successful. The reason for this is that our successive placings in the “Southern” and “National” each year rule out our improving men according to the rules of the South of the Thames Association. In the circumstances, and losing, as we do, two or three men’s eligibility in this race each year, a “placed” team must always be considered a very successful result from our point of view. Just this as a side note : On returning to the dressing room we had no option but to congratulate a member of the “Belgrave Sisters” on her choice of negligée—she certainly looked “in the pink.” m. s. 1. items.label: February-March 1935
items.sum: Syd Ring's report of the Southern Counties Cross-country Championships at Hassocks, where the Juniors won the team race and the “Finch Wayte” Cup for the first time and the Seniors were beaten by Surrey A.C. by 9 points, with an Hon. Editor's note and the Junior result.
items.s: THE SOUTHERN COUNTIES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS. Syd Ring's report of the Southern Counties Cross-country Championships at Hassocks, where the Juniors won the team race and the “Finch Wayte” Cup for the first time and the Seniors were beaten by Surrey A.C. by 9 points, with an Hon. Editor's note and the Junior result. When it was first heard that the “Southern” Championships were to be held at Hassocks, Sussex, it was surmised that the runners would have to tackle the South Downs, perhaps even Ditchling Beacon. When the more enterprising and enthusiastic team members and others arrived early and looked over the course, it was found to be flat (compared with the Downs) but very heavy and rain-sodden meadowland. It was ideal for the spectators, the runners being in sight nearly the whole way. The Juniors were first away, and we must heartily congratulate our team upon its win and some good packing. At the end of 2½ miles Chantler was 13th, Martin 15th, Stimpson 17th, and Chantler 23rd. The two first named put in splendid finishes, and Stimpson found an extra bit to split the Aldershot pack, which incidentally enabled us to win by one point. Jordan backed up in noble fashion, and we were winners of the “Finch Wayte” Cup for the first time. Our team were well away in the “Senior” race and at the end of a mile we had our twelve in the first fifty places. Footer, Ginty and Carter were especially prominent of ours. Returning from the first lap our good start had gone, but we were well placed with Surrey A.C. looking very dangerous. At the end of the second lap (this sounds like a track race!) Close (Reading), Humphris (S.L.H.) and Edwards (Navy) were leading. Ginty, our new acquisition, was fourth, closely followed by the Nichols Bros., of Surrey. Footer (7th) was evidently feeling the effects of a recent change of occupation. Next came Carter 11th, closely followed by four Surrey runners and our rivals had their six in sixteen places. Our next men were D. Patience (21st), Allum (26th), Taylor (37th). Returning to the finishing point, we met our victorious Juniors, now changed, and waited for the finish. After a short while Close finished in fine style beating Humphris by about 50 yards. Edwards, of the Navy, was third, and was followed by Ginty and Footer, of ours. I think the crowd cheered our pair as much as the leaders. Bert must have fought the whole of the last lap, easing only when he caught Jim Ginty near the finish. Then came the others and although we had picked up points, Surrey had held on well and finished distressed but victorious. They had defeated us by 9 points, and deserve our congratulations for a splendid show. Summing up, I think our boys had an off day, and with the exception of Ginty and D. Patience, all should have been up further. [Hon. Editor's Note.—Our contributor is, of course, fully entitled to his opinion expressed in the last sentence above, but I feel this judgment may be a little harsh. Many of us, bearing in mind Penny's absence, and Taylor's recent indisposition, had not expected our team to get near our score of the previous year. That they scored 85 points against last year's 81, and finished six in 26 as against six in 27 last year, seems excellent in itself. That Surrey were able to score under last year's totals reflects the greatest credit on them and, well as our boys ran, we met a better team on the day. In the light of more recent happenings our defeat may well seem surprising, but then the charm of uncertainty is present in Athletics as in most sports. We had the satisfaction of regaining the “Odling-Smee” Cup for the first Surrey Club to finish twelve men]. RESULT. 24 teams entered 27 teams entered m. s. m. s. 1. D. B. Pell (H.H.H.) 29 58 24. A. items.label: February-March 1935
items.h: A REVIEW OF THE OLD AND NEW SEASONS.
items.sum: Review of the winter season and look ahead: the Inter-Counties at Luton, the London to Brighton Relay (Belgrave holders), the cross-country record for the season, and summer track fixtures and permits at Battersea Park.
e: South of Thames Junior Cross Country Championships
items.s: A REVIEW OF THE OLD AND NEW SEASONS. Review of the winter season and look ahead: the Inter-Counties at Luton, the London to Brighton Relay (Belgrave holders), the cross-country record for the season, and summer track fixtures and permits at Battersea Park. The Winter Season is now rapidly nearing a close, and our Summer programme is fast taking shape, and we hope to have the fixture cards out very shortly. On 30th March will be held the Inter-Counties Cross Country race at Luton. We should have quite a number of men competing for various counties, Footer and Carter for Surrey, Allum, Shields Dan Patience and Taylor for Middlesex, and Parker for Sussex. I still think, however, that this race comes too late in the season to be interesting, but perhaps the Counties will make a move a bring about a change in the date for future years. Then comes the big day, April 13th, the London to Brighton Relay, of which we are the holders, and on the form so far displayed it would be a bold man who would prophesy our defeat. Birchfield H., if they run, are always to be respected, but after their “National” defeat I cannot possibly see them turning the tables on us. No, sir! if anyone may do it, then I think it will be our Southern conquerors, Surrey A.C. On their running in the Ilford race the time put up by the actual first team men was excellent. They hope to field a much stronger ten for the Brighton race, but if there are any doubts, then I think it hinges on the reserve question. There is no possible doubt that so far as bringing men in at the last minute is concerned, we are in an unassailable position. Our “B” team's running in the Ilford Relay proves this, and it is not going too far to say that this team would beat many that will run to Brighton on April 13th. We shall, as mentioned elsewhere, have the usual two vehicles going down with our team and supporters, and if you want a seat on them, then make sure to write straight away and so avoid being disappointed. With this race our Winter season comes to an end, and on looking back I am sure everyone must be more than satisfied with our men's performances. In the races in which the Club has competed, our record is: South of Thames “Junior,” 2nd team; Surrey County Senior, 1st team; Southern Counties Senior, 2nd team; Southern Counties Junior, 1st team; English “National” Championship, 1st team. Quite a good record, don't you think, but one which could be bettered, I agree. However, I think we have now tasted the sweets of victory in every race that is held, that is, as regards the country, so now we had better turn the spotlight on our Track runners and their prospects. As most members are aware, we are dependent upon the L.C.C. for permits for the use of Battersea Park Track, and although we are without dispute the Club with the largest membership using that track, we seem to come off very badly in the allocation of permits. To begin with, we have lost our date on the first Saturday in May, when it will be remembered we usually have a match with the L.A.C.; and in its place we have been given Saturday, May 18th. This date was not suitable for the L.A.C., but I am pleased to say we have fixed May 1st for a match with them at the White City Track. On May 11th we have our, now, annual fixture at Drayton Green Track, with the local club, Ealing Harriers, also our old friends, Ashcombe A.C. and Slough A.C. To come back to May 18th, we have now arranged for a double-barrelled match, with such opponents as Surrey A.C. and Leigh-on-Sea H., and I hope to fix up with two other clubs in order to make it a three-cornered affair for both of our teams. It has been suggested that we make one a Captain's team and the other the Vice-Captain's, so I trust our members will support these matches and so make the arranging of them a worth-while job. In connection with this meeting we shall also hold some Club Handicaps, and here again I hope our members will show better support than last year. After all, your Committee spend a great deal of time in deciding which events would be most suitable for the members, and as you can see from our Balance Sheet our Prize bill is a considerable item, so it is up to the members to justify the continuance of these events by turning out in large numbers whenever they can. There is one other point about our mid-week meetings. That is, this season they will mostly be held on Monday evenings. Here, again, we had to accept what the L.C.C. offered us and I hope the alteration from the usual Wednesday to Monday will not affect our entries in any way. Our Track Championships will be held on the usual Saturday, which is August 3rd, and this year we are departing from the usual custom, and are having Championship events only, with the exception of two Field event handicaps. The reason for this is that on July 29th, which is the previous Monday, we are holding a meeting at Battersea Park and shall devote this entirely to Club handicaps. I expect by this time you will have noticed that I have not mentioned a date for our 3 Miles Championship, and in the absence of a suitable date in June, we have decided to have this race at our meeting on September 14th. This, I know, is rather late in the season, but by this time our men will already be training up for our opening Road Race at Wimbledon, so it should suit them all right. Last year we had an Open Team race at our September meeting, but the support accorded it was rather poor, and so we are staging an equally attractive race in our own 3 Miles Club Championship. Well, I hope this rather brief outline of our Summer programme has given you some idea of what events we are going to have, and I trust our members will be as successful on the track as they have been over the country.
