items.s: THE BRIGHTON WALK. Percy Wright's account of the London to Brighton walk won by H. H. Whitlock in 7 hrs 53 mins 50 secs, with Surrey W.C. beating Belgrave by six points for the team prize and F. E. Bentley first Belgrave man (8th), with the result. Henderson's club is printed as Worthing and District S.C. in the text and Worthing and Dist. A.C. in the result. The team race places Belgrave second on 49 points with team positions printed as 7, 9, 11, 22, unlike the individual places 8, 10, 12, 25 in the result. Ideal weather prevailed, and with an entry of 91, a great race for team and individual honours was expected. At the first stroke of seven o'clock the walkers were off, watched by the usual miscellaneous collection of onlookers, attendants, well-wishers, and early-morning workers. Despite the absence of Tommy Green, who was nursing some slight strains, we had every reason to feel confident of success, for we had last year's winning team and, in addition, Fred Rickards. V. W. Stone, of the Polytechnic Harriers, quickly went to the front and, completing five miles in 43 min. 44 secs., continued to draw away from the rest, passing "The Pied Bull" at Streatham with a twenty yards or so lead. Of our lads at this time the two Freds—Bentley and Rickards—were together in tenth position, Martin fourteenth, and Paul Khlopin well up. Approaching Croydon, Whitlock drew level with Stone, and shortly afterwards went ahead. Even at this early stage it was evident that Ludlow's record was in danger. At the "Chequers," Horley, approaching half-distance, Whitlock had a good lead, about three minutes inside record. Stone was second, with Henderson (Worthing and District S.C.), third. Our boys were in the same position, except Paul, who was having trouble and had dropped a few places. Surrey W.C. just led in the team race, mainly owing to the backward position of our fourth man. Reaching Albourne Green (42½ miles) wild rumours were flying around that Whitlock was fifteen minutes inside record, but subsequently this was found to be an exaggeration. Bentley was moving up and Martin had gained a few places but we still lacked a good fourth man. Surrey W. Club's team was cracking a little, but still held a few points lead. Khlopin, although taking a "hiding," was going much better and looked as if he might recover and win the race for us. This was not to be, however, and eventually he retired a few miles from the goal. Meanwhile, T. W. Richardson (Woodford Green A.C.) was going through strongly, upsetting the prophets, and eventually finishing second. Whitlock broke the tape well inside eight hours, having completed the course in the astounding time of 7 hours 53 mins. 50 seconds. Henderson came in third, Stone falling back to fourth place. In the team race, Surrey W.C. beat us by six points to record their first victory for five years. Heartiest congratulations to them and their gallant lads on a great victory! Our first man to finish was Fred Bentley, who, although inside his last year's time, when he was third; this year could only finish eighth. This gives some idea of the great all-round improvement shown by the competitors. The first four men all beat last year's winning time. Our second man home was Rickards (10th), and Martin (12th) next for us. Thus Fred Bentley again wins the "Belgrave Cup" and the Club Long Distance Championship, with Rickards and Martin in the minor positions. Our scoring team was completed by Bill Holman, who did well; and would be a first-class distance walker had he the necessary time to train. A word of praise to our lesser lights: Allen, Bicknell, Yorwarth, Laurie, Spooner, Wattam and Willis for their efforts. Also, many thanks to the willing band of cyclists who did yeoman work as attendants. We could not possibly do without their services, and so, once again, our grateful thanks! Our supporters on the bus also did great work, although we suspect certain of our racing men of using the bus merely as an excuse for a "pub-crawl," but who am I to criticise such people? (Wait for it!—Ed.). Well, we have lost a walking trophy—the "E. Knott Memorial Shield"—but we are not likely to sit down and moan. Rather, we shall await next year's race with added interest, and, who knows, with keen training and young talent coming along, we may exchange defeat for victory—convincing victory at that! h. m. s. 1. items.s: CLUB MEETING ON JULY 29th. Results of the club handicaps held at Battersea Park on 29 July, including the 100 yards, veterans, 440 yards, junior mile and a new discus handicap. We held a series of Club handicaps at Battersea Park on this evening, and the 100 Yards (under 16) proved a "teaser" for the Judges, who gave the placings with S. A. Bailey 1st, R. Dunford 2nd, and G. H. Aylmer 3rd. The 100 Yards Senior was won by E. J. Johns, our Boxing Day winner, and he certainly seems to have settled down to the sprinting game. B. Saunders, a promising Junior, was second with R. G. Michael once again squeezing into third place. A very poor entry was seen in the Veterans race and here H. E. Jackman proved the winner, with that fine old-stager, Charlie Cook, second; and another one-time stalwart in Dicky Best, third. The 440 Yards was won in fine style by F. W. Nash, who had little to spare over the scratch man, Tommy Scrimshaw, who finished second. W. A. Carnie, our Poly--cum-Belgrave member, was third; which was due reward for his many efforts in club handicaps this season. In the 1 Mile, our Juniors had matters all their own way and with E. S. Stimpson 1st, G. R. Chantler 2nd, and K. N. Wood 3rd, we have the reason why we are Southern Junior C.C. Champions, a title we intend to retain. With the help of the three members above, plus D. W. Martin, we have a team who should fear nobody. An innovation was the Discus Throw handicap, and here we saw a good contest which resulted in C. A. Melchior being first, with that Field Event stalwart, George Powell, second; and none other than our own Jim Ginty third. At least, he was given out as finishing in that position, but we believe Jim had been pulling Bill Sutton's leg! S. A. Bailey S. A. Bailey 1st, 100 Yards (under 16) handicap R. Dunford R. items.sum: Report of the 10 August inter-club match at Imber Court, won by Surrey A.C. from the Metropolitan Police A.C., Belgrave H. and Polytechnic H., with Belgrave's only win in the Javelin team event. "aslo" is printed so.
items.s: INTER-CLUB MATCH AT IMBER COURT. Report of the 10 August inter-club match at Imber Court, won by Surrey A.C. from the Metropolitan Police A.C., Belgrave H. and Polytechnic H., with Belgrave's only win in the Javelin team event. "aslo" is printed so. On Saturday, August 10th, we had a match versus the Metropolitan Police A.C., Polytechnic H. and Surrey A.C. at Imber Court, the fine sports ground of the Metropolitan Police A.A. The weather was perfect and in the running events we did as well as expected, in view of the fact that our team, owing to holidays, was not at full strength. The Poly were in the same position as ourselves, and so it was left to the Police to provide the main opposition to Surrey A.C. The latter fielded a very hot team, supplemented by E. Sears, the Essex County Champion, and R. L. Trapnell, the Achilles runner. Sears broke a ground record in winning the 880 Yards race in 1 min. 58 1-10 sec., with G. A. Smith, also of Surrey A.C., a close second. The 1 Mile team race, 1600 Yards Relay, and 440 Yards Relay were all won by Surrey A.C., with the Metropolitan Police annexing the 660 Yards Relay. R. L. Trapnell aslo broke a ground record when winning the Mile race in 4 min. 28 sec. and A. R. Shaw, in securing second place, is to be complimented on his fine running. We lost to Surrey A.C. by 2 points in the team scoring, the Surrey boys making a great last lap effort. As regards the Field Events, we have a brighter side to the picture. Our men won the Javelin with E. H. Finneron, our young member from Guildford, putting in a fine throw of 158 ft., and G. H. Powell, with C. A. Melchior, completed the team which registered our only win of the meeting. The final points worked out as follows: Surrey A.C. 47, Metropolitan Police A.C. 30, Belgrave H. 24, Polytechnic H. 19. A swim in the widened River Ember, tea in the Pavilion, followed by dancing later, completed a very attractive fixture. E. Sears E. items.s: CLUB MEETING ON AUGUST 19th. Results of the poorly attended club handicap meeting of 19 August: 100 yards, 880 yards (won by Dicky Best), 2 miles (won by Tom Carter) and the walk (won by Frank Jarvis). Entries for this meeting proved very poor, and the question of whether we continue our present programme of evening handicap meetings will have to be seriously considered by the Committee. The 100 Yards handicap was won by R. W. Archer, a reward for his perseverance, with E. J. Johns following up his win by now securing second place, and F. Stower, another consistent trier, third. Then came the "turn-up" of the season. Dicky Best, that "young" veteran, actually walked away with the 880 Yards handicap, and in no uncertain manner, as his time proved. A. A. Bird ran well to finish second, with Frank Webb, finding some of his old form, third. The 2 Miles Run resulted in a popular win for Tom Carter. He ran one of his best races and his handicap time was the second fastest for this race. As he ran from virtual scratch, Tom has proved beyond doubt that he is our best distance runner on the track this season. A. T. A. Jordan, who finished second, was another instance of a member competing without being on the programme, with the result that the handicapping had to be done on the ground, and it is hoped that this practice will not be allowed in future races. These remarks do not, however, detract from Jordan's performance and we are pleased to see him among the prize-winners after being for so long on the fringe. J. Chantler, a brother of G. R., was third; and it is to be hoped that he continues to improve as well as his brother has done. The Walk gave Frank Jarvis (575) his first Club prize; the minor places being filled by C. E. Churcher (160) and W. A. Treacher (60). The time of 13 min. 57 sec. was on the fast side, and Jarvis has undoubtedly shown great improvement during the Summer months. R. W. Archer R. W. items.label: November 1935
items.sum: Report of the last two Southern Amateur Athletic League Division 1 relays (1 mile medley at the White City, 4 x 880 yards at Battersea Park), Blackheath Harriers taking the title with Belgrave second ahead of Herne Hill.
items.s: SOUTHERN AMATEUR ATHLETIC LEAGUE (Division 1). Report of the last two Southern Amateur Athletic League Division 1 relays (1 mile medley at the White City, 4 x 880 yards at Battersea Park), Blackheath Harriers taking the title with Belgrave second ahead of Herne Hill. On August 17th, at the White City Stadium, was held the 1 Mile Medley Relay, and with Tommy Scrimshaw turning out (although coming straight back from holiday) we considered we had a good chance of winning this event. Eddie Pack ran the 440 yards stage and did well in handing over third behind Whittingham and Pallett. Stroud and Bone both did their bit in keeping this position; and Tommy went off about 30 yards behind the leaders, who were A. C. J. Poole, of Blackheath H., and L. J. Wood, Herne Hill H. Putting in a fast lap he caught them, and at the bell was leading by a yard or two. Round the back straight Tom had to fight hard to keep them off, and on coming into the finishing straight, it could be seen that our man had "shot his bolt." Poole. judging his effort finely, won a grand race with Wood beating Tommy for second place. This meant we were now four points behind Blackheath, and two behind Herne Hill. The final event in the League, the 4 x 880 yards, was held at our meeting in Battersea Park, on September 14th. A. A. Bird ran the first leg for us and gave us the lead. Bill Rice went next and was soon passed by two of his opponents. Bill's lack of speed (due to his team work in distance races; or, perhaps, the sickness which was to strike him down three days later), was soon apparent, but, sticking to his task in fine style, Bill handed over less than 20 yards behind the leaders. Fred White ran next and surprised even himself by the way he performed. As the leader he was chasing was none other than the Inter-Counties 440 yards champion, F. S. Whittingham, Fred ran marvellously in handing over as he did inches in front, to put us back into the lead again. Dick Michael very wisely let A. C. J. Poole, the Kent County Champion, go in front and then kept close on his shoulder. Coming to the Long Jump pit "Mike" let loose a link, and rounded the bend a few yards in front. Poole, however, was not finished with; and coming again with a glorious effort, he beat Michael by a few yards in a race that had pulsated with thrills throughout. I ought to mention that the Polytechnic H. finished a poor third, with Mitcham A.C. fourth, Herne Hill H. and South London H. fetching up in the rear. We heartily congratulate Blackheath Harriers on taking the title from us. Their teams throughout the season have done excellently, and they are worthy winners of our division. With Herne Hill only collecting two points to our five, we thus beat them by one point for the second place in the League table. Our old friends Mitcham A.C. were 4th, Polytechnic H. 5th, and South London H. 6th. Thus the S.L.H. will have to perform in a lower division this season, but knowing their lads I fully expect to see them back with us after a season's absence. items.s: INTER-CLUB RELAY COMPETITION. Report of the final meeting of the inter-club relay series at Epsom on 31 July, Mitcham A.C. winning the Shield from Belgrave H., Croydon H. and Epsom H. The final meeting of the series was held at Epsom on July 31st. We were one point behind Mitcham A.C. on the scoring to date and so hoped for the best. As usual with these away fixtures, our sprinters failed to materialise; and so the team which did duty for us in the 4 x 100 yds. finished third, with Mitcham beating Croydon for first place. They did, however, run very well in the 4 x 300 yds. but had to surrender first place to the Mitcham boys. The 4 x 880 yds. was, as usual, an easy win for our lads; although, bearing in mind the shock we had at Epsom last year, it was not surprising to find the local club in second place. Mitcham beat Croydon for third place, so with one event to be decided we were now two points behind Mitcham on the gross total. The Mitcham lads, however, consolidated their position by scoring a fine win in the 1 Mile team race; and they also provided the individual winner in R. Thorogood, who beat Tom Carter in the good time of 4 min. 32 sec. Thus the final points scored were: Mitcham A.C. 52, Belgrave H. 49, Croydon H. 38, and Epsom H. 21. We congratulate Mitcham on securing the Shield for the third time in the series, and hope that the time will come when both Croydon and Epsom have their names engraved on the Shield as winners for the first time. R. Thorogood R. Thorogood won the 1 Mile team race individually in 4 min. 32 sec. Tom Carter Tom Carter 2nd, 1 Mile team race Inter-Club Relay Competition Epsom Mitcham A.C. items.label: November 1935
items.sum: Report of the Club Track Championships at Battersea Park on 3 August, event by event, with the field event handicaps and the standard medal winners.
items.s: THE CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP MEETING. Report of the Club Track Championships at Battersea Park on 3 August, event by event, with the field event handicaps and the standard medal winners. The Club Track Championships were held at Battersea Park on August 3rd, and a good afternoon's sport was witnessed; with the bulk of the performances sound rather than showy. The meeting commenced with the 100 Yards Boys under 15, and in the winner, S. R. Gardner, we appear to have a boy who should make a name for himself in the sprinting world. His time of 11 2-5 secs. equalled the club record, and we hope he will do even better next year. The other boys placed were E. Langrish and S. A. Bailey. The 100 Yards Senior came next, and here the holder, C. H. Brodie had bad luck in that at the moment of starting, the back of one of his holes gave way, and Brodie almost fell. The race was won by F. Stroud, a previous holder of the title, with B. L. Bone at last justifying the good opinions of him, second, and Brodie a gallant third. The time was on the slow side but the track gave no assistance whatever; being very loose and, indeed, rather dangerous for sprinters, especially near the starting holes. A good field lined up for the 880 Yards and they kept well together until 300 yards to go, when R. G. Michael jumped right away to win in handsome fashion. Harry Shields battled his way into second place in his own indomitable style; and A. A. Bird finished very fast to gain third place. The time of 2 min. 1 1-5 sec. was distinctly creditable, and we trust that Michael will make every effort to get inside that magical two minutes next season. The Senior 220 Yards saw the completion of a sprint double by F. Stroud. Eddie Pack made a game effort but could never head his opponent; and Stroud's strength told in a close finish. E. L. Kealey was third. Then came the Junior (under 18) 220 Yards race, and here we have pleasure in proclaiming the unearthing of a most promising young sprinter, B. Saunders, to wit. He ran clean away from his field, and his time of 24 secs. equals the third best time for this event. C. E. Jones and G. Crilly, who were second and third, are also to be placed in the highly promising class, both being lads who are certain to improve if they stick to regular training methods. The 1 Mile came next, and this is always considered by most people to be the tit-bit of the meeting. J. Parker, our new member from Brighton, was an entrant, and right from the start his huge stride took him into the lead. Tom Carter made a game effort to hang on but was plainly feeling it at the bell. Pat Parker, however, kept to his seemingly monotonous stride (in fact, his three laps hardly varied in time); and it was obvious that unless someone produced a startling last lap effort, Pat would win the race at his first time of competing. Albert Shaw, however, had other ideas, and he set about the task of overhauling the leader. He decreased the distance, but on reaching the dressing room, Parker still had sufficient lead to keep his opponent at a respectable distance, and won the race in 4 min. 32 sec.—time which equals the Club record. Tom Carter still had enough strength left to hold on to his forward position, and finished close behind Shaw in third place. It is doubtful whether any Club Championship in the world has come up to that which we saw in the 2 Miles Walk. Don Brown retained his title, as was generally expected, but Bill Treacher (2nd), Len Fletcher (3rd) and Harry Churcher (4th) all finished inside 14 mins. 26 secs. Four men inside a time which has won the A.A.A. Championship—and on a track which was far from perfect! Truly a splendid showing! This excellence extended to the other competitors, and we may look back upon this race with pride, both for the performances and the size of the entry. The 440 Yards final concluded the meeting; and, although we wish to give every credit to R. G. Michael for accomplishing a fine double win, it seemed that in attempting the 220 yards and 440 yards, E. H. Pack fell between two stools. Whereas the eventual outcome of his efforts was two second places, if he had concentrated on the longer distance he might easily be now a Club title holder. H. Jones, who finished third, is, we hope, going to get down to it seriously next season. With more concentration on a particular distance, rather than flirting with them all, he should be a danger to the best in the Club. In addition to the Championships, we held two Field Event handicaps; and in the Long Jump A. J. Hewett showed his versatility by winning, with F. W. Pritchard second, and F. J. Skelly doing even better than previously with a fine actual jump of 19ft. 6ins., which secured him third prize in the handicap. The Shot Putt handicap was won by one of our Veteran members, C. R. Crawley. We like to see the "Vets" bobbing up now and again. S. Jones was second; and he has certainly had a good bag this season, but deserves it for his enthusiasm in the realm of Field Events. Third place was secured by R. E. Stride, and, considering his disability, he is little short of a marvel. Standard medals for the Championship events were won by the following :— 440 Yards.—F. W. items.label: November 1935
items.sum: Report of the final club track meeting at Battersea Park on 14 September: a triangular match with the Metropolitan Police A.C. and Polytechnic Harriers, the Club 3 Miles Track Championship and club handicaps.
items.s: FINAL CLUB TRACK MEETING. Report of the final club track meeting at Battersea Park on 14 September: a triangular match with the Metropolitan Police A.C. and Polytechnic Harriers, the Club 3 Miles Track Championship and club handicaps. September 14th. This was held at Battersea Park on Saturday, September 14th, and a torrential downpour just before the meeting was due to commence rendered the track on the heavy side. We had a triangular match versus the Metropolitan Police A.C. and Polytechnic Harriers, and the 100 Yards match was the first event. Poly had A. W. Green, the Midland Champion, out for them; while we were very pleased to welcome our member, E. Gray, who is the Hants County 100 and 220 yds. Champion. Gray ran finely to beat Green in 10 3-10 secs. and is without doubt going to prove a decided acquisition to our sprinting strength. In the 1 Mile, E. J. Hengle, the Police 880 yds. Champion, ran a well judged race to beat our men, L. J. Cohen and A. R. Shaw, while W. D. Symes (who is also a member of the "Bels") filled 4th place for the Police. Then came the 220 Yards, and here W. W. Pickard, of the Police, narrowly beat A. W. Green, with E. Gray a good third. E. J. Hengle completed a good double by winning the 440 Yards in which Fred White and Hugh Jones were second and third for us. The last of the running events was the 1 Mile Medley Relay, and A. A. Bird ran splendidly in beating A. H. Pettet, of the Police, over the half-mile stage; and then Michael further increased our lead by running a fine quarter. Les Bennett did the 220, and kept his advantage; so that when Gray went off for the final 220 he had a comfortable lead. Pickard, of the Police, made a strong effort but our man won easily in quite good time. As regards the Field Events, E. Gray, a positive glutton for work, won the Long Jump with a fine leap of 20ft. 10ins. F. Grassau credited us with first place in the Shot Putt with 38ft. 6¾in.; but in the absence of Finneron, and with George Powell competing under difficulties, second and fourth was the best we could manage in the Javelin. The High Jump was well beyond the reach of our youngsters, but we hope they will not be discouraged and thank them for turning out as they do. In the Discus Throw, F. Grassau was second to D. L. Grigg, the Police Champion ,with S. Jones filling fourth place. Points were scored 5, 3, 2, 1 for the first four places in each event (except the Relay, which was 4, 2, 1) and the final points scored were: Metropolitan Police A.C. 45, Belgrave H. 39, Polytechnic H. 22. We also held our Club 3 Miles Track Championship at this meeting and in winning for the first time, C. T. Carter ran one of his best races to date. Unlike the 1 Mile Championship, he wisely let J. Parker go and worked up to his man gradually. When he did catch his rival he soon went in front, and Pat was well beaten long before the finish. He managed to retain his hold on second place, and Arthur Allum and Syd Ring had a fine tussle for third position, with Allum proving the speedier when they reached the home straight. Arthur Penny, our Empire Games 6 Miles Champion, made his first appearance of the season after his long enforced rest, and ran very wisely in qualifying for 2nd Class Standard. Even so, he finished 5th, with Cecil Mains, who has also been in hospital following an accident, 6th, and G. R. Chantler also gaining the standard awards. The time of 15 min. 19 2-5 sec. was, considering the conditions underfoot, very good; and on this form Tom should have a very successful Winter season. Included in the meeting were also three Club running handicaps. The 880 Yards was won by Alec Ball, with E. H. M. Williams second, and H. Jones third. Williams showed excellent form. It is a great pity that his schoolmaster's duties take up so much of his time during the Summer. We hope that next year he may see his way clear to turn out more often. A Club 2 Miles Walk handicap enabled some of our Metropolitan Police members to show that Police athletic prowess is not only confined to running and field events. F. Jarvis (500), S. Goold (400), and G. H. Boddington (400), all M.P.A.A. men as well as very loyal Belgrave Harriers, filled the first three places. They are all rapidly improving walkers, and the struggle for places in our Championship teams during the Winter should be very interesting. A. W. Green A. W. items.s: THE THREE MILES ROAD RACE. J. E. Flower's account of the club's annual three miles handicap road race, won by F. G. White, with the full result. As printed, the text credits T. C. Carter with fastest time while the table lists C. T. Carter (14 19 h'cp, 14 24 actual) and A. C. Ball with a 13 59 actual time; several printed handicap times do not equal actual time minus start (rows 9, 10, 19, 22). Again we had a fine day for the annual road race, and all the spectators looked forward to a fast race. Sure enough, we got it! Our old friend, George Tyrer, was away first at a nice, steady pace. Seven minutes later Arthur Penny started in pursuit of a large field of runners, looking as if he meant to catch them all. I took up my usual position about half-way. George Tyrer was leading White by about a hundred yards, the latter being fifty yards ahead of the next man. After watching the majority of runners go by, I decided to get back to the winning post, so took a short cut across the Common for home. Were my eyes deceiving me or was it a tree I saw moving slowly? No! it was Ben—better known to the boys as "King Konk." Ben was using his head and saving his legs by taking a short cut. He also informed me that he was feeling very seedy (but not politely as I have put it). Tough guy, he calls himself! Getting back to the race, J. C. Edwards had put in some very fine running. He was almost on White's heels, and there was a great race between them down the last straight, White getting the better of the battle to win by fine seconds. Edward's effort was a very fine one; and Chamberlain's running, which took him into third place, is full of promise, and shows that we have yet another junior of more than average ability. T. C. Carter must be congratulated on doing the fastest time for the day, and it is very pleasing to see Arthur Penny running so well again. The official result is appended. Posn. Name H'cp. items.s: AT EALING. Harry Parker's report of the annual 5½ miles cross-country race against Ealing Harriers at Drayton Green on 19 October, won by Pat Parker, with the result and team scores (Belgrave 43, Ealing 93). As printed, the result gives 10th to E. G. Saunders (B.H.) while the team scores give 10th to Ealing; the text gives Pat Parker's winning time as 30 mins. 37 secs., the result as 30 31. On Saturday, 19th October, we journeyed to Drayton Green for our annual race with the Ealing Harriers; and our annual football match with the local "small fry." In the latter affair the locals won, as the runners retired to dress for the more serious contest. It was very pleasing to see our Brightonian, Pat Parker, present. To travel 60 odd miles to run 5½ miles is more than keenness, and a club spirit which we should like to see displayed by a few more of our members, particularly those who find the journey from Clapham Junction to Wimbledon so trying! "Our Bert" was also present, but did not turn out, as he said he had a cold through working too hard, We wish him a speedy recovery! It was pleasing to see Arthur Penny out again, although he is not yet fit. Twenty-eight runners turned out (Ealing 11, Belgrave 17) and the course was approximately 5½ miles, mostly grassland with a little road. Edwards, of Ealing, and Pat Parker were early to the fore and made all the running; and Pat eventually left his opponent about a mile from home to win as he pleased in 30 mins. 37 secs. items.label: November 1935
items.sum: Assistant Hon. Secretary E. A. Duffett's notes on the evening runs from the Rising Sun and the cross-country fixtures for November 1935 to January 1936, including the club championships and their trophy holders.
items.s: FORTHCOMING CROSS-COUNTRY FIXTURES. Assistant Hon. Secretary E. A. Duffett's notes on the evening runs from the Rising Sun and the cross-country fixtures for November 1935 to January 1936, including the club championships and their trophy holders. The season has already opened and from the numbers turning up at Wimbledon every Saturday, and from the entry in our Road Race Handicap on October 5th, it would appear that we shall have a most successful season in every respect. The evening runs on Tuesday and Thursday from the "Rising Sun," Ebury Bridge Road, which is quite near Victoria, are not, however, so well attended as in the past. Maybe it is because the season is yet young, but I would like to point out to members, new ones especially, that here is a fine opportunity of becoming better acquainted with your fellow-members. The atmosphere, to say the least, is most congenial and the runs which take place on the adjoining roads and round Rotten Row, in Hyde Park, are certain to be enjoyed. Packs to suit all are sent out in charge of an experienced runner, and all you need is your ordinary running togs plus rubber shoes. If you can afford proper road shoes so much the better, and it is preferable to wear a sweater, (white if you can manage it), as the winter evenings are apt to strike cold until you get warmed up. The packs go out about 8 p.m. and you can arrive at the "Rising Sun" any time after 7 o'clock, so as to make sure you will be ready when the pack leader shouts "All out." After these few remarks, we will now give you a little idea of our coming fixtures, as per fixture card, and if you have not yet received one of these let the Gen. Hon. Sec. know at once so that he can remedy it. On November 9th we have the first of the many Open racing fixtures. This is the South of Thames "Junior" team race, which will take place from the Grandstand, Epsom Downs. The word "Junior" does not apply to age but to ability. All those who have scored for any of our Senior teams are automatically barred. We usually enter three or four teams and all members who are selected to compete for the Club will be advised. On November 16th we have a double-barrelled fixture at Imber Court, the headquarters of the Metropolitan Police A.A. Both our runners and walkers will be in opposition to the might of the Police, and I trust our members will turn up and sample the hospitality of the Force. On November 23rd we shall have a fixture with Ashcombe A.C. and Ealing Harriers at Wimbledon. Our team will be selected (with due regard to the strength of the opposition) and members advised accordingly. November 30th. The day of the Club Open Walk at Wimbledon, and in view of the large numbers competing I wish to point out that NO runners will be allowed to change at the Hall on this day. We trust our runners will appreciate that every inch of space is required to house the walking competitors and so we have accordingly arranged an away fixture for them. This will be held at the Village Hall, Warlingham, the quarters of the Croydon Harriers. Mitcham A.C. and Epsom H. will also be there and packs to suit all will go out over the surrounding country, which should prove very interesting, and probably a little different from that we encounter week by week at Wimbledon. There are frequent Southern Railway trains to Warlingham and if any members wish to have further particulars, I shall be pleased to advise them. The Surrey County Youths' Cross Country race will be held on December 7th, from the headquarters of the Rothery A.C. at Redhill. All members possessing Surrey qualifications, and who are under 18 years of age, are asked to get in touch with our Junior Captain, R. J. Savage, who is always in attendance at Wimbledon. On the same day we have our old friends, Herne Hill Harriers, paying us a visit for a training spin with our lads. The first of the Club Cross Country Championships will be held at Wimbledon on December 14th, when the 7 Miles race for the "Blackstaffe Shield" (Holder, A. W. Penny) will be decided. There is a sealed handicap open to all Club members in conjunction with the championship and I hope they will support this. After the race we shall proceed to lay the table for Tea, and to see some of our lads feeding is really better than a visit to the —— well, I'll let you use your imagination there! After tea the tables are cleared and the floor is all set for dancing, which goes on until 11 p.m. You can bring as many friends as you like, and ladies are doubly welcome. My wife does not read the Gazette, so I feel on safe ground in saying this! On the 21st December we have our Club Junior Cross Country Championship for the "Savage Shield" (Holder, G. R. Chantler). This is held over our 5 miles course and is open to members who are under 21 years of age on day of race. The same day we are entertaining the Metropolitan Police A.C., and St. George's Services S.C., and here is a good opportunity for those who have not as yet sampled any of our racing fare. On Boxing Day, December 26th, we hold our annual Track meeting at Battersea Park. This commences at 11 a.m. and the races held are: 120 Yards Handicap and a 2 Miles Running Handicap. Last year the entries for the sprint were very poor, so much so that it was a moot point as to whether we continued this fixture, and I trust that on this occasion our members will turn out in good numbers and so prove to the Committee that they do appreciate the chance that is given them during the Christmastide festivities. Entries (1/- each event) should be sent to me at least a week before date of meeting, for which many thanks. This brings us to the end of 1935 and the fixtures for 1936 include the County Cross Country Championships on January 4th. The Surrey race is being held at Epsom Downs; but at the time of writing, the venue for the Middlesex race has not been decided upon, although Colindale is a possibility. A week later the Surrey County Junior C.C. Championship will be held from St. George's Services S.C. headquarters at Raynes Park, and I hope our boys will make every endeavour to secure their first win in this race. Another good move is the bringing forward of the Inter-Counties C.C. Championship, which will be held on January 18th. This race has usually been the "Cinderella" of the cross-country season, and I hope that the alteration now made will become a permanent one. We then come to the Club 10 Miles C.C. Championship for the "Macher Shield" (Holder, H. E. Footer), which will be held on January 25th, and by then our teams for the Open Championships will have begun to take shape and our task of defending our title of English Cross Country champions will have become the sacred duty of each one of our cross-country men. Knowing them, I am confident of their ability to do this successfully. All entries and any enquiries to— E. A. Duffett, Asst. Hon. Sec., 10, Barrow Road, Waddon, Surrey. R. J. Savage R. J. items.label: November 1935
items.sum: Walking notes: A. A. Cooper's world 5,000 metres walking record at Battersea Park on 14 September, the walking captains for 1935–36, and the coming walking fixtures including the matches with the Metropolitan Police and Surrey W.C. and the club's Annual Open Walk.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes: A. A. Cooper's world 5,000 metres walking record at Battersea Park on 14 September, the walking captains for 1935–36, and the coming walking fixtures including the matches with the Metropolitan Police and Surrey W.C. and the club's Annual Open Walk. On the occasion of our Meeting at Battersea Park, on Saturday, September 14th, we co-operated with Woodford Green A.C. in promoting an attempt on the World's 5,000 metres Walking Record by A. A. Cooper. Special arrangements were made to have the track in really first-class condition, but these efforts were largely negatived by a torrential shower of rain just as proceedings were about to begin. The start was delayed, but after a while it was found possible to stage the event, and Bert Cooper was able to record new World's figures for the distance. Times were as follows: 1 mile (6 min. 54 sec.), 2 miles (14 min. 1 3-5 sec.), 3 miles (21 min. 10 3-5 sec.) and 5,000 metres (21 min. 52 52 2-5 sec.). The best figures previously recorded for this distance were 21 min. 59 sec. by A. Schwab, in May, 1931. Congratulations to Cooper upon his fine effort, and in overcoming terrible weather conditions. P. G. Wright and C. F. D. Sutton, of ours, assisted in the event at short notice. * * * * * Our Captains and Vice-Captains for 1935—1936 are as follows: Road—C. E. Churcher (Capt.), A. A. Harley (Vice-Capt.). Track—D. E. Brown (Capt.), W. A. Treacher (Vice-Capt.). They rely upon the accustomed loyalty of the walkers, and we look forward to very successful seasons. * * * * * The fixture list has now been circulated and it will be seen that our fixtures remain much the same as before. We shall support the usual Open events as in past years; and have our usual matches v. Metropolitan Police W.C. and Surrey W.C. Club Championships fall on the usual dates and should produce some fine racing. * * * * * We visit Imber Court for our match v. Metropolitan Police W.C. on November 16th, and they will visit us on January 25th, when we also hold our Club 10 miles Championship. As so many of the prominent Police Walkers are also members of our Club, they will find themselves with double interests, and maybe find double speed. There will also be the usual sealed handicap for members, so the race should be crammed full of interest. Our visit to Croydon for the annual match v. Surrey Walking Club over the Croydon to West Wickham and back course, is on December 7th. A win for us here is very much overdue, so how about it boys? Our own Annual Open Walk will take place on November 30th, when there will be no accommodation for runners at Wimbledon. As usual, we expect a splendid entry, and know that every active member on our books will do his utmost to support our own promotion. We have always been helped in the promotion of this event by generous friends, who have contributed towards the Prize Fund, and any donations on this occasion would be gratefully appreciated. One other way in which our own participants can help is by sending in their entries well in advance of the official closing date. Many thanks ! All entries and enquiries should be sent to : A. A. items.label: November 1935
items.sum: Light-hearted piece by "Hundred Per Cent." about the club members' Sunday strolls in search of teas, with mock awards for the walkers.
items.s: THE BELGRAVE STROLLERS. Light-hearted piece by "Hundred Per Cent." about the club members' Sunday strolls in search of teas, with mock awards for the walkers. By Hundred Per Cent. Every Sunday (sometimes even overnight on Saturday) they sally forth in search of the beauties of Nature; the quest of health, the wind on the heath (to borrow a phrase), and all that. Every Sunday afternoon they look about them, seeking to throw down the gauntlet to some unsuspecting tradesman who is rash enough to advertise an ad lib tea. It's a challenge not to be resisted, and like most challenges the Belgrave lads seem to have a way of coming off best! Faith may be able to move mountains, but it's got nothing on Harry Shields. It is not generally known that he had an operation recently which has eliminated his appendix, and increased his scope considerably. He captains my team versus "The Rest of the World" in "The Grub Stakes." My vice-captain would be Mick Walker (who tends to overtrain) and the team completed by the inclusion of Cecil Penny (ranking equal 2, and on his day equal to two); and Big Ben May, who will improve as he grows. This team is in a class by itself, and the introduction of reserves would weaken it considerably; but Pat Parker, A. A. Bird and G. S. Doubleday (the latter specialising in boiled eggs) are training on rapidly. The team is essentially a strolling side. No home fixtures can be entertained! It is an interesting sight (albeit tinged with pathos) to observe a victimised caterer spellbound; torn between pleasure at seeing the sincere appreciation accorded his wares, and pain at the thought of rapidly approaching bankruptcy! Whether these Sunday outings consist of strolls between meals, or meals between strolls, I cannot presume to say with any certitude; but how Napoleon would have rejoiced in such followers of his "army marches on its stomach" dictum! The humorous element is supplied by all at some time or the other; but without a doubt, the most notorious offender, especially in the verbal fields, is Bert Lindsey. He is awarded the prize for The Worst Pun of the Month—a cellophane-wrapped bottle of prussic acid. It's a walk-over! Say what you will, he can always cap it! And talking of caps, Bert has a life-long friend which he sometimes uses to keep his hair from becoming untidy. I believe this originally came from Newington Butts, and I can well understand that thoroughfare having its doubts! To turn to more pleasant subjects, Charlie Churcher (if one excludes oneself) must be acknowledged as The Most Gentlemanly Stroller and is duly gazetted to receive The Purple Garter of the Belgravian Order of Chivalry (1st and 3rd class, Sundays only); and is permitted from to-day to wear his sideboards one inch longer. Musically, Bird (the Cheerful Sparrow) is the chief provider. His favourites are from Gilbert and Sullivan (especially the one about the General); and he usually ends his recital with Chopin's "Dead March," possibly out of respect to the tunes he has murdered. Some of the gang remain unmentioned, but just come along one week-end, and hear them speak up for themselves! items.s: THE ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING. Report of the club's Annual General Meeting at "The Rising Sun" on 19 September 1935, at which W. J. Fish and A. A. Harley were made Life Members and Oscar Horwood was elected President, with the sub-committees then set up. A good crowd of members assembled at "The Rising Sun" on September 19th for the Annual General Meeting. The Hon. Secretary read the minutes of the last A.G.M., which were duly confirmed; and was then called upon for his Annual Report. He rapidly gave an account of the past year's successes and progress; and his report was unanimously accepted. The Hon. Treasurer followed with his financial statement, which disclosed an excess of expenditure over income, despite careful management. After a few questions had been satisfactorily answered, the report was adopted. A proposal from the Committee to honour W. J. Fish and A. A. Harley by making them Life Members was unanimously agreed; and they made suitable response. The business of Election of Officers for the ensuing year then occupied the Meeting's attention. Mr. J. R. McKay proposed from the Chair, that Mr. Oscar Horwood should be the new President of the Club; and told the assembled members of the years of service rendered by Mr. Horwood in many capacities. A. A. Harley seconded, and Mr. Horwood was duly elected, and installed in the Chair. He acknowledged the applause of the meeting, and made an especial appeal to the Junior members to carry on the good work of the Seniors. Other officials were then elected as per the Club handbook, now in the possession of all members. Several suggestions were made under the heading of "Other Business," and were passed to the new Committee for their consideration. * * * * * At the first Committee meeting the following Sub-committees were set up :— Fixtures and Selection.—Sectional Captains, Vice-Captains, and Hon. Secretaries. Finance.—Messrs. A. A. Harley, W. H. Hare, H. Parker and F. G. Thomson. Social.—Messrs. W. Redgrave, Fish, Savage, Carter, Cotton, Shields, F. R. Webb, and Social Hon. Secretary. Building Fund.—Messrs. T. Cotton, F. H. Elson, E. Gordon, A. A. Harley, H. Parker, A. E. Taylor. The President, Hon. Secretary, and Hon. Treasurer are ex officio members of all the above Sub-committees. W. J. Fish W. J. Fish made a Life Member at the 1935 A.G.M. A. A. Harley A. A. items.s: SOCIAL. Social notes on the first dance and social of the 1935–36 season and the list of coming socials and dances, with applications to W. L. Bayliss. Our first Dance and first Social of the season have already been held. Our Dance was held at the Express Rooms, Clapham Junction, on September 14th, and was very successful. The Social at Wimbledon, on October 5th, was well-attended; and the fun fast and furious. Social and Dance dates are given below, and we look to every member to help the social programme along, and do his best to support the functions arranged. Nov. 2nd—SOCIAL, at Wimbledon. Nov. 23rd—DANCE, at Express Rooms, Clapham Junction. Dec. 14th—SOCIAL, at Wimbledon. Dec. 31st—CARNIVAL DANCE, at Queensberry Hall, South Kensington. Jan 25th, 1936—SOCIAL, at Wimbledon. The usual 5 miles Handicap which brings the realities of another busy imminent Winter season home to us, was held on October 5th; and attracted a fine entry of 26. Dick Northover was first away, followed 45 seconds later by Don Heath, and then came the others with varying allowances, until Don Brown left the post of honour. As last year, Harry Churcher again showed that he requires practically no preparation (unlike most of us who have to train for months to achieve something like fitness!) and won fairly easily, recording fastest time in doing so. Colin Sutton won his first prize with us during his three years of membership; and now that he has settled down to training again he should claim his place in our "Junior" team. Jack Rutland took third place and continues to improve. Len Fletcher was noticed moving in something like his old style; and two newcomers in S. R. Wood and W. C. items.label: November 1935
items.sum: T. Cotton's Building Fund notes on unreturned Belgrave Building Bricks, pinboards, the Supporters' Club and the new Building Fund Sub-Committee, with a holiday anecdote about the Hon. Editor and the Editor's bracketed reply.
items.s: BUILDING FUND NEWS. T. Cotton's Building Fund notes on unreturned Belgrave Building Bricks, pinboards, the Supporters' Club and the new Building Fund Sub-Committee, with a holiday anecdote about the Hon. Editor and the Editor's bracketed reply. By T. Cotton. There is one thing puzzling me greatly just at present, and that is where do Belgrave Building Bricks go after being issued? Since September, 1934, we have handed bricks out in plenty, and were inclined to pat ourselves on the back, until we found the discrepancy between exports and imports. Sometimes, very rarely, our young lives have been made joyous by a box suddenly finding its way back. This, as I have already said, very rarely. We can only draw mental pictures of bright yellow boxes used to support aspidasras, or gold-fish bowls; and are considering having some done in pink, or light blue, for the more dainty type of member. Really, we should be hearing more about these bricks. The Supporters' Club scheme is a great success, but one feels that the original plan of the "Building Fund" was so sound that it is disappointing to note the poor efforts made with these bricks. Concerning pinboards, I shall welcome payment for all those completed. We still have a few of the larger boards on hand. Please note that no member can secure more than one "600" board at a time. As everybody seems to know, our Supporters' Club is a great success. Some of the figures I have heard regarding profits have been amazing (especially to Frank Elson and myself, who are responsible for the scheme), but to be candid, we are very delighted with the support given. There are some ways in which you can help Frank and myself a great deal. You know by now that one or other of us is always present on Tuesday and Thursday evenings at "The Rising Sun"; at Wimbledon on Saturdays; and at Battersea Park on Sunday mornings. Please try and square all accounts as quickly as possible, so that we can complete our accounts speedily. Then there is another important point being neglected by some. It is essential that we have the name and address of every member of the Supporters' Club on our books. If you have any outstanding names and addresses, please let me have them immediately. To be of full value, these details should be legible. One hopes after the fine efforts made by all just recently, and with the day when we really can make a move drawing nearer, that many will remain to enjoy the advantages of our our headquarters. I cannot help thinking that a bachelor really does perhaps get more out of such things and I must give warning to my friend the Editor. During our holidays I exerted every possible effort to keep him from the wiles and trickery of women. On board the boat going over I did have a spot of bother over one lady who was greatly impressed by his method of leaning over the rail when sea-sick, but it passed. For two whole weeks did I exert all my known good (?) influence, and many the good talking-to I gave him. Then, gentle reader, then when we have returned with unblemished reputations, I stroll into the "Swan" on the night of our first Social, and behold a sight that tears my heart with pain. The Hon. Editor, plus cigarette and beer, standing by the piano, crooning! Oh, Alfred! beware! [Editorial Interpolation.—Seeing that the above comes from the pen of our old friend, Tom Cotton, it is hardly necessary for me to make reply. You all know what his remarks are worth. (Thank you, Bert!) But what base ingratitude this youngster shows to one who has taken him by the hand for the past five years; and safely seen him through his holidays! Were I given to washing dirty Cotton linen (something wrong here!) in public; never again would waters run clear and undefiled. And so, I refrain, conscious of the old adage, " . . . . where angels fear to tread"] A new "Building Fund" Sub-Committee has been elected and consists of A. E. Taylor, A. A. Harley (the same), H. Parker, E. Gordon, F. H. Elson and yours truly; and, of course, the President, Gen. Hon. Secretary and Hon. Treasurer, ex officio. Frank and I have been specially placed on this Sub-Committee because of our known ability for being cursed by people who cannot obtain sufficient membership cards. So don't mind us, carry on cursing! items.s: IMPORTANT ! Notice of the subscription increase approved at the Special General Meeting of 31 October 1935, including four free issues of the Belgravian, with a request to pay arrears and for Gazette Fund donations. At the Special General Meeting held at "The Rising Sun" on October 31st, after discussion, the proposal of the Committee to increase subscriptions to 8/- per annum for Senior members; 4/- per annum for Junior members (under 18); and 1/- per annum for Boys (under 15); was approved, and becomes operative immediately. This subscription is to include the free distribution of four issues of the "Belgravian" annually, and there is no doubt that our subscription value is still the greatest obtainable among athletic clubs. Arising from the above, all members are asked to settle their liabilities for past "Belgravians" immediately, and so enable the books to be closed. A considerable amount is outstanding and prompt settlement would be appreciated. As hitherto, any donations to the "Gazette Fund" will be gratefully accepted and acknowledged, and should be sent to the Hon. Editors, or to the Hon. Treasurer. Addresses appear on page 1. The Rising Sun

items.label: February 1936
items.h:
THE XIth OLYMPIAD.
Berlin, August 1st to 16th.
items.sum: Preview of the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games describing the flame relay and the Reich Sport Field venues, recalling that Britain's only two winners at Los Angeles in 1932 were Belgrave Harriers.
items.s: THE XIth OLYMPIAD. Berlin, August 1st to 16th. Preview of the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games describing the flame relay and the Reich Sport Field venues, recalling that Britain's only two winners at Los Angeles in 1932 were Belgrave Harriers. Many of our members' thoughts are turning towards the Olympic Games. Some hope to carry the British vest on to track or road, some to attend as spectators, while the great majority will have to be content with the newspaper reports; but all will be interested to know of the preparations being made to receive the World's athletes. Since the Games were revived at Athens in 1896 they have been held in different countries at regular intervals of four years. Berlin will act as host in 1936, and countless thousands will take advantage of the opportunity to pay a visit to the German capital. On the opening day the teams of more than fifty nations will march into the Stadium with their national flags and take the Olympic oath of true comradeship. A great relay of runners will carry the sacred fire from the ancient scene of the games at Olympia in Greece to Berlin, where the Olympic Flame on the tower of the Stadium will be lit while a salute of honour thunders forth. The great white flag with the five linked rings, symbolizing the five continents, will be hoisted on the mast of the arena before the eyes of a hundred thousand spectators. The Olympic Bell will be heard for the first time, summoning, as it is intended to do, "the youth of the world," and then the world championships in more than nineteen forms of sport will be carried out in the course of two weeks. We are, of course, particularly interested in the Athletics part of the programme, and this will extend from August 2nd to August 9th. The track will be at Grunewald, one of the western suburbs of Berlin, and is rapidly nearing completion. Here on the former Race Course, in an area of 262 acres (about three-quarters of the space occupied by Hyde Park) 2,500 men are at work constructing one of the most magnificent sports grounds in the world. Twenty minutes' journey from the centre of Berlin brings one to the South Gate of the Reich's Sport Field. Entering the Field one is immediately confronted with the huge concrete-built Olympic Stadium. This has an outside elevation of 48 feet, while the arena itself is sunk 42 feet below the surface. There is accommodation for 100,000 spectators, most of whom can be seated on its 30 miles of seats. The South side of the Stadium is occupied by the tribune of honour, where the distinguished guests will be seated. At the western curve is an entrance for competitors, and at the eastern end lies the main gate, above which the Olympic Torch will burn throughout the Games. Two tunnel entrances in the west curve lead to the dressing rooms which are under the grandstands. The athletic contests will be staged here, and also the finals of the football, handball and equestrian events. The arena consists of a football field surrounded by a 400-metre track. In the semi-circular spaces between the ends of the football field and the curves of the track are javelin grounds, spaces for high jump and putting the shot, as well as arenas for the discus and hammer events. Outside the 30 feet wide track, down either "straight," are the grounds for the pole vault, the long jump, and the hop, step and jump. Many visitors to the stadium have commented on the excellence of the turf on the infield. The secret is that it has been laid with ten-year-old turf taken from a neighbouring field. North of the Olympic Stadium lies the Swimming and Diving Stadium, with room for 18,000 spectators. The diving and swimming pools are separated by a concrete wall so that it will be possible to hold both diving and swimming contests at the same time. A heating plant has been installed in order that the water may be kept at an even temperature. The International Swimming Association requires that this shall be 70 degrees Fahrenheit. A few inches below the level of the water a curved gutter has been built into the walls of the pool. This will break the waves caused by the swimmers, so that the water will always be comparatively calm. To the East of the Swimming Stadium lie practice grounds, tennis courts, the hockey stadium, and basket ball grounds. The women competitors will live in the Sports Forum during the Games. The men will be housed in the Olympic Village which is being built at Döberitz, nine miles away along the main Hamburg road. Immediately to the west of the main Stadium lies the Assembly Ground, presided over by the 220 feet high Führer Tower. From this Tower will peal forth the Olympic Bell to announce the opening of the Games on August 1st, 1936. A single peal of the bell will also precede the announcement of each result. The Assembly Ground will be used for Polo contests. South of this, occupying the extreme south-west corner of the Sports Field, in a delightful sylvan setting, lies the equestrian stadium. In the north-west corner of the Field is the Dietrich Eckart Open Air Theatre. Here in a vast semi-circular natural arena, surrounded by woodland, the largest open-air theatre in the world has been built. It will seat 20,000 people. The gymnastic contests will be held here and a number of dramatic performances will be given during the Games. The Festival Play to be presented on the evening of the opening day of the Games will, however, be staged in the Olympic Stadium itself. We are, of course, very hopeful that we shall have several members in the British team. It is with pleasure that we recall that Britain's only two winners at Los Angeles in 1932 were both Belgrave Harriers, and that both had carried our colours with distinction prior to their trip across the Atlantic. We trust that the shorter journey to Berlin will provide other Belgrave Harriers with their chance to emulate their club-mates of four years ago. And so, best of luck! Olympic Games Berlin Athens Olympia Grunewald Hyde Park Döberitz Los Angeles Belgrave Harriers

e: South of the Thames Cross-country Championship
items.s: THIS AND THAT. Club notes: subscriptions, members' news (Bill Rice, A. O. Tookey, the Patience brothers in Egypt, new members Verney, Goodale and Kemp), Olympic possibles, a new club tie, early-season cross-country matches and coming fixtures. This is the second issue of our Gazette to be issued quarterly under the new arrangements passed by the Club at the Special General Meeting held on October 31st, 1935. Every member should automatically receive his copy, and members are requested to notify any change of address promptly. It is also pointed out, once again, that this is your Gazette. Your suggestions and contributions are wanted. Team work is a very necessary part in the production of a journal such as this, and you are asked to do your bit Please write to the Hon. Editor saying what you like about the "Belgravian," where you think improvements can be effected, and pass on any bright ideas likely to interest, help or amuse your fellow-members. Thank you! * * * * * Your Hon. Treasurer would be glad to receive outstanding subscriptions (8/- Senior, 4/- Juniors, 1/- Boys) which became due in September. The business of spending the Club's money is quite arduous enough, without reluctant members causing extra work in the collection of subscriptions. Members who have an account outstanding against their names in respect of "Belgravians" received up to our last issue, are asked to send this amount on to the Hon. Editors. It is desired to close this matter as soon as possible, and your co-operation would be welcomed. * * * * * Bill Rice continues to show slow progress, but we are glad to know that his health is improving, even though it will probably be many weeks before he is back to normal. His interest in Club affairs is as keen as ever, although he is unable to come along and enjoy our jokes and take his part in our Club affairs. When he does so, we can all assure him of a very hearty welcome. * * * * * Congratulations and best wishes to A. O. Tookey, who has recently joined the married ranks. * * * * * In October we bade Dan Patience and brother Rod au revoir, when they left England for Egypt, where they will be stationed for some time. Both had endeared themselves to us by their modest bearing and enthusiasm for the Club. We expect to have them out with us again when they return to England. Meanwhile, news comes from Egypt that Dan has recently won the Egyptian Command Championship, upon which we most heartily congratulate him. An old friend in Cotterell was second. * * * * * Writing of Dan Patience reminds us of his splendid running in last year's "Southern," when he had to stop in the early stages to adjust a shoe, losing dozens of places, and yet ran brilliantly to score in our team. Since this race, one of the members of the winning team has been declared ineligible, and so Surrey A.C.'s margin over us was reduced to a bare point. It is as well, perhaps, that we were not made winners of the Championship by this adjustment. We would much rather regain it on our merits this year, although we do not minimise the strength of the opposition. * * * * * The Southern Cross-country Championships are to be held from Sandown Racecourse on February 22nd. Both Junior and Senior events will be decided, and the nearness of the venue should enable many of our members to attend and help our men on. * * * * * We are glad to know that Harry Verney's application to be considered a first-claim member of our Club without serving the usual qualifying period, has been acceded to by the special committee appointed to consider such cases. Verney, a former Civil Service Cross-country champion and Birchfield Harrier, has shown that he has real ability, and we wish him luck in his quest for a place in our championship teams. The A.A.A. 10 miles running and 7 miles walking championships are to be held at the White City on April 11th—during the Easter holiday. No doubt we shall be well represented and it is whispered that Arthur Penny has his eyes on the 10 miles title. * * * * * Our readers are requested to note that the date of the London—Brighton Relay has been altered. It is now intended to hold this event (probably starting from Mitcham) on April 25th. Please note your fixture list accordingly. It will probably be necessary to alter the date of our 5 miles road handicap in view of this change. * * * * * The A.A.A. have recently circularised about 150 athletes, advising them that they are under consideration for Olympic selection, and urging them to take particular care in their preparation. Final selection will be made after the A.A.A. Championships (July 10th and 11th) and, of course, it is quite likely that there will be some "turn-ups'" when the team is finally selected. Our members to receive the official letter are: J. E. Flower (10,000 metres), J. Ginty (Steeplechase), J. Parker (5,000 and 10,000 metres), A. W. Penny (5,000 and 10,000 metres), G. H. Powell (Javelin), and T. H. Scrimshaw (800 metres). No walkers have been advised, but here the A.A.A. are acting in concert with the R.W.A., and there is little doubt that several of our men are on the "probables" list. Good luck to all our athletes in their quest for Olympic honours; those named above, and others! * * * * * The Committee have decided to order a newly-designed tie for the use of members. This tie will have the inner portion of the Club badge (portcullis and cross keys) woven in gold on a dark red background; and will supersede the present striped pattern. Many members have suffered the embarrassment, when wearing the old pattern tie, of being asked if they are an "Old Reptillian," etc., and we do not doubt that many South London Harriers have been surprised (albeit flattered) when claimed as a Belgrave Harrier by those whose colour values are not their strong point. The new design should obviate all this, and should, in addition, by reason of its better toning with the ordinary lounge suit, prove very popular and be much in evidence at Club functions and elsewhere. This tie will sell at 3/- each and be obtainable from our Hon. Treasurer, so advise him of your requirements at once. Some of the well-known rugby clubs have adopted such badge-woven ties which are sold at 6/6 to 8/6 each, but, as far as is known, we shall be the first athletic club to favour this new development in sports ties. Among others we have welcomed to the Club recently are T. F. Goodale and J. W. Kemp. The latter has shown up prominently in Bank races, has been third in the Southern Junior Cross-country Championship, and generally given evidence that he will be an asset to our teams in due course. Goodale was third in the Southern Counties 880 yards Championship last season, and won the Army Championship at this distance. He has well-beaten two minutes for the distance on several occasions, and as he expects to settle down in the South before long, he, too, should add to our strength. * * * * * Congratulations to our team in the Surrey County Cross-country championship on holding their title. Also to Arthur Penny on his success in the Surrey race; to Pat Parker upon winning the Sussex title; and to E. Simpson upon winning the Middlesex Junior Championship and so following in the footsteps of Harry Shields, with, of course, something to spare. * * * * * One of our early races of the season was versus University of London A.C., at Coulsdon. We had a very easy win (98 points to 202), supplying the first seven men to finish. Parker, Penny and Cohen finished equal first, closely followed by Shaw, Williams and Verney. We were obviously much too strong for our University friends, who lacked the assistance of Etheridge; but, nevertheless, the sporting match was greatly enjoyed by all. * * * * * On the same day the remainder of our forces met Thames Valley Harriers over their Cranford course, and in a very exciting race we managed to win by four points (148 to 152, scoring 12 aside). Arthur Allum, followed by George Chantler, led the field home. * * * * * Our encounter with Metropolitan Police A.C. at Imber Court on November 16th showed us in a very heartless mood, for we had no fewer than the first fourteen home! Then came W. D. Symes, for the Police (he is also a member of our Club); and final scores, twenty aside, were 220 points to 716 points by the Police. Pat Parker was the actual winner of the race. A visit to Imber Court is always most enjoyable, and many of our runners and walkers (the walk is described elsewhere) remained to tea, and for the dancing which followed. * * * * * Track fixtures are at the moment the concern of the appropriate sub-committee; and they are busily planning our summer season. We have been able to book six Wednesday dates at Battersea Park for our evening meetings, and two Saturday afternoons, but we are not yet sure of a Saturday fixture in May, with which we usually open the season. * * * * * Our Championship Day has been arranged for July 25th. This is a week earlier than usual, and has been so arranged to allow those of our members who intend visiting the Olympic Games, either as competitors or spectators, to do so without missing the Club Championships. * * * * * A final word. The Championship season is fast approaching. "South of the Thames Senior," "Southern," "Junior" Walk "National" (English Championship, strictly), and "Senior" Walk follow one another rapidly. See that you do your little bit to help our teams along. Buy a new tie, and a packet of throat lozenges, and help things along! Bill Rice Bill Rice recovering slowly from ill health A. O. Tookey A. items.s: THE HIGHGATE HARRIERS' OPEN WALK. Report and result of the Highgate Harriers' open walk (short of seven miles), won by A. A. Cooper, in which Belgrave won the team race with 19 points and regained the Berman Cup (as printed, T. W. Green's handicap time does not match his time less allowance, and the placings 3, 4, 5 and 8 add to 20, not 19). The first Open event of the season was promoted by the Highgate Harriers on the last Saturday in October. It was necessary to find a different course from that generally used, owing to road-work, and it would appear that the course chosen was well short of the advertised seven miles. From the start our men were prominent, and at the half-way mark Harry Churcher led the field. He was forced to yield to Cooper and Stone before the end was reached, but this effort of Harry's must rank as one of his best. Tommy Green, young as ever, and Len Fletcher, who we were all glad to see on the road once again, and Bill Treacher, completed our team. Our score was the very low one of 19 points; and second came Surrey Walking Club, with 73 points. This win brought the "Berman Cup" back to our possession. The form of our men was quite encouraging and we left the first race of the season, feeling confident of more successes to come. Handicap awards eluded us, but Bill Snell won a special prize for the fastest handicap time from the Club providing the largest entry. Pos. Name Act. Time Allce. H'cap Time 1 A. A. Readman walked splendidly in his first Open race and promises to do well in the future; and the walking of our men generally gave great satisfaction. 103 finished. Pos. Name Act. Time Allce. items.label: February 1936
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's sixteenth open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon, where Woodford Green A.C. narrowly won the scratch team race and Percy Wright took the first handicap prize.
items.s: OUR OPEN WALK. Report of Belgrave's sixteenth open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon, where Woodford Green A.C. narrowly won the scratch team race and Percy Wright took the first handicap prize. Our open 7 miles event—the sixteenth we have promoted—took place at Wimbledon on the last Saturday in November, as usual. Compared with other entries this season, ours was the best received, but, unfortunately, there were 31 fewer than last year. One hundred and fifty-eight names came in this year (19 teams) and these figures condemned us to a financial loss, despite the very generous support given by several friends. Athletically, the event was the usual success, and our race with its by no means easy course seems to exercise a hold over the ordinary walker, which makes him come along year by year to see if he really can get up those hills without undue distress! This year we saw one of the finest tussles ever for scratch team honours. The teams concerned were Woodford Green A.C. and ourselves. Up to the half-distance the advantage was ours, but shortly afterwards Green, in attempting to race Cooper, was ruled out. This levelled matters, and the team fight was on. Eventually, victory went to our Woodford friends. We finished our fourth man before theirs, but Woodford's 1 and 3 points for their first two men home gave them the advantage and a few points win. Well done, Woodford Green! Meanwhile, Percy Wright, of our D team, was doing splendidly and with 19th position and 7 mins. 10 secs allowance, claimed the first handicap prize. Well walked, Percy! Our "D" team (Wright, Readman, Goold and Earle) took the first handicap team prizes, and so we can consider we had our share. Other awards appear below. Len Fletcher took the prize for the first Belgrave Harrier not gaining any other award, and a special prize (presented by Mr. W. Allen) for the first man in the scratch race with an allowance of 7 mins. or over, and not gaining any other award, went to R. A. Staker, of Highgate Harriers. We were particularly pleased to welcome teams from Dunlop W.C. and Leicester W.C., from the provinces; but they were unable to record any successes. Our own Club entry was very good and four teams were entered. In concluding, we should like to record our very sincere appreciation of the help given us by R.W.A. officials and others, and offer our thanks to the competitors who entered our race. We are also especially grateful to Messrs. Askew, Bayliss, Elson, Gordon and Thomson for their support of the Prize Fund, and to Mr. W. Allen for presenting a special prize. 129 finished. P. G. e: Belgrave Harriers v Metropolitan Police Walking Club
items.s: AT IMBER COURT. Report and result of the seven miles walking match against the Metropolitan Police Walking Club at Imber Court on November 16th, which ended in a dead-heat at 134 points each. On November 16th we met the Metropolitan Police Walking Club, at Imber Court, over their usual seven miles course. We were without the two Churchers and one or two other stalwarts, but our team looked good enough to win. From the command to start, Len Fletcher and Don Brown took the lead, which they gradually increased throughout, without ever distressing themselves. Places were changing continually among the rest of the field, and eventually we finished six men in the first eight home—and yet the complete team result proved a dead-heat! The reason for this was the splendid packing of our Police friends in the middle portion of the field—a factor which has led to our defeat in the past. Among those who enabled the Police to level-up the advantage gained by our earlier men were noticed several Police walkers who are also Belgrave men. Full details appear below. Pos. items.s: THE 7 MILES "JUNIOR" WALK. Report of the club 7 miles "Junior" walk for the "Horwood" Cup, won by C. E. Churcher from the holder C. Speechley, with "Doug" Earle taking the sealed handicap. Competition to hold the "Horwood" Cup was expected to be very keen, and 14 competitors lined up to take their chance in championship and handicap. A terrific struggle was expected between the holder, C. Speechley and our Captain, C. E. Churcher. This was forthcoming from the first few yards. Charlie, the elder, tried his hardest to get away on the hills, but Charlie, the younger, had a very slight advantage on the flat—and this advantage enabled him to show slighty more speed over the finish, and to win by seven seconds. This reversed the result of last year's race, when Speechley gained a very narrow victory over Churcher. P. G. Wright again showed improved form and the time he recorded was very creditable. He will certainly strengthen our "Junior" team. Rutland can do better than the time he recorded on this occasion. The fifth man, "Doug" Earle, with a 5-min. allowance, carried off the sealed handicap, with Frank Jarvis, who followed him in, and with the same allowance, second. There were a few absentees from this race, which is, of course, confined to those members possessing the R.W.A. "Junior" qualification; and it would have been interesting to see how Storey, R. F. Elson, Brian, Readman, Goold and Boddington (to mention a few) would have fared, had it been possible for them to turn out. Pos. Name Act. Time H'cap H'cap Time H'cap Pos. 1 C. E.
