items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Report and result of the Belgrave Open Walk of 26 November 1938, won by Harry Churcher in a course record from E. A. Staker, with Belgrave's C and A teams first and second in the scratch team race.
items.s: The Belgrave Open Walk. Report and result of the Belgrave Open Walk of 26 November 1938, won by Harry Churcher in a course record from E. A. Staker, with Belgrave's C and A teams first and second in the scratch team race. 26th November, 1938. By knocking 43 seconds off the course record (held by V. W. G. Stone, Poly), Harry Churcher treated a large crowd of onlookers to an excellent display of fast walking and his fellow-competitors to a clean pair of heels. At a signal from our President, 176 walkers sped up Lauriston Road. The judges soon got to work, for Colin Sutton was disqualified when he had only covered about a quarter of a mile. After a small lap of the Common, Harry was already in front, and Belgrave vests were already prominent. At the half-way stage it became evident that, barring accidents, Belgrave were due for a lion's share of the prizes; for our men who were prominent at the start maintained their positions. Harry eventually won from E. A. Staker (Highgate H.) by the comfortable margin of 1 min. 30 secs. Joe Coleman gave us his usual sound performance to fill third place, whilst Percy Wright walked hard all the way to finish fifth. The performances of the rest of our lads can best be shown by looking at the team results. In the scratch team results a preliminary word of explanation is necessary. Our A and C teams (captain's and vice-captain's) were chosen from our best men, and, on paper, there appeared little to choose between them. The chances of the A team were weakened by the disqualifications of Sutton and Treacher. This caused them to have to go into the forties for their fourth man—Stan Goold, who, by the way, is performing well this season. Thus handicapped, they were beaten by the C team, but they were worthy runners-up. To finish two scratch teams first and second in an open race (22 teams taking part) and having accomplished this with two men ruled out, speaks volumes for our present strength. Our B team were only a few points behind the A team, and occupied fifth posiition; that is, only two other clubs could beat our third team. Looking at the handicap section, it was no great surprise to find that our B team had returned the lowest aggregate time. The individual handicap prize went to the Highgate Centurion, A. D. McSweeney. Charlie Churcher won the special prize awarded to the first Belgrave Harrier not gaining any other award. The special prize for Police competitors was won by the man who won it last year—R. C. Aylen. This account would be incomplete without recording our most sincere thanks to the following: Messrs. T. Askew, C. E. Churcher, F. H. Elson and E. Gordon for their donations to the prize fund; also to W. Allen, who provided a special prize. Then there is our indebtedness to the R.W.A. officials and handicappers, the local police and the many Club members who acted as pointsmen. Lastly, to those Clubs and Individuals who supported the event and helped to make it the success which deservedly rewarded the efforts of those responsible for its organisation. items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Report and result of the club seven mile "junior" walk for the Horwood Cup on 17 December 1938, won by Bert Clayton from Eddie Heather and Syd Roberts, with Frank Jarvis winning the sealed handicap.
items.s: The Seven Mile "Junior" Walk. Report and result of the club seven mile "junior" walk for the Horwood Cup on 17 December 1938, won by Bert Clayton from Eddie Heather and Syd Roberts, with Frank Jarvis winning the sealed handicap. Saturday, 17th December, 1938. This race for the Horwood Cup was held a week later than was originally arranged, and fourteen walkers shivered in Lauriston Road, waiting for the word to start from Oscar Horwood. Bert Clayton immediately went into the lead, accompanied by Bert East, with Syd Roberts leading the rest in pursuit. After a small lap of the Common, Clayton was still leading, Eddie Heather having worked his way into second place. These two were still leading at the top of the hills, with Roberts leading Thaxter and Doubleday for third place. Going round the common again, Heather was a few yards in front, but there was little to choose between them when the hills were tackled again. Roberts seemed to be moving better now and appeared to be gaining on his rivals. Coming up the hills the second time Clayton, after a ding-dong battle, had gained a lead of twenty yards or so, but Heather stuck gamely to his task, and finally had to admit defeat after a most thrilling race. Roberts maintained his position and was a worthy third. Harry Thaxter gave an excellent performance to finish fourth. Clayton's victory bears out the form which he has shown in open races this season. It is a fitting reward for his keenness, for, living at Eastleigh, he has not had the advantage of training with a pack. He is, however, under the watchful eye of Tommy Green, to whom, no doubt, his success will be a source of satisfaction. The performances of the others will assure the Club that our reserve talent will become worthy successors to the traditions set by our teams. L. Little, one of this season's newcomers, shows continued improvement, whilst W. F. Brunning progresses steadily and will perform better over the longer distances. Frank Jarvis won the sealed handicap, and our old friend, Bill Snell, worked his way into second place. A comparative newcomer, W. H. Jones, gave evidence of his prowess by claiming third place. No doubt this will be a great encouragement to him, and his improvement will continue. The race was slightly marred by the absence of Bridger, Elliott and Speechley, whose presence would most certainly have made the race keener. RESULT. Pos. Name Act. Time Allce. items.sum: Report and result of the London Transport Open Walk on 4 February 1939, won by Harry Churcher, with Belgrave winning the scratch team race and the B team second in the handicap team race.
items.s: The London Transport Open Walk. Report and result of the London Transport Open Walk on 4 February 1939, won by Harry Churcher, with Belgrave winning the scratch team race and the B team second in the handicap team race. 4th February, 1939. This event is usually a bogey race for our men, as many of them manage to get "pulled." This year's race was no exception, for only a bare four of our "A" team got through to complete the course. The course, which is aptly described as two and a half laps of housing estate and gasworks, would appear to be, judging from the times returned, a good seven miles. The walkers were pleased to find that the steepest hill on the course, a narrow lane with muddy banks on each side, had been modernised to form a wide concrete "speedway." This appeared to render the hill a little less formidable. The usual men soon found their way to the front, and by the time that the headquarters were reached (after about a mile) Harry Churcher was at the head of a well strung out field. On the first of the two large laps came catastrophe number one. Charlie Churcher, after having steadily worked his way into a useful position, suffered disqualification. Alan Bridger and Bill Treacher also shared a similar fate. This reduced our "A" team to four (seven only starting). A quick reckoning by our Walking Hon. Sec. made us potential winners of the scratch team race, so he gave our men a timely warning to watch their step. Harry was first home exactly two minutes ahead of his nearest rival, H. H. Whitlock (Metropolitan W.C.), who must have given some of the short distance specialists a shock. Joe Coleman was fourth, whilst Percy Wright and Len Coleman completed the team. Our "B" team (Clark, Doubleday, Roberts and True) managed to get in the prize-winners again, taking second handicap team prize. Brunning, Jones and Little also gave us encouraging performances, and their constant support of open races is an excellent testimony to their keenness and club-spirit. RESULT. items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Report and result of the club Ten Miles walking championship on 28 January 1939, won by Harry Churcher from his brother Charlie and Joe Coleman, with Belgrave also beating the Met. Police W.C. in a match held in conjunction.
items.s: The Ten Miles Championship. Report and result of the club Ten Miles walking championship on 28 January 1939, won by Harry Churcher from his brother Charlie and Joe Coleman, with Belgrave also beating the Met. Police W.C. in a match held in conjunction. Saturday, 28th January, 1939. An ex-holder of this Championship, Harold King, started a large field of walkers, which included members of the M.P.A.A. and Surrey A.C. Three men immediately shot to the front—Harry Churcher and the Coleman brothers. After two laps of the Common, Harry already had a good lead, whilst his brother Charlie, after a modest start, had now got well into his stride and was close on the heels of Percy Wright, who then occupied fourth position. Out to Roehampton and back there were many private "dust-ups," and on reaching the War Memorial there were many who wished that the race finished at Lauriston Road. But, alas, there were two laps of the Common to be done. By this time the cold was beginning to take its toll and some gave it best and retired. On his final lap of the Common, Harry Churcher got a view of some of his fellow-competitors—they were still struggling on the first of their two laps. This meant that he was a mile in front of them! Brother Charlie showed a welcome return to form by finishing second, Joe Coleman being third. When the handicap result was announced, the name of Churcher was again at the head, for not only did Harry win from scratch (he's done that before!) but Charlie's efforts were rewarded with second prize. Alan Bridger, who is now finding his form after a slight setback in the shape of a bad leg, followed by a cold, was a worthy third. We were again successful in our match v. the M.P.A.A., which was held in conjunction, and the usual practice of having our Police members scoring for the "boys in blue" was adhered to. RESULT. Pos. items.s: The Ashcombe-St. George's Open Walk. Report and result of the Ashcombe-St. George's Open Walk on 21 January 1939, won by Harry Churcher, with Belgrave winning the scratch team race and so retaining the R.W.A. Berman Cup. 21st January, 1939. There was added interest in this race this year as the R.W.A. "Berman" Cup was awarded in conjunction with the scratch race. The day was very muggy, and some hundred odd competitors, after many almost bewildering left and right turns, found themselves in Richmond Park. As can be well imagined, there were some small ups and downs, but no severe gradients, the tendency of the course being uphill on the outward journey and downhill coming home. It was very pleasing to see some of our runners in the Park, and their vocal encouragements were both welcome and much appreciated. Harry Churcher recorded his customary win, Vic Stone (Poly) beating E. Staker (Highgate) for second place. Another Poly man, H. D. Neilson, was fourth. Joe Coleman and Charlie Churcher were fifth and sixth, the latter having made a moderate start, his position improving as the race progressed. Our Junior Champion, Bert Clayton, was tenth to complete the team; his getting into the scoring four was as popular as it was well-merited. Thus we retained the Berman Cup and, whilst we cheer the men who won it, we must not forget to add a word of congratulation to Harry Thaxter, who gained third prize in the handicap. RESULT. items.label: March 1939
items.h: The Valentine's S.C. Open Ten Miles Walk.
items.sum: Report and result of the Valentine's S.C. Open Ten Miles Walk at Goodmayes on 18 February 1939, won by D. Christie-Murray, with Belgrave's A team winning the scratch team race in Harry Churcher's absence and the B team second in the handicap team race.
e: Valentine's S.C. Open Ten Miles Walk
items.s: The Valentine's S.C. Open Ten Miles Walk. Report and result of the Valentine's S.C. Open Ten Miles Walk at Goodmayes on 18 February 1939, won by D. Christie-Murray, with Belgrave's A team winning the scratch team race in Harry Churcher's absence and the B team second in the handicap team race. This race was held on February 18th, in the Goodmayes neighbourhood, and attracted a large entry, including 22 Belgravians. This is the only ten miles open handicap of the season, and we had high hopes of maintaining our sequence of scratch team race wins in open events. The news that Harry Churcher, hero of a dozen or more successive Open race wins, was prevented from turning out owing to a bout of influenza was disappointing, and the fact that Percy Wright was recovering from similar trouble, seemed to make scratch team prospects more open than has been the case in recent races. Both Metropolitan Walking Club and Surrey Walking Club seemed to be at full strength and we anticipated a keen struggle with both these old-standing rivals. The brothers Coleman and E. A. Staker led the field at the start, until Len found the pace a little too warm and dropped back. Mile after mile Joe Coleman and Highgate's E. A. Staker kept shoulder to shoulder in the lead, until about six miles or more, when D. Christie Murray, of Surrey W.C., came through the field with a determined and extraordinarily well-judged turn of speed. Staker attempted to go after him, but later had the mortification of slipping back to eighth position. Meanwhile, Harold Whitlock had been gaining places and eventually beat our Joe by a small margin. An attempt to total the team scores at six miles (approx.) showed that we were scoring 35 points to the 36 of the Metropolitan W.C.! Whitlock, of the Met., appeared likely to gain places and it will be realized that excitement reigned. Our boys were apprised of the facts and immediately responded. Joe Coleman was determined to finish well up. Colin Sutton set about gaining places, as did also our Captain, Charlie Churcher. Len Coleman, fourth "A" team man, also moved up, and Eddie Heather, of the "B" team, and Bert Clayton, fifth and non-scoring "A" team man, rendered yeoman service. They were told to overtake the Metropolitan men and right well they set about their task. The position improved and at eight miles approximately we were leading with 30 points to the 42 of Metropolitan W.C., whilst Surrey Walking Club were also improving their position. Still, our walkers gained places, and their determination was grand to see, and a tribute to their loyalty to their Club and team-mates. At the finish we were comparatively easy winners, and whilst the efforts of our scoring four were splendidly maintained and worthy of the highest praise, they will be eager to join in the tribute to Clayton and Heather. Unable to score in the team themselves, these two did marvellous work in pushing the other clubs back; and displayed team spirit at its very highest level. May both receive the reward merited in the "Junior" Championship, which follows a fortnight later! While our six aforementioned men were finishing in the first twelve places, our other walkers were also striving hard and with some effect. Messrs. Roberts, Doubleday, Clark and Heather, of the "B" team, walked well and comprised the second handicap team. Eddie Heather's forward walking, his best to date, earned third individual handicap prize. All things considered, we can look back with a deal of pleasure on this event. We regretted the absence of Harry Churcher from our team, but it was pleasing to find that we had others in plenty to give of their best and make up for his absence. RESULT. E. C. items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Walking column on the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship win (the club's seventh), the coming walking fixtures and training, a call for new walkers, and an appeal to join the Road Walking Association as individual members.
items.s: With The Walkers. Walking column on the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship win (the club's seventh), the coming walking fixtures and training, a call for new walkers, and an appeal to join the Road Walking Association as individual members. So we have won the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship once again. A full account must follow in our next issue, but we heartily congratulate the team responsible for our seventh win in this series of races. No other club can approach this record of success, the next best being the four wins of Surrey Walking Club. As we won last year's race (with a record score) and this team was no longer eligible, we were set the task of finding four new scoring men. This we succeeded in doing, and two successive wins is of the greatest credit to all concerned. Next year we shall be out to put up a "best-ever" performance and score another win. It must be admitted that this presents many difficulties We have some very fine young walkers coming along but they will probably not be sufficiently matured in time for next March. So we shall, in all probability, rely upon this year's candidates for places in our team, plus the new members that we hope will be forthcoming during the next few months. We trust that all members will keep a keen look-out for new talent, and we can assure all who join the ranks of the walkers a cordial welcome, good times, and a guaranteed measure of success if they are prepared to persevere. * * * * * Now for the "Senior," to be held on May 13th from the Police quarters at Hendon. As the title-holders, we shall use all our endeavours to hold on to the Championship. It would be a wonderful feat to win once again all three "R.W.A." titles in one season, and one which is within our capabilities. * * * * * We hope to have all last year's men again representing us, supplemented by some of those who have now left the "Junior" ranks behind for ever. The Club Championship at 20 miles, with sealed handicap in conjunction, will be held at Wimbledon on April 22nd. The Metropolitan Police W.C. and Surrey A.C. will also be visitors. It is unfortunate that the postponed "Godstone" Walk is to be held on the same day, but our S.W.C. friends realise that we have to carry through with our arrangements. * * * * * The following Saturday we expect to travel eastwards for the Colchester to Ipswich Walk, won by Colin Sutton last year. * * * * * The R.W.A. 50 kilos Championship is to be held from De Bohun's Farm, Southgate, on July 22nd. This is another title to be defended and we have every confidence in our men. With the Olympic Games to follow in 1940, we shall be looking to this Championship event to give us some guide as to England's representatives the following year. * * * * * Our Inter-club scratch Walks will be held at Battersea Park Track on Wednesday, May 31st, when we expect to receive the usual very fine support of clubs in the Metropolitan area. * * * * * We should like to add twenty new walkers to our ranks during the Summer months. The Hon. Secretary, Track Captain, and other officials will do all in their power to assist the newcomer to walking and put him on his way to success. All enquiries and entries should be addressed to— A. A. Harley, 39, Roxborough Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. * * * * * Training for the Track Walking season will take place on Tuesday evenings at Battersea Park, commencing when the clocks are adjusted to Summer time. Any member, especially the newer ones, who require further particulars, should write to the Track Captain, P. G. Wright, 23, Campana Road, S.W.6, who will gladly give any information needed. The Road Walking Association has, in recent years, found it very difficult to function at its highest point of efficiency, by reason of its limited finances. The only income the Association receives is in the form of 25% of the affiliation fees paid by Clubs to the District Associations, and any profits that may be made on the three Championships promoted. It is obvious that with no "gate" to call upon, the Championships are more likely to show a loss than a profit, and so it becomes increasingly difficult to carry on if further progress is to be made. Accordingly, an appeal is made to those interested in road walking to join the Road Walking Association as indvidual members at an annual subscription of 5/-. There is no desire on the part of the Association to bring about any diminution of support by members to their clubs, but it is thought that those who can afford to do so will welcome the chance to assist the Association's finances by enrolling as Honorary Members. Any Belgrave member desirous of so doing is asked to get into touch with A. A. Harley. Colin Sutton Colin Sutton won the Colchester to Ipswich Walk last year A. A. Harley A. A. items.sum: Look back to 1929: Belgrave's first South of the Thames cross-country title, the Southern and National championships, second place in the R.W.A. "Junior" walk, and club news of that year.
e: South of the Thames Cross-country Championship
items.s: Ten Years Back. Look back to 1929: Belgrave's first South of the Thames cross-country title, the Southern and National championships, second place in the R.W.A. "Junior" walk, and club news of that year. The Championship season of 1929 provided us with a great success. For the first time we succeeded in winning the South of the Thames Cross-country Championship, and also the "Colman" Cup as the first club to finish its complete team of twelve men. It was certainly a proud moment for W. H. Hare, the first Belgravian to be President of the South of the Thames Association; and all other Club members present, when the trophies were awarded. Our winning team consisted of W. S. Mitchell (4), A. W. Penny (7), A. Allum (13), W. G. Webb (16), P. Khlopin (23), A. Robertshaw (26), giving us a total of 89 points. Herne Hill Harriers were second with 139 points, and Horsham Blue Star A.C. third with 211 points. The other members of our team were A. E. Smith (44), K. B. O'Kell (56), W. A. Rice (66), A. G. Jones (87), W. L. Bayliss (116), and S. Drake (144). With this first "Senior" Championship win to encourage us, we went hopefully to the "Southern" held at Horton Kirby, but could only finish tenth of the 29 clubs that started. A fortnight later, in the "National" held at Beaconsfield in brilliant sunny weather, our team did not close in. Only four of our runners finished : W. G. Webb (87), A. W. Penny (120), W. L. Bayliss (122) and F. G. Ford (197). Turning to the walking side we find that we were placed second in the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship held at Birmingham in 1929. Surrey W.C. were the winners, and our team consisted of J. E. Field (9), J. Rathbone (11), E. Saunders (13) and F. H. Elson (18). Three members of this team were destined to be in the winning team the following year; and Jack Rathbone was in our winning "Senior" team later in the season. The Southern Amateur Athletic League had just been formed and its first fixture list announced. Our Field Events men were doing their utmost to arouse more interest and enthusiasm, and the conditions to decide the first holder of the "Harry Wright" Shield appear in the April, 1929, issue of "The Belgravian"—the first to be published under the editorship of A. A. Harley. These were the happenings of our Club life ten years ago! W. H. Hare W. H. Hare first Belgravian to be President of the South of the Thames Association W. S. Mitchell W. S. items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Survey of Belgrave athletes with a chance of selection for the 1940 Olympic Games at Helsingfors, event by event from the sprints to the field events and walks, with a summary of Percy Wright's article "Which Walkers for Finland?" and an editor's note.
items.s: Helsingfors, 1940. Survey of Belgrave athletes with a chance of selection for the 1940 Olympic Games at Helsingfors, event by event from the sprints to the field events and walks, with a summary of Percy Wright's article "Which Walkers for Finland?" and an editor's note. The next Olympiad is due to be held in Finland next year, and those athletes who entertain hopes of inclusion in the British team are already planning their training. What are Belgrave's chances of having some of its members in the team? On current form, and with no unlucky breaks, we have many potentialities, and this brief analysis of our own members is intended to give a few ideas as to who may be honoured with selection for the team. In the sprints, S. C. Botwright's name stands out; he also does a very good "quarter." Our other sprinters, judging by last season's results, are on the up-grade, and if some can clip off a few tenths of a second, they will be attracting the selectors' eyes. H. E. Pack has already gained representative honours in the 440 yards, although his times are apt to be dimmed by the performances of A. G. K. Brown and W. Roberts. Our man, however, has beaten 50 seconds on several occasions, recording times which would have won an A.A.A. championship in many years, and if only Eddie could find a sustained finishing effort I am sure we have a world-beater in our ranks. In the 880 yards, A. A. Bird is already inside two minutes, and with a little more age and experience will be doing better. Another man to watch over these distances is S. Jarlett, who last year showed great improvement. We must not, of course, forget T. H. Scrimshaw, who in his day was one of the leading half-milers in the country. Whether Tommy can recover his old form remains to be seen, but I am sure we all wish him the very best of luck. In the 1500 metres, L. W. Herbert and W. E. Lucas are our best, and although neither has yet beaten 4.20 for the Mile, they cannot be overlooked. Lucas gained inclusion in last year's A.A.A. Mile final, while Herbert also gained an A.A.A. standard by beating 4.25. Both of these runners are yet young, and we look forward to still better performances from them both during the coming track season. We have to turn to our cross country men for the 5,000 and 10,000 metres (3 and 6 miles roughly). For the shorter race, C. T. Carter, J. Parker, J. C. Smart and L. J. Cohen can all give good acccounts of themselves, and if only Pat would get down to some serious training, I am sure he could make the team. For the longer race A. W. Penny, an ex-Empire Games 6 miles champion, is still a strong candidate, and although just failing to make the team at the last Olympic Games, we wish him better luck for 1940. D. Patience, S. T. Ring and E. S. Stimpson are three more who do well at these distances, and the latter, an ex-Southern Junior C.C. Champion, is particularly promising and should have a good season. Both having well beaten three hours, A. F. Mitchell and F. A. Walker are well in the running for honours in that classic race—the Marathon; whilst if H. E. Footer should train for the distance—as is probable—he might well win this event for Gt. Britain. For the Steeplechase (3,000 metres) we naturally think of J. Ginty, who was Belgrave's only representative in 1936, but whether Jim's duties will permit of him giving time to the necessary training is rather doubtful. Two others who shine at this branch of athletics are C. T. Carter and A. R. Shaw, and both have good performances to their credit. As regards the Hurdle races, it must be confessed that our chances are extremely remote, the ordinary clubs seem to be rather overshadowed by the Universities and Services in these events, due in the main to lack of training facilities. At the last Olympiad, Great Britain sent very few Field Events competitors, as the performances by Britishers are lamentably below the standards of most other countries. Whether they adopt this procedure again remains to be seen, although we are glad to see that the ruling body have taken steps to encourage this side of athletics among the clubs. Naturally our own club performers are below International standards, but I think that our men deserve attention. That our Field Events section is one of the strongest is evidenced by our performances in the S.A.A.L. Field Events League. In the Shot and Discus, S. Jones, W. H. J. Sutton and L. J. Worrad form a powerful trio who gain us many points in Club matches. In the Javelin, E. H. Finneron, C. A. Melchior, G. H. Powell and Ron Jeal are a useful quartet, whilst our Club champion, H. M. Quackenbos, with more strength and experience, will throw further. For the High and Pole Jumps, our Northern member, J. Dodd, who won the A.A.A. Pole Vault title in 1937, would already have gained International honours but for the fact that he is barred by tht International rules. F. J. Skelley is certainly a bright hope for the Long Jump, he has already cleared 22ft. 8in. and will undoubtedly profit by maturer years. Our Field Events men have been training under F. Stampfl during the Winter, and their performance next Summer will be watched with hope and interest by all. Coming to the Walkers, it is noted that a 10,000 metres walk is planned. For this we have many members who give good accounts of themselves over seven miles. On the form which he has shown in the "Open" races, H. G. Churcher is undoubtedly selection number one, whilst D. E. Brown, C. E. Churcher, H. G. Clayton, J. G. and L. J. Coleman and P. G. Wright are names usually prominent in "Open" races. In the 50 kilometres (31¼ miles) walk, F. E. Bentley, J. C. Bidgood, F. Rickards and C. F. Sutton are strong candidates. Bentley has already represented Great Britain in the European Championships, whilst Sutton was selected as a reserve. At the last Olympiad the only Britisher to win an Individual Championship was H. H. Whitlock in the 50 kilometres walk; whilst in the 1932 Games our own T. W. Green was victorious, and I am sure that if Britain wins this event through a Belgrave Harrier, Tommy will be as pleased (if not more) as all of us. No doubt there are some names which may catch the selectors' eyes which have not been mentioned. These are the members who, by their efforts and enthusiasm will better their past performances. Who are they to be? * * * * * Since writing the above I have received an article from Percy Wright entitled "Which Walkers for Finland?" Economy of space prevents its appearance in full, but here is a brief summary. It deals with the 10,000 metres walk only, and the hope is expressed that the maximum possible number of men will be sent. H. G. Churcher is the first name mentioned, and his classic race with Mikaelsson (Sweden) in 1937 (when Harry returned the fastest time done by an Englishman in the Championships) is cited as proof of his ability on the track. The distance may prove too far for A. A. Cooper (Woodford Green), who has held the two miles championship for several years. F. J. Redman (Metropolitan W.C.) may now be past his best, but a tribute is paid to his fine style. This brings out the important point that the Olympic Race will be a severe test of style, a point to which the selectors will give their fullest and most careful consideration. A Staines (Leicester W.C.) possesses good style as well as speed. Our own Coleman brothers too, will be in the reckoning. Four younger walkers, in H. G. Clayton (Belgrave), D. Kenney (Leicester W.C.), J. V. Sweeney (Metropolitan W.C.) and W. A. Webster (R.A.F., Halton) are also mentioned; Kenney gaining special mention as he is not yet twenty years old. To this Percy adds that he (no doubt like many others!) will try his hardest to gain Olympic colours. In conclusion, he predicts that the following will be the four from whom the team will be chosen: H. G. Churcher and J. G. Coleman (Belgrave), A. Staines and D. Kenney (Leicester W.C.). [Editor's Note.—This addition represents, of course, the personal views of P. G. Wright. Some will agree and some will differ, but nobody will doubt the honesty and sincerity of his views on a topic which can be so full of controversy]. S. C. Botwright S. C. items.sum: Article comparing performances using the I.A.A.F. scoring table of 1934, ranking world records and A.A.A. standards by points.
items.s: Who's Best ? Article comparing performances using the I.A.A.F. scoring table of 1934, ranking world records and A.A.A. standards by points. Some interesting results emerge from a study of the Scoring Table for Track and Field Events as adopted by the I.A.A.F. Congress at Stockholm in 1934. This table, in addition to giving a means of scoring for Decathlon competitions, satisfies the curiosity of those who would like to know, for example, if a hundred in "evens" is better than a quarter in 49 seconds. Looking up the former, we find that it scores 872 points whilst the latter obtains 954 points, so that the quarter is better. A scale of points is given for all metric running distances, except the steeplechase and marathon; and for all the Field Events, including the standing jumps. The points range from 1360 down to 1 by intervals of one point. Opposite each number the corresponding performances, in the different events, are listed. The compilers have catered for everyone, from the superman of many years hence, who will run 800m. in 1 min. 41.5 sec., to score 1360 points, to the champion of the kindergarten, who toddles round the metric half mile in 3 min. 17.6 sec., thus getting one point. Arranging the world's records in order of merit, we find that the Field Events occupy most of the leading positions with Jack Torrance's shot putt of 57ft. 1in. topping the list and scoring 1202 points. If it has been adopted as a world's record, Owen's 20.3 sec. for the 200 metres is the best pure running performance. The middle and long distance records are in the lower half of the list. Wooderson's 800 metres record is worth 1109 points as against 1088 due to Lovelock's 1500 metres in Berlin. Rather surprisingly the "worst" record is the 10,000 metres recently put up by Maki, which scores 1075 points. Coming nearer home, to A.A.A. standards, we discover, as expected, that the running events score consistently higher points (about 840 on the average) than the Field Events, which average 670 points. The influence of cross-country running is shewn by the fact that the most difficult standard to obtain is the three miles (14m. 50s.) which, converted to 5,000 metres, scores 884 points compared with the easiest, the discus (120ft.), which obtains 613 points. In fact, excepting the high and long jumps, the man who wins an A.A.A. standard in a Field Event does not put up quite so good a performance as he who attains Middlesex county standard in any running event. It must be realized that this table is true only if the performances are done under standard conditions (say ideal conditions) and makes no allowance for wind, heavy or loose track, etc. To compare one running performance with another or a Field Event with another Field Event, the table can be used with confidence, but the comparison of a track record with a field record does not give such good results. From the above facts it appears that in the region of World's records the running events do not score enough points while in the part of the table corresponding to A.A.A. standards, the Field Events, even allowing for their low rating in England, should be given more credit. items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Report of the club's Boxing Day Christmas Social, with tea, dancing and a members' performance of "Little Nell".
items.s: The Christmas Social. Report of the club's Boxing Day Christmas Social, with tea, dancing and a members' performance of "Little Nell". This was held on Boxing Day, and some 90 odd members and friends sat down to a hearty tea. Then came a bout of dancing, a little breathing-space followed, during which some of our dramatically-inclined members gave us their version of "Little Nell." The following gentlemen formed the cast—let their names speak for themselves! F. A. Walker—the Father—complete with beard (and how it shook when he laughed!), Wellington boots and other clothes which looked as though he was just off on a Polar expedition! A. A. Bird—Little Nell (a little fast, perhaps, but she does a 1.59 "half"). She wore black shoes and stockings, a pale yellow shirt which hid a sausage balloon. Evidently the "Pidge" did not wish to give the impression that she lacked maternal affection. C. T. Carter—the Policeman, complete with coat and helmet, trundling a toy tricycle around—and who can blame him for deserting his running legs in these mechanical days? Besides, his mount added to the dignity and poise of authority. P. G. Wright—the Villain. Percy undoubtedly knew his villains well, for he was rigged up in evening dress, collar and bow, and spats. He tried to disguise himself by hiding behind a moustache, and by smoking a cigar (real) completed the picture of wanton dissipation. Suffice it to say that, notwithstanding a few "divertissements" such as the Lambeth Walk, their acting was powerful enough to send the audience into hisses and boos ("booze?"). A band was engaged and Bill Sutton operated a radio amplifier. Even this did not render Bill free from the sudden (but well-calculated) embraces of one of the ladies, who, after careful manœuvering, caught him unawares. A frame-up is strongly suspected. After the interval, when cries of "Where's the M.C.?" (Les Bennett) had died down, Bert Footer, dressed up as a jockey and mounted on his bucking steed, Syd Jarlett, gave us a quick Rodeo act. They were faithfully followed by Micky Walker in the rôle of stable-boy. Thus the party amused itself until it broke up at 11-30. Everybody voted the party a success, and it seems to have found a place in our Social calendar. Although not run for profit, a balance on the right side resulted. Finally, mention must be made of the good work of our Social Committee who, working under our popular Hon. Social Secretary, Tommy Morrell, were responsible for a most enjoyable evening. To them we all express our warmest thanks and gratitude. F. A. Walker F. A. Walker played the Father in "Little Nell" A. A. Bird A. A. Bird played Little Nell C. T. Carter C. T. items.label: March 1939
items.h: The Lighter Side of the Club.
items.sum: Social notes on the loss-making second dance at Zeeta House, the coming Social on March 25th, and the Annual Dinner and Dance at the Empire Restaurant, Victoria, on May 6th.
items.s: The Lighter Side of the Club. Social notes on the loss-making second dance at Zeeta House, the coming Social on March 25th, and the Annual Dinner and Dance at the Empire Restaurant, Victoria, on May 6th. Unfortunately, the success of our first Dance at Zeeta House was not maintained at the second. In an effort to prevent overcrowding our Social Sub-committee did not use their high-pressure salesmanship in disposing of the tickets. As a result the Dance showed a loss, many regular Club members not appearing on February 11th. Now, come, boys! Do not leave it to outsiders to make these dances successes. I'm sure everyone present had an enjoyable time, including our Cross-country Captain who, between dances, made repeated dives to the Bar. Looking through some old issues of the "Belgravian," I see mention of a Club record made at a social on November 22nd, 1930. The report is very interesting. Firstly, that 140 sat down to tea on this occasion and secondly, that we had two vocalists, both members of the Club (Tom Cotton and Billy Williams) who sang old favourites with great success. Now, the purpose of our Social, on March 25th, is to break this very old record, also to discover talent, which I am sure still exists among the many members of the Club. In the old days we had such artists as Bill Williams, T. Cotton, "Castor and Oil," the Nonesuch Girls and the Belgrave Sisters, to mention only a few, who were always willing to oblige for the enjoyment of those present. The chance is yours! Now see what you can do to brighten our Socials in the future. You will receive full support from the Social Sub-committee. Do not be afraid to make any suggestion if you think that it will make our socials sucesses! * * * * * I would like to bring to your notice the Club's Annual Dinner and Dance which, this year, is to be held at the Empire Restaurant, Victoria, on Saturday, May 6th. Although this date seems a long way off, I ask you all to make a note of it, and to make your reservations as early as possible. With your co-operation, the Social Sub-committee hope to make this the Social Event of the year. Tickets will cost: Single 6/-, Double (lady and gent.) 11/6. Everything possible is being done to ensure a function worthy of the Club. Members wishing to use instalment cards for the payment of Dinner Tickets should get in touch with me as soon as possible—the strictest privacy will be assured in this matter. * * * * * For any further Social particulars, please apply to T. F. Morrell, Social Hon. Sec.. 3, Florian Road, S.W.15. items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Short notes on the club's junior cross-country runners, praising the Junior Championships winner, Lionel Penny and J. R. Shotter, and urging juniors to start track training.
items.s: With the Juniors. Short notes on the club's junior cross-country runners, praising the Junior Championships winner, Lionel Penny and J. R. Shotter, and urging juniors to start track training. Our junior runners have given plenty of evidence of their ability during the present season; and we have every confidence that they will also be prominent in Track events this coming Summer. Herbert has been our best man this season, and deservedly won the Junior Championships, but Lionel Penny and J. R. Shotter deserve mention as a more than useful recruit and for great improvement respectively. The others, whose form is well known, have all shown improvement on last season. Perhaps I can best conclude these short notes with the warning that the track season is almost upon us and an exhortation to non-cross-country juniors to start their training with plenty of long, slow work, preferably with the sprinters' pack from Belgrave Hall on Saturday afternoons. items.label: March 1939
items.sum: Notes for the club's marathon runners on the coming season: the Finchley 20 miles, a likely Surrey race and the Poly's Windsor to London marathon, with their standard medals.
items.s: Marathon Notes. Notes for the club's marathon runners on the coming season: the Finchley 20 miles, a likely Surrey race and the Poly's Windsor to London marathon, with their standard medals. During the last two seasons we have entered teams for this type of race. That these teams have always been in the first three shows that this little band is already attaining the high standards set by our other teams. By the time that these notes appear our marathon runners will be starting training on the road. For those who do not fancy the full 26 miles, there is the Finchley Harriers open 20 miles race, with a team race held in conjunction. The Surrey County A.A. will probably be holding a similar race. Standard medals are awarded in each race. In the Finchley race it is 2 hours 15 mins.; in last year's Surrey race it was calculated on the winner's time. What it will be this year remains to be seen. Later on comes the Poly's classic race from Windsor to London (Chiswick). Last year three Standards were awarded, viz., 3 hours, 3 hours 15 mins. and 3 hours 30 mins. This gives the more moderate performers a chance to gain a medal. Even if one fails to gain a Standard and finishes the course, there is the satisfaction of having done the distance, and the urge to train on to a better performance. Experience counts a great deal, and a certain amount of experiment is needed to adapt one's pace and style to suit the longer distance. In this connection the writings of Arthur Newton can be studied with advantage. Well, if these notes have attracted any potential "pavement pounders," and if further information is desired, the following will be at Wimbledon on Saturdays until May: F. G. Ford, A. S. Lindsey, A. F. Mitchell, F. A. Walker and F. G. White. Any member who would like to join the pack for one lap (eight miles) is cordially invited to do so. In conclusion, I might add that much useful advice can be obtained from our old friend George Still, who was a first-class marathon runner during the early part of this century. items.sum: Preview of the London to Brighton Relay and the Club 5 miles road race, complaints about Battersea Park Track, and lists of the club's track fixtures and the open meetings for the coming season.
items.s: Forthcoming Fixtures. Preview of the London to Brighton Relay and the Club 5 miles road race, complaints about Battersea Park Track, and lists of the club's track fixtures and the open meetings for the coming season. The Cross Country season is now drawing to a close and our thoughts are turning towards the London to Brighton Relay Race. On March 25th at Wimbledon we hold our Club 5 miles Road race, with the usual sealed handicap in conjunction. I hope we shall see a good field out for this race, and there is bound to be a rare old tussle for the leading places, as our "Brighton" team is selected after this race. The day of the Relay is Easter Saturday, April 8th, and the start will be from Mitcham, as last year. Our rivals from Mitcham will be out for blood, as another victory this year will see them equal our record feat of three wins in succession. I expect the Birchfield boys to put up their usual good show, but if Mitcham are to be beaten then it is up to the "Bels." to do the trick. Our team should be as good as last year, when although only finishing third, I think it is generally agreed that but for our bad luck on the second stage, and seeing the way our lads ran on the subsequent stages (especially Harry Verney on the third and Pat Parker over the final leg), given ordinary luck this time we shall be right there. There is always the chance of a runner breaking down, but for it to happen again this year is not to be thought of, and so I can see no reason why we cannot this time turn the tables on our conquerors. A few words about the coming Track season may be of interest to our members, and as usual the bulk of our meetings will be held at Battersea Park Track, which I hope the L.C.C. will put into much better condition than last season. I agree that this track is probably the most used of any London one, but a little foresight on the Parks Committee's part could help this "old dust-heap" regain a little of its former fine running surface. Meetings are held there every day of the week and hundreds of school children use the ground, but surely if the track was closed from 5 p.m. to 6-30 p.m., and some attention given to it, the surface would not be as it is at present. However, I suppose we must hope for the best and so I give a list of our fixtures to be held during the coming season :— We have again arranged to hold the Club Championships at Tooting, as this venue proved popular with our members last season. The fact of it being rather late was due to no fault of ours, as this was the only date that the L.C.C. could offer us. We had asked for a date in June, but were unable to obtain one, and so had to accept August 5th, which, no doubt, some members will recall was always the day fixed for the Club Championships in the past. This is the Saturday before August Bank Holiday, and I hope that our members will take note of the date, and, if possible, arrange their Summer holidays, if any, accordingly. I have also been able to ascertain some of the other "Open" dates, and so that members can make a note of these, I have asked our Editor to allow me to append the following list of meetings :— In addition to the above, we hope to arrange several Inter-Club matches both for Seniors and Juniors; these will be given on our Summer fixture card, which will be issued when our fixtures are completed. Thus it will be seen that our members will be kept busy during the Summer, and if any new members are desirous of any further information I shall be pleased to assist them.
